In-repo examples are only the three session-store adapters.

note: 4 languages, 21 concepts, 70+ tool pages, Studio no-code
details: Docs now versioned (`docs/edge` plus frozen `docs/v1.x.y` snapshots) in English, Arabic, Korean and Brazilian Portuguese, with 22 concept pages, 35 learn pages, 12 frontend guides and 17 observability integrations; AMP docs moved off-repo to docs-platform. Crew Studio (AMP) is a no-code builder, and JSON/YAML-first crews and declarative flows let non-engineers edit prompts and roles. `SKILL.md` authoring is feasible for Product/Data.

note: Bilingual EN/ZH, Chinese deeper than English
details: English plus Simplified Chinese. The English site gained the full v0.9 quickstart (11 chapters), release notes, a Cancel/TurnLoop guide and a failover guide, narrowing the gap, but middleware pages and issue threads are still richer in Chinese; prompts and READMEs are bilingual. `SKILL.md` and `AGENTS.md` middleware are authorable by non-engineers, while tools require Go.

genkit.dev now has a per-language path and lists Go on 89 of 109 pages, including the full Agents section, durable streaming, MCP, middleware, testing and evaluation (earlier 'Go trails JS' gap largely closed; correction/upstream). GoDoc is excellent and was audited so examples compile; `go/README.md` is ~1,400 lines. `.prompt` files (YAML plus Handlebars) are editable by non-engineers and `DefinePromptAgent` can back an agent with one; remaining JS-only pages are multi-agent, some deployment and tutorial pages. (Report 0.7)

note: Deep docs, autogen API ref, no markdown skills
details: Docs at docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph are deep on graph mechanics, ReAct, persistence and human-in-the-loop; reference docs are generated from docstrings, and an `llms.txt` is now produced from the docs build. Non-engineers can read the concepts but cannot author content without Python; there is no markdown-driven skill flow.

note: Extensive Starlight, deep concepts, low non-eng access
details: Starlight markdown site under `docs/src/content/docs/framework/` with Concepts, Getting Started, Understanding (Agent ~1,100 lines, RAG, Workflows, Evaluation, Tracing, Deployment) and per-provider module guides. Workflow docs moved under the LlamaAgents section and LlamaHub links were retired. Non-engineer accessibility is low: pages are Python code walkthroughs with no GUI or markdown authoring model.

note: Deep TS-flavored Mintlify docs, SKILL.md path
details: Deep, TypeScript-flavoured docs in the monorepo with their own `AGENTS.md` and migration guides for breaking package majors. A Product/Data person can author `SKILL.md` unaided, and file-based agents (`instructions.md`, since 1.48.0) let non-engineers edit instructions without TypeScript; tools and processors still require code.

note: learn.microsoft.com, formal ADRs, migration guides, SKILL.md
details: Official docs on learn.microsoft.com/agent-framework (tutorials, user guide, migration guides from Semantic Kernel and AutoGen), feature docs in-repo, and 40+ numbered ADRs that record design intent. Skills are YAML-frontmatter Markdown (agentskills.io spec), so a Product/Data author can write one unaided, though registering sources and approval rules needs an engineer. Some ADR numbers are duplicated.

MkDocs Material site with JA/KO/ZH translations and per-feature pages (agents, tools, sessions, guardrails, HITL, MCP, sandbox, tracing, voice, testing). Depth has grown: pages now spell out trust boundaries and failure modes (server-side HITL, SQLite storage trust, Unix-local sandbox limits). Cross-team accessibility is medium: it assumes a Python developer, with no markdown-only authoring flow outside sandbox `SKILL.md` files.

note: Astro/Starlight, ja/zh/ko translations, large examples dir
details: Astro/Starlight site with English plus ja/zh/ko translations; guides cover agents, sessions, streaming, tools, MCP, handoffs, HITL, guardrails, tracing, sandbox, voice, troubleshooting and a new Testing guide, and pages spell out replay, approval and redaction semantics. The examples directory is large and runnable. A non-engineer would need TypeScript and CLI familiarity; no no-code surface.

note: Deep code-tested docs, AgentSpec YAML for non-engineers
details: Deep, code-tested docs (`tests/test_examples.py` runs doc snippets), now at pydantic.dev/docs/ai, covering agents, capabilities, hooks, agent-spec, persistence, workspaces, realtime, ~50 Harness pages and a V1 to V2 migration map. Non-engineer accessible: `AgentSpec` YAML, `SKILL.md` skills, markdown sub-agent definitions and Logfire-managed prompts editable from a UI.

Docs at rig.rs/docs (moved from docs.rig.rs) plus Rustdoc; `rig-agent` denies missing docs and `MIGRATING.md` (4,624 lines) gives before/after snippets per release, which helps through heavy breaking churn. Aimed at Rust engineers: no skills, no markdown agent configs and no playground, so non-engineers can read but not author. Kept at 2 because no non-engineer surface exists and the site depth is not evidenced beyond Rustdoc.

note: Deep in-repo Starlight docs, SKILL.md, CLI wizard
details: English docs at strandsagents.com are now sourced from `site/` in the same repo and are deep, with SDK, harness, evals, deploy and changelog sections and per-feature pages (context management, storage, interrupts, sandbox, memory). Non-engineers can drop `SKILL.md` files for the AgentSkills plugin, and the CLI setup wizard lets them configure and export an agent project; there is no web authoring UI. Some root README links returned 404 on 2026-10-01. Raised from 3 on the docs expansion and wizard. (Report 0.7)

note: Shared portal, compiled TS snippets, SKILL.md
details: Same strandsagents.com portal as the Python SDK, sourced from `site/` with TypeScript snippets as compiled `.ts` files next to the `.mdx` pages, a TS API reference and a changelog generated from releases. In-repo `AGENTS.md`, TESTING and DEPENDENCIES guides plus a middleware design README. `SKILL.md` and `GoalLoop` natural-language goals are authorable by non-engineers; everything else is code. Raised from 3 for parity with the Python SDK on the shared docs site. (Report 0.7)

note: Deep TS docs, new Harnesses section
details: Deep TypeScript-centric docs at ai-sdk.dev, expanded with a full AI SDK Harnesses section, code mode, tool search, evaluation, batch, realtime, policy-based approvals and a 1,278-line lifecycle-callbacks reference, plus in-repo architecture notes. Non-engineers still cannot author behaviour without code (even harness skills are a TypeScript array). Raised from 3 on the expanded coverage and to match other deep-docs, no-non-engineer-path peers (LangGraph, OpenAI Agents JS). (Report 0.7)

Heavy Go framework (v2.5.0) with bundled run loop, graph workflow engine, REST/A2A servers with authn/authz, embedded web UI, OTel, session/memory/artifact stores, context compaction, plugin and skill systems. Not a thin SDK; comparable scope to Mastra.

Heavy Python platform: FastAPI-based AgentOS with routers for auth, scheduler, durable job queue, tracing, evals, approvals and an MCP server, plus an Agent class with ~110 constructor parameters (~455k lines of Python in libs/agno).
Multi-crate Rust workspace; you embed it in whatever Rust binary you build. Core surface is focused (agent/executor/memory/tool/runtime); features gated via Cargo flags.

Thin Python shim (~12.9 kLOC across 26 files) that subprocesses a bundled Claude Code Node/native binary (~100 MB wheel) which actually runs the agent loop. Closest to a wrapper around a vendor-managed CLI.

TypeScript shim (~1.2 MB sdk.mjs, 5.4 MB unpacked package) over a 225-242 MB bundled Claude Code native binary. The loop, system prompt, tools and skills run inside the spawned subprocess; the SDK is a control-protocol bridge. Proprietary licence.

Heavy Python framework (~127 kLOC) bundling crew/flow runtime, conversational flows, memory (LanceDB), checkpointing, MCP, A2A, event bus, CLI and telemetry. Optional AMP SaaS adds hosted deploys, tracing, evaluation and registries.

Go library (~60 kLOC non-test across compose, adk, schema, callbacks, components) with no HTTP server, UI or eval. Rich runtime primitives (graph, ADK, middlewares, cancel, TurnLoop) plus eino-ext, but you assemble the application. CloudWeGo-owned, ByteDance-internal use case drives the roadmap.

Medium-heavy Go framework (go/v1.13.1) with registry, 17 plugin directories, prompt loader, experimental agent runtime, stateless HTTP handler factory and a dev-only Reflection API server. The JS dev-tools CLI is optional and dev-only.

OSS graph runtime (libs/langgraph) plus the source-available (ELv2) langgraph-api server for queue/auth/multitask/MCP routes, which needs a paid licence in production. Pure OSS is a library; the full product is hybrid OSS plus paid platform.

Python library: agent/Workflow runtime in-process, no HTTP server, scheduler or UI. Production serving is punted to the separate llama-agents project (llama-agents-server, llamactl), which replaced the deprecated llama_deploy.

Heavy TypeScript framework. @mastra/core (~933 source files, agent.ts ~10.7k lines) bundles agents, workflows, durable agents, workers, memory, storage, RAG, voice, MCP, deployers, scorers, RBAC/FGA and Studio.

Heavy SDK (~51 kLOC Python core, 42 Python packages, 35 .NET projects) for Python and .NET. Ships agents, workflows, sessions, compaction, MCP, middleware, observability, skills, security labelling, evaluation, harness and 20+ provider connectors. Azure-tilted but core has no hard Azure dependency.

Medium-heavy Python library (v0.22.3). Ships agents, 10 session backends, guardrails, MCP, sandbox runtime, tracing, realtime, testing utilities and a REPL, but no dev UI, scheduler, deployer, or eval harness.

TypeScript library: agents-core, agents-openai, agents-realtime, extensions. agents-core now carries a sandbox runtime and a testing module. No bundled storage backends, eval, dev UI, or plugin system. The umbrella @openai/agents re-exports the parts.

Python library with a medium core (Agent, pydantic_graph, hooks, toolsets, ASGI adapters) plus a heavy optional layer: the first-party pydantic-ai-harness (0.x, ~53 kLOC, now in the monorepo). Durable execution via opt-in temporal/dbos/prefect/restate.

Medium-heavy Rust workspace of 28 crates: rig-core (portable contracts), rig-agent (agent runtime), providers, vector stores, MCP (rig-rmcp), record/replay and an experimental Bevy runtime. No HTTP server or dev UI.

Medium-heavy Python library (python/v1.57.1, ~70.6k lines in 25 sub-packages): agent, event loop, hooks, middleware, interventions, multiagent, sessions/storage, memory, sandbox, MCP client, OTel, plugins. AWS-leaning default but provider-agnostic.

Heavy Node library (~50.6k non-test lines, ~35 modules, Agent class ~2.7k lines) with hooks, middleware, plugins, interventions, multiagent, sessions/storage, memory, sandbox and telemetry. Analysed from harness-sdk/strands-ts now that sdk-typescript is archived.

Thin TypeScript SDK (ai@7.0.126): generateText/streamText/ToolLoopAgent plus 50+ provider adapters and UI stream protocol. No sessions, durable runtime, RAG or dev UI in ai; experimental harness, sandbox and workflow packages are separate opt-ins.

Loop is plain Go in your binary: runner/runner.go:568-626 hands an LlmAgent root to a single-node workflow (runner/run_node.go:136-143), whose ReAct loop is internal/llminternal/base_flow.go Flow.Run. No subprocess or sidecar; only outbound HTTPS to the LLM provider (Gemini, or experimental OpenAI). First-party REST/A2A servers run in the same process.

Agent.run dispatches to agno.agent._run (a 16-step run with retry attempts) inside your Python uvicorn worker. Memory and learning extraction run as background futures, and durable queue workers (v3.0.0) are in-process too. No subprocess or vendor cloud unless you opt into managed or external-framework agents.
Loop runs on the caller's tokio runtime (direct.rs and react.rs TurnEngine). LLM calls are plain async HTTP from the same process. Optional in-process ractor actor runtime; never a separate process.

Loop runs in a spawned Claude Code Node/native binary, not in your Python; Python is a JSON-over-stdio control-protocol shim that, since 0.2.160, also tracks CLI session_state frames to know when a run is over but makes no model or tool decisions. You cannot fork the loop without forking Claude Code; only hooks and canUseTool extend it. Acceptable for Claude-only tools, weak for the benchmark's open multi-provider goal.

Same architecture as the Python SDK: agent loop, system prompt, tool dispatch, permissions, compaction, skill discovery, sub-agent fan-out and Workflow scripts all run inside a spawned native binary. The vendor hosting doc states one agent session maps to one subprocess. The TS package is a transport and RPC bridge; hook callbacks and SDK MCP servers run in your Node heap.

Crew.kickoff runs in your Python process; the default AgentExecutor (experimental/agent_executor.py) is a Flow subclass that plans todos and runs tool calls, and the legacy CrewAgentExecutor is now deprecated. LLM HTTP calls go straight from the same process via native SDKs or LiteLLM. No subprocess, no vendor binary.

TypedChatModelAgent.Run (adk/chatmodel.go) spawns a goroutine that runs a compiled ReAct compose.Graph in your Go process. Workflow agents fan out goroutines coordinated by sync.WaitGroup. No subprocess at any layer.

ai.GenerateWithRequest (go/ai/generate.go) is the single Go function that loops model, tools, model in your binary. The experimental agent runtime (go/ai/exp/agent.go) calls the same function each turn, and detached turns run on in-process goroutines. The Reflection server only starts when GENKIT_ENV=dev.

CompiledStateGraph.stream/invoke drives PregelLoop.tick directly in your Python process; tools and checkpointer I/O are in-process. The source-available (ELv2) langgraph-api server wraps the same loop with queue/auth/multitask but does not subprocess it.

FunctionAgent.run resolves to Workflow.run which schedules @step methods on the asyncio event loop. No subprocess or vendor cloud round-trip. HTTP/distribution is BYO or via separate llama_deploy repo.

packages/core/src/loop builds a Mastra workflow stream (AgenticLoopBuilder) that runs in your TypeScript runtime. DurableAgent can move steps to worker processes, still Mastra code on your infrastructure. The new agent-sdks packages (@mastra/claude, @mastra/openai) wrap other runtimes, and then the loop runs in the vendor SDK; scored on the default path.

Python agent.run uses BaseChatClient.get_response with FunctionInvokingChatClient tool loop; .NET uses Microsoft.Extensions.AI's FunctionInvokingChatClient via DelegatingAIAgent. Both run inside your host process — no subprocess, no bundled CLI.

Runner.run drives run_internal/run_loop on the asyncio event loop you own. No bundled CLI or sidecar. Opt-in exceptions: experimental OpenAIHostedMultiAgentModel (sub-agent orchestration on OpenAI's service) and Programmatic Tool Calling (hosted V8), while function tools still run locally. Scored on the default path.

Runner.run is a single while(true) loop in packages/agents-core/src/run.ts (~lines 1643-2203) calling prepareTurn, getResponseWithRetry, processModelResponseAsync and resolveTurnAfterModelResponse. No subprocess or vendor binary. Opt-in exception: experimental OpenAIHostedMultiAgentModel moves sub-agent orchestration to OpenAI while local tools still run in your process.

Agent.run opens iter(), which builds a pydantic_graph run over UserPromptNode, ModelRequestNode and CallToolsNode. Every model call is host-process HTTPS; no subprocess. Optional cloud sandbox workspaces run commands and file I/O remotely, not the loop; durable variants (temporal/dbos) run the same graph under their workers.

Loop is plain Rust async: AgentRunner drives drive_agent (crates/rig-agent/src/agent/engine.rs) over a sans-IO AgentRun state machine, with I/O dispatched on an in-process effect bus. Runs on your executor (tokio or any other; rig-core no longer depends on tokio). No subprocess or IPC; an experimental Bevy runtime (rig-ecs) runs the same protocol.

event_loop.event_loop_cycle is a pure-Python async generator called from Agent._execute_event_loop_cycle. No subprocess. A ConcurrencyException guards one stream_async per Agent instance, pushing one Agent per active session but many sessions per process.

Agent.stream is an async function* whose body loops until stopReason != toolUse, dispatching tools through the local ToolRegistry. Providers do outbound HTTP/SSE but orchestration is local. No subprocess.

generateText/streamText is a do/while loop in packages/ai/src/generate-text/generate-text.ts and ToolLoopAgent wraps it, all in your Node process. Exceptions: the experimental HarnessAgent hands the loop to a third-party runtime (Claude Code, Codex, Pi) inside a sandbox, and WorkflowAgent runs steps on Workflow DevKit workers. Scored on the default path.

Go 1.26.6 (go.mod), one Go binary with no bundled binaries or native libs. Only an LLM provider is mandatory (Gemini/Vertex, experimental OpenAI or OpenAI-compatible, or BYO model.LLM). Postgres/SQLite/MySQL/Spanner, Vertex Agent Engine, GCS, BigQuery and MCP servers are optional; with the database session store you must run AutoMigrate on every startup (v2.5).

note: Python plus DB driver, MCP optional
details: Python 3.9+; agno[os] adds fastapi, uvicorn, sqlalchemy, PyJWT, opentelemetry-sdk, croniter and pytz. You pick a DB driver plus an LLM provider key, and background runs and the durable queue now require a database (v3.0.0). Redis/Valkey (cross-replica cancel, SSE resume) and S3/GCS media storage are optional. Heavier than thin SDKs but no daemons or native binaries.

Rust (edition 2024, latest stable) and tokio are mandatory; ractor backs the actor runtime (default off wasm). Optional Cargo features pull wasmtime, deno_ast/rquickjs, rmcp, qdrant-client, llama.cpp/mistral-rs; WASI builds of the OpenAI client are supported. No mandatory DB or vendor. Compile time is the real cost.

Python 3.10+ and a bundled Claude Code binary (wheel ~93-103 MB per platform) or a system-installed claude; no wheel is published for Windows at 0.2.163. Anthropic API key (or Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry credentials) is mandatory. The loop only works with the CLI and you cannot replace it. No Postgres/Redis/vector DB required.

Node 18+ (or Bun/Deno) plus a 225-242 MB platform-specific Claude binary pulled as optionalDependencies, practically mandatory; the SDK throws if it is missing unless pathToClaudeCodeExecutable is set. Installing linux x64 and arm64 together carries about 480 MB. Anthropic API (or Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry) is required; bubblewrap is optional for the Linux sandbox.

Python >=3.10,<3.14, pure Python: no bundled binaries, no Node, no vendor CLI. Default LanceDB writes to disk, checkpoints go to ./.checkpoints and flow persistence to local SQLite; Redis is used for locks only when REDIS_URL is set. An LLM provider endpoint is required. Optional E2B/Daytona sandbox and MCP servers; AMP cloud is opt-in.

Go toolchain only: core go.mod declares go 1.18 (some eino-ext modules need 1.23-1.25); the May note of Go 1.25 was wrong for core. No bundled binaries (the local PDF backend moved from cgo go-fitz to WASM go-pdfium) and no daemons. Postgres/Redis/vector stores only if you wire them via eino-ext. Lightest deployment story alongside adk-go and rig.

Go ≥1.25, pure-Go modules. Optional Node.js + genkit CLI for dev UI/eval/init helpers only — not required at runtime. Optional GCP credentials, OTel exporter, Postgres/Firestore via plugins. ~30 MB binary, ~30 MB RSS idle.

Python >=3.10 for the library; langgraph dev needs Python >=3.11. Storage (Postgres via psycopg, or SQLite) is optional and LLM providers come via langchain-* packages. For an HTTP server you add langgraph-cli[inmem], which pulls the ELv2 langgraph-api and runtime packages; production images need a LangGraph licence key, and platform deployments also need Redis for API/worker pub/sub.

Python 3.10+ with SQLAlchemy, httpx, pydantic, tiktoken, aiohttp, nltk, tenacity, banks, aiosqlite, llama-index-workflows. No bundled binaries. No mandatory infra; default Memory uses aiosqlite. Each provider/store integration adds its own SDK.

Node >=22.13 (packages/core/package.json; the May note of Node >=18 was wrong), or Bun and edge runtimes via deployers. The default in-memory store must be replaced for production (libsql/pg/redis/d1/dynamo/mssql among 31 adapters). The model router resolves 210 providers; optional vector store, Redis/Pub/Sub for workers, observability storage (needed by TokenCostControl) and sandbox providers.

Python >=3.10 or .NET 8/9/10. No external binaries the SDK subprocesses by default (opt-in MCP stdio, shell tools, Hyperlight sandbox). Optional stores include Redis, Cosmos DB, Blob, Valkey and several vector DBs; one LLM provider is required. Since Python 1.13.0 feature-usage telemetry is added to the provider User-Agent unless disabled.

Python 3.10+, pure Python with no bundled binaries or Node CLI. Core now requires openai>=3 with HTTPX2 (0.21) and accepts MCP SDK v1 or v2. OpenAI API by default, or LiteLLM/any-llm for 100+ providers. All session backends (SQLAlchemy/Redis/Mongo/Dapr) are optional and the default is in-memory; sandbox agents need Docker or a hosted provider for real isolation.

Node 22+, Deno or Bun; no bundled binaries or subprocess. OpenAI API for the default Model (apps passing their own client need openai >=7.2); the AI-SDK extension brings Anthropic/Gemini/Bedrock. MCP server subprocesses and sandbox providers (Docker needs /bin/sh and GNU utilities) are opt-in. Cloudflare Workers is experimental with nodejs_compat.

Python 3.10+, pydantic/pydantic-core/pydantic-graph/genai-prices/opentelemetry/anyio. No external binaries, no required infra. LLM provider key required. Durable execution via opt-in temporal/dbos/prefect/restate extras.

Rust 1.95.0+ (MSRV) and an async executor: rig-core is executor-agnostic and tokio is the usual choice; HTTP transport is rig-reqwest by default or any HttpClientExt. WASM-compatible. No bundled subprocesses or CLIs and no required infra; companion crates (rig-bedrock, rig-vertex, rig-memory, rig-candle) are opt-in.

Python ≥3.10 with boto3 in core (Bedrock default). Optional provider extras: anthropic/gemini/litellm/llamaapi/mistral/ollama/openai/writer/sagemaker. Optional S3 for sessions, OTLP collector for traces. No bundled CLI.

Node >=22 (required since v1.17), plus @aws-sdk/client-bedrock-runtime and small utilities. All other LLM providers, OTel, MCP, Express and S3 are optional peer deps. No bundled CLI; Docker/SSH sandboxes need a running container or host. Local file storage by default or S3; no mandatory Postgres/Redis.

Node 22, 24 or 26 (raised from 18 in 7.0.0), ESM-only. No native libs or bundled binaries; the database is BYO. Only an LLM provider account (or AI Gateway) is needed. Optional pieces add dependencies: HarnessAgent needs a sandbox provider and an external runtime, WorkflowAgent needs Workflow DevKit (beta peer dependency).

README states containerized deployment is supported with strong Cloud Run support, and adkgo deploy generates Dockerfiles for Cloud Run or Agent Engine. cmd/launcher composes web UI, REST and A2A. The natural shape is one binary per app serving many users keyed by (AppName, UserID, SessionID); since v2.5 the web launcher binds 127.0.0.1 by default, so containers need -host 0.0.0.0, and the REST server godoc says network-reachable servers need an Authenticator.

Canonical pattern is agent_os.serve(app=..., reload=True) calling uvicorn.run; the README points to template repos for Docker, AWS, GCP, Azure, Railway, Fly, Render, Modal and Helm. One process serves many agents and sessions and replicas scale out against a shared DB; v3 adds a durable job queue with leases and multi-replica reclaim, optional Redis for cross-replica cancel, and stateless MCP serving. Auth, RBAC, scheduling and tracing live in the same process.

Docs describe direct vs actor agents but do not prescribe container-per-tenant vs shared process. README's "horizontal scaling with multi-agent coordination" refers to the in-process actor runtime, not multi-process deployment. You embed it in whatever Rust binary you build.

The vendor hosting guide (code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hosting, language-agnostic with Python tabs, checked 2026-10-01) documents four patterns: ephemeral, long-running (Python holds a `ClaudeSDKClient` per session), hybrid (requires `session_store=`) and multi-agent container. It adds sizing (1 GiB RAM and 1 CPU per agent), consistent hashing on `sessionId`, and a multi-tenant recipe (`setting_sources=[]`, `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY`, per-tenant `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` and `cwd`). Practical shape is N CLI subprocesses per pod. The repo ships only `Dockerfile.test`, has no `startup()`/`prewarm()` equivalent and no queue or scheduler, so you build the pool. Raised from 2 to match TS.

The vendor hosting doc documents four patterns (ephemeral, long-running, hybrid with a required SessionStore, multi-agent container) and recommends pinning sessions to containers by consistent hashing on sessionId. Practical shape is N CLI subprocesses per pod with idle eviction; startup() and alpha prewarm() help build pools. The runAssistantWorker blueprint was removed in 0.3.181 and there is no first-party queue or scheduler, so you build the pool yourself.

OSS docs (docs/edge) still assume one Python process per Crew/Flow kickoff and cover crew design, not horizontal scaling. Frontend guides add a self-hosted shape: a FastAPI plus ag-ui-crewai process behind a CopilotKit runtime. AMP deploys from GitHub or ZIP to a managed runtime (AMP docs moved off-repo to docs-platform.crewai.com). No tenant primitive in OSS.

No vendor topology doc since it is a library; the v0.9 quickstart web chapter runs one Go process with a Hertz server and file-backed sessions and labels sessions, memory and UI protocol as business-layer code. Confirmed in production at Dailymotion: one Go process per pod behind its own router with shared DB state. A TurnLoop is per session, so a pod hosting N sessions holds N loops. Multi-tenancy guidance is minimal.

Samples target Cloud Run (stateless instances behind a load balancer), with docs for Cloud Run and any platform. One Go binary serves N routes via genkit.Handler and, since v1.10, genkitx.AgentRoutes per agent; the basic-agents-server sample shows store-backed and client-managed state. Per-tenant identity flows via headers to ContextProvider, with a tenant prefix on the session store. No worker-per-session recommendation.

Platform docs recommend one-process-many-tenants: API pods sharing Postgres for state and Redis for pub/sub with worker pods. Self-host follows the same pattern (langgraph up compose, Helm chart), and langgraph deploy can now target a listener in your own cluster (hybrid) or push a prebuilt image. Production use of the server needs a licence; pure-OSS users bring their own HTTP, queue and auth.

The in-repo deployment tutorial is still a TODO stub. The vendor path is now the separate llama-agents repo (llama-agents-server wraps a Workflow as a REST API; llamactl deploys to LlamaParse, AWS Bedrock AgentCore or your infra), which replaced the deprecated llama_deploy and was read only at README level. Kept at 0 because nothing in the framework repo documents a topology; open question whether llama-agents should count.

Documented one-process-many-tenants with a stateless server; replicas share storage and pub/sub, and resumable streams (observe with offset) remove session-affinity needs. Mastra({ workers }) runs orchestration, scheduler and background-task workers, splittable from the API via MASTRA_WORKERS, and graceful shutdown is configurable. Deployers package for Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Workers, Mastra Cloud and a new sandbox deployer.

No single canonical topology, but samples exist per option: .NET Hosting (`AddAIAgent`, `AgentSessionStore`, isolation-key scoped stores), Foundry Hosted Agents (container per agent), DevUI for local work, and the first-party Durable Task extension. Checked microsoft/agent-framework-durable-extension (MIT, Microsoft-maintained): Azure Functions is the documented production host (`ConfigureDurableAgents` / `AgentFunctionApp`, generated `/api/agents/{name}/run` endpoints), with console/generic-host and Durable Task Scheduler options and per-agent session TTL. Capability alone would merit 5, but the extension labels itself preview (NuGet 1.16.0-preview.260922.1, PyPI 1.0.0b260922, `Development Status :: 4 - Beta`) and the in-repo Python hosting packages are alpha, so 4 under the maturity cap. No turnkey multi-tenant server.

The SDK has no vendor opinion on topology. Examples assume one Python process per host serving many sessions via asyncio; for horizontal scaling run N stateless workers with a shared store (SQLAlchemy/Redis/Mongo). The closest guide is the server-side HITL doc (keep RunState in app storage, owner-checked atomic resume), whose example is explicitly not a deployable service. No first-party container-per-tenant recommendation.

Docs do not prescribe a topology. examples/nextjs/ shows one-process-many-requests in a Next.js Route Handler; there is no built-in worker pool, queue, or cluster mode. Cloudflare Workers is documented as experimental. Experimental hosted Multi-agent supports one active run per model instance and approvals must resume on the same instance, which forces sticky routing for that feature.

Not opinionated; docs treat Agent as stateless and global, so the default is one process serving many tenants with per-call deps. UI adapter docs assume the endpoint runs inside your authenticated route, and the cancel-endpoint example needs a single process or sticky routing. Durable patterns are documented for Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate, and Harness SqliteConversationStore must not be shared between hosts.

Not opinionated; no production deployment guide. The README positions rig-agent for hosts that bring their own HTTP and runtime, and Agent, AgentRunner and ToolServerHandle are asserted Send + Sync + 'static for shared host state. One process serving many tenants is the natural default; the serializable AgentRun plus Agent::resume lets any instance continue a run, but the wiring is yours.

Not prescribed by the SDK, but the docs list deploy targets: AgentCore Runtime (session-per-microVM), Lambda, Fargate, App Runner, EKS, EC2, Docker, Kubernetes and Terraform, plus an operating-in-production page. A concurrency lock still pushes one Agent instance per active session with many sessions per process. A2AServer(agent_factory) encodes the same pattern.

The SDK repo prescribes nothing, but the docs site has deploy pages for AgentCore, Lambda, Fargate, App Runner, EKS, EC2, Docker, Kubernetes and Terraform plus an operating-in-production page (same docs as the Python SDK). The A2A server runs one agent per contextId, LRU-capped at 1000. Practical patterns: one Agent per request or session, or container-per-tenant. Raised from 2 to match the Python peer; no shipped runtime daemon keeps it at 3.

The SDK ships no hosting recipes for ToolLoopAgent; docs and examples/next-agent mount createAgentUIStreamResponse in a Next.js route (many tenants per process, state in your DB). For the experimental HarnessAgent the documented topology is one sandbox per chat: stable sandboxId from the chat id, detach per request, resume on the next, with long turns run under Workflow time slices. No queue or worker pool.

Sub-second from main() to first run and tens of MB RAM baseline (not measured in this analysis). Binary is tens of MB, larger with the embedded Web UI. No JVM/Python/Node interpreter and no bundled vendor binary. Expected fastest cold start of the benchmarked stacks.

Cold start is dominated by Python import, the FastAPI app and AgentOS init (DB initialisation, tables auto-provisioned on boot by default). v3.0.1 caches derived tool schemas and loads session history incrementally; v3.0.4 lazy-imports file/knowledge tools. RAM and disk are not measured; the package is ~455k lines but most toolkits and providers import lazily.

Release binary cold start ≈ process startup time (typically <100ms). Memory baseline small unless you enable llama.cpp/mistral-rs features. Compile time is the real cost — full cargo build with all features is heavy, but runtime is light.

Each connect() runs a version check, spawns the CLI subprocess and does an initialize handshake (timeout min 60 s); latency is dominated by Node startup, and open issue #333 reports 20-30 s cold start in some multi-instance setups. Estimated 200-500 MB RAM per active session (not measured). Wheel is ~93-103 MB per platform, and since 0.2.160 a run can keep the subprocess alive up to 10 minutes while background agents finish.

No vendor cold-start number. The vendor hosting doc gives 1 GiB RAM, 5 GiB disk and 1 CPU per agent as a floor; issue #372 reports 99% CPU and P95 103 s at 40 concurrent sessions and open issue #268 reports 900 MB+ for listSessions(). Binary is 225-242 MB per platform. startup()/WarmQuery and alpha prewarm()/SpareProcess mitigate spawn latency. Plan for at least 1 GiB per concurrent session.

Cold start is roughly a second dominated by provider SDK imports (1.14.7 lazy-loads docling); estimates, not benchmarked. RAM baseline ~150 MB Python interpreter plus framework, growing with the memory store. Disk ~50-100 MB of wheels; LanceDB grows linearly with memory. No 20-30 s subprocess penalty.

Negligible startup latency: NewRunner is struct allocation. Core is ~60k non-test LOC (adk ~29k) but nothing loads eagerly; the local PDF backend lazily starts a pdfium WASM pool. Per-session memory is dominated by runSession.Events accumulation; zero disk baseline. Large cold-start advantage for serverless and horizontal scaling.

Init dominated by plugin Init() calls (googlegenai sync HTTP/credential check, typically <1s with cached ADC). Cloud Run instance cold-boot <<1s after image pull. ~30 MB RSS for minimal binary; growing with model SDKs (~50 MB once Vertex gRPC initialized).

Pure-OSS embedding: few hundred ms import, RAM baseline tens of MB beyond model client. Platform/self-host runs Starlette+Uvicorn worker pods; multi-tenant Postgres connection pool dominates RAM. Closed-source server hides exact numbers.

Pure-Python import overhead is non-trivial — SQLAlchemy, pydantic, tiktoken, nltk, banks, httpx, aiohttp all pulled in. No published baseline RAM. Cold start dominated by LLM SDK warm-up, not the framework. Reasonable but not measured.

note: tens of MB, slow on edge
details: No public benchmark in-repo. @mastra/core is heavy (~933 non-test source files, agent.ts ~10.7k lines) though some dependencies are lazy-imported. Realistic baseline for a 5-agent app: tens of MB RAM and sub-second cold start on Node, longer on Cloudflare Workers because of bundle size. Not officially reported.

Not advertised. Startup is dominated by provider SDK initialisation and context-provider work (skill scans, MCP connects). Python 1.11.0 made root exports lazy and 1.18.0 lazy-loads Foundry/OpenAI integrations to cut import cost. Thin assembly otherwise; no documented multi-second startup issue.

import agents triggers openai SDK + pydantic imports; lazy SQLiteSession and extension backends amortize. ~100-150 MB RAM baseline. Tens of MB disk for the package. No 20-30s startup; sub-second cold start in practice.

No bundled binary. Pure JS/TS startup is typical Node baseline (~200-400 ms). Minimal RAM beyond Node baseline; MemorySession in-memory. Loop starts on run() invocation in milliseconds. No equivalent of Claude Agent SDK issue #333.

Pure-Python import; startup is the interpreter plus the chosen provider SDKs (tens of MB RAM). V2 resolves deferred provider imports and price data at Model construction, moving first-request latency to construction. A cloud-sandbox workspace adds provider boot time per run. No bundled binaries and no documented multi-second startup.

Rust binary startup typically <500 ms once compiled (no JIT, no Python interpreter). No vendor binary downloaded; no Node sidecar. Memory baseline small — Agent struct is a few Arcs plus a RwLock-wrapped ToolServerState.

Construction is in-process and light, but Agent.__init__ now wires more subsystems (tool, hook, middleware and intervention registries, context manager, memory manager, background tasks, sandbox, storage). Import cost is dominated by boto3, pydantic, OpenTelemetry and mcp. No subprocess warm-up and no published benchmark.

Not measured but expected light because no subprocess starts. Lazy-loaded peer-deps mean tree-shaken bundles stay small. CI includes browser bundle check, suggesting modest baseline footprint. No subprocess-spawn overhead.

ai cold start is a JS import, tens of ms, with no bundled binaries; the first LLM call is dominated by provider latency. The experimental HarnessAgent adds sandbox creation, bootstrap and runtime start, mitigated by snapshot-able sandbox templates; no published latency or RAM figures exist for it.

LLM: medium; model.LLM is open but requests and responses still embed genai types, and first-party impls are gemini, apigee and the experimental openaimodel (Responses/Chat Completions, any OpenAI-compatible BaseURL). No native Anthropic/Bedrock adapter. Hosting: low-medium; runs anywhere Go runs, but the deploy CLI, IAP/OIDC authenticators, Agent Engine backends and Agent Registry are GCP-specific. Eval: Python-only (N/A in Go). Observability: low (OTel). Net unchanged: LLM axis improved, GCP tilt grew.

note: 52 LLM providers, no hosting, no eval
details: LLM: minimal; 52 provider packages behind an abstract Model base. Hosting: none; a uvicorn process (the os.agno.com UI is optional). Eval: none; evals, scorers and environments are in-repo and OTel tracing is provider-neutral.

note: low LLM lock-in, OTel, no eval
details: LLM: low; a unified LLMProvider trait covers 10 cloud and 3 local providers plus a generic OpenAI-compatible provider. Hosting: none; runs anywhere Rust runs (WASI for parts of the LLM crate). Eval: none, no eval framework. Observability: OTel via autoagents-telemetry with optional Langfuse, both swappable.

LLM: strongly Anthropic-locked — alternative providers route only via Anthropic gateway (Bedrock/Vertex), only Claude models first-class. CLI binary: strongly Claude-Code-locked — wire protocol closed-source, CLI-version-specific. Hosting low. Eval/observability OTel-only.

LLM: high; Anthropic models only, with Bedrock/Vertex/Foundry/gateway being hosting routes for Claude rather than other model families, and the skill/sub-agent format is Claude Code-shaped. Hosting: low for self-host, high for the claude.ai bridge and remote isolation. Licence: proprietary bundle under Anthropic Commercial Terms, no source to fork. Eval/observability: low (standard OTel env vars).

OSS path open: 100+ providers via LiteLLM, none for hosting/eval/skills/memory/persistence. AMP path heavy lock-in: AMP-only deploys, automations, triggers, Studio, Traces dashboard, hallucination guardrail, PII redaction, RBAC, Agent Repositories. Stay OSS to keep portability.

LLM: low; all providers sit behind model.BaseModel interfaces (10 providers plus 6 agentic variants in eino-ext), though AgenticMessage with provider-hosted server tools raises coupling. Hosting: none. Eval: none, BYO. Tracing: low (OTel via APMPlus/Langfuse, or LangSmith/CozeLoop). Persistence: none, CheckPointStore is two methods on []byte.

LLM: multi-provider; native plugins for Google AI/Vertex, Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, DeepSeek, DashScope, Kimi, Z.ai, OpenRouter, Ollama and Model Garden, plus a Fallback middleware. Hosting: slight GCP tilt; samples target Cloud Run, the telemetry plugin is GCP-only and Firestore is the only managed session store, but nothing GCP is required. Eval: no lock-in. Tracing: OTel-standard.

LLM: low; any langchain-* chat model works via init_chat_model. Hosting/platform: medium; the HTTP server, auth, run queue, multitask coordination and /mcp routes ship only in the source-available ELv2 langgraph-api package, which needs a paid licence in production, so pure OSS means BYO HTTP, queue and auth. Eval: medium; cost in USD requires paid LangSmith.

note: ~100 LLMs, no hosting, no eval lock-in
details: LLM: none; pluggable abstraction with ~100 implementations. Hosting: none; llama-agents-server is OSS too and LlamaParse (formerly LlamaCloud) is for parse/ingest, not serving. Eval: none; LangSmith, Arize, Langfuse, Opik and Phoenix integrations exist.

LLM: low; accepts AI SDK v4-v7 models plus a provider/model router over 210 providers. Hosting: low; eight server adapters and four platform deployers, nothing requires Mastra Cloud. Storage: low, 31 adapters. Eval/observability: medium; MastraScorer/runEvals and the span model are proprietary, with exporters for OTel, Langfuse, LangSmith, Datadog and others, so migrating scorers is a rewrite.

LLM: open; Python clients for OpenAI, Azure/Foundry, Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini, Mistral, Ollama and others, and .NET accepts any IChatClient. Hosting: Azure is first-class (Foundry, Cosmos, Blob, AI Search) but core has no hard Azure dependency, and .NET 1.21.0 dropped Azure.AI.OpenAI. Eval/observability: OTel-native. Feature-usage User-Agent telemetry is on by default (opt-out).

LLM: low; MultiProvider supports openai/litellm/any-llm prefixes (100+ providers), but Responses-only features (tool search, Programmatic Tool Calling, hosted multi-agent, server-side compaction) are widening the gap to other providers. Hosting: none. Eval/observability: none; default OpenAI Traces exporter is replaceable by 25+ partner exporters. Session: none; 10 backends plus the Session Protocol.

LLM: medium; default is the OpenAI Responses API (default model gpt-5.6-luna since 0.15.0), pluggable via custom ModelProvider, with Anthropic/Gemini/Bedrock/Vertex through the AI-SDK bridge. Hosted tools and hosted Multi-agent are OpenAI Responses-only. Hosting: low. Tracing defaults to the OpenAI Traces dashboard but is escapable via setTraceProcessors.

LLM: low; ~20 provider modules, FallbackModel, SelectModel and custom Model subclasses (V2 made the openai: prefix mean the Responses API). Hosting: none. Eval: low; pydantic-evals is in-repo with OTel export. Observability: low; OTel-first, Logfire is one backend, though the optional ManagedPrompt ties prompt management to Logfire.

LLM: low; 26 in-tree providers plus Bedrock, Vertex, Candle and others as companion crates, with a serializable ProviderRef for runtime selection. Hosting: none. Eval: none; the in-tree evals module was removed in 0.40.

LLM low — 12+ providers (Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, LiteLLM, Llama, Llama.cpp, Mistral, Ollama, SageMaker, Writer, OpenAI Responses). Hosting low — pure Python, no managed runtime. Eval low — no built-in eval. Default-Bedrock posture biases AWS shops but nothing about SDK is AWS-only.

LLM low — Bedrock default but Model base class provider-agnostic; shipped adapters for Bedrock/Anthropic/OpenAI (Chat+Responses)/Google/VercelModel shim. Hosting none — pure library. Eval/observability OTel-native, so any OTLP backend (Datadog/Honeycomb/Tempo/Grafana/Phoenix) works.

LLM: low; 50+ adapters behind LanguageModelV4. Hosting: low for ToolLoopAgent, medium for the experimental WorkflowAgent (Vercel-first Workflow DevKit) and HarnessAgent (Vercel Sandbox is the only first-party network sandbox). Agent runtime: HarnessAgent makes the runtime swappable but behaviour belongs to the runtime. Eval: none required. Lowered from 5 because the new optional layers carry a Vercel tilt.

Heavy, and heavier than at v1.2 (+156k/-8.7k lines incl. tests and embedded UI). Bundles run loop, graph workflow engine, session stores, context compaction, memory, artifacts, REST server with authn/authz, A2A server, outbound auth, Agent Registry client, plugins, skills, MCP client, OTel, web UI and CLI. Comparable scope to Mastra without RAG, scheduler or eval; lighter than LangGraph Platform, heavier than Vercel AI SDK.

Very heavy platform: ~455k lines of Python in libs/agno (+177k/-31k since May), ~40 subpackages (agent, team, workflow, tools ~150 modules, models 52, db, knowledge, memory, eval, scorer, guardrails, skills, scheduler, job_queue, tracing, os FastAPI server ~62k lines). Agent has ~110 constructor parameters. Raised from 4: v3 added a durable queue, tool-result offloading, an MCP server, an eval suite and pluggable authz, level with CrewAI and Mastra.

Heavy by total LOC (multi-crate workspace including speech, vector stores, derive macros, guardrails, WASM sandbox) but core surface (autoagents-core) is focused: agent/executor/memory/tool/context/hooks/runtime. You only pull what you use via Cargo features.

Thin Python SDK relative to the work it delegates: ~12.9k lines across 26 files in src/claude_agent_sdk (up from ~10.6k), led by types.py (2,545 lines), _internal/query.py (1,228), subprocess_cli.py (1,228), __init__.py (772) and client.py (631). Heavy lifting is in the bundled CLI binary (~100 MB per platform), which is not source-distributed.

TS shim at 0.3.286: sdk.mjs 1.2 MB, bridge.mjs 1.3 MB, core.mjs 123 KB plus chunks, 5.4 MB unpacked. The bundled native CLI is 225-242 MB per platform, the heaviest of the stacks by bytes on disk. sdk.d.ts grew to 9,890 lines (from 5,722) and sdk-tools.d.ts to 4,172. Neither a thin SDK nor a heavy framework conceptually.

Very heavy: ~127 kLOC under lib/crewai (re-measured with wc -l; the May ~70 kLOC was an estimate), six packages and 163 event classes. Bundles agent classes, two executors, crews, flows (DSL, declarative, conversational), memory, knowledge, RAG, MCP client, A2A, event bus, interception hooks, telemetry, checkpointing, CLI with TUIs, skill loader, tool catalog and guardrails.

Heavy library, no platform: ~60k non-test LOC (the May figure of ~12k was wrong), of which adk is ~29k (cancel, TurnLoop, retry/failover and the typed layer added ~14k in v0.9). 8 in-tree middlewares and 3 prebuilts. Zero platform code (no HTTP server, UI, eval or marketplace); rich runtime primitives, you assemble the application. Kept at 3 for calibration with strands and rig libraries.

Medium-heavy and growing: 483 .go files under go/ (224 non-test, non-sample), core packages genkit, ai and core, 17 plugin directories (anthropic, alloydb, compat_oai, evaluators, firebase, googlecloud, googlegenai, localvec, mcp, middleware, ollama, pinecone, postgresql, server, vertexai, weaviate, a2ui) and 36 samples. The stable Generate call is one function, but the experimental agent runtime (snapshots, detach, artifacts) is a sizeable subsystem. Heavier than Eino; no bundled UI.

Heavy. The graph runtime is ~2k LOC, but ToolNode, prebuilt, checkpointers and the SDK add many thousands more (the SDK gained ~5k LOC of v3 streaming client), and the BaseStore/BaseCheckpointSaver interfaces invite ecosystem packages. The ELv2 platform server adds queue, persistence, auth and multitask coordination on top and is not counted by bytes.

Heavy ecosystem (300+ integration packages) but the core is modular. The agent layer (agent/workflow/) is ~2,900 lines: base_agent 836, multi_agent_workflow 900, codeact 400, react 330, function 196, plus context, events and prompts.

Very heavy framework. @mastra/core has ~933 non-test source files (agent.ts alone is 10,679 lines) and bundles agents, workflows, durable agents, workers, memory, storage, RAG, voice, MCP, deployers, schedules, scorers/datasets/experiments, RBAC/FGA, Studio and AgentController. Trade-off is coupling: Agent knows about Mastra, Storage, Memory, Workspace, MCPServer and pub/sub.

Very heavy: the Python core alone is ~51 kLOC (up from ~27k), with 42 Python packages and 35 .NET projects. Bundles agents, workflows, sessions and stores, compaction, MCP, middleware, agent-hooks enforcement, observability, skills, FIDES security labelling, evaluation, harness providers, vector-store abstractions and 20+ provider connectors. Raised from 4: scope broader than LangGraph and now at CrewAI/Mastra scale.

Medium-heavy for a library and growing (src/agents ~134k lines). Ships agents, 10 session backends, guardrails, MCP client, sandbox runtime with Docker, Unix-local and 7 hosted providers, tracing, realtime voice, Codex extension, hosted-tool wrappers, a REPL and first-party test doubles. No dev UI, frontend SDK, scheduler, deployer or eval harness.

Mid-weight and growing. The umbrella @openai/agents re-exports agents-core, agents-openai and agents-realtime; agents-core now carries a sizeable sandbox runtime (manifests, capabilities, path grants, snapshots, memory generation) plus a testing module, and extensions add AI SDK, Cloudflare, Twilio and 7 sandbox providers. Still no bundled storage backends, eval UI, dev UI or plugin system. Raised from 2 because the refreshed report no longer describes it as lean.

Medium core, heavy optional layer. Core: agent/__init__.py ~4.9k LOC, _agent_graph.py ~3.3k, messages.py ~5.1k, still storage-free. The first-party Harness (0.x, now in the monorepo) is ~53 kLOC across 50+ capability packages: file/shell tools, sandboxes, memory, step persistence, spend limits, guardrails, compaction, code mode and integrations, all opt-in per capability. Raised from 2 for the Harness.

Medium-heavy library, and growing: 28 crates including rig-core (contracts), rig-agent (runtime), an experimental Bevy ECS runtime, effect bus, rig-cassette record/replay, 26 provider integrations, 12 vector stores, MCP (rig-rmcp), memory policies, Candle local inference and a CLI chatbot. No HTTP server, dev UI or plugin marketplace. The 0.43 split trimmed rig-core dependency weight (no reqwest or tokio).

Medium-heavy now: strands-py/src/strands grew from 13 to 25 sub-packages and ~70.6k lines (+43.6k/-11.3k). Bundles tool registry, MCP client, multiagent orchestrators, middleware, interventions (Cedar, HITL), memory manager, unified storage, sandbox, background tasks, context manager, model routing, bidi, vended tools and OTel. Kept at 3 for calibration with the other medium-heavy libraries.

Heavy library: ~50.6k non-test TS lines across ~35 modules (agent.ts 2,728 lines) covering middleware, routing, memory, context management, background tasks, storage, sandbox, hooks, plugins, interventions, multiagent, sessions and telemetry. A full agent SDK rather than glue; harness-ts and strands-cli sit on top. Kept at 3 for calibration with Eino and strands-py.

ai remains a thin SDK: generate/stream text/object/image/speech/video, embeddings, tool loop, telemetry, UI stream protocol, tool authoring, tool search and evaluation. It does not ship sessions, a durable runtime, RAG, a skill loader for ToolLoopAgent, or an HTTP server. The ecosystem got heavier (@ai-sdk/harness ~16k LOC plus adapters, sandbox, workflow and TUI packages), but those are experimental opt-ins that delegate the runtime to third parties, so the score is unchanged.

No in-repo CHANGELOG.md, but v2 ships an in-repo migration guide (README-v2.md) and GitHub Releases carry explicit breaking-change sections. Cadence is steady: v1.3/v1.4 (May), v2.0 (2026-06-30, module path /v2), then v2.1-v2.5 by 2026-09-30, with a parallel v1 maintenance line, release-please and an apidiff CI guard. Breaking changes still land in minors (v2.5: new events columns needing AutoMigrate, loopback bind default). Raised from 2.

No in-repo CHANGELOG.md; release notes live on GitHub Releases and docs.agno.com/other/v3-changelog, and v3 ships an in-repo V3_MIGRATION_GUIDE. Cadence is high (58 releases since 2026-05-15, 2.6.7 to 3.0.11) and v3.0.0 is a breaking storage release with a mandatory migration. Breaking renames also landed in minors (v2.7.0 MCP surface 19 to 8 tools). Kept at 2: no in-repo changelog and high churn.

No CHANGELOG.md, HISTORY.md or RELEASES.md in the repo; history comes from GitHub Releases (v0.4.0, 2026-07-08) and commit messages. PUBLISH.md documents the release process and v0.4.0 added a version-consistency release gate. Cadence slowed after v0.3.7 (Mar) and the last commit is 2026-08-26. v0.4.0 breaking changes (new Task field, Environment::run signature) appear only in release notes.

CHANGELOG.md is maintained per release with PR numbers and mirrored by GitHub Releases (0.2.82 to 0.2.163 since May, 80 releases, most of them bundled-CLI bumps). Breaking items are called out, e.g. skill-name validation raising ValueError (0.2.129, CHANGELOG.md:247) and the Message union widening (0.2.137, CHANGELOG.md:188). Recent themes: run lifecycle with background tasks (0.2.160), SessionStore resume, argv-injection hardening and verbatim_prompts.

Maintained CHANGELOG.md plus one GitHub Release per version; it grew by 787 lines between 0.3.143 and 0.3.286 and lists breaking or behaviour-changing entries (0.3.286 permissionMode default CHANGELOG.md:10, 0.3.217 sub-agent nesting cap, 0.3.162 Bash find/grep). The ./assistant export was removed in 0.3.181 without a changelog entry. Repo commits in the window are almost all changelog updates plus CI hardening. SessionStore is still @alpha.

docs/edge/en/changelog.mdx is the canonical in-repo changelog (mirrored to GitHub Releases) with line-level entries per version. Cadence moved from nightly alphas to roughly weekly stable patches (1.14.5 to 1.15.23); churn shifted from renaming core runtime pieces (CrewAgentExecutor deprecated in 1.14.5) to additive platform surface, and conversational flows went stable in 1.15.18. Still pin an exact version before bumping.

No in-repo CHANGELOG.md; releases are documented on the CloudWeGo docs site (migration pages now include v0.9) and as auto-generated GitHub Releases. v0.8.13 to v0.9.21 (126 commits, 22 patch tags) added AgenticMessage, cancel, TurnLoop and failover, and marked agent transfer and workflow agents NOT RECOMMENDED. Still pre-v1 with a v0.10 alpha branch; pin minor versions, and checkpoint compatibility relies on explicit gob shims.

No in-repo Go CHANGELOG; GitHub Releases (go/vX.Y.Z) are detailed and include 'Before you upgrade' sections. The Go SDK has been 1.x since go/v1.0.0 (the May note of pre-1.0 was wrong) and shipped v1.9 to v1.13.1 in four months, including a retracted v1.13.0. Behaviour changes: default MaxTurns 5 to 50 and partial responses on failure; untyped Define* functions are deprecated and the agents API is experimental.

No in-repo CHANGELOG.md for libs/langgraph; release notes are GitHub Releases (auto-generated lists per package tag). New libs/sdk-py/CHANGELOG.md and MIGRATION.md cover the v3 streaming client. 1.2.0 to 1.2.12 in four months added typed interrupt responses, TracePolicy, store tenancy and security fixes; create_react_agent and AgentState stay @deprecated and DeltaChannel is still beta.

A single combined CHANGELOG.md covers all packages. Core releases 0.14.22 (2026-05-14) to 0.14.25 (2026-09-21) are roughly monthly (CHANGELOG.md:55-61, 685-704, 903-921) and no breaking agent-API changes landed. The workflows runtime (separate repo) moved from 2.21 to 2.25 with a timeout behaviour change for long-suspended runs. The most decision-relevant breaking change remains the move to the external workflows package and the deprecation of OpenAIAgent/ReActAgent.from_tools.

Active per-package changesets: packages/core/CHANGELOG.md spans 1.36 to 1.73 in ~21,700 lines (~15 stable core minors in 7 weeks). Breaking items are called out, e.g. @mastra/mcp 2.0 dropping the standalone HTTP+SSE transport and AgentController renames; 1.73.0-alpha.0 changes default error processors and 1.51.0 added anonymous telemetry. Very fast-moving runtime/session layer; pin versions and read changesets.

python/CHANGELOG.md follows Keep a Changelog with semver and flags breaking entries (1.6.0 instrumentation on by default, 1.15.0 semconv consolidation); .NET changes are only in GitHub Release notes. Python shipped 1.5 to 1.19 (roughly weekly) and .NET 1.7 to 1.23 since May, backed by 40+ ADRs. Durable Task / Azure Functions moved to a separate repo in 1.14.0, and the .NET AgentSessionStore promotion was marked [PREVIEW BREAKING].

Documented in-repo at docs/release.md (breaking changes per minor, with line refs) and GitHub Releases. 0.17.2 to 0.22.3 in ~4 months (22 releases): 0.21.0 requires openai v3 and HTTPX2, 0.22.0 tightened failure handling and data isolation, 0.20.0 changed the default model; the RunState schema went from 1.10 to 1.18. Cadence is roughly one minor every 2-3 weeks; pin a minor and read release.md.

Per-package CHANGELOGs with commit refs (packages/agents-core/CHANGELOG.md). 0.11.4 to 0.18.0 in ~16 weeks: 0.15.0 default model gpt-5.6-luna and MCP 2026-07-28 negotiation, 0.16.0 testing utilities and Standard Schema, 0.17.x replay-safety fixes; the sandbox beta label was removed on main. A high volume of preserve/redact/fail-closed fixes shows the serialized RunState contract is still hardening. No dedicated breaking-changes doc.

docs/changelog.md and docs/migration.md track releases (v2.52.0, near-daily cadence). V2 breaking changes are listed in docs/changelog.md:97-238 (behaviour kwargs moved to capabilities, MCP classes collapsed, end_strategy default changed, pydantic_graph.persistence removed). Two GHSA advisories were fixed in the window and Harness joined the monorepo on 2026-09-26. Recurring renames, though V1 message history still deserializes.

In-repo CHANGELOG.md (0.38 at :791-828, 0.43 at :11-147) plus a long MIGRATING.md with per-release notes. Seven releases in ~4 months (0.37.0 to 0.43.0, 2026-09-30), every one breaking; 0.43 warns persisted 0.42 histories and runs may not load (MIGRATING.md:1344-1351). The evals and pipeline modules were removed. Documentation quality is high, but the churn and single-maintainer concentration (82% of commits) are signals.

No CHANGELOG.md; release notes live on GitHub Releases and the docs changelog. Weekly minors from v1.41 to v1.57.1, plus the move to the harness-sdk monorepo (sdk-python archived). Deprecations noted in code: experimental.bidi alias, bash tool replaced by shell, cache_tools replaced by CacheConfig.tools_ttl, most of strands-agents-tools. Several README doc links moved and now 404.

Still no cancel endpoint and no run ID. The SSE handler runs on `req.Context()`, so closing the connection cancels the run; v2 fixed event-loop handling after cancel and propagates cancellation into workflow nodes. `/run_live` accepts `{"close": true}`. Cross-pod cancel is BYO.

`POST /agents/{id}/runs/{run_id}/cancel` sets a flag checked at loop checkpoints; with a Redis-backed `QueueConfig` it works from any replica, and queued jobs are cancellable while pending. Cancelled runs persist a `cancellation_stage` (v3.0.11). Same route exists for teams and workflows.

No HTTP API. In-process you can drop the run's future/stream; for actor runtimes `Environment::shutdown()` or the new `shutdown_with_timeout()` stop the whole runtime, not one task. `Environment::run()` no longer returns a `JoinHandle`, and there is no per-task cancellation token.

Library-only. `ClaudeSDKClient.interrupt()` is the in-process primitive (result `terminal_reason` is `aborted_streaming` or `aborted_tools`; SDK MCP tools are cancelled on mcp 2.x), and `stop_task(task_id)` stops one sub-agent task. Mapping it to a DELETE endpoint is BYO.
Library-only. `Query.interrupt()` (returns a receipt, optional `cancel_queued`), `Query.close()` and `AbortController` are in-process primitives; the DELETE endpoint is yours to build.

No `cancel()` on `Crew`, `Agent` or `Flow`, and AMP has no documented cancel endpoint (not re-verified). A hook raising `HookAborted` gives cooperative cancellation at the next model, tool or step boundary, but the flag and any HTTP route are BYO.

No HTTP route, but a first-class in-process cancel API: `adk.WithCancel()` returns an `AgentCancelFunc` with modes (immediate, after chat model, after tool calls), timeout escalation and a resumable checkpoint. You expose it behind your own DELETE handler.

Experimental agent routes add `POST /agents/{name}/abort` for detached runs: the snapshot flips to `aborting`, the worker cancels and an `aborted` snapshot is committed. Synchronous turns cancel on disconnect and also commit an aborted snapshot. Capped at 4: needs `detach` plus a snapshot store, and durable flow streams run on a detached context with no cancel endpoint.

`POST /threads/{tid}/runs/{rid}/cancel?action=interrupt|rollback&wait=0|1`: interrupt halts and persists, rollback discards and reverts state. Disconnecting does not cancel unless `on_disconnect: cancel` is set. The v3 client has no cancel command, so cancel still uses the v2 endpoint. Endpoint behaviour is evidenced by the SDK, not by server source.
`WorkflowHandler.cancel_run()` is in-process. The AG-UI router has no cancel endpoint (it only calls `cancel_run()` when the stream errors); HTTP wiring is BYO.

New explicit `POST /agents/:agentId/threads/abort` (with optional `expectedRunId`) aborts the active run on a thread behind thread-access and permission checks; dropping the SSE connection also cancels via the request `AbortSignal`, and `/threads/signals/cancel` cancels queued input. Capped below 5 because cancellation is per thread rather than per run ID, and runs without memory rely on connection close.

DevUI ships `POST /v1/responses/{id}/cancel` with auto-cancel on disconnect, and the .NET `Hosting.OpenAI` package adds `POST /{agent}/v1/responses/{responseId}/cancel` plus GET and DELETE, mirroring the OpenAI Responses API. AG-UI Python has detached runs with timeouts. Capped at 4 because the evidence is DevUI (beta, not for production) and a .NET package with experimental pieces.
Library-only. `RunResultStreaming.cancel(mode="immediate"|"after_turn")` exists in-process; the cancel endpoint and disconnect-to-cancel plumbing are yours to design.

Library-only. `options.signal: AbortSignal` aborts the model call and, since 0.14.0, propagates to function tools and MCP requests; you wire `request.signal` into it yourself. No DELETE/cancel endpoint.

First-party `CancellationToken` passed to `adapter.run_stream(...)`: you expose your own cancel route that calls `token.cancel()`, the adapter emits a Vercel `abort` chunk and `on_cancel` receives the partial messages. A plain client disconnect tears the run down without an abort chunk. No shipped cancel endpoint, and multi-worker routing is yours, so this stays at 3.
Library-only. `AbortHandle`/`Abortable` exists in-process; no HTTP cancel endpoint is shipped.

Over A2A, `tasks/cancel` transitions the task and calls the agent's cooperative cancel (`executor.py:547`), and invocations accept a `cancel_signal`. This works only on the A2A surface (agent-to-agent, in-memory task state, no auth); a chat endpoint such as `DELETE /runs/{id}` is yours to build.

`agent.cancel()`, `InvokeOptions.cancelSignal` and tool-level `cancelSignal` are the in-process primitives (in-flight Bedrock/OpenAI/MCP calls abort). The A2A server does not support cancel: `cancelTask` throws unsupported. The recommended DELETE shape is described but not shipped.

BYO patterns: same-server `chat.stop()` maps to `request.signal` into `streamText({ abortSignal })` (abort reasons now reach tools); multi-server uses an example `DELETE /api/chat/:id/stream` writing `canceledAt` to a DB. `HarnessAgent` sessions add `stop()`/`detach()`. No shipped framework endpoint.

`GET .../sessions/{session_id}` returns persisted events for client-side rendering; no `Last-Event-ID` or server-side stream replay. Resumption is implicit: call `/run_sse` again with the same `sessionId`, and workflow-based HITL pauses are rebuilt from session history. No dedicated `/resume` or `/replay` route.

`POST /agents/{id}/runs/{run_id}/resume` takes `last_event_index`, replays missed events from the in-memory or Redis stream (falling back to stored events), then continues live. `GET` run and session-run routes return persisted output, and checkpoint routes list run boundaries. External-framework agents run inline and are not resumable.
No HTTP API; no resume primitive even in-process.
`ClaudeAgentOptions.resume=<session_id>` is a parameter, not an endpoint. HTTP exposure is BYO.
`query({ options: { resume: sessionId } })` is the in-process logic, including `resumeSessionAt: messageUuid`. The endpoint is BYO.

OSS: in-process only. Conversational Flows restore session state via `handle_turn(session_id=...)`, and `Crew.from_checkpoint`/`flow.resume` continue runs, but you wire your own `/sessions/:id/resume` and keep your own event log. AMP: re-kickoff via API.
`Runner.Resume(ctx, checkPointID)` and `TurnLoop` resume from a checkpoint ID exist at the Go level; no HTTP wrapper ships and the event stream itself is not persisted, so replay needs your own log.

Experimental agent routes reopen a session via `init.sessionId` or a specific `init.snapshotId`, with `getSnapshot` and `waitForSnapshot` companions for detached runs. Durable streaming (experimental) replays buffered chunks to a client that reconnects with `X-Genkit-Stream-Id`; in-memory and Firestore `StreamManager`s ship. Capped at 4: agents and durable streaming are experimental, and event replay of a past turn is not provided (you get the snapshot).

v2: `GET /threads/{tid}/runs/{rid}/stream` with `Last-Event-ID` re-attaches (needs `stream_resumable: true`). v3: the client resubscribes with a `since` sequence cursor and dedupes by `event_id`, on explicit reattach and automatic reconnect. State endpoints (`/state`, `/state/{checkpoint_id}`) round it out.
Pattern is to serialize `Context` keyed by `session_id`. The AG-UI router is stateless per request (the client resends full messages and state), and no replay endpoint ships in this repo.

`POST /agents/:id/observe` (`runId`, `offset`) re-attaches and replays from an index; `POST /agents/:id/threads/subscribe` streams a thread's runs, optionally with stored history first. `GET /agents/:id/suspended-runs`, `resume-stream` and `recover` (orphaned durable runs) cover suspended and interrupted work. The observe route changed from `GET .../observe-stream`.

DevUI and the .NET endpoints reuse a `conversation` ID or `previous_response_id`; `GET /v1/conversations/{id}/items` and `GET .../responses/{id}` fetch stored history. AG-UI has opt-in thread snapshot hydration and interrupt/resume metadata. No dedicated resume endpoint or stream replay.
`RunState.to_state().to_json()` / `RunState.from_json` are the primitives; you build the `/runs/{id}/resume` endpoint.
`RunState.toString()` / `RunState.fromString` exist; no endpoint shipped.

No resume endpoint: Vercel AI and AG-UI clients send full history each request, and server-authoritative history needs your own persistence by `conversation_id` passed as `message_history`. No server-side event replay buffer for reconnecting to an in-flight stream.
Resume via `ConversationMemory` is in-process only; no HTTP surface.

No resume endpoint. Rebuilding the agent with the same `session_id` restores a conversation, and `idempotency_token` lets a retried request attach to the in-flight invocation (in-process). No event replay buffer.
`SessionManager.restoreSnapshot` and `agent.invoke([interruptResponseBlock])` are in-process; endpoint is BYO.

Resumable streams come from the third-party `resumable-stream` package plus Redis in an example (not part of `ai`); `WorkflowChatTransport` provides resumable streaming for `WorkflowAgent`. `HarnessAgent` reopens via `createSession({ sessionId, resumeFrom })` with no replay of past UI events.

Approvals reuse `/run_sse` with a `functionResponse` carrying the same call `id` (`adk_request_confirmation` for tool confirmation, `adk_request_input` with a response schema for v2 workflow nodes). The runner routes the reply to the agent that asked, and v2 added fixes that reject conflicting or non-agent-authored confirmations. No separate approval endpoint and no run-status endpoint: the pause is visible only via event content and `longRunningToolIds`.

Tools with `requires_confirmation`, `requires_user_input` or `external_execution` emit `RunPaused` and set the run to `PAUSED`; `POST /agents/{id}/runs/{rid}/continue` (also accepts `input`, `fork`, `regenerate`) resumes it. A separate `/approvals` admin namespace persists approval rows that operators resolve over HTTP. Pause state is readable from the stream, the run row and the approval status route.
Only `HookOutcome::Abort` skips a tool call. No pause/wait-for-approval state, no persistence/resume primitive. HTTP surfacing is fully BYO.

`can_use_tool` is an intra-process callback (now also usable with `query()` since 0.2.140); cross-request HITL requires keeping the `ClaudeSDKClient` and its CLI subprocess alive across the user's round trip. A `PreToolUse` hook returning `defer` ends the turn with `deferred_tool_use` set, which does not pin a subprocess. No HTTP endpoint ships.

`canUseTool` is the in-process primitive and can be answered out of band by returning `null` after sending the `control_response`. Pause state is now observable on the stream via `session_state_changed: requires_action` and `pending_permission_requests` (opt-in), but no endpoint ships.

Flow-level `@human_feedback` with async `HumanFeedbackProvider` raising `HumanFeedbackPending` is the production pattern — auto-persists state and returns. Tool-level and task-level helpers are console-only (sync, not API-friendly). HTTP wiring is yours; AMP ships a Flow HITL UI.

`adk.Interrupt`/`StatefulInterrupt` plus `ResumeWithParams` work in-process with checkpoints. No HTTP route; the pause is visible only through the interrupt event your serializer emits (or the `eino:interrupted` meta chunk in the ACP bridge).

Experimental agent route: the turn ends with `finishReason: interrupted`, the pending request is observable via `getSnapshot`, and the client resumes on the same route with `data.resume` (respond/restart). The runtime validates each entry against a tool request the model really issued, which blocks injected tool executions. On the stable flow path the HTTP payload is still yours to design. Capped at 4 as the agent API is experimental and there is no dedicated approval endpoint.

`POST /threads/{tid}/runs/stream` with `command: {resume: ...}` (or per-interrupt map) resumes paused threads; state can be edited first via `POST /state`. v3 uses an `input.requested` event and an `input.respond` command, and `interrupt(value, response_schema=...)` exposes and validates the expected answer shape. Pause state is observable via `StateSnapshot.interrupts`.

In core, `Context.wait_for_event(HumanResponseEvent)` is first-class in-process and the host must route the verdict to `ctx.send_event`. The only HTTP shape in the repo is the AG-UI router, where approvals are frontend tools: the run ends after the tool call and the client sends the result in the next `POST /run`. No pause status, server-side persistence or approval endpoint, and a 0.x satellite package.

Dedicated `POST /agents/:id/approve-tool-call` and `decline-tool-call` (decline takes an optional `reason`), each returning a new SSE stream, plus `send-tool-approval` for a client that does not own the stream and `resume-stream` for generic suspend/resume. Pause state is discoverable via `GET /suspended-runs`. The `tool-call-resumed` chunk is from 1.73.0-alpha.1.

Tools with `approval_mode=always_require` emit `function_approval_request`; the client returns a `function_approval_response` on the same conversation. The framework accepts only responses that match a request it recorded, and DevUI rebuilds the call from server-stored data. DevUI surfaces requested/responded SSE events and AG-UI uses `RUN_FINISHED` interrupts; resume uses the same endpoint rather than a dedicated approval route.

`function_tool(needs_approval=True)` and `RunState.approve/reject` are in-process primitives, and docs now prescribe a server-side pattern (authenticate the reviewer, authorize each pending call, accept only decision IDs, consume atomically); the example is explicitly not a deployable service. The wire format and endpoint are yours.

`RunToolApprovalItem` interruptions come back from a run (and stream as `tool_approval_requested`); `state.approve/reject` resumes, and approvals are now bound to the canonical invocation and input. The HTTP shape is yours, e.g. the Next.js example's `decisions` payload on the same POST.

Deferred tools are first-class in core (`requires_approval`, `ApprovalRequired`, `DeferredToolRequests`). The Vercel adapter (SDK UI v6+) streams `tool-approval-request` chunks and accepts `approval-responded` tool parts; AG-UI carries interrupts. Approval responses are trusted from the request by design, so binding them to server state is yours, which keeps this at 3.

No HTTP surface. In-process patterns ship as examples: an async `on_dispatch` hook can await an approval inline, and a serialized `AgentRun` can be resumed for durable approval. The pause is not observable to an HTTP client unless you expose it.

Interrupts are first-class in the loop (`stop_reason=interrupt`), and over A2A the executor publishes an `input_required` status listing pending interrupts and resumes from an `interruptResponse` DataPart. This covers only the A2A surface, with no auth boundary; for chat HTTP the approval endpoint is BYO.

`context.interrupt` and `InterruptError` are first-class in the SDK, resumed via `agent.invoke([interruptResponseContent])`, and the vended `HumanInTheLoop` handler maps onto an HTTP pause/approve/resume flow. The TS A2A server has no interrupt handling (Python only), so HTTP wiring is BYO.

Server emits `tool-approval-request` chunks and the client re-POSTs messages with `addToolApprovalResponse`; the next call re-validates approvals server-side (HMAC signature when a secret is set, input schema, policy) so a client cannot forge a pre-approved call. No separate endpoint; the pause is observable client-side as `approval-requested`.

SSE frames are `models.Event` JSON: text deltas (`partial: true`), partial tool arguments (`partialArgs`/`willContinue` forwarded from the stream aggregator) and complete tool-call/tool-result, state-delta, transfer and workflow-output events. Partial args only appear for backends that stream them (Vertex; the genai SDK marks them unsupported on the Gemini API). No explicit start/end lifecycle frames.

Named SSE events with `event_index`: `RunContent` deltas, `ReasoningContentDelta`, `ToolCallStarted/Completed/Error`, model-request and hook events, linked by `tool_call_id`. Partial tool arguments are not streamed: `ToolCallStarted` carries the complete args once the provider finishes the call, which keeps this at 4.
No HTTP API. In-process `StreamChunk::ToolUseInputDelta`, text chunks, and lifecycle events do exist and would form a complete stream once you serialize them yourself.
No HTTP API. In-process all three dimensions are available (`include_partial_messages` for token deltas + `input_json_delta`, plus `Message` lifecycle frames).
No HTTP API. `includePartialMessages: true` exposes `SDKPartialAssistantMessage` with text + tool-arg `input_json_delta` + lifecycle in-process, but you serialize the wire format.

OSS ships no HTTP stream. In-process `StreamFrame`/`StreamChunk` carry text deltas, incremental tool-call arguments and tool lifecycle frames, but SSE serialization is yours (or the third-party AG-UI bridge). AMP webhook events carry stream chunks, but delivery is not a live stream unless `realtime=true`.
No HTTP API. Tool-call deltas come through model chunks with `ToolCalls.Index` for merging — but no separate tool-arg-fragment event type and no wire framing ships.

SSE frames are `{message: chunk}` with text deltas; `ToolRequest.Partial` carries partial JSON args (provider-dependent, Gemini supported); tool results arrive as `role: tool` chunks linked by `Ref`. Experimental agents add `artifact`, `customPatch` and `turnEnd` frames. No dedicated tool-input start/delta/end sub-taxonomy.

`messages/partial` carries `AIMessageChunk.tool_call_chunks` (partial tool args) and text deltas, alongside `values`/`updates`/`checkpoints`/`tasks`/`metadata`/`end` events, all linked by `tool_call_id`. v3 exposes typed projections (messages, tool_calls, subgraphs), and sub-agent lifecycle events link back to the spawning tool call.

The AG-UI router (0.x satellite package) streams per-token `TextMessageChunk`, run start/finish frames and state/messages snapshots, with `toolCallId` linkage. Tool calls arrive as one chunk with complete JSON args after the LLM turn, so partial tool arguments are not streamed. Core agents expose `AgentStream` deltas in-process, but wire framing there is BYO.

SSE forwards `fullStream` chunks as `data:` JSON: `tool-call-input-streaming-start`, `tool-call-delta` (`argsTextDelta`), `tool-call-input-streaming-end`, text deltas and lifecycle chunks (`tool-call`, `tool-result`, `tool-output`, `tool-error`, approval/suspend/resume). All three dimensions stream with `toolCallId` linkage.

DevUI/.NET emit OpenAI-Responses-compatible SSE including `response.output_text.delta` and `response.function_call_arguments.delta` plus output-item and lifecycle events. AG-UI emits `TOOL_CALL_START/ARGS/END`, step and text events. Linkage is by `call_id`/`item_id` (Responses) or `toolCallId` (AG-UI).
No HTTP API. In-process the Responses API emits `response.function_call_arguments.delta` via `RawResponsesStreamEvent` plus `RunItemStreamEvent` lifecycle.
No HTTP API. `RunRawModelStreamEvent` exposes provider events but the SDK doesn't normalize into a typed tool-call-delta. Wire format is yours.

Vercel adapter SSE frames cover `start`, `text-delta`, `tool-input-start`/`tool-input-delta`/`tool-input-available`, `tool-output-available`, data chunks and `finish`, with `toolCallId` linkage; partial args come from `ToolCallPartDelta.args_delta`. Delivered through the adapter with your own route, so kept at 4 against Vercel AI SDK's 5.
No HTTP API. In-process `StreamEvent::Text` deltas and tool/lifecycle items exist, but partial tool-argument streaming was removed in 0.43 (tool calls stream whole); serialization is yours.
No first-party chat HTTP. In-process `ToolUseStreamEvent` carries partial tool args and the stream yields message and lifecycle events; wire framing is yours.
No first-party chat HTTP. `ModelStreamUpdateEvent` carries `toolUseInputDelta` partial JSON in-process; you serialize.

UI Message Stream Protocol v2 ships explicit `tool-input-start`, `tool-input-delta` (`inputTextDelta`), `tool-input-available` plus `text-delta`, `start`/`start-step`/`finish-step`/`finish` lifecycle. `useChat` automatically transitions `ToolUIPart.state` from `input-streaming` to `input-available`. All three dimensions stream with explicit `toolCallId` linkage.

Since v2.4/v2.5 `adkrest.ServerConfig` takes an `Authenticator` (`authn.NewHeader`, `NewIdentityAwareProxy`, `NewGoogleOIDC`, `NewCustom`) that guards every route except `/health` and `/version`, and an `Authorizer`; `authz.NewStrict()` requires the caller to equal the request `userId` across runtime, sessions and artifacts. Claims such as a tenant ID can be read from `authn.Caller` in tools. Gaps: defaults are open (Noop), and there is no tenant-, app- or resource-level authorization or RBAC (`appName` is not checked).

A single `AuthMiddleware` terminates JWT (JWKS/verification keys) or service-account PATs across REST, MCP and WebSocket.
