RBAC scopes `agent-os:<os>:<type>:<id>:<action>` are enforced per route, and `user_isolation=True` (v3.0.0) scopes sessions, memories, knowledge and more per JWT `sub`; `dependencies_claims` copies claims such as tenant into run dependencies. Pluggable authorization (managed roles, OpenFGA) and audit sinks exist only on `main` (unreleased at analysis time) and are not counted. No built-in tenant model.
No HTTP API; auth is fully BYO.
SDK is unaware of HTTP; auth is your concern.
SDK does not validate JWTs, OAuth, or anything else. Auth termination is in your HTTP handler; tenant context is passed via `cwd`/`env`/closure-captured hooks.
OSS: BYO. AMP supports a bearer token per automation and webhook callbacks can carry their own auth. No tenant-aware RBAC at the HTTP boundary.
No HTTP API; auth is host responsibility.

Not terminated by the framework: a `ContextProvider` maps headers to `ActionContext` and can reject, and a Firebase auth provider ships. No tenant model or RBAC, and for agent sessions the snapshot-path prefix is the only scoping (`getSnapshot`/`abort` are otherwise unscoped by snapshot ID). Stdlib middleware covers the rest.

`@auth.authenticate` runs on every request and `@auth.on.*` handlers apply per-resource filters (threads, runs, assistants, crons, store), so auth is terminated at the API boundary and identity reaches nodes via runtime context. `actions=` on resource decorators is now enforced, but unmatched paths are allowed by default, so a global default-deny handler is recommended. The server is source-available (ELv2) and not in this repo.
Not provided: neither core nor the AG-UI router terminates auth or extracts tenant identity (`POST /run` has no tenant header handling). Add FastAPI dependencies yourself.

`coreAuthMiddleware` terminates auth on `/api/*` (JWT, cookies, API keys) with provider integrations (Auth0, Clerk, WorkOS, Supabase, Firebase, Better-Auth, Okta, Google, Neon, Studio). Routes declare `requiresPermission` for RBAC, FGA (enterprise) checks agent execution and thread ownership, and a middleware-set resource ID wins over the client-supplied one for tenant scoping. `/health` is registered before auth.

On .NET, `UseClaimsBasedAgentIsolation` derives an isolation key from the authenticated claims and partitions Responses/Conversations storage, sessions and A2A tasks by it (strict when a provider is registered); authentication itself is the ASP.NET Core pipeline. AG-UI Python offers FastAPI `dependencies=` and a `snapshot_scope_resolver` for stored threads. DevUI has bearer-token auth only, the Python hosting helpers have none, and JWT validation and route-level authorization are BYO.
SDK consumes validated identity via `RunContextWrapper.context`; HTTP-layer JWT/Okta/API-key validation is yours.
Auth in your host middleware before calling `run()`.

Docs explicitly say "Treat the adapter endpoint as an internal backend service, running it inside your own authenticated route handler." Auth is the route's job — typical pattern is a FastAPI dependency validating JWT and building `TenantDeps` passed via `agent.run(..., deps=...)`.
No JWT validation, no tenant scoping at the network boundary.

Verified in source (strands-py/src/strands/multiagent/a2a/server.py:32-141, executor.py:154-155): `A2AServer` takes no user, auth or context builder, so the TypeScript `userBuilder` has no Python counterpart; `to_starlette_app(app_kwargs=...)` and `to_fastapi_app` only forward constructor kwargs to the ASGI app. The executor warns that `context_id` is not an authentication boundary and multi-tenant deployments must authenticate at the transport or gateway. After your layer authenticates, identity goes into `invocation_state`, where Cedar interventions can enforce per-tool authorization. Score stays 0 (1 to 0 was applied in the refresh).
`A2AExpressServerConfig.userBuilder` integrates with `@a2a-js/sdk` for per-request user auth on the A2A path. Browser-chat auth is BYO middleware.

Not terminated by the SDK: your framework validates JWTs and derives tenant identity before the agent runs, and there is no route, thread or resource authorization. v7 redacts server error details from UI streams by default, and `@ai-sdk/policy-opa` can enforce per-tool authorization at tool dispatch only.

Runner is stateless per call; storage layer enforces isolation via one GORM transaction per applyEvent plus a stale-session optimistic-concurrency check (session/database/service.go:410-492). Local sessions use a sync.RWMutex and, since v2.4, Events() snapshots under the read lock. Agent mode is now resolved per invocation rather than mutating the shared agent (internal/llminternal/mode.go:19-25). Strong single-writer-per-session guarantees, but parallel turns on one session ID fail the second append. Live bidi sessions are pod-local and need sticky routing.

Each run()/arun() builds its own RunContext and reads/writes its AgentSession by session_id through BaseDb; the shared Agent instance is not mutated per call (v3.0.2 stopped writing session metadata back onto it). AgentOS(user_isolation=True, released in v3.0.0) scopes sessions, memories, metrics, schedules, knowledge and traces per user_id, with the JWT sub forced as user_id (os/app.py:377-378). AgentFactory + TrustedContext can build the agent per request from verified claims. Isolation holes found and fixed in this window (tool-result cache keys v2.9.0, SQLite bulk upsert owner check v3.0.8) show active hardening. Still user-level, not tenant-level (no tenant_id, issue #9831); lands at the same level as Mastra and Pydantic AI for per-call isolation plus enforced identity scoping.

Each BaseAgent owns its own Arc<Mutex<MemoryProvider>> (base.rs:65), so spawning one agent per session isolates naturally. There is no first-class Session concept: sharing one agent across sessions leaks memory, because no per-call isolation exists. v0.4.0 added Task::app_meta (could carry a session_id) but the runtime never reads it. No tenant-scoped primitives.

Each ClaudeSDKClient/query() spawns its own claude CLI subprocess with its own cwd, env, JSONL transcript, and MCP connections. State cannot bleed across subprocesses except via shared filesystem or your shared SessionStore. Concurrent @tool handlers in the same Python process share closures/globals — engineer must avoid module-level mutable state.

Spawning one subprocess per (tenant, session) is the only safe model — sharing a subprocess across tenants bleeds cwd, MCP servers, settings, JSONL targets. The SDK does not enforce isolation; the host is responsible. Open issue #122 documents an in-process MCP host race when multiple query() calls share an SDK MCP server name — a real concurrency hazard with workaround (unique names).

Better than in May. Event-bus runtime state is now scoped per outermost kickoff in ContextVars (events/event_bus.py:84-90, 1.14.7), each run has an execution UUID, and contextvars.copy_context() carries request-scoped values into threaded tools, MCP and guardrails. Gaps remain: hooks (@on, @CrewBase) still register on process-wide lists (hooks/dispatch.py:97-121, project/crew_base.py:599-616), event-bus listeners see every crew's events, and the per-execution scoped_hooks() registry is not wired into any entrypoint. So a hook for tenant A can still fire for tenant B unless you wrap kickoff yourself. Moved from 2 to 3: per-run isolation is now real, hook/listener scoping remains host-built.

ctxWithNewTypedRunCtx (adk/runctx.go:537-558) seeds a fresh runContext per Runner.Run call and lives in context.Context. runSession mutexes guard internal maps; parallel sub-agents fork ctx via forkRunCtx and rejoin via joinRunCtxs, and cancel scopes are per run. Risk remains for closures that capture singletons outside runSession.Values; the framework does not enforce that (v0.9 fixed one internal race of this kind). TurnLoop is per-session but the host still tracks N loops itself.

Each request has its own context.Context; the registry is shared but concurrency-safe, and middleware-contributed tools go into a child registry per Generate call (go/ai/generate.go:467-512). Agent turns deep-copy inputs at the framework boundary, and middleware config is copied per JSON-dispatched call (v1.13 fix #6092, previously one call's fields could leak into the next). Session state lives in your session store; WithSnapshotPathPrefix gives store-level tenant partitioning (experimental), otherwise all sessions share one global prefix. Standard Go isolation, no enforced tenant boundary.

OSS: each PregelLoop is a fresh Python instance per run; state is checkpointer-keyed on thread_id. BaseStore namespaces are tenant-scoped by convention but not enforced; before checkpoint-postgres/sqlite 3.1.1 a prefix search on ("acme",) also returned ("acmecorp",) rows (LIKE without separator), fixed at this commit. Platform adds the @auth.on.* filter chain enforcing resource scoping at the data layer, raising isolation to first-class for the hosted product.

Each workflow.run() creates a new Context (unless ctx=existing_ctx is passed to resume), and Context.store is a per-context KV with no global sharing. A cross-run bleed was fixed: agent initial_state was shallow-copied or not copied at all, so a tool mutating nested state polluted every later run on the same agent instance; both agent paths now deepcopy it (base_agent.py:302-303, multi_agent_workflow.py:287-288). Tools with closures and LLM clients on the agent object are still shared across runs. No tenant primitives beyond per-Context isolation.

RequestContext and MessageList are per-call inside loop(); sub-agents get a derived copy without identity keys (agent.ts:5362-5373). Persistence is per-thread via SaveQueueManager keyed on threadId (agent/save-queue/index.ts:30-47). Reserved request-context keys (MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY, MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY) are server-authoritative: mergeBodyRequestContext never overwrites keys the server set, and thread access is checked with enforceThreadAccess (server/handlers/utils.ts:70-81, :157), so clients cannot spoof tenant identity at the HTTP layer. AgentController sessions (experimental) own their own event bus. A first-class tenant-isolation primitive most peers lack.

Sessions hold mutable state (session_id, service_session_id, a state bag); SessionStore.get returns independent copies so concurrent continuations cannot mutate each other's snapshot, but AgentState provides no locking and the README makes the app responsible for single-writer advancement. Agents are singletons by default. .NET adds an experimental IsolationKeyScopedAgentSessionStore that partitions every session key by the current AgentIsolationKeyProvider and throws in strict mode when no key is available; OpenAI hosting and A2A task storage use it too. Python has no equivalent tenant primitive, and the stores and Python hosting packages are experimental/alpha, so the score stays at 4.

Session protocol binds one session_id per instance; SQLiteSession scopes every row by session_id. RunContextWrapper is a fresh dataclass per Runner.run (run.py:669); approvals and tool-invocation records are per-wrapper (run_context.py:193-198). Since 0.18-0.20 the SDK snapshots the agent tool list per run and raises UserError if a hook replaces agent.tools on a shared agent, but in-place mutation of shared tool objects is not isolated (lifecycle.py:40-47). Cross-session bleed is impossible inside the SDK unless you share mutable TContext or shared agent/tool objects.

Each run() constructs a fresh RunState wrapping a fresh or caller-supplied RunContext (run.ts:1262-1273). RunContext carries app context by reference, so you decide what is shared; approvals and usage are shared with forked nested contexts (runContext.ts:256-268). Recent releases isolated SDK-owned data (detached interruption snapshots, private MCP tool caches). OpenAIHostedMultiAgentModel supports only one active run per instance and must not be shared across concurrent requests. Isolation is otherwise trivially correct if you do not share mutable objects.

Fresh RunContext per run() (deps, usage, metadata, run_id, conversation_id, workspace) plus a ContextVar _CURRENT_RUN_CONTEXT (_run_context.py:938, :955) so concurrent runs in one process do not bleed; toolsets and capabilities get per-run instances via for_run, and Harness Memory.for_run resolves the tenant namespace once per run. The refreshed report documents a bleed risk: a shared MCPToolset holds one MCP session for all concurrent runs, so per-request credentials leak across runs unless you build the toolset per run (docs/mcp/client.md:487-489). Moved from 5 to 4 on that documented caveat (see changes.md); otherwise the strongest per-call isolation in the Python peer group.

Run state is per-run: each AgentRunner builds its own AgentRun, HookContext and ToolContext clone, and overrides never mutate the source agent (rig-agent runner.rs:54-75, hook.rs:124-160); a test pins that concurrent runs on one agent are independent. The shared surface is the ToolServerHandle (Arc<RwLock>): add_tool/remove_tool affect every user of the handle, though each turn uses a catalog snapshot. Conversation-memory isolation lives in your ConversationMemory backend keyed by ConversationId, and hooks are shared objects (per-run state belongs in HookContext::scratchpad).

Agent.stream_async holds a lock that raises ConcurrencyException if two invocations enter the same instance (agent/agent.py:1378-1383, agent/_concurrency.py). Each Agent owns its own messages, state, registries, hooks, interrupt state, metrics and sandbox, so isolation is by construction. Caveats: ConcurrentInvocationMode.UNSAFE_REENTRANT skips the lock, shared plugin instances must keep per-agent data in agent.state (the Cedar handler warns about leaking rate-limit counts), and invocation_state is shared by reference with hooks and tools.

acquireLock() throws ConcurrentInvocationError if invoke() is called while another invocation is in flight (agent.ts:854-861); agent.isInvoking lets a host check. Each Agent instance owns its messages, appState, modelState, registries and interrupt state, so multi-tenant fan-out must use a per-request new Agent(); sharing across tenants is unsafe by design. The experimental A2A agentFactory mode builds one agent plus one AsyncLock per contextId, but contextId is documented as not an authentication boundary and direct tool calls can still hit the same instance state.

ToolLoopAgent has no in-process session bag: each request has its own messages and runtimeContext, so provided those come from the request there is no shared mutable state in ai (telemetry registration is process-wide by design). The new HarnessAgent enforces isolation at the sandbox boundary: one sessionWorkDir per session, one sandbox per chat in the documented pattern, and model credentials kept out of the sandbox via brokering. Resume state may contain bridge tokens and must be treated as sensitive. Isolation is still the request-handler boundary for the core path.

Session state is externalized to the database (session/database) or Vertex Agent Engine (session/vertexai), so N pods share the session pool, and the stale-session check (service.go:424-434) prevents lost updates between racing pods. Workflow HITL pauses survive across pods because pause state is rebuilt from session events on the next turn (runner/run_node.go:179-194), though a crash mid-graph is not resumable. No leader election; live bidi sessions are pod-local and need sticky routing; auth.InMemoryCredentialStore is process-local.

Stateless replicas share one DB, and v3.0.0 added explicit multi-replica machinery: a durable job queue (agno_jobs) with leases, heartbeats and fenced writes so any replica can claim or reclaim a run; optional Redis/Valkey for cross-replica cancel and SSE resume; DB-backed scheduler polling with leader election; and stateless MCP serving so /mcp needs no affinity (job_queue/config.py:56-116). Caveat: a reclaimed run re-executes from the start (max_attempts default 1 fails visibly) rather than resuming from the last checkpoint. Moved from 4 to 5 for released, first-class multi-replica coordination, level with LangGraph.

Runtime is SingleThreadedRuntime (event-loop ownership; single_threaded.rs:70): no leader election, distributed lock, shared store or pod-pool pattern. v0.4.0 only improved in-process lifecycle (run/wait/run_background, shutdown timeout). Horizontal scaling is entirely BYO.

The SessionStore adapter (reference Postgres, Redis and S3 adapters under examples/session_stores/) lets any pod resume a session: store to temp JSONL to --resume, and since 0.2.137 settings.json is copied into the temp config dir so apiKeyHelper auth and hooks survive the hop. Limits: the store is append-only, two pods writing the same session interleave unsafely, there is no leader election or coordinator, and SessionKey.project_key (types.py:1515-1534) is only a sharding/tenant lever. Moved from 2 to 3 for parity with the TypeScript SDK, which has the same store design and was already 3; the refresh also added the cross-pod resume fix.

SessionStore interface (sdk.d.ts:6482, still @alpha) plus Postgres, Redis and S3 reference adapters lets any pod resume any session ID; forkSession and the other session helpers are store-aware. The hosting doc gives two patterns: pin each session to a container by consistent hashing on sessionId, or hybrid resume-from-store, noting a store-resumed run deletes its local copy so the store holds the only durable copy. No leader election, shared coordinator or distributed lock.

Still no shared session store, leader election or queue in OSS, but 1.14.7 added startup-time factories to point flow persistence, memory and knowledge defaults at a shared backend (set_flow_persistence_factory, set_memory_storage_factory, set_knowledge_storage_factory) and a Redis-backed lock store (crewai_core/lock_store.py; REDIS_URL or set_lock_backend). Conversational Flow state is keyed by session_id and restored from flow persistence each turn, so with a shared FlowPersistence any worker can serve the next turn, but there is no locking around concurrent turns on one session and checkpoints support only JSON or SQLite. AMP hosts the runtime for you. Moved from 1 to 2: partial primitives, level with other BYO-store peers.

Stateless Go binary; pods scale trivially. CheckPointStore is the cross-pod seam: point all pods at the same Postgres-backed store and any pod can resume any session (Runner.Resume) or restart a TurnLoop from its CheckpointID. Leader election, session-to-pod affinity and locking are not provided; a TurnLoop is in-memory, so two pods running one for the same CheckpointID would race and you must add optimistic concurrency or advisory locks.

Stateless workers with a shared session store as system of record: any instance can resume a session by sessionId/snapshotId, SaveSnapshot is an atomic read-modify-write contract (go/ai/exp/session.go:150-191), detached turns heartbeat every 30 s and read as expired after 60 s, and Firestore listeners (or directory polling for the file store) let an abort issued on instance A stop a detached turn on instance B. Limits: no leader election, work does not migrate if the worker dies (it expires and must be resumed from the last snapshot), and the agent runtime and stores are experimental (exp/ packages), hence the cap of 4. Moved from 3 to 4 for concrete cross-instance coordination comparable to ADK Go's stale-session check.

OSS: shared PostgresSaver checkpointer with thread_id as partition key — any worker replays from any checkpoint. Platform: closed-source langgraph_api adds a Postgres-backed run queue serializing per-thread work via multitask strategy and re-attachable SSE streams. First-class horizontal scaling at both layers.

In llama-index-core: BYO. Serialize a Context (ctx.to_dict(serializer=JsonSerializer())), stash it in Postgres/Redis, and re-hydrate on the next request from any worker. No leader election or built-in coordination. The separate run-llama/llama-agents repo (llama-agents-server with SQLite or BYO store, llama-agents-dbos coordination backend) provides a control plane; llama_deploy, named in the earlier analysis, is deprecated. Neither is in scope here.

Stateless API workers share storage and pub/sub with no leader election. DurableAgent chunks flow through pub/sub so any replica can serve /observe with an offset, and with recovery.durableAgents: 'auto' (default since 1.68.0) running checkpoints are persisted so recoverActiveRuns() re-drives runs orphaned by a crashed process (durable-agent.ts:3625-3655). Background tasks are fenced by a persisted expiring ownership lease (1.72.0) so two replicas do not run the same task, and suspended HITL state is durable via workflow snapshots. Moved from 4 to 5: crash recovery across processes plus lease fencing is released, not labelled experimental, and matches Agno and LangGraph.

Stateless workers plus a shared store: Cosmos (history provider and checkpoint storage), Redis (keys scoped by provider and session identity since 1.19.0), Valkey, and Azure Blob for .NET sessions; the AgentSessionStore contract is experimental. There is no optimistic concurrency, leader election or sticky routing, so same-session concurrency is the host's problem. The Durable Task / Azure Functions answer cited in May was extracted to the separate microsoft/agent-framework-durable-extension repo (Python 1.14.0), which this refresh did not inspect; scored on in-repo stores only.

Ships session backends (SQLAlchemySession, RedisSession, MongoDBSession, DaprSession, OpenAIConversationsSession and others), all designed for stateless workers plus a shared store; sticky routing is not required if the store is consistent. InputItem.input_id gives exactly-once input tracking across resumes, and there is retry logic for OpenAI-managed conversation locks (run.py:624-626). No leader election or centralized scheduler: the docs require an atomic owner-checked transition when two workers might resume the same RunState (docs/human_in_the_loop.md:204), and hosted multi-agent cannot resume in-flight in another process.

As long as session state lives in an external store (a custom Session backed by Postgres/Redis), any number of pods can serve the same session pool; no leader election, no shared in-process state. RunState.toString()/fromString() serialize a paused run to any KV store, and the schema is versioned (1.21 with 1.0-1.20 still readable, runState.ts:190-214) so pods on adjacent SDK versions can share checkpoints. SessionHistoryTransactionAwareSession provides an idempotency key for retried writes across pods. No Postgres/Redis store ships in-box.

Stateless by default: N workers serve the same Agent and the caller owns message history. Optional shared state by feature: MongoStepStore or your own StepStore (Harness step persistence), PostgresMemoryStore, and RedisSpendStore for cross-process budget counters (Lua-atomic). Cancel-by-id across workers needs your own broker. Durable engines (Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, Restate and others) give per-workflow recovery on any worker. No leader election or shared session pool in-tree.

Rig ships no multi-pod machinery: no shared store, leader election or session routing, and ConversationMemory backends are yours. New in the refresh: AgentRun is Serialize + Deserialize and Agent::resume(run) continues it on any process running the same rig version, re-binding tool names to that process's implementations (completion.rs:636-678, engine.rs:377-390). The classic AgentRunner does not persist automatically, so the host must hand-drive AgentRun (examples/agent_with_durable_approval). Moved from 1 to 2: a real cross-process resume primitive now exists.

Stateless workers rehydrate from shared storage. New: SnapshotSessionManager persists the whole agent as one versioned blob through any Storage backend (in-memory, local file, S3 or your own protocol implementation), with a mutable snapshot_latest plus optional immutable history (session/snapshot_session_manager.py:244-260); S3SessionManager gained endpoint_url for S3-compatible stores. The older FileSessionManager, S3SessionManager and RepositorySessionManager remain. No leader election or distributed locking, so two workers writing the same session concurrently is your problem.

N stateless Node processes behind a load balancer each hydrate an agent from a SessionManager backed by a shared S3Storage (storage/s3-storage.ts:37) or your own Storage (unified Storage plus SnapshotStorageAdapter; legacy classes deprecated). Nothing prevents two pods restoring and saving the same sessionId at once, and there is no worker registration or heartbeat. In-process background tasks are not portable: on restore every non-terminal task is marked failed (background-tasks.ts:451-462).

Stateless-worker model: N Node processes each pulling session state from your shared store; the canonical resumable-stream example uses the third-party resumable-stream package plus Redis. No leader election or shared in-memory map. For HarnessAgent any instance can serve the next turn if it can reattach the sandbox by id and load the caller-persisted resume state; for WorkflowAgent / workflow-harness the Workflow backend owns scheduling and replay across instances. No built-in session store or pluggable store interface in ai.

First-party Pub/Sub and Eventarc triggers in the REST server (server/adkrest/controllers/triggers/). PubSubTriggerHandler accepts Cloud Pub/Sub push messages throttled by a MaxConcurrentRuns semaphore, and RetriableRunner retries with exponential backoff on resource exhaustion; trigger routes fall under the 10 MiB body limit since v2.5. Workflow HITL pauses can resume on a later request. No in-box cron: wire Cloud Scheduler to Pub/Sub to an ADK trigger.

ScheduleManager + SchedulePoller + ScheduleExecutor are cron-driven with DB-stored schedules (agno_schedules, now keyed by user_id and name) and DB-backed leader election. POST /agents/{id}/runs with background=true persists a PENDING run and executes it detached (default 32 concurrent per replica); the streaming variant buffers SSE for /resume. v3.0.0 adds QueueConfig(durable=True) so accepted runs survive crashes and deploys, with Idempotency-Key dedupe and 429 backpressure. Hooks can also run in the background (@hook(run_in_background=True)). First-class on every axis except webhook-in triggers beyond the REST API.

No cron, no schedulers, no webhook receivers. v0.4.0 added Environment run()/wait()/run_background() and shutdown_with_timeout, which manage runtime lifecycle rather than scheduling. Long-running background work is possible via tokio::spawn and Topic<Task>, but there is no first-party primitive.

`AgentDefinition.background` (types.py:124) and `run_in_background` sub-agents keep running after a `ResultMessage`; since 0.2.160 the SDK keeps stdin open until the CLI reports idle (ceiling `CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS`, default 10 min) and `stop_task` (client.py:443) stops one. The bundled CLI (2.1.286, the same version the TS report analyses) also provides model-invoked in-session scheduling (CronCreate/CronDelete/CronList with durable persistence to `.claude/scheduled_tasks.json`, ScheduleWakeup) and a RemoteTrigger tool; the Python SDK has no typed inputs for them but surfaces fired schedules through `MessageOrigin` subkind `scheduled-trigger` (types.py:1062, 1093-1097). Session-local, not a distributed scheduler; webhook intake is BYO. Raised from 1 to match TS; the Cron tools were not exercised from this repo.

AgentDefinition.background and AgentInput.run_in_background give sub-agents that run in the background by default and emit task_notification when done; BashInput.run_in_background (timeout default 30 min, max 2 h) covers long commands, and perTaskStopAffordance keeps background work alive across interrupt(). New model-invoked in-session scheduling: CronCreate/CronDelete/CronList (durable: true persists to .claude/scheduled_tasks.json) and ScheduleWakeup, plus a RemoteTrigger tool for Anthropic-hosted triggers tied to a claude.ai account. Local to the session or process, not a distributed scheduler (the runAssistantWorker scheduler cited in May was removed in 0.3.181); webhook intake on your infrastructure is BYO.

OSS: Crew.kickoff() is blocking; there is no scheduler module and the CLI's `crewai triggers` commands operate on AMP triggers. AMP ships Automations with triggers for Gmail/Calendar/Drive/Outlook/OneDrive/Teams/HubSpot/Salesforce/Slack/Zapier plus webhook/API kickoff and cron, vendor-managed, with no OSS equivalent (docs moved to docs-platform.crewai.com; the trigger list was not re-verified).

No cron, webhook trigger system or scheduled-job framework on main. TurnLoop.Push is a clean entry point for externally triggered work (a webhook handler can Push into a session's loop), but scheduling and durability across pods are yours. A background-task manager and durable background tasks exist only on the unreleased alpha/10 branch and are not scored.

First-party background agent runs: AgentInput.Detach / RunDetached returns a pending snapshotId while the turn keeps running, followed via task.Poll/Wait or POST /agents/{name}/waitForSnapshot and stopped via /abort, with a 30 s heartbeat, expiry after 60 s, and cross-instance abort (go/ai/exp/task.go, go/genkit/exp/routes.go:89-109). Also async background sub-agents (middlewarex.Agents{Async}), BackgroundModel/GenerateOperation for long model jobs, and experimental durable streaming with a StreamManager. All of the agent pieces are experimental (exp/) and need a SnapshotSubscriber store; cron and webhook triggers are BYO. Moved from 2 to 3: a first-party background-run lifecycle now exists, capped by experimental status.

Pure OSS: not provided — BYO Celery/arq/Temporal/cron. Platform: first-party crons (crons.create/search/delete in langgraph_sdk/_async/cron.py) and webhooks (run create accepts webhook URL); Platform queue persists scheduled runs in Postgres. Strong story when the Platform is in scope; OSS-only is BYO.

No cron, scheduler or webhook primitives in llama-index-core; BYO Celery, Temporal, RQ or asyncio. The separate run-llama/llama-agents project (replacing the deprecated llama_deploy) is out of scope for this analysis.

Three first-party mechanisms. Schedules: a unified mastra.schedules API for cron-style agent and workflow runs (renamed from heartbeats in 1.50.0; file-based agent schedules in 1.58.0) executed by a scheduler worker. Background tasks: tools or sub-agents run as background tasks with per-call dispositions, backgroundTaskPolicy/disableBackgroundTasks, and a dedicated chunk family. Signals and channels: sendMessage/queueMessage and SignalProvider (webhook, polling) wake agents from external events, and channels (Slack, Discord, Teams, Telegram) run agents from chat events, with waitUntil so background runs survive serverless responses.

In-repo: `BackgroundAgentsProvider` (Python and .NET) runs sub-agents in process, not durable across restarts. The first-party durable extension adds durable orchestrations that checkpoint every agent call, human-in-the-loop waits that can last days with zero compute, fire-and-forget HTTP runs (202 with `x-ms-wait-for-response: false`), a long-running-tools sample, `DurableAgentContext.ScheduleNewOrchestration` from tools and MCP tool triggers. I found no agent-specific cron/timer abstraction in it, so schedules rely on native Azure Functions or Durable Task timers. The extension is labelled preview/beta (1.16.0-preview, 1.0.0b), so 4 under the cap, level with ADK Go. Restored from 3 now that the extension was inspected.

No scheduler, cron, webhook trigger or background-agent runtime. The optional temporal extra (pyproject.toml:88) integrates Temporal workflows for durable orchestration, but Temporal is a separate runtime you stand up yourself. Remains the biggest architectural gap versus Mastra (schedules, background tasks) or LangGraph Platform (crons, background runs).
No cron, webhook trigger primitives, or queues. Run a worker process (BullMQ, AWS SQS, etc.) and call run() from inside.

No first-party scheduler, cron or webhook trigger. New since May: Harness BackgroundTools (pre-1.0 first-party package) lets selected tools run in the background while the agent continues, and Shell background processes persist across runs of a conversation. Durable long runs integrate Temporal, DBOS, Prefect, Restate, AWS Lambda durable, Kitaru, Airflow and Absurd, but these are external engines you stand up. Moved from 1 to 2: first-party in-run background work in addition to the durable-engine integrations.
No cron, webhook trigger, or background agent. Tokio runtime can spawn tasks but Rig offers no scheduling abstraction.

Scheduled, cron and webhook triggers are not provided (the tools-repo cron tool is deprecated). New since May: Agent(background_tasks=True | BackgroundTasksConfig) runs tools as in-process background tasks chosen by policy (always/never/agentic), with max_concurrency 4, per-task timeout, wait_for_completion and a strands_manage_background_task tool (agent/agent.py:231, background_tasks/_types.py:13-31). This is intra-invocation concurrency that dies with the worker, not a job scheduler. Moved from 0 to 1: a small first-party primitive exists.

No cron primitive and no webhook trigger surface. Since v1.16.0 AgentConfig.backgroundTasks runs ordinary tool calls asynchronously in the same process, selected by the model (agentic mode), with maxConcurrency 4, an optional timeout, a strands_manage_background_task tool, and results re-entering the conversation through the continuation mechanism. Only the config is public (BackgroundTasks and the manager are @internal), and non-terminal tasks are marked failed on restore. Moved from 0 to 1, matching the Python SDK; scheduling stays BYO (BullMQ, Cloud Tasks).

No cron, scheduler or webhook trigger primitive in ai; use Vercel Cron, Cloud Scheduler or Trigger.dev. New first-party pieces for long-running work: WorkflowAgent (@ai-sdk/workflow, now needing the Workflow 5 beta) runs the loop as durable steps, @ai-sdk/workflow-harness runs HarnessAgent turns as durable time slices or semantic steps, and experimental provider batch APIs (experimental_startTextBatch) support completion webhooks for offline bulk inference. All depend on the separate Vercel Workflow product and you write the 'use workflow' wrappers. Moved from 0 to 1.

Triggers ship a semaphore-based concurrency limiter (MaxConcurrentRuns, triggers/pubsub.go:102-104), a thin worker pool. The workflow engine adds in-process concurrency control (workflow.WithMaxConcurrency, ParallelWorker maxConcurrency) and per-node Timeout/RetryConfig, but there is no durable queue: a run lives as long as the request or iterator driving it. For long work use workflow HITL pauses or fire-and-forget Pub/Sub triggers.

New in v3.0.0: a first-party durable job queue (job_queue/, os/job_queue.py) stored in the AgentOS DB or a dedicated DB/Redis. Jobs are committed rows (agno_jobs) claimed by any replica's worker with leases, heartbeats and fenced writes; knobs include max_concurrency, max_queue_depth (default 1000), max_attempts (default 1 = a crashed run fails visibly), jittered retry backoff, per-run timeout and retention. Idempotency-Key dedupe, 429 backpressure, a dead-letter state with requeue, and /queue/jobs and /queue/stats endpoints. Gap: reclaim re-executes a run from the start. Moved from 1 to 5 at parity with LangGraph's run queue, but released and OSS.

Tasks are delivered to actors via actor_ref.cast(message) in ractor. No durable queue and no retry semantics at the queue layer (LLM-level retries exist in optim::RetryLayer). v0.4.0 only made runtime processing errors propagate out of the event loop (#304) instead of being dropped.

Runtime model is one CLI subprocess per active session, lifetime owned by the calling Python coroutine. For queue-shaped workloads layer your own (Celery, RQ, Temporal, SQS workers). Background sub-agents can now extend a run well past the first ResultMessage, which matters for worker timeouts.

streamInput(), stopTask(), interrupt({cancel_queued}) and queued_turn_count / command_lifecycle frames give primitives for a long-lived session with queued user sends, but there is no shipped job queue, lease or enqueue() API. Use BullMQ, Cloud Tasks or Temporal around query().

OSS: none. AMP: implicit, each Automation is a separate managed deployment receiving trigger events. The OSS repository ships no queue primitive; internal thread pools (event bus, memory save pool, async tasks) are not exposed as a worker model.

New in v0.9: TurnLoop is an in-process, per-session queue. Push buffers items (adk/turn_buffer.go) with optional preemption of the running turn, GenInput decides what each turn consumes, and unprocessed items are returned in TurnLoopExitState.UnhandledItems and persisted in the TurnLoop checkpoint (adk/turn_loop.go:942-950). It is not a worker pool: there is no cross-session pool, priority queue or distributed queue, so cross-pod long-running work still needs Asynq, Temporal or Cloud Tasks. Moved from 0 to 2: partial first-party queue with checkpointed items, level with ADK Go's trigger limiter.

No queue, concurrency cap, retry scheduler or work stealing. Detached agent runs (experimental) are goroutines in the accepting process, bounded only by process limits, and abandoned detached turns are only marked expired by heartbeat. For durable queued work put requests on Pub/Sub, SQS or Cloud Tasks and have a worker invoke the agent or genkit.Generate.

langgraph_api ships a Postgres-backed work queue with one logical lane per thread_id. Long-running runs (minutes or hours) are the default expectation; re-attaching clients pick up via GET /threads/{tid}/runs/{rid}/stream with a Last-Event-ID header when stream_resumable: true (a header, not a query parameter; _async/runs.py:1146-1150), or with the v3 client by reopening client.threads.stream(thread_id=...) from a since cursor. OSS-only mode has no queue; you wrap it in your own.

Not provided in llama-index-core. The separate run-llama/llama-agents project (control plane plus server runtime around Workflows; it replaces the deprecated llama_deploy) provides this outside the scope of this analysis.

Corrected: a first-party worker model already existed in May. Mastra({ workers }) creates orchestration, scheduler and background-task workers (packages/core/src/worker/workers/) that consume events from the configured pub/sub; step execution can be in-process or HTTP-remote with bearer/API-key auth, a pull transport exists for polling setups, and MASTRA_WORKERS splits API and worker roles across processes (mastra/index.ts:1575-1600). Pub/sub backends: in-process default, Redis Streams, Valkey Streams (new) and Google Cloud Pub/Sub. Gaps: no generic job-queue API outside agent/workflow execution, and no documented dead-letter or backpressure model. Score 4 (previously 1, based on the May report that missed this model).

No queue API in the core repo, only in-process background sub-agents. The first-party durable extension supplies the worker model: each agent session is a Durable Task entity (`dafx-` prefix), the entity framework serializes messages per session, any worker on a Durable Task Scheduler or Azure Functions task hub can resume a session, and HTTP calls can be fire-and-forget. That is a first-class queue-backed worker model on capability (5), capped at 4 because the extension is preview/beta (1.16.0-preview, 1.0.0b). Level with Mastra at 4; Agno and LangGraph keep 5 for stable queues. Restored from 2.

No internal task queue and no worker pool. For long-running agents expose a streaming endpoint over run_streamed(), or persist RunState.to_json() and resume later from a worker pulling jobs off your own queue (Celery, RQ, SQS). ToolExecutionConfig.max_function_tool_concurrency (run_config.py:139) bounds concurrent function tools within one run, not across runs.

SDK assumes short-lived request scope by default and provides no queue or worker pool. Long-running agents need a serialized RunState checkpoint pattern (examples/agent-patterns/human-in-the-loop.ts:84-111); RunState.addInput() (0.15.0) stages new user input onto a paused state and survives serialization until the next safe model request.

No built-in queue. UseThreadExecutor (capabilities/thread_executor.py:17, formerly ThreadExecutor) lets you supply your own concurrent.futures.Executor for sync tools in long-running servers. Otherwise request-scoped execution is assumed and queueing is the durable engine's (Temporal, DBOS, Prefect and others) or your job.

Not provided for agent runs. The new in-process effect bus (bounded by ServingPolicy: command_capacity 16, stream_capacity 64 by default) is an internal command queue between the run loop and its handlers, not a job queue. Long runs either stay attached to a request (stream_prompt) or are persisted as AgentRun and resumed by your own worker.

No inter-session queue; session-level queueing is BYO. Intra-agent only: ConcurrentToolExecutor (tools/executors/concurrent.py:19) parallelizes tool calls within one cycle, and the in-process background task manager tracks statuses queued, working, input_required and completed. Both die with the worker.

Not provided for agent runs: you wrap agent.stream() in your own request handler or queue consumer. The only queue is internal to background tool calls: InProcessTaskEngine keeps a queue and active executions bounded by maxConcurrency with per-task timeouts (background-tasks/in-process/engine.ts:16-21), behind a BackgroundTaskManager interface whose only implementation is in-process and @internal. Moved from 0 to 1 for parity with the Python SDK, which has the same in-process task manager and scored 1.

Not provided in ai; the SDK assumes request scope. For queued work use an external queue (BullMQ, SQS) or the Workflow DevKit (queuing, retries, durability as a separate Vercel product). WorkflowAgent (@ai-sdk/workflow@2.0.57, now requiring Workflow 5 beta) is the first-party way to get queue-backed, retryable tool steps, but it is not a horizontal multi-tenant worker runtime.

Strong typed session.Session interface plus storageSession/storageEvent GORM models with composite primary key (AppName, UserID, ID). Event-sourced model with scoped state (app/user/temp) in separate tables; v2 adds workflow columns (Routes, Output, NodeInfo, RequestedInput, IsolationScope) and live-transcription columns to the event row. No first-class tenant_id, but the composite identity gives a natural multi-tenant key.

AgentSession dataclass with session_data, metadata, agent_data, summary, timestamps and sibling TeamSession/WorkflowSession types. Since v3 the runs live in a separate agno_runs table (run_id, session_id, user_id, parent_run_id, status, run_index, run_data) and are re-attached on load, with fork/regenerate lineage fields. No first-class tenant_id (user_isolation scopes by user_id), but rich enough to scope via session_id and user_id.

AutoAgents has no Session type. Closest equivalents are Task (input only, now with a free-form app_meta whose doc names session/chat isolation but which no framework code reads), AgentState (in-memory for one Context run), and MemoryProvider (SlidingWindowMemory). No id, tenant_id, user_id, created_at, parent_session_id, usage or model field on any session-like type.

Sessions identified by session_id (UUID) plus project_key for tenant scoping in the SessionStore via SessionKey TypedDict. SDKSessionInfo carries summary, last_modified, custom_title, first_prompt, git_branch, cwd, tag, created_at. CLI writes opaque JSONL transcript entries; SDK treats entries as pass-through dicts.

SDKSessionInfo (sessionId, summary, customTitle, gitBranch, cwd, tag, createdAt) plus SessionKey (projectKey, sessionId, subpath). projectKey is explicitly documented as the multi-tenant scope. Per-message types carry session_id, uuid, parent_tool_use_id, subagent_type. Strong session model among the JS frameworks.

Conversational Flows (stable since 1.15.18) add a real chat-session primitive: ConversationState{id, messages, events, agent_threads, last_intent, ended}, persisted per turn via FlowPersistence under a caller-chosen session_id. Chat flows can declare their own state shape, so tenant_id is a subclass field. Still no built-in tenant_id, user_id, created_at or parent_session_id, and plain Crew/Agent kickoffs remain frozen-UUID runs with no conversation model. Richer than OpenAI JS (id + items) but less standardised than ADK/Strands, so 3.

No Session type per se. runSession is run-scoped (per Runner.Run call) with Values/Events/LaneEvents; the new TurnLoop adds a persisted turnLoopCheckpoint (runner state + queued and interrupted items) for per-session multi-turn use. The serialization checkpoint payload carries RunCtx plus interrupt state. Traditional session fields (tenant_id, user_id, created_at, summary) are not in the framework; the quickstart builds them in the business layer.

The old typed-state-only Session[S] was removed. The experimental agent layer now has SessionState{SessionID, Messages, Custom (typed), Artifacts} and SessionSnapshot{SnapshotID, ParentID, Status, FinishReason, Error, HeartbeatAt, timestamps}, with a live aix.Session handle inside a turn. Absent: tenant_id, user_id, model, usage, summary, metadata (tenant scoping is a storage-path concern). Scored on capability and capped at 4 because the layer is gated behind WithExperimental().

Thread is the session primitive with first-class Checkpoint TypedDict (v, id, ts, channel_values, channel_versions, versions_seen, updated_channels) and CheckpointMetadata (source, step, parents, writes). CheckpointTuple persists config/checkpoint/metadata/parent_config/pending_writes/pending_sends. Models full history (one per super-step), replayable.

No formal Session type. Memory carries session_id, token_limit, memory_blocks, insert_method and sql_store (now any AsyncDBChatStore, since 0.14.24). Workflow Context is a separately serializable state bag with KV store and queue position. The two-piece model (Memory + Context) covers conversation and run state but lacks a unified Session entity.

Mastra calls the session a thread, paired with a resourceId (typically user/tenant id). MastraDBMessage has id, threadId, resourceId, role, content, createdAt, metadata, plus suspendedTools/pendingToolApprovals for HITL. resourceId gives natural per-tenant scoping at the model level.

AgentSession class (Python and .NET) with session_id, service_session_id (for provider-managed threads), state dict namespaced by ContextProvider.source_id. .NET uses AgentSessionStateBag (ConcurrentDictionary). No first-class tenant_id/user_id but state bag is extensible.

Session Protocol with session_id, optional SessionSettings, and items (TResponseInputItem). Concrete SQLiteSession adds created_at/updated_at columns. Minimal surface area on purpose; tenant scoping is BYO via session_id namespacing or TContext.

Session interface is just { sessionId, items: AgentInputItem[] } with 7 methods. No first-class tenant_id, user_id, cwd, model, metadata, usage, or summary fields. Reasoning-item IDs are persistable via opt-in. Slim by design.

Core still has no Session object: conversation_id (UUID7), run_id, metadata and caller-owned message_history only. The first-party pydantic-ai-harness (0.x, version-locked to core) adds RunRecord, ContinuableSnapshot, StepEvent, ToolEffectRecord with parent_run_id lineage, plus SqliteConversationStore with ConversationSummary and revisioning. No tenant/user fields. Capped by the pre-1.0 Harness label and by the fact that core callers still persist everything themselves.

No Session type. ConversationMemory is keyed by a ConversationId newtype over (Vec<Message>) with load/append/clear, and the serializable AgentRun carries chat_history, usage, completion_calls, current turn and hook RunEntries. No tenant_id, user_id, created_at or metadata on either. The memory contract itself still does not persist usage or attachments.

Message-log dataclasses are unchanged: Session (session_id, session_type, timestamps), SessionAgent (agent_id, state, conversation_manager_state, internal state) and SessionMessage (with durable tracking_id). The recommended path is now a Snapshot (schema 1.0) persisted by SnapshotSessionManager: messages, state, conversation/context-manager state, interrupts, model state, system prompt and app_data. Still no tenant_id, user_id, parent_session_id or session-level metadata (BYO via agent.state).

Snapshot interface with scope (agent|multiAgent), schemaVersion, createdAt, framework data, and appData (caller-owned). SnapshotLocation tuple (sessionId, scope, scopeId). Snapshot is a JSON-serializable agent-state snapshot, not a wire chat session.

ToolLoopAgent still has no Session/Thread type; you persist UIMessage[] yourself. The new experimental @ai-sdk/harness HarnessAgent has a live session object (runtime, sandbox, work dir, pending approvals) whose persisted form is an opaque adapter-specific resume blob with no documented field list. Gains one point for a session object that exists at all, but it models an external runtime's session rather than a chat model.

Three first-party session.Service implementations: InMemoryService, GORM-backed database service (Postgres, SQLite, MySQL, Spanner dialectors; NewSessionServiceFromDB shares an existing pool) and Vertex AI Agent Engine. AutoMigrate must run on every startup, and v2.5 un-migrated databases fail writes. No first-party Redis, S3 or JSONL store, but GORM coverage makes any SQL backend viable.

Fourteen adapters ship under libs/agno/agno/db/: Postgres (sync+async), MySQL, SQLite (sync+async), Redis, Valkey (new), Mongo, DynamoDB, Firestore, SingleStore, SurrealDB, GCS JSON, JSON file, in-memory, plus ClickHouse (traces-oriented). All inherit BaseDb/AsyncBaseDb; v3 stores runs in a per-run table on every adapter and requires a MigrationManager step. Best-in-class breadth.

No persistence stores ship. No JSONL, no SQLite, no Postgres, no Redis, no S3. Only the in-memory SlidingWindowMemory (VecDeque<ChatMessage>). MemoryProvider trait has clone_box/preload/export hooks for BYO storage.

Default is local-disk JSONL written by the CLI to ~/.claude/projects/. InMemorySessionStore reference. Postgres/Redis/S3 reference adapters live under examples/session_stores/ (added 0.1.64) but are not shipped in the wheel; you copy them in. Solid local story, but no first-class server-side adapters in the package.

Default JSONL on local disk plus InMemorySessionStore class. Postgres, Redis, S3 reference adapters under examples/session-stores/ with conformance tests. Marked @alpha. SQLite, MongoDB, DynamoDB, Cassandra, R2, Vercel Blob are BYO. Strong local default but production adapters are not first-party.

Two checkpoint providers ship: JsonProvider (one file per checkpoint) and SqliteProvider (WAL, one DB file). Flow persistence adds SQLiteFlowPersistence, the default for conversational sessions, swappable process-wide via set_flow_persistence_factory. No Postgres/Redis/S3/cloud-blob providers; Redis appears only as an optional lock backend. Adequate for local dev, BYO for production.

None. CheckPointStore is interface-only and eino-ext ships no implementation (verified by grep). The bridgeStore is framework-internal in-memory only. Possibilities (Postgres/Redis/S3/SQLite/BoltDB) are all BYO.

The experimental agent layer ships three SessionStore implementations: InMemorySessionStore, FileSessionStore (atomic temp-file + rename, cross-process status polling) and FirestoreSessionStore (per-turn JSON-Patch diffs over periodic sharded checkpoints, real-time status listener). Tenant isolation is available through WithSnapshotPathPrefix on the file and Firestore stores. No Postgres, SQLite, Redis or S3/GCS adapter, so a SQL-backed multi-tenant agent still implements the store itself. Comparable to Strands (file + cloud) at 3.

Four production-grade checkpointers ship: InMemorySaver (dev), PostgresSaver + AsyncPostgresSaver, SqliteSaver + AsyncSqliteSaver. PostgresSaver also implements BaseStore for namespaced KV + vector search. No bundled Redis/S3/Mongo but the Postgres story is the gold standard.

Memory uses SQLAlchemyChatStore by default, covering any SQLAlchemy-supported DB (SQLite default, Postgres, MySQL), and since 0.14.24 accepts any AsyncDBChatStore. Core ships only the SQLAlchemy implementation. The Postgres/Redis/DynamoDB/Mongo/Azure chat stores are separate integration packages that implement the legacy BaseChatStore for the deprecated ChatMemoryBuffer, not the new Memory. Context serialization is BYO storage.

Thirty-one adapters under stores/: relational/KV (libsql default, pg, mysql, mssql, dsql, oracledb, spanner, turso, duckdb, clickhouse, cloudflare, d1, dynamodb, mongodb, couchbase, convex, redis, upstash, valkey) plus a dozen vector/search stores. Storage domains are split (memory, workflows, observability, scores, thread-state and more) and MastraCompositeStore can route each domain to a different backend. Breadth leader, with opt-in retention/prune.

In-memory (both platforms), file (Python, experimental), Redis (Python), Valkey and Azure Blob (.NET), Cosmos NoSQL (both), Foundry hosted/persistent stores, and a vector-store history provider (Python, experimental). Python SessionStore/FileSessionStore are experimental and the .NET AgentSessionStore is preview. Solid Azure-aligned coverage, uneven between Python and .NET.

Ten first-party backends: SQLiteSession (default, WAL), OpenAIConversationsSession (hosted), OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession, AdvancedSQLiteSession, AsyncSQLiteSession, SQLAlchemySession (Postgres/MySQL), RedisSession, MongoDBSession, DaprSession and EncryptedSession (Fernet/HKDF wrapper). Largest set of any framework in the comparison. Note: the SDK is pre-1.0 (0.22.x) but unlabelled, so the 5 is kept; see open questions in changes.md.

Three session impls: MemorySession (in-process), OpenAIConversationsSession (OpenAI hosted), OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession (wraps another session for server-side compaction). No SQLite, Postgres, Redis, S3, or JSONL on disk built-in. Example adapters (file, Prisma) live under examples/.

Core ships no store: you serialize all_messages_json yourself. The first-party Harness (0.x) ships InMemoryStepStore, FileStepStore, SqliteStepStore (WAL) and MongoStepStore for StepPersistence, SqliteConversationStore for chat heads, and Memory stores incl. Postgres. There is no Postgres or Redis step store, and the Harness API is explicitly allowed to move between minors.

Only InMemoryConversationMemory ships in-tree (single-process). rig-memory adds policies (sliding window, token budget, compaction) that wrap a backend, not new backends. rig-ecs save_world and rig-cassette EffectLog checkpoints produce JSON you store yourself. rig-postgres/sqlite/mongodb remain vector stores, so Postgres/Redis/S3 session stores are BYO.

SnapshotSessionManager over a unified Storage protocol (InMemoryStorage, LocalFileStorage, S3Storage) is the recommended path, alongside the message-log FileSessionManager, S3SessionManager and RepositorySessionManager. Postgres/Redis/DynamoDB are BYO via Storage or SessionRepository; community adapters are only listed in docs. File + S3 covers a typical multi-tenant deployment.

Persistence is now layered: SessionManager over a unified Storage interface with InMemoryStorage, LocalFileStorage and S3Storage (namespaced prefixes, optional BM25 search on local files). The old FileStorage/S3Storage/SnapshotStorage trio is deprecated but still works. This is the same shipped set as Strands Python (memory + file + S3), so it is scored equal. Postgres, Redis and DynamoDB are BYO.

None in ai: no JSONL, SQLite, Postgres, Redis or Blob adapter, and you persist messages via onStepEnd/onEnd callbacks. The experimental HarnessAgent relies on the external runtime's own on-sandbox history plus sandbox snapshots, and WorkflowAgent relies on the Workflow backend's event log. The resumable-stream recipe uses Redis but is example code, not a built-in store.

session.Service is a clean 5-method interface (Create, Get, List, Delete, AppendEvent) and the returned Session is itself an interface. v2 tightened the godoc contract (wrap session.ErrNotFound, assign event IDs, round-trip Compaction) and exposes a public conformance suite, session/sessiontestsuite, to validate custom backends. You can BYO Redis/S3/Cassandra/proprietary backends.

BaseDb / AsyncBaseDb is the plug point, now with about 82 abstract methods covering sessions, memories, metrics, evals, knowledge, traces, components, schedules, approvals and learnings. The v3 per-run APIs are concrete with fallbacks, so an adapter can keep runs inline until it opts in. Well-typed but a heavy contract compared with a 5-method interface.

MemoryProvider trait (remember, remember_many, recall, clear, memory_type, size, clone_box, preload, export, plus optional summary hooks) is the BYO plug point; remember_many lets a provider write a tool-call batch atomically. ChatMessage is Serialize/Deserialize so a Postgres/Redis/S3 backend is straightforward. The provider receives no Task or app_meta, so a multi-tenant store must be built per session, and every consumer must BYO.

`SessionStore` Protocol (types.py:1609) with two required methods (`append`, `load`) and four optional (`list_sessions`, `list_session_summaries`, `delete`, `list_subkeys`), a 13-contract conformance harness (`claude_agent_sdk.testing.run_session_store_conformance`), `InMemorySessionStore` and S3/Redis/Postgres reference adapters. Among the best plug-store stories in the set. The feature itself carries no alpha or experimental label (none in types.py, session_store.py, the README or the session-storage docs page, checked 2026-10-01); only the package classifier is `Development Status :: 3 - Alpha` (pyproject.toml:16), and a whole-package label does not cap under the clarified rule. Restored from 4 to 5; TS stays at 4 because its SessionStore is tagged `@alpha`. The store mirrors the CLI's local JSONL rather than replacing it.

SessionStore mirrors the Python protocol: six methods (two required), with a 13-contract conformance suite under examples/session-stores/shared/conformance.ts. The type is explicitly marked @alpha and the shape is unchanged since May; adapter authors should treat uuid as an idempotency key. Capped at 4 under the shared rule that alpha-labelled first-party APIs cannot score 5. delete is a no-op for WORM stores and load() has no streaming form (issue #426).

Three separate interfaces: BaseProvider ABC for checkpoint state (discriminated union on CheckpointConfig.provider), FlowPersistence ABC for Flow state and conversational sessions (now installable process-wide with set_flow_persistence_factory), and StorageBackend Protocol for memory (also with a factory). Comprehensive but the surface is wider than typical.

CheckPointStore interface is just Get/Set on []byte (gob-serialized), with an optional CheckPointDeleter that TurnLoop calls on clean exit. Minimal contract: you implement two methods, and there is no schema, migration helper or versioning hook on the user side. Very BYO-friendly if you want full control.

SessionStore[State] combines SnapshotReader (GetSnapshot, GetLatestSnapshot) and SnapshotWriter (SaveSnapshot with an atomic read-modify-write function), plus an optional SnapshotSubscriber needed for detach/abort. The interface docs spell out a Postgres mapping (SELECT FOR UPDATE, LISTEN/NOTIFY). Experimental, and coupled to the generic State type.

BaseCheckpointSaver abstract class with get_tuple/list/put/put_writes plus async siblings. Conformance harness lives in libs/checkpoint-conformance/. Postgres saver also implements BaseStore for cross-session KV. Gold-standard pluggability.

Memory now plugs into AsyncDBChatStore (abstract async get/add/set/delete/archive methods, documented in memory.mdx), while BaseMemory and the legacy BaseChatStore remain. SQLAlchemyChatStore is the only shipped AsyncDBChatStore; community Redis/Postgres/Azure stores implement the legacy interface. Reasonable extension surface with no conformance suite.

MastraStorage with per-domain abstract classes (memory, workflows, observability, scores and more); a custom adapter implements the domains it needs and is passed via new Mastra({ storage }). A FactoryStorage contract owns domain initialization and readiness. Powerful but more domain interfaces than typical.

Python HistoryProvider (get_messages/save_messages) plus an experimental SessionStore (get/set/delete); .NET AgentSessionStore (promoted into Abstractions in 1.22.0, experimental MAAI001, partitioned AgentSessionStoreKey) plus ChatHistoryProvider and a DelegatingAgentSessionStore for decorators. Clean per-platform interfaces with a small surface; the session-store contracts are still labelled experimental or preview.

Session Protocol (4 methods: get_items, add_items, pop_item, clear_session) or SessionABC, duck-typed with no inheritance required. Since 0.20 a custom session that declares a wrapper parameter on all four methods receives the active RunContextWrapper, which the docs name as the tenant-routing hook. Minimal surface so a custom store is short to write. Pre-1.0 (0.22.x) but unlabelled, so the 5 is kept; see open questions.

Session needs five core methods (getSessionId, getItems, addItems, popItem, clearSession), with a 119-line file-store reference. Optional capability interfaces now cover run-context routing (RunContextAwareSession), history rewrite and idempotent transactions with a stable operationId (SessionHistoryTransactionAwareSession), and Responses compaction. That matches the Python Session protocol including its context-aware tenant routing, so the two are scored equal. Same pre-1.0 (0.18) caveat as Python; see open questions.

Core has no store interface: message_history is caller-owned. The first-party Harness (0.x) defines a StepStore Protocol (register_run, append_event, save_snapshot, latest_snapshot, record_tool_effect, list_unresolved_tool_effects and more), with MemoryStore and SpendStore protocols alongside. A Postgres store is BYO against the protocol. Scored 3 because the contract is ten methods, covers only the optional StepPersistence capability, and ships with no conformance suite.

ConversationMemory trait (load/append/clear on async fn returning Vec<Message>) sits behind Arc<dyn ConversationMemory> on Agent::memory. Async-safe, WasmCompat bounds. Clean three-method contract for BYO Postgres/Redis/Mongo/S3 backends.

Two seams: SessionRepository ABC (create/read/update on session, agent and message, plus list_messages) and the unified Storage protocol (write, read, delete, list, search, namespace views) that backs snapshots, file memory and context offloading. Implementing Storage once covers all three. Reasonable surface for Postgres/Redis BYO.

Implement the unified Storage interface (six methods, namespace and search optional) and pass it as AgentConfig.storage or SessionManagerConfig.storage; the legacy six-method SnapshotStorage is deprecated. FileStorage/LocalFileStorage and S3Storage are the reference implementations, and subsystems auto-namespace under their own prefixes.

No SessionStore or Checkpointer abstraction. Persistence is entirely your callback inside onStepFinish / onFinish. The SDK does not formalize how your DB exposes session reads/writes. Plug-store ergonomics are the weakest in the benchmark.

Every non-partial event is persisted synchronously inside one GORM transaction, so a crash loses at most the in-flight LLM response or tool batch. New in v2: HITL pause/resume rebuilds workflow node state from session events (ReconstructRunState), but a crash mid-graph is not resumed (it returns nil when no interrupt history exists) and the next message starts a fresh run. Per-event granularity, not per-task durability like LangGraph.

Agent(checkpoint='tool-batch') persists the run row after every tool batch (released in 2.6.19), and continue_run(continue_from=N) plus checkpoint-listing endpoints resume from a boundary. Gaps: per-tool-call mode raises 'not available yet', a tool in flight at crash time re-runs, and the durable queue's automatic reclaim re-executes the run from the start rather than from the checkpoint. Opt-in, so 3 rather than 4.
Not provided. Crash mid-tool-call loses all in-memory state. SlidingWindowMemory holds a bounded VecDeque<ChatMessage> only for the agent's lifetime.

Best-effort: CLI flushes JSONL per entry to local disk so a crash mid-tool-call leaves everything up to that point on disk; resume <id> re-loads it. No transactional commit-per-tool-write the way LangGraph's _runner.commit/put_writes does. SessionStore mirror is batched (~100ms) so external store may lag.

The subprocess writes each transcript entry to local JSONL line by line; that is the durability boundary, and an external SessionStore is a post-local, batched (~100 ms) mirror. Since May the CLI marks automatic re-runs of a host-restart-interrupted turn with resume_reason, re-runs deferred tool calls at resume start and restores background-agent state. Still turn-level recovery: no per-task commit like LangGraph.

With on_events=['*'] or tool events a checkpoint fires per tool call. Crew.from_checkpoint restores and _restore_runtime walks the event record to find tasks that started but did not complete, sets executor._resuming and resumes on the next kickoff(). Since 1.14.6 the default AgentExecutor can also restore from a checkpoint. Gold-standard mid-tool-call resumability.

Checkpoints are now saved on interrupt, on cancel (adk.WithCancel at safe points) and when TurnLoop stops, which makes graceful stops resumable and persists queued inputs between turns. There is still no per-step or per-task durable commit: a process crash without a prior interrupt or cancel loses everything since the last checkpoint. Same level as other HITL-plus-graceful-stop designs at 2.

Experimental agent layer snapshots once per turn, and since v1.13 a failed or aborted turn commits the tool rounds that completed so a retry does not repeat them. Detached runs heartbeat and surface as expired when the worker dies, and resume restarts from the last committed snapshot. A turn in flight at process death is discarded whole, and tools inside it run again; there is no per-task commit.

Gold standard. _runner.commit() calls put_writes per task — so each parallel tool call's result is durable as it completes. _put_checkpoint runs once per super-step. Under durability=async (default) next super-step starts while previous persists. If 4 parallel tool calls run and the process crashes after 3 finish, on resume the 3 completed tool results are durable and not re-executed.

Not automatic. A workflow can be paused at ctx.wait_for_event for HITL and serialized with ctx.to_dict, but a crash mid-tool-call loses the in-flight tool result. The workflows runtime (2.21-2.25, separate repo) mentions durable ticks and snapshot replay via llama-agents-dbos, but the report did not verify per-step crash recovery for FunctionAgent runs.

HITL suspension persists workflow snapshots (survives restarts, discoverable via suspended-runs), and DurableAgent adds crash recovery: with recovery.durableAgents='auto' running checkpoints are written per step and recover()/recoverActiveRuns() or POST /agents/:id/recover re-drive orphaned runs. Gaps: auto-recovery is off by default since 1.68.0, applies to DurableAgent only, and is step-granular so a tool that crashed mid-execution re-runs. Strong with non-default setup, so 4.

Agent level: opt-in per-service-call history persistence resumes a run after a crash between model calls, and workflows write `CheckpointStorage` checkpoints between supersteps (Cosmos, file), replayable since 1.13.0. The first-party durable extension goes further: conversation state is persisted in a Durable Task entity after every message, orchestrations checkpoint each agent call and replay deterministically after failure, and workflows run as durable orchestrations. Granularity is the agent call (the entity runs the full tool loop, then persists). Capability alone would merit 5 against LangGraph and CrewAI, but the extension is preview/beta (1.16.0-preview, 1.0.0b), so 4. Restored from 3.

RunState.to_json() is the durable checkpoint primitive (schema 1.18, with per-checkpoint usage and add_input for staging durable input on resume). It captures input, current agent and turn, items, model responses, guardrail results, approvals and sandbox resume state. Per-turn session persistence is automatic; per-tool-call or interruption checkpoints require you to call result.to_state().to_json() yourself, and from_json does not authenticate the snapshot.

No automatic mid-tool-call durability. Closest is RunState serialization at HITL halts: state.toString()/RunState.fromString and run(agent, state), which since 0.15.0 carries durable pendingInput, structured tool outputs and invocation evidence so approved tool calls are not re-executed. Schema is versioned (1.21) but this is not a substitute for per-tool checkpoints.

Core still has no checkpointer and true mid-tool-call resume needs Temporal/DBOS/Prefect/Restate. The first-party Harness (0.x) StepPersistence snapshots history after each settled tool batch, keeps a tool-effect ledger, and provides continue_run and inspect_recovery; tools left 'started' are flagged unknown_after_crash. Docs state automatic execution recovery is not implemented, so replay decisions stay with the host. Equal to Agno's tool-batch checkpoints at 3.

AgentRun is Serialize/Deserialize and Agent::resume(run) continues it, with a durable-approval example that writes the run to disk at CallTools. The classic runner persists nothing itself, pending tools re-execute on resume, and a run must be resumed on the same rig version. rig-ecs (experimental) adds durable tool-turn checkpoints that reissue unfinished effects. Primitive plus host wiring, so 2.

Agent(checkpointing=True) now wires the experimental checkpoint into the loop: the run stops with stop_reason='checkpoint' at after_model and after_tools and resumes via checkpointResume. The checkpoint carries position and cycle index only, so it must be paired with a session manager; per-tool granularity is the ToolExecutor's job and a crash during a tool call re-runs the tools.

Durable checkpoints exist but are marked experimental (agent.checkpointing=true, exported from @strands-agents/sdk/experimental): the run pauses with stopReason 'checkpoint' at afterModel and afterTools, and resumes via checkpointResume. The payload is only position and cycle index, not conversation state, so it must be paired with a SessionManager and you persist it yourself. HITL pauses also persist via the SessionManager; a crash mid-tool still loses that tool's work. Now equal to Strands Python at 2.

ToolLoopAgent still has no durability: a crash mid-tool-call loses the run, and the resumable-stream recipe only re-attaches a client to a stream. The first-party WorkflowAgent (@ai-sdk/workflow, on the Workflow DevKit, now in Workflow 5 beta) makes each tool execution a durable step with retries and surviving HITL approvals, and the experimental HarnessAgent offers turn-level continuation via suspendTurn. Needs the separate Workflow runtime and a different agent class, so 3.

note: no fork, Branch is sub-agent path
details: No fork/branch model. Branch is a dotted-path label (agent_1.agent_2) for parallel sub-agents, and the new IsolationScope filters task-mode sub-agent history; both are horizontal visibility filters over shared storage, not vertical forks.

First-class branching since v2.6.19: continue_run(fork=True) clones a run into a sibling with forked_from_run_id and forked_from_message_index, regenerate=True re-generates the last response with lineage, and POST /agents/{id}/sessions/{session_id}/fork forks a whole session. Lineage is stored on the run rows. Not a LangGraph-style multi-branch graph inside one session, so 4 alongside Claude and CrewAI.
No thread/branch model. To fork, clone_box the memory provider and start a fresh agent. No parent-child session relationship.

Forking supported: fork_session=True + resume=<id> creates a new session id branching from a prior session, and the top-level fork_session() helper does it from outside a client. Since 0.2.137, resume_session_at and resume_drops_turn allow forking or retrying from an earlier transcript entry safely. Not LangGraph-style multi-branch within one session, but a clean fork primitive.

forkSession(sessionId, { upToMessageId?, title?, sessionStore? }) branches at a specific message UUID with UUID remapping, and resumeSessionAt/resumeDropsTurn plus a rewind_conversation control request cover truncation and rewind. Several fork-correctness fixes landed since May. A fork is a new sessionId, so there is no multi-branch graph per session.

Branching via checkpoint fork: Crew.fork(config, branch=experiment-1) restores from a checkpoint then forks the underlying RuntimeState to a new branch label. Same for Flow.fork and Agent.fork. Conceptually similar to LangGraph's checkpoint forks.
No fork/branch model — you cannot session.fork() LangGraph-style. Thread of execution is linear; only parallel sub-agents inside one run get lanes. A new checkPointID equals a new session.

A session is a chain of snapshots linked by ParentID, and resuming from an older snapshotId effectively forks (rewind). The docs state ParentID is informational and that when history forks the most recently created branch wins; there is no branch or thread API. Parent-child history exists, but branching is implicit and experimental.

First-class: graph.get_state_history(config) returns every step; graph.update_state(config_at_step_N, values) creates a new branch from step N. Multiple branches per thread are first-class via Pregel checkpointer. The reference design for this row.
No fork/branch primitive in the OSS framework. Workflow Context resume after pause is the closest mechanic. To branch, you copy the session in your DB and feed messages to a new run.

Fork/branch is not first-class. memory.cloneThread copies a thread to a new id with message-id mapping, AgentController can clone threads, and updateThreadResourceId transfers ownership; none keeps a parent-child graph or multiple branches per thread.

No fork/branch model on AgentSession. SessionStore.get returns copies, so saving a post-run session under a new id gives simultaneous branches (the previous_response_id pattern), and workflows can resume from any checkpoint. That is copy and checkpoint-replay rather than a parent-child session tree.

Correction: AdvancedSQLiteSession ships a real branch model (create_branch_from_turn, create_branch_from_content, switch_to_branch, delete_branch, list_branches) and existed at 0.17.2 too. It is an extension backend, not part of the Session protocol, so other backends need separate session_ids with copied prefixes. RunState.to_json remains interruption resume rather than forking. Usable but backend-specific, so 3.
Single linear conversation per session. No fork / branch model and no parent_session_id. To branch you would implement a graph layer on top.

Core only offers conversation_id='new' to branch off a message_history. The first-party Harness (0.x) adds fork_run(store, run_id) that returns a history to branch from any stored snapshot, continue_run, and parent_run_id lineage linking delegate runs into a tree. There is no addressable checkpoint tree with time-travel, so it sits below LangGraph.

There is no branch API and conversation memory is linear per ConversationId. Because AgentRun is serializable, a host can copy a run and resume two copies, which is a manual fork primitive. Scored equal to Strands TypeScript's snapshot-copy fork.

Still no branching primitive: one linear conversation per (session_id, agent_id). SnapshotSessionManager now writes immutable history snapshots restorable by id, and take_snapshot/load_snapshot can hand a state blob to another agent, which mirrors Strands TypeScript's snapshot-copy fork. Rollback and copy, not a parent-child tree, so 1.
Forking is take a snapshot, hand it to another Agent instance, load it — the Snapshot is a JSON blob you copy. Not a first-class branch model.
Single linear conversation per id. No branch/fork model. No checkpoint graph. If you want branching, you implement it as N sessions in your DB.

Event-sourced model means you can List/Get sessions and walk events, but no first-party replay engine. To replay you would re-feed events to a new runner with mocked LLM responses. Tracing exports OTel.

Export via db.get_session(session_id).to_dict() and db.get_runs(...) for direct per-run export (v3). No deterministic re-execution helper: continue_run(regenerate=True) or continue_from=N re-runs from a past boundary against the live model, and agno.environments exports rollouts as SFT JSONL.
Partial: MemoryProvider.export() returns Vec<ChatMessage> and preload() re-hydrates one. Replay (deterministic re-execution of past events) is not provided — events are emitted but not stored.

Top-level list_sessions/get_session_messages/list_subagents helpers plus _from_store siblings. On-disk JSONL is transparent append-only and can be replayed by passing resume=<id> to a new query. import_session_to_store migrates local to remote. Strong export/replay among the field.

getSessionMessages and listSessions for read; deterministic replay via query({ options: { resume, sessionStore } }). resumeSessionAt: messageUuid replays up to a specific point. listSubagents lists subagent transcripts. foldSessionSummary helper for summary sidecars.

crewai replay -t <task_id> CLI lets you re-run from a saved task output. RuntimeState.event_record is fully serializable JSON, captures emission sequence, restored on from_checkpoint. crewai_event_bus._replaying contextvar signals listeners to suppress side effects. Replay is deterministic enough to reconstruct UI state but not to remake real HTTP calls.

Export via r.store.Get(ctx, checkPointID) returns the gob blob. Replay via Runner.Resume re-enters from the saved point. No deterministic replay-from-start framework (frozen RNG, recorded LLM responses) — BYO with a mock model.

A snapshot is a self-contained JSON document exported via GetSnapshot/GetLatestSnapshot and the getSnapshot HTTP companion (metadata-only reads available). Replay is resume from a snapshotId (WithSnapshotID) or an empty AgentInput to re-run the last turn on committed messages, which re-issues model calls and is not deterministic. Experimental; no session-timeline replayer in the Dev UI.

Strongest replay story. graph.get_state(config) returns current StateSnapshot; graph.get_state_history(config) returns every step. Both serialize via langgraph-checkpoint's codec. Replay: pass config['configurable']['checkpoint_id'] to graph.stream(None, config). is_replaying observable on the loop.

Context.to_dict(serializer=JsonSerializer()) / Context.from_dict is the canonical export/import pattern, and workflows 2.21+ add JsonSerializer(allowed_types=...) to allow-list deserialized types. For deterministic replay you re-feed chat_history to a new run with a mock LLM (MockFunctionCallingLLM can now replay tool-call blocks); there is no built-in record/replay harness.
