Export via storage.getMessages({ threadId }) plus resumable-stream / observe-stream endpoints. _llm-recorder package (packages/_llm-recorder) is used for test fixture replay. Solid export, replay is more test-fixture-oriented than user-facing.

AgentSession.to_dict()/from_dict() exports a typed JSON envelope (FileSessionStore writes JSON or MessagePack), and workflow checkpoints are fully replayable from initial input and HITL responses since 1.13.0. AG-UI thread snapshots can be persisted. The DurableTask replay-from-checkpoint path moved to an external repo (not re-verified), and deterministic agent replay is not provided.

RunResult.to_input_list exports a run as input items, and RunState.to_json/from_json enables cross-process state replay with an explicit schema-version contract (now 1.18). New agents.testing.ScriptedModel replays a scripted model conversation deterministically against the real Runner. No first-party replay viewer beyond the tracing dashboard.

RunResult.history and RunResult.state serialize via JSON (schema 1.21, older versions still readable), and RunState.fromString rebuilds state for replay. ScriptedModel (0.16.0) gives deterministic model replay in tests, and the Traces dashboard at platform.openai.com/traces is a hosted viewer. Solid baseline.

AgentRunResult.all_messages_json() exports the full conversation as JSON bytes, and ModelMessagesTypeAdapter round-trips messages. Replay is Agent.run(..., message_history=...) against the live model. The first-party Harness (0.x) adds continue_run/fork_run from any stored snapshot and inspect_recovery for crashed runs, but no deterministic record/replay engine.

New rig-cassette records effect logs (AgentBuilder::record_to), stamps them with agent identity, refuses replay when run spec or handlers differ, and replays saved tool outputs; provider HTTP cassettes give deterministic provider replay. Export also comes from PromptResponse.messages or the serialized AgentRun. Pre-1.0 with breaking format changes between releases (0.42 runs may not load in 0.43), and no viewer, so 4.

Agent.take_snapshot(preset=session, include=..., exclude=..., app_data=...) returns a Snapshot dataclass capturing messages, state, conversation_manager_state, interrupt_state, system_prompt. Agent.load_snapshot restores. Experimental checkpoint wraps this for durable pause/resume.

agent.takeSnapshot({ preset: 'session' }) returns a JSON-serialisable Snapshot and loadSnapshot restores it; SnapshotStorage keeps immutable history. Experimental checkpoints now let you resume at a cycle boundary, matching the Strands Python feature set. Deterministic event-by-event replay is not a primitive and re-invoking re-calls the model, so 3 like Python.
Export is JSON.stringify(messages) — you already have the messages. Replay = pass the same messages and pin model + seed. Determinism is not a first-party feature.

llmagent.New wires llminternal.Flow, the ReAct loop (request processors -> LLM call -> tool dispatch -> repeat until IsFinalResponse(), base_flow.go:127-176). In v2 the runner wraps an LlmAgent root in a single-node workflow, and agents gain ModeChat/ModeTask/ModeSingleTurn placements. New guards cut off a model that emits 10 consecutive thought-only turns. The harness owns continuation and supports agent transfer and HITL pauses out of the box.

Each Model adapter (libs/agno/agno/models/base.py) ships the LLM-tool-LLM cycle; agent.run() drives it with tool_call_limit (open bug #8304 reports the limit not stopping the loop), HITL pause/resume and continue_run. An explicit reasoning phase runs only when reasoning_model or reasoning_agent is set; reasoning=True was removed in v3. With checkpoint='tool-batch' the adapter persists a running checkpoint after each tool batch. User only configures tools and hooks.

Prebuilt ReActAgent uses the shared TurnEngine.run_turn (turn_engine.rs:148) bounded by max_turns; also ships BasicAgent and CodeActAgent variants and lets users implement custom AgentExecutor. Loop fully owned by framework.

The ReAct loop runs inside the Claude Code CLI; Python harness only ingests the JSONL frames. It is the canonical Anthropic agent loop with tool-use, hooks, permission gating, sub-agents and resume — but you cannot intercept call->tool->call at the Python layer.

Same CLI-hosted ReAct loop as the Python SDK, with hook fan-out (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolBatch at sdk.d.ts:2619), maxTurns, maxBudgetUsd, a permission step that includes the auto classifier, and SDK MCP round-trips back to the host. A Stop hook can now return additionalContext to continue the turn. Fully framework-owned, but the loop runs in the closed CLI subprocess and is visible only through .d.ts and the changelog.

The default Flow-based AgentExecutor (experimental package, plan -> todo steps -> LLM-tool loop bounded per todo) and the legacy CrewAgentExecutor both implement the LLM-tool-LLM cycle; a ReAct text path remains the fallback for LLMs without native function calling. Native tool calls from one LLM response run in parallel on a thread pool (corrected: the May claim of first-tool-only execution was wrong). Still opinionated: the default loop is a plan/todo state machine and is shaped mainly through hooks or executor_class.

adk.NewChatModelAgent compiles a fixed Init -> ChatModel -> ToolNode -> ChatModel ReAct graph (adk/react.go:354-562), now with cancel-check and after-tool-calls nodes, a MaxIterations cap (default 20), returnDirectly support, retry/failover wrappers and a middleware chain. ReAct is the default loop with no graph-building required; the legacy flow/agent/react remains for old code.

note: automatic tool loop, no explicit ReAct prompt
details: ai.GenerateWithRequest runs an automatic call->tool->call loop (turnBody, go/ai/generate.go:620-771) bounded by MaxTurns, whose default is now 50 (was 5), with parallel tool dispatch via goroutines. It relies on native function-calling, with no Reason/Act/Observe scaffolding. Errors now return a partial response with history up to the last completed tool round. Experimental aix agents wrap the same loop per user turn.

create_react_agent ships a ReAct loop but is @deprecated in favor of langchain.agents.create_agent (chat_agent_executor.py:274-277). Pregel super-step engine is the real primitive; you typically assemble the agent/tools nodes yourself for production.

ReActAgent (react_agent.py:38) parses Thought/Action/Observation for non-tool-calling models; FunctionAgent uses native function-calling. Both drive the same workflow event graph (init_run -> setup_agent -> run_agent_step -> parse_agent_output -> call_tool* -> aggregate_tool_results) bounded by max_iterations (default 20).

loop() builds an iteration workflow (llmExecutionStep -> map-tool-calls -> foreach toolCallStep -> llmMappingStep -> backgroundTaskCheckStep -> signalDrainStep -> isTaskCompleteStep -> goalStep) repeated via dowhile (loop-builder.ts:345-414, 688). It supports HITL suspension, completion scorers, a durable thread-scoped goal judged in-loop, background tasks and opt-in eager tool execution. Fully framework-owned with strong ReAct semantics.

Python's FunctionInvocationLayer (_tools.py:4888) drives the call->tool->call loop until no tool calls remain or a limit trips (max_iterations, max_function_calls, max_duration_seconds, max_consecutive_errors_per_request), then disables tools and forces a text answer. .NET delegates the loop to Microsoft.Extensions.AI's FunctionInvokingChatClient. AgentLoopMiddleware (Python) and LoopAgent (.NET) add an outer re-run loop but sit in the experimental HARNESS feature stage. Kept at 4 because the .NET loop still lives mostly outside MAF.

Runner.run / run_streamed implement the documented ReAct cycle (run.py:281-286; loop in run_internal/run_loop.py and turn_resolution.py) with handoffs, tool_use_behavior modes (run_llm_again / stop_on_first_tool / StopAtTools / ToolsToFinalOutputFunction), max_turns and resumable RunState. 0.19 adds ProgrammaticToolCallingTool, letting the model emit one program that calls several tools within a single turn (Responses API only). Framework owns every step.

run() implements the same canonical loop as the Python SDK (docstring at run.ts:693): final_output -> stop, handoff -> swap agent, else dispatch tools and re-run. Bounded by DEFAULT_MAX_TURNS=10 (null disables since 0.10.0); errorHandlers can recover from max-turns and, since 0.12.1, invalid final output. Fully framework-owned.

Agent graph nodes UserPromptNode -> ModelRequestNode -> CallToolsNode form the ReAct cycle (_agent_graph.py:582/1292/2086), terminated by end_strategy (early/graceful/exhaustive; the default is now 'graceful') and bounded by UsageLimits (default request_limit=50). Provider-invalid history is repaired automatically. First-class ReAct without user wiring.

Agent::prompt builds an AgentRunner whose drive_agent (crates/rig-agent/src/agent/engine.rs:132-460) loops model call -> tool batch until AgentRunStep::Done, bounded by max_turns (which now counts all model calls including retries). Tool calls run concurrently up to tool_concurrency, and malformed calls go through an on_invalid_tool_call repair/retry hook. No separate thought channel beyond provider reasoning blocks and the built-in ThinkTool. Effectively ReAct without an explicit thought scaffold.

event_loop_cycle (event_loop/event_loop.py:189-410) plus recurse_event_loop (:413) drive the call -> tool -> call cycle with hook fan-out (BeforeModelCall, BeforeToolCall, After*), invocation limits and tool-as-async-generator yields. Loop-shaping plugins (GoalLoop, steering handlers) and internal middleware stages sit on top. Multi-agent and conversation manager plug into the same loop.

Agent._stream() (strands-ts/src/agent/agent.ts:1513; while(true) at :1584) is the ReAct loop, with deferred append for crash safety, BeforeInvocation/BeforeModelCall/BeforeTool* hooks, InvokeModelStage/ExecuteToolStage middleware, concurrent or sequential tool executors, invocation limits and StopReason-driven termination.

generateText/streamText contain a do { } while(...) ReAct loop (generate-text.ts:867) with parallel tool execution. ToolLoopAgent defaults stopWhen to isStepCount(20); raw generateText stops after one step unless stopWhen is set (isLoopFinished, hasToolCall and custom conditions are available). Callers must configure the loop primitive explicitly.

handleFunctionCalls (internal/llminternal/base_flow.go:1306-1507) runs one task per FunctionCall through platform.RunTasks (concurrent goroutines by default; since v2.1 platform.WithTaskRunner lets the host bound concurrency or run sequentially), wrapping tool.Run in plugin and agent Before/After/OnToolError callbacks, then merges all FunctionResponse parts into one session.Event. Results are matched by FunctionCall.ID; LongRunningToolIDs surface HITL pauses. Streaming tools (functiontool.NewStreaming) bypass the tool callbacks.

Each Model adapter drives FunctionCall.execute() (tools/function.py:2589): pre_hook, per-user-keyed result cache, tool_hooks chain, entrypoint, post_hook. Model-supplied values for framework-owned parameters (run_context, identity) are dropped. Results are written back as role=tool messages and ToolExecution records, and oversized results can be offloaded to a ResultStore. Approval gating is built in via pause/requires_confirmation. Concurrency depends on each provider adapter.

ToolProcessor.process_single_tool_call_with_hooks dispatches via tool.execute(parsed_args), fires on_tool_call/on_tool_start/on_tool_result/on_tool_error hooks and emits ToolCallRequested/Completed/Failed events (tool_processor.rs:50-108). Linear name lookup; the assistant tool-use message and its results are now stored as one atomic memory batch. Hooks observe or abort only.

Three dispatch paths inside the CLI: built-in tools, MCP processes, and SDK MCP tools that round-trip back via control_request: mcp_message (Query._handle_sdk_mcp_request, _internal/query.py:753-782) to an in-process SdkMcpBridge serving @tool-decorated handlers. Results return as ToolResultBlock matched by tool_use_id. Caller cannot intercept dispatch beyond the MCP/hook surface.

Same three dispatch paths as the Python SDK; SDK MCP tools defined via createSdkMcpServer + tool() (sdk.d.ts:613, 9667) run inside the Node host. PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolBatch hooks gate every call, and tool_result blocks are matched by tool_use_id. Since 0.3.216 a tool_result_meta sidecar distinguishes denied, interrupted and cancelled calls without text parsing.

For native tool calls, both executors run the calls from one LLM response in parallel on a ThreadPoolExecutor (up to 8 workers, contextvars copied) and fall back to serial only when a tool has result_as_answer or max_usage_count; this corrects the May claim of first-tool-only execution. before/after tool-call hooks can mutate input, abort or replace the result, result_as_answer ends the loop, and tools can now return a structured ToolFailure so failed runs are not recorded as successes. Results are matched back by tool_call_id. No per-call approval primitive and the thread-pool model is less isolated than peers' task contexts.

compose.ToolsNode (compose/tool_node.go:81-92) resolves name and argument aliases, dispatches each ToolCall to the matching tool (default ExecuteSequentially=false -> goroutine per call) and emits one schema.Message per call, matched back via ToolMessage.ToolCallID == ToolCall.ID. UnknownToolsHandler covers hallucinated names; ToolArgumentsHandler and invokable/streamable middleware chains are available.

handleToolRequests (go/ai/generate.go:1572-1745) spawns one goroutine per Part.ToolRequest, runs the WrapTool chain, and folds responses in request order into a single tool-role message; tool streaming sends are serialised under a mutex. Interrupts are first-class and surface FinishReason=interrupted. A tool error now discards the whole round and returns a partial response instead of feeding the error back to the model.

ToolNode.invoke (tool_node.py:743) splits tool_calls into parallel executions via Send in v2 ReAct, appends one ToolMessage(tool_call_id=...) per tool to the messages channel. Linkage always explicit; you can also build custom dispatch nodes in any StateGraph.

parse_agent_output emits one ToolCall event per call; the workflow runtime fans them out to parallel @step call_tool invocations (base_agent.py:621-630) and aggregate_tool_results fans them in via ctx.collect_events (:680-682). Context-aware FunctionTool wiring injects the workflow Context where requested.

toolCallStep (loop/workflows/agentic-execution/tool-call-step.ts) rejects unknown or inactive tools with ToolNotFoundError, supports requireApproval/needsApprovalFn (emits a tool-call-approval chunk and suspends durably via workflow snapshots), and runs tool.execute inside beforeToolCall/afterToolCall hooks. The iteration workflow runs calls through a concurrency-controlled foreach (opt-in eagerToolExecution can start them mid-stream), and llmMappingStep runs processToolResult processors before folding results into the next prompt.

Python _try_execute_function_call_groups (_tools.py:2379) runs each call in its own task with copied contextvars, concurrently via asyncio.gather by default (also true in May) or in model order when allow_concurrent_invocation=False. .NET delegates to FunctionInvokingChatClient, where concurrent invocation is opt-in (AllowConcurrentInvocation, default false). Inline approval gating emits function_approval_request, approval responses are bound to session-recorded requests, and MiddlewareFailure aborts the batch fail-closed. Most .NET loop logic lives in Microsoft.Extensions.AI.

Dedicated dispatch modules in run_internal/tool_execution.py (function tools, local shell/shell, apply_patch, computer actions) plus MCP approvals in tool_planning.py. Each call gets a ToolContext (tool_name, tool_call_id, arguments, RunContextWrapper) and results are FunctionToolResult items threaded back via run_items_to_input_items. Since 0.17: tool_not_found_behavior, tool_name_collision_policy, per-tool timeout_seconds/timeout_behavior and custom_data_extractor.

runner/toolExecution.ts (executeFunctionToolCalls, :320) runs concurrent function tool calls up to toolExecution.maxFunctionToolConcurrency with sibling cancellation on failure, and per-tool input/output guardrails wrap tool.invoke. Unknown tool names can be returned to the model as an error (toolNotFoundBehavior). Results become RunToolCallOutputItem fed back next turn.

CallToolsNode -> ToolManager.handle_call validates JSON args with the tool schema and fires before/wrap/after_tool_validate, approval/deferral checks, then before/wrap/after_tool_execute hooks; ToolReturnPart or RetryPromptPart (on ModelRetry) is appended to the next ModelRequest. Parallel calls run as asyncio tasks with a selectable mode ('sequential', 'parallel', 'parallel_ordered_events') and a per-tool sequential barrier. Deferred tools must be revealed through tool search before they can be called.

Each call is an EffectKind::ToolCall dispatched on the effect bus: on_dispatch can patch args, skip, deny or stop, on_outcome can rewrite the result, and unknown or malformed calls go to on_invalid_tool_call (fail/retry/repair/skip). Calls run concurrently up to tool_concurrency (engine.rs:607) with results committed in call order, against a per-turn ToolCatalog snapshot and a fresh ToolContext per call; tool errors become model-visible feedback. Kept at 4 because HITL approval is a hook pattern (async on_dispatch, or serialising the AgentRun), not a first-class interrupt primitive.

ToolExecutor._stream (tools/executors/_executor.py:153) dispatches through the ExecuteToolStage middleware chain to the selected tool's stream(); tools are async generators yielding intermediate ToolStreamEvents ending with a ToolResultEvent. BeforeToolCall hooks can swap the tool, rewrite tool_use, cancel or raise an interrupt; AfterToolCall can retry (and now reports duration). Unknown tools still produce an error result through the chain, and tools can be routed to background execution.

executeTool (strands-ts/src/tools/executors/executor.ts:107) fires BeforeToolCallEvent (hooks may mutate input or name, swap the tool or cancel; the model-issued toolUseId stays authoritative), runs ExecuteToolStage middleware, streams tool.stream() as ToolStreamUpdateEvents and fires AfterToolCallEvent (hooks may mutate the result or retry). ConcurrentToolExecutor (default, Promise.race over per-tool generators) and SequentialToolExecutor are exported and swappable at runtime; interrupts are deferred until sibling tools finish.

executeTools (generate-text.ts:1632) runs approved client tool calls in parallel via Promise.all (:1666); resolveToolApproval (:1222) gates each call (approved/denied/user-approval). In streamText, tool execution is now delayed until the model call finishes. tool.toModelOutput reshapes raw output, results are ordered by tool call, per-tool timeouts are configurable, and ToolUIPart tracks each call from input-streaming through output-available.

Streaming is first-class via the same iter.Seq2[*session.Event, error] iterator; partial assistant deltas have Partial=true on LLMResponse, are not persisted, and live alongside tool/state events. RunLive adds bidi audio/video streaming via channels wrapped back into the iterator.

_run_stream is a generator yielding RunOutputEvent instances including RunContent for text deltas, ReasoningContentDelta for reasoning, and ModelRequestStarted/Completed for usage. Stream is plain Python yield with 37 distinct event types in RunEvent (run/agent.py:144-194); every streamed event now carries a monotonic event_index used for exact replay on resume.

TurnEngine.stream_with_tools accumulates LLM StreamChunks (Text, ReasoningContent, ToolUseStart/Delta/Complete, Done, Usage) and emits Event::StreamChunk per chunk plus Event::StreamToolCall. Delivered via tokio mpsc::Sender stored on Context.tx.

Token streaming is opt-in via include_partial_messages=True; SDK then yields SDKPartialAssistantMessage / StreamEvent carrying raw Anthropic SSE events. Default iterator only sees assembled assistant messages, so consumers must opt in to get token-level deltas.

Same as Python — includePartialMessages: true makes the Query iterator yield SDKPartialAssistantMessage (type: 'stream_event') carrying raw BetaRawMessageStreamEvent. Off by default; consumers re-stream over their own SSE/WS.

Crew(stream=True) projects bus LLMStreamChunkEvents into StreamChunk(content, chunk_type=text|tool_call) via CrewStreamingOutput; Flows, conversational turns and LLM.stream_events now yield StreamFrame objects (channels llm/flow/tools/messages/lifecycle) through a StreamSession. LLMStreamChunkEvent and LLMThinkingChunkEvent flow on the bus for richer observability.

Streaming is the default representation: ChatModel.Stream returns *schema.StreamReader[*schema.Message], MessageVariant.IsStreaming surfaces it in the AgentEvent, and the graph reducer concatenates chunks. Tool calls also stream via streamToolCallMiddlewares.

ai.WithStreaming(cb) invokes the ModelResponseCallback per chunk; GenerateStream returns iter.Seq2[*ai.ModelStreamValue, error]. Chunks carry Role and Index; tool results flow as role=tool chunks (go/ai/generate.go:1724-1734) and experimental tools can push partial output (tool.SendPartial). Experimental agents add a typed AgentStreamChunk (model chunk, artifact, state patch, TurnEnd).

stream_mode='messages' yields (AIMessageChunk, metadata) tuples per token via StreamMessagesHandler.on_llm_new_token (pregel/_messages.py:151-164); modes can be combined (values, updates, messages, custom, checkpoints, tasks, debug). An experimental stream_events(version='v3') adds typed projections. Per-call SyncQueue/asyncio.Queue is the in-process delivery.

_get_llm_response writes AgentStream events as tokens arrive (base_agent.py:340-350); handler.stream_events() yields them. AgentStreamStructuredOutput streams structured output progressively. Per-token delta surfaced on event.delta.

agent.stream returns MastraModelOutput exposing fullStream (ReadableStream<ChunkType>) with text-start/text-delta/text-end, reasoning-*, tool-call-delta, etc. ~50 agent chunk variants in the ChunkType union (stream/types.ts:1082). Plus per-property promises for text/usage/toolCalls.

stream=True returns ResponseStream[AgentResponseUpdate, AgentResponse]; .NET RunStreamingAsync returns IAsyncEnumerable<AgentResponseUpdate>. Each update is a partial Message; DevUI mapper splits these into OpenAI Responses-shaped frames (response.output_text.delta etc.).

run_streamed returns RunResultStreaming whose stream_events() yields StreamEvent = RawResponsesStreamEvent | RunItemStreamEvent | AgentUpdatedStreamEvent. Raw text deltas, function-call-arg deltas and reasoning deltas all surfaced via the underlying OpenAI Responses API events.

StreamedRunResult yields async iterable of RunStreamEvent including RunRawModelStreamEvent (e.g. output_text_delta) and RunItemStreamEvent for assembled items. Sub-agent stream events can be forwarded via Agent.asTool({ onStream }).

Each graph node implements async def stream(ctx) yielding PartStartEvent/PartDeltaEvent/PartEndEvent (messages.py:4112-4213); text and tool-call-argument deltas are both surfaced. Agent.run_stream_events() (an async context manager only in v2) yields AgentStreamEvent + AgentRunResultEvent, and event_stream_handler / event hooks let you intercept the stream.

agent.prompt(p).stream() returns a Stream of MultiTurnStreamItem carrying part-lifecycle StreamEvent items (Start/Text/Reasoning/Arguments/End) plus tool-call and committed-result items; hooks include on_text_delta and on_reasoning_delta, and run_channel() exposes RunEvents for hosts with their own executor. Incremental tool-argument streaming was removed in 0.43 (tool calls stream whole), and the blocking path has no stream, which keeps this at 4.

Agent.stream_async yields AsyncIterator with TextStreamEvent for token deltas, ToolUseStreamEvent for streaming tool-arg JSON, ReasoningTextStreamEvent for thinking, and ModelStreamChunkEvent for raw Bedrock chunks. Pure async generator under the hood.

Agent.stream() is a native AsyncGenerator yielding AgentStreamEvent class instances; ModelStreamUpdateEvent carries token deltas (textDelta, reasoningDelta, toolInputDelta) and ContentBlockEvent yields assembled blocks. Hooks invoked synchronously before each yield.

streamText(...).stream (fullStream is deprecated) yields TextStreamPart (26 variants including text-start/-delta/-end, reasoning-*, tool-input-*); toUIMessageStream emits wire-format UIMessageChunk (28 variants) on SSE. Both push (callbacks) and pull (iterator) surfaces exist.

A turn ends when event.IsFinalResponse() returns true (session/session.go:218-232; compaction events are explicitly not final). Every event carries InvocationID and Branch, so the 'invocation' is the modeled outer cycle, and workflow node events carry NodeInfo.Path. There is no dedicated Turn type, but boundaries are explicit and observable via the event stream.

Agno calls a turn a 'run': one run() call = one turn = one model loop with N tool calls. RunOutput.run_id (uuid4) is the turn-level identifier; in v3 each run is stored as its own agno_runs row with a run_index, and AgentSession.runs is re-attached on read. RunStarted/RunCompleted events demarcate boundaries.

TurnEngine.run_turn is one explicit turn; Event::TurnStarted{turn_number, max_turns} and Event::TurnCompleted{final_turn} bracket each iteration (autoagents-protocol/src/protocol.rs:128). max_turns cap is first-class. Among the clearest turn taxonomies in the benchmark.

ResultMessage marks the end of a turn and carries num_turns (internal LLM<->tool exchanges), stop_reason, terminal_reason (completed, max_turns, aborted_streaming, ...), total_cost_usd and model_usage. ResultMessage.origin distinguishes turns the session injected itself (background-task notifications, scheduled triggers, peers) from ones you submitted, and the run now stays open until the CLI reports idle. max_turns caps the internal loop. No explicit start-of-turn event, but boundaries are reliable.

SDKResultMessage (subtype success / error_max_turns / error_max_budget_usd / ...) ends each request loop with num_turns, total_cost_usd, usage, modelUsage, permission_denials and terminal_reason. Newer fields add result_index, queued_turn_count, user_message_uuid(s) and command_lifecycle frames (queued/started/completed/cancelled/discarded), which make multi-send turn bookkeeping observable. Still no per-model-call turn event, so kept at 4.

Inside an executor a turn is one LLM call plus its tool calls, bounded by max_iter (default 25; per todo in AgentExecutor), with no Turn object. Conversational Flows (stable since 1.15.18) add an explicit user-facing turn: one handle_turn() call bracketed by ConversationTurnStartedEvent/CompletedEvent/FailedEvent (events/types/flow_events.py:205-219). LLMCall* and Task* events give implicit boundaries elsewhere. Raised from 3 on that new stable evidence; boundaries are explicit only at flow level.

Inside one run there is still no Turn type or TurnStarted/TurnCompleted event; an iteration is the ChatModel -> ToolNode trip bounded by MaxIterations (default 20). New in v0.9, adk.TurnLoop makes the turn explicit across runs: one GenInput decision -> PrepareAgent -> agent run -> OnAgentEvents, with a TurnContext (consumed items, Preempted/Stopped channels). AgentEvent remains the smallest emitted unit, so this stops at 3 rather than 4.

Stable loop: a turn is one trip through the tool loop, counted by MaxTurns, with no Turn type; GenerateParams.Iteration now exposes the index to WrapGenerate middleware and each turn opens a generate span. Experimental agents (aix, WithExperimental gate) define a turn as one AgentInput processed to completion, ending with exactly one TurnEnd{FinishReason, SnapshotID} chunk and a turn-end snapshot. Experimental, so capped below a first-class score.

No 'Turn' object; the closest first-class boundary is the Pregel super-step. A ReAct turn is roughly: agent node (one LLM call) -> tools node (one or more ToolMessages). stream_mode='tasks' or 'updates' surfaces super-step starts/ends but you must reconstruct a 'turn' yourself.

A turn is one LLM call -> N parallel tool calls -> fan-in. max_iterations (default 20) caps the count, early_stopping_method = 'force' | 'generate' tunes overflow behavior (base_agent.py:519-541). AgentInput/AgentSetup/AgentOutput events bracket each turn on the stream.

A turn (called a 'step' in Mastra) is one full pass through the 6-step workflow chain. The fullStream emits start-step / step-finish / finish chunks demarcating turn boundaries; isStepCount-style stop conditions and isTaskCompleteStep scorers control termination.

Implicit: a run ends when the model returns no actionable tool calls, when a loop limit triggers (stop reason recorded), when an approval pause is raised, or when MiddlewareTermination/MiddlewareFailure is raised. No explicit Turn type. AgentLoopMiddleware (experimental) introduces a 'user turn' scope above individual runs, used by after_run_once_per_turn providers.

Documented: 'A turn is defined as one AI invocation (including any tool calls that might occur)' (run.py:301-302). max_turns (default 10, None for unlimited since 0.16.0) is first-class; resumed runs continue from the turn count stored in RunState, and RunState.add_input() refuses to stage input when no model turns remain. Boundaries are explicit and serializable via RunState.

A turn is bounded by prepareTurn -> model call -> resolveTurnAfterModelResponse -> applyTurnResult; state._currentTurn (runState.ts) increments at the start of each turn, and since 0.15.0 StreamedRunResult.currentTurn counts only turns that reached the model request boundary. Task and turn spans (on by default since 0.14.0) make the boundary visible in traces. maxTurns defaults to 10 (null disables since 0.10.0); the loop terminates only on next_step_final_output or next_step_interruption.

A turn is one model request plus the tool calls it produced. RunContext.run_step (_run_context.py:225) increments per step and UsageLimits bounds total requests; model-request hooks fire once per model turn even when a provider pauses mid-turn and the agent continues transparently. end_strategy controls termination, but there is no Turn lifecycle event type.

A turn is one model call plus its tool batch. AgentRunStep::CallModel{turn} carries a one-based model-call index, max_turns counts model calls including retries, and the on_model_turn_finished hook can accept, Retry or Stop each turn; the stream also emits CompletionCall and ModelTurnRetried items. Still no dedicated TurnStarted/TurnCompleted event type, so 4 rather than 5.

One event_loop_cycle is one model call plus zero-or-many tool calls, and Limits.turns formalises it ('One turn is one model call plus any tool execution that follows', types/agent.py:160-162). The invocation ends with a stop_reason such as end_turn, limit_turns, cancelled, interrupt or checkpoint (types/event_loop.py:39-52), and AfterToolsEvent.end_turn can end the turn after a tool batch. Each tool batch recurses into a fresh cycle, so cycle boundaries are observable via hooks.

A cycle is one model call plus any tools it triggered (this._meter.startCycle(), agent.ts:1600), and limits.turns counts these cycles. StopReason (types/messages.ts:710-726) now includes limitTurns/limitTotalTokens/limitOutputTokens, checkpoint (experimental), pauseTurn and refusal, so the reason a cycle ended is observable. A full invocation may span many cycles.

A step is one LLM call plus parallel tool executions; stopWhen (isStepCount, hasToolCall, the new isLoopFinished, or custom) defines termination. start-step / finish-step stream parts bracket each step and onStepStart/onStepEnd callbacks fire (onStepFinish remains as a deprecated alias). Step boundaries are first-class. HarnessAgent (experimental) uses 'until the runtime finishes the prompt' turns.

Idiomatic Go 1.23 iter.Seq2[*session.Event, error] is returned by Runner, workflow, node, agent and flow at every layer (runner/runner.go:536). Composable via for-range, no EventEmitter or callback hell. The workflow scheduler uses an internal buffered channel drained by one consumer goroutine and RunLive uses channels underneath, both re-wrapped as iter.Seq2.

_run_stream is a Python generator yielding RunOutputEvent; _arun_stream is an AsyncIterator. Events come from helpers in agno.utils.events and pass through handle_event, respecting events_to_skip and store_events. 37 distinct event types in the RunEvent enum, each stamped with a monotonic event_index at publish time.

Events emitted via mpsc::Sender<Event> on Context.tx, wrapped by EventHelper. Two consumption modes: DirectAgent fans out via EventFanout (BoxEventStream), ActorAgent uses runtime Environment.take_event_receiver or subscribe_events. DEFAULT_CHANNEL_BUFFER bound.

Single anyio memory-object stream with max_buffer_size=100 (_internal/query.py:229-231). The transport read loop pushes typed dataclasses and routes control-protocol frames aside; receive_messages pops. Backpressure via the bounded buffer means a slow consumer blocks the read loop after 100 buffered messages. One taxonomy on one iterator, deliberately simple; asyncio and trio backends both supported.

Query extends AsyncGenerator<SDKMessage, void>; consumers iterate with for-await-of and dispatch on msg.type. A single discriminated union (39 SDKMessage members, up from ~30) covers stream events, turn results, tool/sub-agent/hook/notification lifecycle. The Node process peels control-protocol frames off the CLI stdout stream and yields the rest. Same simple design as the Python SDK.

CrewAIEventsBus is a process-wide singleton with sync handlers dispatched to a ThreadPoolExecutor and async handlers on a daemon asyncio thread (events/event_bus.py:95). 163 event classes across 20 modules cover crew/agent/task/LLM/tool/memory/MCP/checkpoint/HITL/skill/reasoning/guardrail/conversation categories. Runtime state is now per run via ContextVars, and streaming sinks (StreamFrame) are scoped per execution; the singleton design still limits horizontal isolation.

*AsyncIterator[*AgentEvent] backed by an unbounded internal channel (adk/utils.go:31-60) returned by Runner; consumers loop with iter.Next(). One event per assistant/tool message; sub-agent events multiplex via RunPath. With TurnLoop the same iterator is handed to OnAgentEvents once per turn. Callback hook events are a separate subsystem and not mixed in.

Stable path: a ModelStreamCallback (one function, go/ai/generate.go:87) or GenerateStream's iter.Seq2 wrapper; tools can push partial output into the same stream. Experimental agents add AgentConnection.Receive() returning iter.Seq2[*AgentStreamChunk, error] with model chunks, artifacts, state patches and TurnEnd. No async EventEmitter or topic bus, and the stable stream still carries no lifecycle events, so kept at 3.

Per-run SyncQueue / AsyncQueue (pregel/main.py:2748, 3156) plus a parallel LangChain callback handler chain for token streaming (pregel/_messages.py:151-164). stream() yields between super-step ticks; seven StreamPart TypedDicts (values, updates, messages, custom, checkpoints, tasks, debug). Experimental stream_events(version='v3') routes the same parts through StreamTransformers into typed projections.

Two complementary mechanisms inside the workflow runtime: (1) @step routing via return / ctx.send_event with ctx.collect_events fan-in, (2) ctx.write_event_to_stream pushes onto handler.stream_events() consumer iterator. Rich event taxonomy with HITL InputRequiredEvent/HumanResponseEvent first-class.

loop() returns a web-standard ReadableStream<ChunkType>; MastraModelOutput exposes fullStream plus per-property promises (text, usage, toolCalls, finishReason, messageList). Processors push custom data-* chunks via the processor stream writer (transient chunks streamed but not persisted), and agent.subscribeToThread() gives thread-level consumers a stream that can open with thread history.

Python returns AsyncIterable<AgentResponseUpdate>; .NET returns IAsyncEnumerable<AgentResponseUpdate>. Middleware composes via with_transform_hook / with_result_hook; ContextProvider lifecycle hooks fill the gap. No in-process event bus or observer pattern — the only fan-out is middleware.

Internal asyncio.Queue[StreamEvent | QueueCompleteSentinel] (result.py:638) plus a separate _input_guardrail_queue. Three event flavors (RawResponsesStreamEvent / RunItemStreamEvent / AgentUpdatedStreamEvent) cover token deltas, run-item generation, and agent handoffs. RunHooks fire synchronously inside the loop.

Dual surface: AgentHooks/RunHooks EventEmitter for lifecycle (agent_start/end/handoff/tool_start/end, lifecycle.ts:101-181) and StreamedRunResult async iterable of RunStreamEvent (events.ts:1-83). Asymmetric but flexible.

Agent.run_stream_events() returns an AgentRunEvents async iterator (agent/abstract.py:138) that starts a background run on first __anext__ and forwards typed events over a memory stream, ending with one AgentRunResultEvent. Nodes implement async def stream(...). Interception via event_stream_handler, the ProcessEventStream capability, wrap_run_event_stream / on_event hooks and @agent.on_event listeners; tools and hooks can push custom events with ctx.emit.

Streaming returns a futures::Stream of MultiTurnStreamItem, and run_channel() returns the driving future plus a RunEvents stream (with try_next() for synchronous ticks) for hosts with their own executor. A 12-method AgentHook trait fires in both blocking and streaming runs, tracing emits invoke_agent/chat/execute_tool spans, and AgentBuilder::record_to receives every bus dispatch, stream event and outcome. The blocking path still returns only a PromptResponse, so 4 rather than 5.

Agent._run_loop is a Python async generator yielding TypedEvent instances; stream_async routes each through event.prepare and callback_handler (agent/agent.py:1432-1439). A rich hook event bus (BeforeInvocation/BeforeModelCall/BeforeToolCall/AfterToolsEvent/etc.) is layered alongside, and the whole pass is wrapped by an internal AgentStreamStage middleware.

Native AsyncGenerator<AgentStreamEvent, AgentResult, undefined> from Agent.stream(); every yielded value is a discriminated AgentStreamEvent class (16 union members). Hooks run in-line through _invokeCallbacks before each yield, so they can mutate events before they leave the generator, and InvokeModelStage/ExecuteToolStage middleware can yield extra events.

Two parallel mechanisms via notify(): push (onStart, onStepStart, onLanguageModelCallStart/End, onToolExecutionStart/End, onStepEnd, onEnd, plus onChunk/onError/onAbort on streamText; stable names since v7, experimental_* and onStepFinish/onFinish kept as deprecated aliases) and pull (streamText().stream: AsyncIterableStream<TextStreamPart>). The ai package also publishes event data on Node diagnostics/tracing channels. 26-variant TextStreamPart in-process plus 28-variant UIMessageChunk on the wire.

Native adapters are Gemini/Vertex (`model/gemini`), an Apigee Gemini proxy, and a new experimental `model/openaimodel` (Responses or Chat Completions, `BaseURL` for OpenAI-compatible endpoints; EXPERIMENTAL in `doc.go:17-18`). A name-based registry (`model.Register` / `model.NewLLM`, `model/registry.go:74,102`) is opt-in. Still no native Anthropic, Bedrock or Azure adapter (issues #225, #1097 open); BYO means implementing `model.LLM`, which forces marshalling through `genai.Content`. Up from 1 because a second first-party provider now exists; stays below genkit-go, which has many plugins.

`libs/agno/agno/models/` ships 52 provider packages (41 at 2.6.7): Anthropic (plus Bedrock/Vertex Claude), OpenAI (Chat + Responses, Azure Responses), Gemini/Vertex, Bedrock, Azure AI Foundry, Cohere, Mistral, Groq, DeepSeek, xAI, Ollama, vLLM, LiteLLM, OpenRouter, Portkey, Cloudflare AI Gateway and many more. `provider:model-id` strings resolve through a lookup table. Among the broadest native catalogues in the benchmark.

Native backends in `crates/autoagents-llm/src/backends/`: OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, xAI, Phind, Groq, Google, MiniMax, Ollama, plus local-model crates (llama.cpp, mistral-rs, experimental Burn/Onnx). The public `OpenAICompatibleProvider` (#294) covers vLLM, LM Studio, gateways and LiteLLM proxies, and the README now has a per-provider capability matrix with typed errors for unsupported features. No first-party Bedrock or Vertex backend and no LiteLLM adapter.

The SDK serves Claude models only. The CLI can reach them through the first-party API, Bedrock, Vertex, Azure Foundry, Anthropic AWS/Google Cloud, Mantle and gateways, and `ModelUsage.provider` reports which one served each model (`types.py:1333-1336`). Provider selection is CLI configuration (env vars / settings), opaque to the SDK. No OpenAI, Gemini or LiteLLM path, so multi-provider is effectively out of scope.

Claude models only, through several hosting providers: `AccountInfo.apiProvider` is `firstParty | bedrock | vertex | foundry | anthropicAws | anthropicGoogleCloud | mantle | gateway`, selected by environment or settings, not an `Options` knob. `modelUsage[*].provider` reports which provider served each model, and `Settings.allowedProviders` lets an admin restrict them. No native OpenAI, Gemini or open-weight support; the report calls this the largest gap against ADK, OpenAI Agents, Mastra, Vercel AI and LangGraph.

Native SDK providers under `lib/crewai/src/crewai/llms/providers/`: OpenAI (Chat + Responses), Anthropic, Azure, Bedrock, Gemini, Snowflake Cortex (new in 1.14.7) and an `openai_compatible` adapter (DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Ollama, vLLM, Cerebras, DashScope). Anything else routes through LiteLLM in `LLM.__new__` (`llm.py:283`), and a `litellm-removal-guide` page signals a move toward native providers. Each agent can use a different `llm`, and crew-level `manager_llm`/`planning_llm` exist.

`eino-ext/components/model/` ships adapters for OpenAI (Azure via compatible endpoint), Claude (Anthropic direct, Bedrock and Vertex with service-account JSON), Gemini (Vertex + AI Studio), Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen, Qianfan, Ark/Arkbot and OpenRouter, plus new `agentic*` adapters (OpenAI Responses, Claude, Gemini, Ark, DeepSeek, Qwen) for `AgenticModel`. Any `model.BaseModel[M]` implementation plugs in. No bundled LiteLLM-style gateway. Corrected from May: Bedrock is reachable through the Claude adapter, so it is no longer a gap; stays at 4 because Bedrock/Azure are only via Claude/compatible adapters.

Plugins now cover `googlegenai` (Gemini + Vertex), Vertex Model Garden (Claude, Llama, Mistral), `anthropic`, OpenAI (rebuilt in v1.12), `compat_oai` plugins for xAI, DeepSeek, DashScope, Kimi and Z.ai, OpenRouter as a gateway, and Ollama. Every plugin accepts a `Models` map to override capabilities for newer models. No first-party Bedrock plugin (only through anthropic-sdk-go helpers) and no LiteLLM aggregator, though OpenRouter fills that role. Up from 3 because breadth now matches eino and autoagents.

`init_chat_model("anthropic:...")` / `openai:` / `google:` / `bedrock:` / Azure / Vertex / LiteLLM-as-OpenAI-proxy — native via the langchain ecosystem, not a third-party shim. Effectively unlimited provider breadth.

`llama-index-integrations/llms/` holds 101 LLM packages: Anthropic, OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Bedrock and Bedrock Converse, Vertex, Google GenAI, Cohere, Mistral, Groq, Together, Fireworks, DeepSeek, Cerebras, Databricks, Cloudflare AI Gateway, Heroku, HuggingFace, IBM, Ollama, vLLM and more, with new-model support landing quickly. Each agent has its own `llm:`; there is no first-party `Router`. Among the broadest native coverage in the benchmark (count corrected from ~104 to 101).

A model router resolves `provider/model` strings over a generated registry of 210 providers (`packages/core/src/llm/model/provider-registry.json`, from models.dev and custom gateways), and AI SDK v4-v7 model objects are accepted directly. Gateways are pluggable (`MastraModelGatewayInterface`), custom OpenAI-compatible configs can target the Responses API, and unsupported sampling params are stripped for models that dropped them. Reasoning effort is normalised across providers. Broadest registry-based coverage in the benchmark.

Python packages and .NET libraries cover OpenAI (Responses + Chat), Foundry/Azure OpenAI, Foundry Local, Anthropic, Bedrock, Gemini (beta), Mistral (new, official SDK), Ollama, TypeSafe (alpha), plus agent wrappers for Claude Agent SDK, GitHub Copilot SDK and Copilot Studio. On .NET any `IChatClient` works; several providers are Python-only or arrive via MEAI. Solid breadth but with beta/alpha providers, so 4.

`MultiProvider` (`src/agents/models/multi_provider.py:62`) routes by string prefix: native OpenAI (Responses incl. WebSocket, Chat Completions) by default, plus `LitellmProvider` and `AnyLLMProvider` extensions that unlock 100+ providers (Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Vertex, Azure, OpenRouter). Custom prefix maps are supported via `MultiProviderMap`. Responses-only features (tool search, hosted multi-agent, compaction) are rejected on other backends, so behaviour is not fully consistent across providers.

OpenAI is first-party (Responses over HTTP or WebSocket, Chat Completions; `packages/agents-openai/`). Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Vertex, Mistral and compatible gateways flow through `@openai/agents-extensions/ai-sdk` (`aisdk(model)`), which now accepts AI SDK v2-v4 model specs and AI SDK 7. Custom providers implement `Model` + `ModelProvider`. Wide coverage but heavily mediated through the Vercel adapter, and there is no task-class router.

`pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/models/` ships native modules for Anthropic, Bedrock (and Bedrock Mantle), Cerebras, Cohere, Crusoe, GitHub Copilot, Google (Gemini API + Vertex), Groq, HuggingFace, Mistral, Ollama, OpenAI (Responses default, Chat via `openai-chat:`), OpenAI Codex, OpenRouter, Snowflake, xAI, Z.ai and TypeSafe, plus many OpenAI-compatible providers and an AI Gateway prefix. V2 removed `outlines` and the old `gemini` module (use `google`). Comprehensive first-party coverage.

`crates/rig-core/src/providers/` has 26 native providers: Anthropic, Azure OpenAI, ChatGPT, Cohere, Copilot, DeepSeek, Doubleword, Gemini, Groq, Hugging Face, Hyperbolic, llama.cpp, MiniMax, Mira, Mistral, Moonshot, Ollama, OpenAI (Chat + Responses), OpenRouter, Perplexity, Together, Venice, VoyageAI, xAI, Xiaomi MiMo and Z.ai. Bedrock and Vertex AI live in companion crates (`rig-bedrock`, `rig-vertexai`), and `ProviderRef::parse("deepseek:deepseek-chat")` allows runtime selection with a `ProviderCapabilities` check. All providers decode through one typed decoder per wire format. Galadriel and llamafile were replaced or removed.

`src/strands/models/` ships Bedrock (API-key auth, Mantle), Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenAI Responses, Gemini, LiteLLM (100+ providers), Llama API, llama.cpp, Mistral, Ollama, SageMaker and Writer, with a context-window table for known model ids. The harness adds `provider/model` string shorthand (`bedrock`, `anthropic`, `openai`, `google`, `ollama`, `litellm`) and a unified `effort` knob. Native breadth plus the LiteLLM long tail.

`strands-ts/src/models/` has `BedrockModel` (API-key auth, Guardrails), `AnthropicModel` (server-tools seam, `pause_turn` continuation), `OpenAIModel` (Responses default, Chat via `api: 'chat'`, Bedrock Mantle), `GoogleModel` and `VercelModel`, which wraps any `@ai-sdk/provider`. Smaller native surface than the Python sibling and no Mistral, Ollama, LiteLLM or SageMaker adapters, but the Vercel adapter reaches the AI SDK ecosystem. Custom providers subclass `Model`.

50+ first-party provider packages implement `LanguageModelV4` (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure, Bedrock, Vertex, Mistral, Cohere, DeepSeek, Groq, Together, xAI, Fireworks, Cerebras, Moonshot, Alibaba, ByteDance, Hugging Face, OpenAI-compatible, Open Responses, new `anthropic-aws`), plus AI Gateway as a meta-provider with plain string model ids. No LiteLLM dependency. Broadest provider-package set in the TypeScript field.

No model-fallback primitive. `retryandreflect` retries on tool errors only, and workflow `NodeConfig.RetryConfig` retries a node on the same model. Fallback on outage means an `OnModelErrorCallback` that calls another `model.LLM`, or a wrapping model like the `resilientModel` in `examples/workflow/complex` (timeout, retries, static text), all host-built. The new model registry helps construct models by name but does not route.

`FallbackConfig` (`libs/agno/agno/models/fallback.py:21-45`) keeps separate fallback model lists for `on_error`, `on_rate_limit` and `on_context_overflow`, plus a callback for instrumentation. Wire it through `Agent(fallback_config=...)` or the `fallback_models=[...]` shortcut; error classification is `ModelProviderError.classify` (v3.0.0). The fallback response is persisted in history (v2.6.22 fix). No in-stream switching: a fallback retries the whole request. Best-in-class for this row.

`FallbackLayer` (`crates/autoagents-llm/src/optim/fallback.rs:116`) composes with `RetryLayer` in a `PipelineBuilder`: `PipelineBuilder::new(openai).add_layer(RetryLayer::with_defaults()).add_layer(FallbackLayer::new(vec![anthropic, ollama]))`. `default_is_fallbackable` (`fallback.rs:93`) falls back on transport, provider, generic and capability errors but not on auth, invalid-request, JSON/tool-config or guardrail errors. `RetryLayer` now honours `Retry-After` with jittered backoff (#265). Streaming falls back only on the initial call, and the crate is pre-1.0 (v0.4.0).

`ClaudeAgentOptions.fallback_model` (`types.py:2076-2077`) gives a single-step fallback on overload or outage handled by the CLI; `ResultMessage.model_usage` shows the per-model split with cost. It is not a multi-rung chain and stays inside the Anthropic family. `ClaudeSDKClient.set_model` switches at turn boundaries (`client.py:341-362`).

`Options.fallbackModel` (`sdk.d.ts:1682`) is a single-step fallback; since 0.3.174 consumers get `system/model_fallback` for every trigger (`overloaded`, `server_error`, `last_resort`, `model_not_found`, `permission_denied`). A separate refusal fallback retries a refused response on another model and reports `system/model_refusal_fallback`. Not an N-model chain, retry policy is still not configurable (#313 open), and it stays within Anthropic-family models. `Query.setModel()` plus `PreModelSwitch`/`PostModelSwitch` hooks cover turn-boundary switching.

No built-in 'if provider A fails, use model B' configuration. New since May is same-model rate-limit retry (`llms/retry.py`: 429 and throttling errors, 3 attempts, 1-8 s backoff with jitter, honours `Retry-After`), and `Agent.max_retry_limit=2` retries the task without switching models. `llm_overlay` (`llm_overlay.py:128`) remaps models per run but is not failover. A fallback chain stays host-built (custom `BaseLLM` wrapper, LiteLLM router or gateway); kept at 1 because same-model retry gives only a small primitive.

New in v0.9: `ChatModelAgentConfig.ModelFailoverConfig` (`adk/chatmodel.go:409-414`, `adk/failover_chatmodel.go:128-167`) with `MaxRetries`, `ShouldFailover` and `GetFailoverModel`, which can also rewrite the input for the backup model. Failover wraps retry and sees `RetryExhaustedError`, keeps the last successful model, and skips on cancellation or interrupts; the summarizer has its own failover. Scored 4 on capability alone: both callbacks are mandatory and host-written, with no declarative backup list and no default error classification, unlike Pydantic AI's `FallbackModel`, Agno's `FallbackConfig`, Strands' `ModelRouter` and Mastra's model array (5). Pre-1.0 status plays no part in the score.

`middleware.Fallback{Models: []ai.ModelRef{...}}` (`go/plugins/middleware/fallback.go:59-70`) takes an ordered list and triggers on UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, ABORTED, INTERNAL, NOT_FOUND and UNIMPLEMENTED, overridable via `Statuses`; unclassified errors propagate. It composes with `middleware.Retry` (backoff and jitter) as `Retry` outside, `Fallback` inside. Since v1.12 every provider plugin classifies its SDK errors, so the middleware sees real statuses. OpenRouter's `ChatConfig.Models` adds gateway-level fallback.

`langchain-core`'s `Runnable.with_fallbacks([...])` wraps the model passed to `create_react_agent` and fires on `Exception`. Generic — no built-in rate-limit-aware or error-class policy; you encode classification yourself.

No first-class fallback primitive in core. The `llama-index-llms-cloudflare-ai-gateway` integration delegates to Cloudflare's AI Gateway; otherwise you wrap an `LLM` with retry/fallback logic yourself. Per-turn model switching works by changing the agent's `llm`, and there is no first-party router.

`model` accepts an ordered array of `{model, maxRetries}` entries (`agent/types.ts:734-776`); `llmExecutionStep` iterates `models.slice(startIndex)` and moves on after failures (`llm-execution-step.ts:1155-1183`), with OTel `MODEL_GENERATION` spans re-stamped for the fallback. Since 1.73.0-alpha.0 default error processors also retry transient provider failures. A new `ModelSelectionProcessor` (1.70.0) routes simple requests to a cheaper model, and `prepareStep`/`processInputStep` can set the model per step. First-class ordered chain with observability and routing; core is currently an alpha build on top of stable 1.72.

No fallback chain: the report confirms nothing first-party retries on another model, and .NET `RoutePersistingRoutingChatClient` defers 'content-based or failover routing' to `Microsoft.Extensions.AI` (`.cs:54-55`). New in .NET 1.19.0 (experimental) is that client itself, which holds named inner clients and stores the active route in session state so `SetActiveRoute` can switch model between turns. Python only has per-run `options={'model': ...}`. Up from 0 for the experimental routing primitive; failover remains BYO via a custom `IChatClient` decorator.

`ModelRetrySettings` + `RetryPolicy` (`src/agents/retry.py:185,210`) handle intra-provider retries with structured advice, session-history preservation and an opt-in `approve_unsafe_replay`; `ModelSettings.timeout` (0.21.1) raises a per-attempt `ModelTimeoutError`. Cross-provider fallback is not provided: wrap `Runner.run` and re-run with another `RunConfig.model`, or write a custom `Model` that delegates to a list. No per-turn model selector either.

`getResponseWithRetry` (`packages/agents-core/src/runner/modelRetry.ts:1153`) retries the same model per `modelSettings.retry`, honouring provider retry advice and replay safety (`approveUnsafeReplay`, 0.15.0); per-call `timeoutMs` (0.16.1) bounds attempts. No cross-provider fallback: wrap several `Model` instances in a custom `Model`/`ModelProvider`. Model switching happens at handoff or turn boundaries only.

`FallbackModel` (`models/fallback.py:90`) wraps an ordered list and `fallback_on=` accepts exception types, exception handlers or response handlers (fall back on a bad `ModelResponse`), default `(ModelAPIError,)`; rejected-response cost is still counted. AI Gateway adds server-side priority/failover and weighted load balancing. The `SelectModel` capability and `DecisionModel` (v2.50.0) add per-step and model-driven routing, and `before_model_request` can swap the model per request.

Rig has no automatic provider fallback: in the classic runtime the driver ends on a provider error (`crates/rig-agent/tests/runtime_model_swapping.rs:1844-1852`), and the `http_client::retry` module was removed in 0.43 (`MIGRATING.md:1396`). What is new is a routing primitive: models registered under labels (`AgentBuilder::named_model`/`model_route`) and picked per call in the `on_model_select` hook, which sees `previous_model`, so a hook can re-route the run's own retries to a backup model but not outages. Only experimental `rig-ecs` retries transient provider failures with backoff. Up from 0 for the routing primitive; outage fallback remains host-built.

New: `ModelRouter([primary, fallback, ...], strategy=...)` is accepted directly as `Agent(model=...)` (`models/routing/router.py:130-176`). The default `FallbackStrategy` does ordered failover until a candidate starts failing repeatedly, `ClassifierStrategy` picks a candidate per call with a model-based classifier, and routing runs as `InvokeModelStage.Input` middleware. It composes with `ModelRetryStrategy` (6 attempts, 4-240 s backoff, configurable retryable exceptions). Caveat: context compression sizes against `agent.model`, so candidates should have comparable windows. Up from 1; equivalent in capability to Pydantic AI's `FallbackModel` plus a classifier router.

New: `ModelRouter` (`strands-ts/src/models/routing/router.ts:129`, first shipped v1.15.0) is accepted as `Agent({ model })`, with a default `FallbackStrategy` (fewest recorded failures, ordered by declaration), an LLM-based `ClassifierStrategy` and custom `RoutingStrategy`. Any error type can trigger a switch after `DefaultModelRetryStrategy` has given up on the same model, and the retry budget resets on switch. The API is marked 'provisional and may change' (`routing/index.ts:4-5`), so capped at 4 under the maturity rule although the capability matches the Python SDK's 5. Retryable exceptions are configurable only by subclassing.

Correction: AI Gateway's `providerOptions.gateway.models` is an ordered fallback list configurable from the SDK, with `order`/`only` for provider routing (`packages/gateway/src/gateway-provider-options.ts:93-106`); the May report wrongly said it was not. Anthropic also supports its native `fallbacks` parameter via provider options, and `prepareStep` can switch model per step. For direct providers there is still no outage chain: `customProvider({ fallbackProvider })` only resolves unknown model ids, `streamRetries` retries the same model, and cross-provider fallback needs `LanguageModelMiddleware`. Up from 2 because a configurable ordered chain exists, but it depends on the hosted gateway.

Since v2.3.0, `session/compaction` ships two first-party strategies: sliding-window summarization every N invocations (`CompactionInterval`/`OverlapSize`) and token-threshold tail retention (`TokenThreshold`/`EventRetentionSize`) that fires inside the request pipeline. The default `LLMSummarizer` uses the root agent's model (60 s timeout) and is replaceable through `Summarizer`; wiring is `runner.Config.Compaction` or `ServerConfig.Compaction`. History is never deleted: a summary event with `Actions.Compaction` substitutes the covered range. Gaps keep it at 4: tail-retention summaries bypass plugins (a redaction plugin never sees them) and the report documents no reactive handling of context-overflow errors.

`CompressionManager` compresses tool results when `compress_tool_results=True`, but there is no automatic message-history compaction when context fills up. Hard caps (`num_history_messages`, `num_history_runs`) and optional session summaries are the only history controls; you compose them yourself.

`SlidingWindowMemory` with `TrimStrategy::Summarize` only marks memory as `needs_summary` on overflow; it does not summarize. Since v0.4.0 (#262) further writes fail until you call `MemoryProvider::replace_with_summary(...)`, so an un-summarized memory now makes the next turn error instead of growing. No built-in summarizer agent ships; `TrimStrategy::Drop` (FIFO) is the default.

Auto-compaction is built into the Claude Code CLI subprocess and runs when context nears the model window. The Python SDK exposes `PreCompact` hook (with manual/auto trigger discrimination and custom instructions), `autoCompactThreshold`, and `get_context_usage()` for live inspection. The algorithm itself is opaque but the integration is first-class.

Same CLI-driven auto-compaction as the Python sibling, plus `PreCompact` and `PostCompact` hooks. `SDKCompactBoundaryMessage` (`type: 'system', subtype: 'compact_boundary'`) cleanly marks where compaction happened and lists `preserved_segment`/`preserved_messages` for resume. First-class but trigger is implicit (no SDK threshold option).

`Agent.respect_context_window=True` calls `handle_context_length()` to summarize/truncate when the LLM raises a context-length-exceeded error. It is reactive only — no compaction before the limit is reached and no `PreCompact` hook. Adequate but not proactive.

Ships `adk/middlewares/summarization/` with a token and/or message-count trigger (default 160k tokens; the earlier 190k figure was wrong), a pluggable `TokenCounter`, custom summary prompt, retry/failover for the summarizer model and an on-demand `Summarize` method (v0.9). It fires inside `BeforeModelRewriteState` and replaces the message list; an optional transcript-file pointer lets the model re-read full history. Best-in-class for a Go framework.
No built-in summarization or truncation. BYO by writing a `WrapGenerate` middleware that watches `len(messages)` or token count and rewrites earlier messages into a summary.

`pre_model_hook` is the documented place to wire trimming/summarization, but the OSS runtime ships no first-party summarizer — engineers compose `trim_messages` (LangChain-core) or `langgraph-deepagents`'s third-party `compress` tool. Primitive is excellent; built-ins are missing.

`Memory` has a token-budget-driven FIFO flush — when chat history exceeds `chat_history_token_ratio * token_limit`, oldest messages are flushed into memory blocks. `ChatSummaryMemoryBuffer` (deprecated) does explicit summarization and `FactExtractionMemoryBlock` can summarize ejected messages. Usable but rougher than first-class strategies.

Three first-party layers: `TokenLimiterProcessor` drops the oldest messages over a token budget, `memory.options.messageHistory` bounds recalled history by tokens (1.68.0), and observational memory uses Observer and Reflector models to replace raw history with LLM-written notes once a token threshold is crossed (`failurePolicy`/`maxRetries`, 1.72.0). This is real LLM-summarizing compaction, which the May cell said you must compose yourself. It stays at 4 because it is a memory feature rather than a drop-in summarizing history manager and no reactive context-overflow handler is documented.

First-class `CompactionProvider` with `TruncationStrategy`, `SlidingWindowStrategy`, `SelectiveToolCallCompactionStrategy`, `ToolResultCompactionStrategy`, `SummarizationStrategy`, `TokenBudgetComposedStrategy` and `ContextWindowCompactionStrategy`; .NET adds `ChatReducerCompactionStrategy` and `PipelineCompactionStrategy`. Strategies can be set per run or on the client, and function-call/result pairs stay atomic (1.13.0). `create_harness_agent` (stable 1.12.0) wires compaction by default; .NET `HarnessAgent` made it opt-in (1.10.0, needs `MaxContextWindowTokens`/`MaxOutputTokens`). ADR 0019 documents the design.

`OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` (~521 LOC) runs server-side compaction on the OpenAI Responses API with `auto`/`previous_response_id`/`input` modes. Restricted to OpenAI; for LiteLLM/Any-LLM you BYO via `session_input_callback` or `call_model_input_filter`.

Three mechanisms, none generic: the `OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession` wrapper calls `responses.compact` after completed turns (with thresholds and a rollback item budget on main), `modelSettings.contextManagement` with `type: 'compaction'` asks the Responses API to compact server-side, and Sandbox Agents have a `compaction()` capability. Not built into the generic `MemorySession`; other providers need BYO truncation or summarization via `callModelInputFilter`.

Core ships provider-native `OpenAICompaction` and `AnthropicCompaction`, `ProcessHistory` for custom processors and `ctx.context_window_used` for trigger decisions. The first-party `pydantic-ai-harness` (0.x, now version-locked in the monorepo, 'APIs may still move') adds model-agnostic `TieredCompaction`, `SummarizingCompaction`, `SlidingWindowCompaction`, `ClearToolResults` and `FallbackCompaction`, triggered at a `max_fraction` of the model's context window. Capped at 4 because the provider-agnostic strategies live in a 0.x package.

The first-party `rig-memory` crate provides `SlidingWindowMemory`, `TokenWindowMemory`, `DemotingPolicyMemory` and `CompactingMemory`, which prepends a rolling summary of demoted history through the `Compactor` trait. The built-in `TemplateCompactor` is non-LLM, so an LLM summarizer is BYO, summaries are process-local, and compaction runs on memory `load` (run start), not mid-run. Mid-run compaction needs a hook returning `RequestPatch::history`. Partial primitive, production use is host-built.

`SlidingWindowConversationManager` (default window 40, `should_truncate_results=True` by default, optional `per_turn`) and `SummarizingConversationManager` are first-class, triggering after each cycle and reactively on `ContextWindowOverflowException`. A new `context_manager='auto'|'agentic'|config` parameter adds proactive summarization at 85% utilization and a model-driven mode; its types are exported as experimental. `NullConversationManager` is forced for stateful models.

`SlidingWindowConversationManager` (window 40) is the default, with `SummarizingConversationManager` and `NullConversationManager` also shipped; reduction is reactive on `ContextWindowOverflowError`, and proactive compression only runs with `proactiveCompression: true` (threshold 0.7). A newer `ContextManager` (`@experimental`) adds a strategy pipeline with offload, summarize at 0.85 utilization and an emergency drop, plus an agentic mode. Kept at 5 because the stable managers and summarizer are built in; the May claim that proactive triggering is default was wrong.

No automatic compaction and no built-in summarization step. A documented manual pattern checks a token estimate in `prepareStep` and returns `messages: pruneMessages({...})`; because `prepareStep` message overrides now persist, the pruned list carries forward. `pruneMessages` is a small first-party primitive, but the trigger and any summarizer are BYO; the experimental `HarnessAgent` only exposes `session.compact()` where the underlying runtime supports it.

Twelve callbacks across plugins and `llmagent`: `OnUserMessageCallback`, `BeforeRunCallback`, `AfterRunCallback`, `OnEventCallback`, `BeforeAgentCallback`, `AfterAgentCallback`, `BeforeModelCallback`, `AfterModelCallback`, `OnModelErrorCallback`, `BeforeToolCallback`, `AfterToolCallback`, `OnToolErrorCallback`. Plugins fire across all agents and short-circuit agent-level callbacks; per-agent variants exist too. Caveat: streaming tools bypass the tool callbacks, and tail-retention compaction summaries bypass plugins.

`pre_hooks`, `post_hooks`, `tool_hooks` (middleware chain), per-tool `pre_hook`/`post_hook`/`tool_hooks`, `BaseGuardrail` subclasses, and `@hook(run_in_background=True)`. Covers run, tools, and per-tool slots; no per-LLM-call slot or `SessionStart`.

`AgentHooks` trait with 10 methods (`on_agent_create`, `on_run_start/complete`, `on_turn_start/complete`, `on_tool_call`, `on_tool_start`, `on_tool_result`, `on_tool_error`, `on_agent_shutdown`). Covers the lifecycle adequately but most slots are read-only.

11 first-class hook events (`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PostToolUseFailure`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SessionStart`, `Stop`, `SubagentStop`, `SubagentStart`, `PreCompact`, `Notification`, `PermissionRequest`). Hook matchers can target tool names; outputs schema is rich.

33 hook events from `HOOK_EVENTS`, including the Python set plus `PostToolBatch`, `UserPromptExpansion`, `SessionEnd`, `StopFailure`, `PostCompact`, `PermissionDenied`, `Setup`, `TeammateIdle`, `TaskCreated/Completed`, `Elicitation`/`ElicitationResult`, `ConfigChange`, `WorktreeCreate/Remove`, `InstructionsLoaded`, `CwdChanged`, `FileChanged` and the new `PreModelSwitch`, `PostModelSwitch`, `DirectoryAdded`, `MessageDisplay`. Matching hooks run in parallel on the original payload. Strictly the broadest surface in the comparison.

Since 1.15.3 one dispatcher (`hooks/dispatch.py`) exposes 10 interception points: EXECUTION_START/INPUT/OUTPUT/EXECUTION_END, PRE/POST_STEP, PRE/POST_MODEL_CALL and PRE/POST_TOOL_CALL, with `@on(point, agents=[...], tools=[...])` filters, `HookAborted`, `HookDispatchedEvent` telemetry and the legacy `before/after_llm_call` families as adapters. Crew callbacks, a 163-event bus and an httpx `BaseInterceptor` sit alongside. Still no `SessionStart`, no `PreCompact`, and hooks are sequential and synchronous.

Three layers: graph-level `callbacks.Handler` (5 timings), the deprecated `AgentMiddleware` struct, and the `ChatModelAgentMiddleware` interface with 9 methods (`BeforeAgent`, new `AfterAgent`, `BeforeModelRewriteState`, `AfterModelRewriteState`, four `Wrap*ToolCall` variants, `WrapModel`). Per-run `WithAfterToolCallsHook` and `TurnLoop` hooks add turn-level slots. Embed `BaseChatModelAgentMiddleware` for no-op defaults.

Three composable middleware points: `WrapGenerate` (per tool-loop iteration), `WrapModel` (per model API call), `WrapTool` (per tool exec). No traditional `SessionStart`/`BeforeMessage`/`AfterMessage`/`OnTurnComplete` lifecycle hooks; intentionally hook-light.

`pre_model_hook` and `post_model_hook` on the prebuilt `create_react_agent` (read+mutate+block+branch), `wrap_tool_call`/`awrap_tool_call` around every tool dispatch (override request, return synthetic ToolMessage, re-execute), `GraphCallbackHandler` for interrupt/resume, plus full LangChain `BaseCallbackHandler` observe-only set.

No Claude-style hook system. You subclass `BaseWorkflowAgent`'s `@step` methods (`init_run`, `setup_agent`, `run_agent_step`, `parse_agent_output`, `call_tool`, `aggregate_tool_results`) and use `FunctionTool(callback=...)`. Dispatcher tracing is read-only.

`Processor` interface with 9 method slots (`processInput`, `processInputStep`, `processLLMRequest`, `processLLMResponse`, `processOutputStream`, `processOutputStep`, `processToolResult`, `processOutputResult`, `processAPIError`), agent/run-level `beforeToolCall`/`afterToolCall` tool hooks (1.42.0), and loop callbacks (`onChunk`, `onStepFinish`, `onFinish`, `onError`, `onAbort`, `onIterationComplete`, delegation callbacks). Covers every stage of the loop.

`AgentMiddleware`, `ChatMiddleware` and `FunctionMiddleware` wrap run, model call and tool call, plus `ContextProvider` with `before_run`/`after_run` only (the May cell wrongly listed `before_chat_call`/`after_chat_call`). `HistoryProvider`, `MessageInjectionMiddleware`, `AgentLoopMiddleware`, `ToolApprovalMiddleware`, `MiddlewareFailure` (fail-closed) and an experimental AGENT-HOOKS bundle (agent_startup/input/pre_model_call/post_model_call/pre_tool_call/post_tool_call/output/agent_shutdown) complete the surface; .NET has equivalent builder hooks.

Global `RunHooks` and per-agent `AgentHooks` with `on_llm_start/end`, `on_agent_start/end`, `on_handoff`, `on_tool_start/end`. Plus `call_model_input_filter`, `session_input_callback`, `tool_error_formatter`, and four guardrail decorators (`input`, `output`, `tool_input`, `tool_output`).

`RunHooks`/`AgentHooks` with `agent_start/end/handoff/tool_start/tool_end`, `InputGuardrail`/`OutputGuardrail`/`ToolInputGuardrail`/`ToolOutputGuardrail`, plus `callModelInputFilter`, `sessionInputCallback`, `toolErrorFormatter`, `errorHandlers`, `HandoffInputFilter`. No `SessionStart` or PreCompact.

`Hooks` capability gives decorator sugar over 20+ slots: `before_run`/`after_run`/`run`(wrap)/`run_error`, per-node variants, `before_model_request`/`after_model_request`/`model_request`(wrap), `prepare_tools`/`prepare_output_tools`, `before/after_tool_validate`(+wrap), `before/after_tool_execute`(+wrap), `before/after_output_validate/process`(+wrap), `deferred_tool_calls`, `run_event_stream`, `event`. Tool hooks support filtering and timeouts.

`AgentHook` (12 methods in `rig-agent/src/agent/hook.rs`) covers `on_run_start`/`on_run_settled`, `on_model_select`, `on_completion_call`, `on_model_turn_finished`, `on_invalid_tool_call`, three streaming-delta callbacks, and `on_dispatch`/`on_outcome` around completions and tool calls (optionally memory and retrieval effects). Hooks fold sequentially with an `observes(kind)` opt-in; sibling tool calls can interleave. Breadth matches ADK Go; there is no session-start-with-context or pre-compaction event and no way to emit extra tool calls. The old `PromptHook` trait is removed.

Lifecycle events (`AgentInitializedEvent`, `BeforeInvocationEvent`, `AfterInvocationEvent`, `MessageAddedEvent`, `MessageUpdatedEvent`, `BeforeModelCallEvent`, `AfterModelCallEvent`, `BeforeToolsEvent`, `BeforeToolCallEvent`, `AfterToolCallEvent`, `AfterToolsEvent`) plus multi-agent events and Bidi events. An interventions layer (`Proceed`/`Deny`/`Guide`/`Confirm`/`Transform`) and ordered callbacks (`order=`) sit on the same points. Per-turn middleware (`InvokeModelStage`/`ExecuteToolStage`) exists but is private API in Python. Sync and async callbacks supported.

Hookable events for invocation, model, tools batch, individual tool call, streaming, message, result and interrupt events plus 9 multi-agent events, ordered by the `HookOrder` enum (now with `MODEL_ROUTING`). New public middleware (`agent.addMiddleware`, stages `InvokeModelStage` and `ExecuteToolStage`) wraps each model and tool call, and typed intervention handlers return proceed/deny/guide/confirm/transform. Hooks always fire outside middleware; the README says middleware will replace hooks long term.

`prepareCall` and `prepareStep` (mutate model/tools/instructions/messages), `onStart`, `onStepStart`, `onLanguageModelCallStart/End`, `repairToolCall` (now stable), `experimental_refineToolInput`, per-tool `onInputStart/Delta/Available`, tool approval functions or `opaPolicy`, `onToolExecutionStart/End`, `onStepEnd`, `onEnd`, plus `LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams/wrapGenerate/wrapStream`. Callbacks for one event run concurrently with errors swallowed, and the execution-end callbacks are read-only. Broad and granular.

Callbacks can mutate `*model.LLMRequest`, tool `args map[string]any` in place, and `result map[string]any`. Returning a non-nil value short-circuits the underlying call (e.g. LLM cache or tool fast-path). `OnModelErrorCallback` and `OnToolErrorCallback` can convert errors to responses/results.

`pre_hooks` mutate `run_input` and raise `InputCheckError` to block; `post_hooks` mutate `run_output` and raise `OutputCheckError`. `tool_hooks` form a nested chain that can short-circuit, retry and transform results, but arg forcing only works by mutating `args` in place: kwargs passed to `next_func` are ignored and zero-arg calls seed a fresh `{}` (`tools/function.py:2485-2496`). There is no per-LLM-call mutation hook, and guardrails are re-ordered first only in global background mode.

Hooks are observe-and-abort. `on_run_start` and `on_tool_call` can return `HookOutcome::Abort` but receive immutable `&Task`/`&ToolCall`. None of the mutate scenarios (force tool args, summarize tool result, rewrite messages) are supported as first-party; you must wrap the executor or hide context inside tool struct fields.

Hooks can return `updatedInput`, `updatedToolOutput`, `additionalContext`, and `decision: 'block'` / `permissionDecision: allow|deny|ask|defer`. `continue_: False` halts. The in-flight messages array is not directly mutable from Python — the CLI owns it — so message-array surgery is restricted to `additionalContext`.

Same `updatedInput`/`updatedToolOutput`/`additionalContext`/`decision: 'block'`/`permissionDecision` surface, plus `AsyncHookJSONOutput` to defer with `asyncTimeout`. Matchers fire per tool name; last-wins merge on `updatedInput`. Messages list still owned by the CLI.

`before_llm_call` and `before_tool_call` mutate `ctx.messages`/`ctx.tool_input` in place and return `False` or raise `HookAborted` to block; `after_llm_call`/`after_tool_call` return a `str` to replace the response or result; EXECUTION_START/INPUT/OUTPUT replace payloads. Only `HookAborted` propagates: any other hook exception is swallowed fail-open. Event listeners cannot block.

`BeforeModelRewriteState` mutates the message list before each model call; `WrapModel` can replace the model entirely (routing, retry, mid-stream tool filtering); `WrapInvokableToolCall` wraps tool endpoints to mutate args and results; `BeforeAgent` mutates Instruction/Tools/ReturnDirectly. Real-world `summarization` middleware proves the mutation depth.

`WrapGenerate` mutates `params.Request.Messages` (Skills uses this for `injectSkillsPrompt`); `WrapTool` mutates `params.Request.Input` and rewrites `resp.Output`/`resp.Content`; `WrapModel` short-circuits with cached responses. Hooks can interrupt and emit extra stream chunks via `params.Callback`.

`pre_model_hook` emits `messages` or `llm_input_messages` (one-shot) updates; `post_model_hook` can append `AIMessage` with new `tool_calls`, route, block, or short-circuit. `wrap_tool_call` can return synthetic `ToolMessage` without executing, call `execute()` zero/one/many times, return `Command(goto=Send(...))` to fan out. `ToolRuntime`/`InjectedState` strip+inject trusted args.

note: subclass to mutate, callback to rewrite
details: Subclassing `@step` methods (`init_run`, `setup_agent`, `run_agent_step`, `call_tool`, `aggregate_tool_results`) gives full read/mutate/block/branch. `FunctionTool(callback=...)` can return a new `ToolOutput` or string to override. `partial_params` only fills defaults — LLM values still win. Verbose vs. dedicated hooks.

`processInputStep` replaces `model`/`tools`/`toolChoice`/`activeTools`/`messages`/`systemMessages`/`providerOptions`/`modelSettings`/`structuredOutput`; `processLLMRequest` returns `{ response }` to skip the LLM; `processOutputStream` drops or rewrites chunks; `processToolResult` rewrites results; `abort({ retry: true })` self-corrects with feedback. Tool input has no documented rewrite path: `beforeToolCall` can block (`{ proceed: false, output }`) but has no `updatedInput`, `processOutputStep` only receives `toolCalls` to validate or abort, and arg forcing relies on in-place mutation (undocumented) or rebuilding wrapped tools per step. Lowered from 5 to 4: Rig's first-class `rewrite_tool_args`/`rewrite_tool_output` and ADK Go's documented in-place args mutation keep 5, while Mastra sits with Vercel AI (`experimental_refineToolInput`) and CrewAI at 4.

`AgentMiddleware`/`ChatMiddleware` mutate `AgentContext.messages` and can raise `MiddlewareTermination`; `FunctionMiddleware` mutates `arguments` and `result` around tool calls; `ContextProvider.before_run` injects instructions/context messages/tools/middleware. Sequential chain via `await call_next()`.

note: filter mutates input, output guardrail replaces
details: `call_model_input_filter` is the only first-class mutate-before-LLM hook (replaces `input`/`instructions`). `RunHooks`/`AgentHooks` are read-only (raise to abort). `@tool_output_guardrail` + `reject_content(message=...)` replaces tool results. No mutate-args hook for tool input; rely on `ctx.context` reads inside the function.

`callModelInputFilter` mutates `{ input, instructions }` before each model call and `sessionInputCallback` replaces merged input. `RunHooks`/`AgentHooks` are read-only. Tool guardrails (`ToolGuardrailBehavior` = allow | rejectContent | throwException) can block a call or replace its output with a string, but cannot rewrite LLM-emitted arguments or restructure results; the May report overstated this. Adequate but narrower than Mastra or the Claude SDKs.
