Every stage exposes `before_*`/`after_*`/`wrap_*` variants. `SkipModelRequest(response)`, `SkipToolValidation(args)`, `SkipToolExecution(result)` short-circuit cleanly. `before_model_request` mutates the request; `before_tool_validate`/`before_tool_execute` mutate args; `after_tool_execute` returns replacement results. Fold semantics across hooks and recovery via `on_*_error`.

`on_dispatch` can patch tool args (`DispatchAction::rewrite_tool_args`) or deny, `on_outcome` can replace tool results (`rewrite_tool_output`), `on_completion_call` returns a per-turn `RequestPatch` (preamble, history, `active_tools` allow-list, context, params), `on_run_start` rewrites the prompt, `on_model_turn_finished` can retry and `on_model_select` routes models. Patches merge in registration order (`active_tools` intersect). The May cell scored 0 because the old `PromptHook` was read-only; history patches are per-turn only and there is no way to emit extra tool calls.

note: writable events incl. tool_use/result, retry, resume
details: `BeforeInvocationEvent.messages`, `BeforeToolCallEvent.{cancel_tool, selected_tool, tool_use}`, `AfterToolCallEvent.{result, retry}`, `AfterModelCallEvent.retry`, `AfterInvocationEvent.resume` are all writable. Interrupts via `InterruptException`. Hooks can mutate `agent.messages` directly. Strong mutate+block surface.

`BeforeToolCallEvent` mutates `toolUse.{name,input}`, sets `selectedTool`, `cancel` or `interrupt(...)`; `AfterToolCallEvent.result` is writable plus `retry`; `AfterInvocationEvent.resume` re-enters the loop. Public `InvokeModelStage` middleware can rewrite messages, system prompt, tool specs, tool choice and model per call, and `BeforeModelCallEvent` can mutate `agent.messages`. Correction: `BeforeInvocationEvent` fires before the new user message is appended, so expanding the input needs middleware or `resume`.

note: prepareStep mutates almost everything; tool result via toModelOutput
details: `prepareStep` returns overrides for `model`, `toolChoice`, `activeTools`, `instructions`, `messages`, `toolsContext`, `runtimeContext`, `providerOptions`, `sandbox`. `experimental_refineToolInput[name]` mutates tool args (Q6.4). Tool result mutation is per-tool only via `toModelOutput`; no harness-level post-tool mutate hook. `LanguageModelMiddleware.wrapGenerate` can block/retry/cache.

No automatic breakpoint placement. `model.LLMRequest.Config` (`*genai.GenerateContentConfig`) can include `CachedContent` (a Gemini feature) but you configure it by hand; no stable-prefix preservation policy ships.

`Claude(cache_system_prompt=True, extended_cache_time=True, cache_tools=True)` and `system_prompt_blocks=[SystemPromptBlock(text=..., cache=True, ttl='1h')]` place breakpoints on the system prompt and last tool, and `cache_read_tokens`/`cache_write_tokens` appear in metrics. Support is Anthropic-specific, OpenAI caching is provider-automatic, and there is no automatic breakpoint placement on history messages. Comparable to the OpenAI-only cache-key support in the OpenAI SDKs.

`CacheLayer` in `autoagents-llm/src/optim/cache.rs` is a response-level cache for identical message+tool+schema inputs, not a stable-prefix breakpoint mechanism. Re-verified in the refresh: no `cache_control` marker anywhere in `autoagents-llm`. Only the llama.cpp provider reuses KV-cache prefixes (v0.4.0), which helps local inference only.

The CLI handles Anthropic prompt caching automatically and surfaces cache tokens on `AssistantMessage.usage` and per model. `SystemPromptPreset.exclude_dynamic_sections` strips per-user sections out of the system prompt and re-injects them into the first user message for cross-user cache hits. New `snapshot` (default true since 0.2.153) keeps the first-recorded system prompt across resumes so the cached prefix survives; prompt edits on resumed sessions are ignored unless `snapshot: False`. Manual breakpoint placement is BYO (the CLI owns it).

Four mechanisms: `systemPrompt: string[]` with `SYSTEM_PROMPT_DYNAMIC_BOUNDARY` splits a static cacheable prefix from a dynamic suffix (fixed for Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry in this window); `excludeDynamicSections: true` strips per-user content for cross-user cache hits; `reloadPlugins({ holdOnCacheImpact })` and the `PreModelSwitch` hook report cache warmth and estimated re-cache cost; and the CLI places breakpoints on stable-prefix content. Cache stats appear on `SDKResultMessage.usage` and `modelUsage`.

`mark_cache_breakpoint(message)` helper is auto-applied in `_setup_messages` to tag the system prompt and per-task user prompt as stable prefixes. Provider adapter translates to Anthropic `cache_control: {type: 'ephemeral'}`; OpenAI/Gemini cache implicitly. Solid but you cannot add your own breakpoints from a `before_llm_call` hook without re-applying the marker.

note: Claude auto cache control, stable prefix
details: The eino-ext Claude adapter supports explicit breakpoints (`SetMessageBreakpoint`, `SetToolInfoBreakpoint`), per-request `WithAutoCacheControl`, and a new `Config.AutoCacheControl` that places breakpoints on system, tools and the last user message every request; the agentic adapters (Claude, Ark, OpenAI Responses, Gemini) gained cache-control support. The framework keeps history order stable and documents that changing tools in `WrapModel` breaks the cache. Automatic only for Claude with the option set, manual elsewhere; the May claim of no helper was wrong. `CachedTokens` and `CacheWriteTokens` expose hit rate.
Plugin-specific not generic: `googlegenai/cache.go` lets you attach `cachedContents`. No generic `cache_control` mechanism across providers — each plugin handles its own cache features.

Engineers wire Anthropic `cache_control` flags into specific `SystemMessage`/`HumanMessage` content blocks; `pre_model_hook` is where you ensure the stable-prefix invariant. No automatic breakpoint placement.
`ChatMessage` supports a `CachePoint` content block which Anthropic/OpenAI providers honor — but the framework does not auto-place breakpoints; the developer inserts them. Not first-class.

Processor pipeline supports caching via `processLLMRequest` returning `{ response: <cached chunks> }` (skip LLM entirely). Built-in `ResponseCacheProcessor` ships. Anthropic-style cache breakpoints are not auto-managed — you place them in the system prompt yourself or via a processor.

The first-party OpenAI client exposes `prompt_cache_key`, `prompt_cache_retention` and `prompt_cache_options` with `mode='explicit'` honouring per-part `prompt_cache_breakpoint` markers (1.12.1); the Anthropic client takes structured system blocks carrying `cache_control`. There is still no generic stable-prefix controller, so placement is manual, and cache read/write tokens surface in `UsageDetails`. Scored 3 in line with the other OpenAI-only cache support.

`PromptCacheKeyResolver` generates a per-run cache key threaded through model settings to opt into OpenAI prompt-caching pricing; the key survives `RunState` round trips. `Usage.input_tokens_details` now tracks `cache_write_tokens` as well as `cached_tokens`. Anthropic `cache_control` is not natively wired; via LiteLLM you pass provider-specific extras.

`modelSettings.promptCacheRetention` (`in-memory` | `24h`) and, since 0.13.2, `promptCacheOptions: { mode: 'implicit' | 'explicit', ttl }` opt into OpenAI prompt caching, and the AI SDK adapter forwards retention (0.15.0). `previousResponseId`/`conversationId` keep a stable server-side prefix. No Anthropic-style `cache_control` breakpoint API; scored in line with the Python SDK's OpenAI-tier support.

Cache breakpoints are first-class: the `CachePoint` message part, `cache_write_tokens`/`cache_read_tokens` on usage, and provider flags. `InstructionPart` is split into static versus dynamic so the stable prefix stays cache-friendly, and Harness capabilities inject without busting the cache; `WarnOnCacheBusts` (Harness, 0.x) warns when hit rate collapses. Breakpoints are mostly automatic per provider; explicit placement is via `CachePoint`.

Anthropic `with_prompt_caching()` places breakpoints on the system prompt, last tool and last message, `with_automatic_caching()`/`_1h()` advances a top-level breakpoint with the conversation, and `with_static_prefix_cache_ttl` sets a separate TTL for tools+system; Bedrock mirrors it. Gemini now creates explicit caches automatically for long runs (`CacheBook`), and OpenAI Responses cache parameters are preserved. `Usage` and `CacheCost` expose hit rate, and 0.43 fixed byte-stability bugs. Opt-in per provider with no agent-level breakpoint planner, hence 4; the May cell missed the Anthropic helpers.

`CacheConfig` (`strategy='auto'`, `ttl`, `system_prompt_ttl`, `tools_ttl`, `cache_key`) detects support and injects `cachePoint`s on Bedrock, Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral, Ollama, Writer, SageMaker and llama.cpp; the harness enables it by default. Manual `cachePoint` blocks still work, and injected content (skills XML, memory, `ContextInjector`) is placed behind cache points. Same level as the TypeScript SDK.

Per-provider `CacheConfig` (`strategy`, `ttl`, `toolsTTL`, `systemPromptTTL`, `messagesTTL`, `cacheKey`) injects cache points on tools, system prompt and the last user message for Bedrock and Anthropic, maps `cacheKey`/`ttl` to OpenAI's `prompt_cache_key`/retention, and keeps injected dynamic blocks behind cache points via `dynamicTrailingBlocks`. TTLs must be non-increasing across tools, system and messages. Placement is automatic once configured.

`LanguageModelUsage.inputTokenDetails` exposes `noCacheTokens`/`cacheReadTokens`/`cacheWriteTokens`, which is better visibility than most stacks. The SDK still places no breakpoints: set `providerOptions.anthropic.cacheControl` yourself or via `LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams`. New `toolOrder` and code-mode `toolDiscovery: 'conversation'` help keep the tool prefix stable, while direct-call tool search can invalidate it.

No first-party clearing primitive. `AfterToolCallback` can replace the result map before it is persisted and `BeforeModelCallback` can rewrite `req.Contents` (prompt only, not storage). Compaction eventually folds old tool output into a summary, and `LLMSummarizer` truncates long tool content in the transcript it summarizes (`MaxToolContentChars`). BYO.

`offload_tool_results=True` (or `ResultStore(threshold_chars, preview_lines, ttl_seconds)`) writes results over 16k characters to AgentFS and leaves a preview, size and `result_id` in the message, with `read_result`/`search_result` tools to page back. `compress_tool_results` + `CompressionManager` summarize in place, and `store_tool_messages=False` drops tool messages from the stored run. Stable since v3.0.0 and aimed exactly at this row.
Tool results go directly into `MemoryAdapter::store_tool_interaction`; the only knob is the sliding-window size which evicts old messages but does not target tool results specifically.

`PostToolUse.updatedToolOutput` replaces a tool's output with a stub or summary before the model sees it, for any built-in or MCP tool; built-in tools require the replacement to match their output schema or the original is kept. There is no API to clear a result already in visible history; `resume_session_at` truncates and resumes instead. Ergonomic and first-class, but no stash or handle helper.

`PostToolUse.updatedToolOutput` (any tool) and `updatedMCPToolOutput` (MCP, deprecated) replace the tool result in-place before it reaches the model — the canonical use is truncating/summarizing/redacting. `getContextUsage()` and per-category breakdown help decide when to clear.
`after_tool_call` returns a `str` to replace the result — e.g. `return ctx.tool_result[:5000] + '... [truncated]'` for any oversized output. Manual but ergonomic; the docs show the exact pattern.

`adk/middlewares/reduction/` has two phases: truncation right after a tool returns (full content to the configured `Backend`, truncated notice naming the read tool) and a clear phase in `BeforeModelRewriteState` that offloads older tool calls and results to stubs once `MaxTokensForClear` is exceeded, with exclusion lists and custom handlers. It supersedes the older filesystem-middleware `large_tool_result.go`, which is marked deprecated. First-party, configurable, zero-code.
Filesystem middleware has a `fileUnchangedStub` to short-circuit re-reads of unchanged files. No generic clearing/summarization primitive for tool results — BYO.

Two manual primitives: emit `RemoveMessage(id=...)` from a node or `pre_model_hook` (or return a replacement with the same id) to delete or replace a `ToolMessage` in the `messages` channel, and use `wrap_tool_call` to rewrite the `ToolMessage` before it reaches state. `BaseStore` is a natural stash. No first-party 'clear old tool results' policy; `TracePolicy` only trims what is traced.
`FunctionTool(callback=...)` or `async_callback=...` can return a summary string and stash the full payload elsewhere. Manual; no first-party clearing primitive.

Tools declare `toModelOutput(output)` to give the LLM a truncated view while the full result stays in storage. New `processToolResult` (1.57.0) rewrites a result in history before the next LLM call via `messageList.updateToolInvocation`, and `ToolCallFilter` removes tool-call/result pairs from later prompts. Kept at 4: the primitives are hooks and filters rather than a threshold-driven clearing policy like Eino's reduction middleware.

`ToolResultCompactionStrategy` explicitly clears or summarizes tool results once they exceed a threshold — a first-party compaction strategy dedicated to this benchmark row. Wired into `CompactionProvider` so it runs automatically.

`@tool_output_guardrail` with `reject_content(message=summary)` replaces a tool result with a synthetic message — usable for clearing/summary. Codex/Shell tools have `tool_output_trimmer` extension that truncates output before it goes back to the model. Solid but not branded as such.

No first-party clearing primitive. `ToolOutputGuardrail` can replace a tool output with a message via `rejectContent(message)` (string only, no structured rewrite), and `callModelInputFilter` can drop or replace items before each call without changing stored history. `SessionHistoryRewriteAwareSession.applyHistoryMutations` only supports `replace_function_call`. Sandbox Agents offer a workspace for large outputs.

`after_tool_execute` returns a replacement value at production time, and the first-party Harness `ClearToolResults(max_tokens, keep_pairs=3)` replaces the oldest results with a placeholder in place; `ProcessHistory` can rewrite older `ToolReturnPart`s. Capped at 4 because the policy-driven clearing lives in the 0.x Harness package.

`on_outcome` can replace a tool result before it enters history (`OutcomeAction::rewrite_tool_output`), and `RequestPatch::history` sends a modified history for one model call. Clearing older results later is per-turn only and there is no stub or handle API or threshold policy. The May cell scored 0 because the old hook was read-only.

`SlidingWindowConversationManager(should_truncate_results=True)` (default) truncates oversized tool results, `context_manager='auto'` truncates results above about 1,500 tokens (strategies `drop`, `truncate`, `summarize`; experimental types), and the vended `ContextOffloader` plugin moves large results to `Storage` with a retrieval handle and turn-based eviction. Agentic mode lets the model call `truncate_context` itself.

`ContextOffloaderPlugin` registers an `AfterToolCallEvent` hook that stores large payloads in configurable `Storage` keyed by `mem_<id>` and replaces in-context content with a preview + reference. Plus sliding/summarizing managers as a secondary path.

`pruneMessages({ toolCalls: 'before-last-N-messages' | [{ type, tools }] })` removes tool-call/result pairs (optionally per tool name) from a message list; used inside `prepareStep` the pruned list now persists for the rest of the run. It removes rather than stubs, and there is no automatic clearing policy, so the trigger is BYO. `toModelOutput` still reshapes per-tool output at authoring time and `onToolExecutionEnd` is read-only.

Staged through tools rather than a generic mechanism: skill frontmatter sits in the system prompt with the body fetched via `load_skill` and files via `load_skill_resource`; `loadartifactstool` lists artifact names and loads content on demand (sub-agents can share artifacts since v2.5); `loadmemorytool` is on-demand versus `preloadmemorytool`. There is no filesystem-stash or summary-handle primitive for arbitrary tool outputs.

Skills keep only metadata in the prompt with bodies fetched on demand; offloaded tool results are paged through `read_result`/`search_result`; `Agent(filesystem=...)` gives a durable DB-backed filesystem; and `CodeMode` (v3.0.0) runs tool compositions in an IPython kernel so intermediate results skip the transcript. Knowledge page tools and `query_<id>` context providers add further lazy fetch. First-party and stable since v3.

With `CodeActAgent`, the LLM writes TypeScript that calls tools inside a sandbox; intermediate tool results stay in the JS runtime and only the returned value plus capped console output (`max_console_bytes` 32 KiB) reach the model. ReAct and Basic executors have no filesystem stash, summary handle or lazy fetch, and MCP `resources()`/`prompts()` are listable but not wired into the loop. A small primitive only.

Skills register only metadata in the system prompt; full body is fetched on demand. Built-in `Read`/`Write`/`Edit` filesystem tools naturally encode the progressive-disclosure pattern (large outputs land on disk, model receives a path and can `Read` slices). No dedicated 'stash large tool result and return summary handle' primitive in the SDK itself — the pattern is straightforward to layer but not branded.

Skills + file scratchpad pattern with built-in `Write`/`Edit`/`Read` (large outputs go to disk, model receives a path and `Read`s on demand). `getContextUsage()` per-category breakdown (system/tools/messages/MCP/memory/agents/skills/commands) supports decisions. MCP tool definitions deferred by default (`alwaysLoad: false`) so descriptions are not in the prompt until tool-search runs. Multiple complementary mechanisms.

Path and registry skills load at metadata level and the agent gets a `load_skill` tool for the full instructions (first-party since 1.15.9, scoped to the execution). Resource files are cataloged only after `load_resources()` and the agent still needs a file tool to read them. Nothing moves large tool outputs out of context, so this covers skills only.

`reduction` offloads oversized tool output to a `filesystem.Backend` and the model re-reads it with `read_file` offset/limit (superseding the older `large_tool_result.go`); skills load bodies on invocation; `toolsearch` hides `DynamicTools` until `tool_search` is called or hands them to the provider as deferred tools; summarization can embed a transcript-file pointer. The most complete set in any Go framework.

`Skills` middleware puts names and descriptions in the prompt and fetches bodies on `use_skill`; experimental `Artifacts` middleware gives `read_artifact`/`write_artifact`, and with `Agents{ArtifactStrategySession}` only artifact names return to the orchestrator; `ai.WithResources` provides URI-templated lazy content and the Filesystem middleware offers bounded `read_file`. No generic stash for arbitrary tool results, and the artifact path is experimental, so capped at 3.

`wrap_tool_call` can rewrite the `ToolMessage` to a summary plus a 'full result available via <resource_id>' pointer using `BaseStore` as a natural stash. The mechanism exists but there is no first-party progressive-disclosure primitive — engineers compose it by hand.

note: stash via callback, no built-in pattern
details: BYO — `FunctionTool` `async_callback` can return a summary string while stashing the full payload elsewhere. No shipped stash+handle+re-read pattern; no skills metadata catalog.

Workspace plus Skills encourage the filesystem-stash pattern: a tool writes full output to a workspace file and returns a short path, and the model reads slices with `mastra_workspace_read_file`/`grep` or the `skill`/`skill_read` tools. `ToolSearchProcessor` keeps large toolsets out of the prompt, `toModelOutput` separates the persisted result from the model-visible summary, and delegation result references (1.67.0) let later delegations reuse sub-agent output by id. First-class staged-handle architecture.

Skills (stable since 1.11.0) keep metadata in the prompt with bodies, resources and scripts fetched via `load_skill`/`read_skill_resource`/`run_skill_script`; `MCPTool(use_progressive_disclosure=True)` loads MCP tool schemas on demand (1.11.0). `FileAccessProvider` ranged reads and `FunctionInvocationContext.add_tools`/`remove_tools` add a file stash and progressive tool exposure but sit behind experimental `HARNESS`/`PROGRESSIVE_TOOLS` flags. Stays at 4 because the stash pieces are experimental and large tool results are not stashed automatically.

`defer_loading: bool` on `FunctionTool` hides the tool definition from the Responses API until `ToolSearchTool` loads it. Coupled with `ToolSearchCallItem`/`ToolSearchOutputItem` items — the LLM searches a catalogue and explicitly loads what it wants; the rest never enter the prompt. First-class progressive disclosure for tool catalogues.

`toolSearchTool()` lets the model load deferred function tools or namespace members on demand (OpenAI Responses, client-side execution supported), Programmatic Tool Calling reduces intermediate results before they reach the context, and Sandbox Agents add lazy skills (`load_skill`), memory summaries with on-demand reads and a filesystem workspace for large outputs. Equivalent to the Python SDK's deferred-tool support; no stash for ordinary tool results outside the sandbox.

Core Tool Search (`defer_loading=True` plus `search_tools`, native on Anthropic/OpenAI or local) and on-demand capabilities (`load_capability`) keep tools and bundles out of the prompt. First-party Harness (0.x) adds `ToolOutputLimits` Spill mode (full payload stored, handle plus preview returned, `read_tool_result` with offset/pattern) and `ConversationSearch` over dropped turns. Capped at 4 because the result-stash pieces live in the 0.x Harness.

`retrieved_tools(...)` advertises only the top-N tools from a vector index per turn, `dynamic_context(...)` pulls retrieved documents via a completion-call hook, and `ToolContext::insert_result` keeps data out of the model context for hooks. There is no filesystem stash, summary handle or on-demand re-read tool, so large outputs are BYO.

The vended `ContextOffloader` plugin moves large content to `Storage` with a retrieval handle, and the context-manager stash (experimental types) keeps offloaded content in durable storage with a retrieval tool, persisted with snapshots. AgentSkills load lazily, the `mcp_router` tool connects approved MCP servers on demand, and `web_fetch` in agentic mode returns an analyst answer rather than the raw page. Brought to the same level as the TypeScript SDK's offloader plus retrieve tool.

`ContextOffloaderPlugin` stores full content in configurable `Storage` keyed by `mem_<id>`, swaps inline with preview + reference, and exposes a sibling `retrieve_offloaded_content` tool with grep / line-range access. Textbook lazy-fetch staged handle, first-party, plug-in shape.

note: tool search + code mode, no stash
details: `toolSearch()` with `deferLoading: true` keeps tool definitions out of context until the model searches for them, and `@ai-sdk/code-mode` (experimental tool callers) lets the model run JS in a QuickJS sandbox so raw tool outputs never enter the context. A sub-agent `toModelOutput` pattern is documented and the experimental `HarnessAgent` delegates skills to its runtime. No filesystem-stash or summary-handle primitive for `ToolLoopAgent` tool results.

`memory.Service` interface with two implementations: in-memory keyword search (v2.5 adds ranking, result limits and non-ASCII handling) and `memory/vertexai` (Vertex AI memory / Agent Engine). Namespaced per AppName+UserID. Population requires an explicit `AddSessionToMemory` call (not automatic). The agent reads memory through `loadmemorytool`, `preloadmemorytool` or `ctx.SearchMemory`. Usable but limited backends and manual lifecycle.

First-class `MemoryManager` with `enable_agentic_memory` (tool-call write/recall) and `update_memory_on_run` (auto-extract user facts; renamed from `enable_user_memories` in v3). `UserMemory` rows keyed by user_id with topics and timestamps; recall via `add_memories_to_context`. The new `LearningMachine` adds user profile, entity memory (isolated per user since v3.0.0) and decision-log stores, and `search_past_sessions` searches earlier sessions. Production-ready out of the box.

No first-party long-term memory abstraction with persistence. `VectorStore` trait with in-memory and Qdrant backends plus embedding abstraction lets you build it. You write a `MemoryProvider` calling into the vector store yourself; no pre-built memory subsystem.

Parity with the TS SDK, which drives the same bundled CLI (2.1.286, `_cli_version.py:3`). `AgentDefinition.memory` ('user' | 'project' | 'local', types.py:119) is serialized to the CLI (client.py:196-201) and selects the CLI's agent-memory directories; CLI auto memory under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` loads into the system prompt (types.py:47 names it; the hosting guide shows the Python `env` switch `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY`), and `get_context_usage()['memoryFiles']` (types.py:818) lists what loaded. Gap versus TS: no typed `SDKMemoryRecallMessage`, so `memory_recall` and `memory_paths` arrive as generic `SystemMessage` data. No own vector index (semantic search is BYO via an MCP tool), and memory is not tenant-scoped by default. Raised from 1 to match TS.

CLI surfaces memory files from `~/.claude/agent-memory/<agentType>/`, `.claude/agent-memory/`, and `.claude/agent-memory-local/`, plus auto memory under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/` loaded into the system prompt. `SDKMemoryRecallMessage` supports `mode: 'select' | 'synthesize'` — selector returns full file bodies, synthesizer returns a Sonnet-authored paragraph distilled from many tiny memories. No own vector index; for true vector-search RAG bring an MCP tool. Open issues #99 and #360 show the SDK path is less complete than the interactive CLI.

Sophisticated `crewai.memory.unified_memory.Memory` with LLM-driven `remember` (extract atomic facts, infer scope/categories/importance, consolidate above similarity threshold) and adaptive `recall` (deeper exploration when confidence low). Tunable recency/semantic/importance weights, hierarchical `root_scope`, LanceDB or Qdrant backends. First-class subsystem.

No `Memory` type, no `MemoryStore`, no auto-recall on `main`. You build cross-session memory by combining `components/retriever` (vector search) with a custom `BeforeAgent` / `BeforeModelRewriteState` middleware that injects recalled facts. Primitives exist but assembly is host-built. An 'automemory' middleware exists only on the `alpha/10` branch, not in the analysed commit, so it is not scored.

Genkit does not ship a memory abstraction (no semantic, episodic, or working memory). The closest pieces are `x/session` for state (not vector recall) and retrievers for query-time semantic search — but you must encode the memory yourself as documents.

`BaseStore` provides namespaced KV with optional vector search and TTL. Tools access it via `runtime.store.put` / `runtime.store.search`. Vector search is backed by Postgres pgvector (in `langgraph-checkpoint-postgres`), SQLite, or in-memory. Memory shape and lifecycle policies are host-built but the primitive is first-class.

First-class `Memory.memory_blocks` accepts `BaseMemoryBlock` subclasses: `StaticMemoryBlock` (fixed system content), `VectorMemoryBlock` (vector search over past messages), `FactExtractionMemoryBlock` (LLM-extracted facts). Blocks processed in priority order; ejected short-term messages pushed into blocks. Comprehensive memory primitive.

`@mastra/memory` ships four memory modes: conversation history (per-thread log), working memory (LLM-summarized rolling notes per resource), semantic recall (vector-store-backed retrieval of relevant prior messages), and observational memory (patterns across many threads). Vector adapters for Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, Astra, Lance, Elasticsearch. Direct fit for the benchmark.

note: Mem0, Azure AI Search, harness store
details: Multiple first-party providers: Mem0 (`agent-framework-mem0` / `Mem0Provider.cs`; storage scope split from search scope since 1.14.0), a new Azure Cosmos semantic-memory provider with fact extraction and user profiles (alpha), `FileMemoryProvider` (harness, stable since 1.12.0), and the harness `MemoryStore` (experimental). Pluggable context-provider model. Several pieces are still alpha/beta/experimental, so capped at 4.

The sandbox `Memory()` capability (`src/agents/sandbox/capabilities/memory.py:18`, `docs/sandbox/memory.md`) distills prior runs into workspace files: after a sandbox session closes, a model extracts summaries and a consolidation agent writes `MEMORY.md` and `memory_summary.md`; the summary is injected into later runs and details are searched on demand. It is file-based (no embeddings), only for sandbox agents, and persists only if you keep or snapshot the workspace. Regular agents have no memory beyond the 10 Session backends (turn history). Score corrected from 0: the capability already existed in May but was missing from the report.

Sandbox Agents ship a `memory()` capability (`packages/agents-core/src/sandbox/capabilities/memory.ts`) where, after runs, a model distils conversations into `memories/MEMORY.md`, `memory_summary.md` and rollout summaries (two-phase extraction + consolidation); the summary is injected into the next run and details are read on demand. It is file-based (no embeddings), only for sandbox agents, and persists only if you keep or snapshot the workspace. Regular agents have only `Session` history. Scored the same as openai-agents-python, which has the equivalent capability.

First-party `pydantic-ai-harness` `Memory` capability (`memory/_capability.py:46`; harness is 0.x, 'APIs may still move'): a Markdown notebook with `MEMORY.md` excerpt injected each request plus `write_memory`/`read_memory`/`delete_memory`/`search_memory` tools, with stores `InMemoryStore`, `FileStore`, `SqliteMemoryStore` and `PostgresMemoryStore`. Search is literal-text only; semantic ranking requires your own `SearchableMemoryStore`, and writes are agent-driven (no auto-extraction). Core also wraps Anthropic's native `MemoryTool`. Raised from 2: a persistent first-party memory with real stores now exists, but pre-1.0 and not semantic.

`ConversationMemory` is in-conversation only (linear history under a single id). For cross-conversation recall you combine `ConversationMemory` with `dynamic_context(sample, vector_store_index)` — the vector store is your semantic-memory substrate. No memory subsystem; you rebuild it via the RAG path.

`Agent(memory_manager=MemoryManager(stores=[...]))` (`memory/memory_manager.py:72`, in the Production/Stable SDK 1.57.1) registers a `search_memory` tool (optional add tool), injects retrieved memories into model input each turn without touching history, and extracts memories every 5 turns client-side (`ModelExtractor`) or server-side. Stores: `BedrockKnowledgeBaseStore` (semantic), `FileMemoryStore`, plus a `MemoryStore` protocol for BYO. Semantic recall depends on Bedrock KB; no in-repo vector store. Raised from 3 (tool-side mem0 tools, now deprecated in favour of this).

`AgentConfig.memoryManager` (`strands-ts/src/memory/memory-manager.ts:87`, shipped v1.5.0, injection v1.6.0, not marked experimental) provides `search_memory` (default) and `add_memory` (opt-in) tools, ephemeral injection into the last user message, and per-store extraction (default every 5 turns; `ModelExtractor` or server-side `addMessages`). Stores: `BedrockKnowledgeBaseStore` (the only semantic backend), `FileMemoryStore` (keyword/BM25) and `TestMemoryStore`; there is no embedding or vector store in the repo. Scored the same as strands-agents-python, which has the same subsystem.
No `Memory` class, no semantic-recall primitive. The SDK has no concept of cross-session memory. Reports contrast this with Mastra and LangGraph, which ship dedicated abstractions.

No first-party pgvector/Pinecone/Qdrant/Weaviate adapter, chunker or reranker. Retrieval is limited to Vertex-backed memory (`memory/vertexai`) and Gemini-native retrieval tools via `geminitool`; `loadmemorytool` is the agent-facing entry point. Anything else means writing your own `memory.Service` or a function tool.

note: Knowledge with many stores, embedders, readers
details: First-class `Knowledge` class (keyword-only since v3.0.7) with many vector DB integrations (PgVector, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, LanceDB, Chroma, MongoDB, Redis, OpenSearch, Elasticsearch, ClickHouse, Cassandra, and more), embedders and readers (text, markdown, pdf, docx, csv, json, sitemap, website, S3, GCS). New since May: digest-driven website/folder ingestion with refresh, page storage with revisions, and a knowledge-level reranker pipeline (`MMRReranker`, `RecencyReranker`). `search_knowledge=True` adds an automatic search tool; `KnowledgeManagementTools` add write tools.

`autoagents-core` ships `VectorStore` trait (in-memory and Qdrant), embedding abstraction, document type, and PDF readers. Examples cover Qdrant and in-memory RAG agents. You assemble retrieval yourself but the building blocks are present.
No first-party RAG. Layer it as an MCP server or SDK tool. No vector store, chunker, retriever, or citation primitive.
Not first-party. No built-in vector store, chunker, retriever, or citation primitive. The supported pattern is defining an `mcp__myrag__search` tool that hits Qdrant/Pinecone/etc.

Separate `crewai.knowledge.Knowledge` subsystem. Source types: String, TextFile, CSV, JSON, PDF, Excel, Docx, CrewDoclingSource for general doc parsing, plus `BaseKnowledgeSource` for custom. Each source is chunked + embedded + stored. ChromaDB default with Qdrant supported. `EmbedderConfig` supports OpenAI, Azure, Cohere, HuggingFace, Bedrock. Set at Agent or Crew level.

First-class primitives: `components.retriever.Retriever`, `components.indexer.Indexer`, `components.embedding.Embedder`, plus `components.document.{Loader,Parser,Transformer}` for ingestion. Eino-ext adapters: Qdrant, Milvus v1/v2, Redis, OpenSearch v2/v3, Elasticsearch v7/v8/v9, Volc VikingDB, Dify, Volc Knowledge. Wired via graph nodes or wrapped as a tool. No first-party citation primitive.

Retrievers, embedders and rerankers are action types. Built-in plugins: `localvec` (in-process), `pinecone`, `weaviate`, `postgresql` (pgvector), `alloydb`, `firebase` Firestore and `vertexai/vectorsearch`. Chunkers, per-provider embedders and a `Reranker` abstraction are included. `ai.WithDocs` inlines retrieved docs as grounding, and since v1.12 `ai.WithDocsFn` lets prompts resolve documents from typed input. Strong end-to-end primitives.

LangGraph does not ship its own retriever but the broader langchain ecosystem (Chroma, Pinecone, Weaviate, Postgres+pgvector) is separately packaged. `BaseStore.search()` covers basic semantic recall in-tree. No first-party chunking or citation primitive in the LangGraph package itself.

Historical core competency. About 78 vector store integrations under `llama-index-integrations/vector_stores/`. Index types include VectorStoreIndex, SummaryIndex, TreeIndex, KeywordTableIndex, KnowledgeGraphIndex, PropertyGraphIndex, ComposableIndex. Retrieval primitives `BaseRetriever`, `RouterRetriever`, `FusionRetriever`. Citations built in via `CitableBlock`/`CitationBlock`; `CitationQueryEngine` now gives each citation its own id and offsets. Expose retrieval as `QueryEngineTool`; the vendor now positions LlamaParse as the ingestion front-end.

`@mastra/rag` ships document processing, chunkers (`recursiveChunker`, etc.), retrievers, rerankers and vector query tools; core has a `knowledge` storage domain. Vector adapters cover Pinecone, Qdrant, Chroma, Astra, Lance, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Azure AI Search, Weaviate, pgvector, libsql and more; embedders live under `embedders/` and `packages/fastembed`. Full end-to-end RAG out of the box.

New shared vector-store abstractions in core (`BaseVectorStore`/`BaseVectorCollection`/`BaseVectorSearch`, portable filters, `InMemoryStore`) plus a `VectorCollectionContextProvider` that injects retrieval into the agent (experimental `VECTOR_STORES` feature). Connectors: Azure AI Search, Redis and Cosmos NoSQL (beta); Qdrant, pgvector, MongoDB, Azure DocumentDB, DuckDB, SQL Server (alpha). .NET adds `TextSearchProvider` over `Microsoft.Extensions.VectorData`. Comparable to rig/eino in shape; capped at 4 because the Python vector layer is experimental/alpha-beta, and no first-party chunker or citation primitive is documented.

`FileSearchTool` integrates with OpenAI's hosted Vector Stores (re-exported from the OpenAI SDK). For non-OpenAI RAG you write a `@function_tool` that queries your own vector store. No chunker, embedder, or citation primitive in-tree.
`fileSearchTool` (OpenAI hosted file search over vector stores) is the closest built-in. Otherwise BYO retriever as a function tool. No first-party chunker/embedder/citation primitive.

Core `embeddings/` package (OpenAI, Cohere, Google, Bedrock, VoyageAI, sentence-transformers), the native provider-hosted `FileSearchTool`, and a pgvector RAG example in the docs. No chunkers, retrievers or citation primitives; vector stores are BYO. Harness `ConversationSearch` (BM25 over persisted history) recalls earlier turns but is not knowledge retrieval.

First-class `rig-core` primitives: `VectorStoreIndex` traits, `InMemoryVectorStore` (LSH), `EmbeddingsBuilder`, rerank models (`rerank.rs`) and loaders for files, PDF and EPUB. Twelve companion vector-store crates (mongodb, lancedb, qdrant, sqlite, surrealdb, milvus, scylladb, postgres, s3vectors, helixdb, vectorize, neo4j). `agent.dynamic_context(samples, index)` retrieves on every model call and injects documents; since 0.43 it is a hook, so ordering relative to your hooks matters. No explicit citation primitive.

Retrieval goes through memory stores: `BedrockKnowledgeBaseStore` (min/max score filtering) and `Storage.search` with BM25/Qmd full-text strategies, surfaced as `search_memory` and optionally auto-injected. No first-party chunkers, embedders or vector-store integrations; ingestion beyond `add`/`add_messages` is the backend's job. The tools-repo `retrieve` tool is deprecated in favour of `MemoryManager` + `BedrockKnowledgeBaseStore(writable=False)`. Bedrock-centric, so scored like the hosted-search cases.

The retrieval primitive is `BedrockKnowledgeBaseStore` (MANAGED, VECTOR, KENDRA and SQL KB types, optional `accessControlList` and `filter`), exposed as `search_memory` and optionally injected into the user turn; `FileMemoryStore` adds keyword/BM25 search. No chunkers, embedders, vector-store integrations, rerankers or citation helpers. For anything else, build a retrieval tool yourself. Raised from 1 and scored the same as strands-agents-python, which has equivalent retrieval support.

SDK ships `embed`/`embedMany`, `rerank` and `cosineSimilarity`, but no vector store, chunker or retriever. `source-url`/`source-document` stream parts carry citations only when providers return them. Use `@ai-sdk/langchain` or `@ai-sdk/llamaindex` adapters for higher-level RAG, or roll your own with a vector DB.

`SearchRequest.AppName` + `SearchRequest.UserID` give per-user scoping in every memory search. For tenant scoping use one `AppName` per tenant (fully isolated memory across apps) or encode the tenant in `UserID`. The report corrects an earlier suggestion to carry the tenant in `app:` state: `app:` state is shared by every user of the AppName and would leak across tenants. Natural shape but not a dedicated tenant axis.

v3.0.0 adds per-user RAG isolation: every chunk has an owner `user_id` and scoped search returns own-or-shared results (`knowledge.py:584-657`; backend support varies, and LightRAG/LlamaIndex/LangChain wrappers cannot scope). Memories and entity-memory learnings are also keyed by `user_id`. There is still no tenant axis: map tenant to `user_id` (losing per-human isolation) or filter on `knowledge_filters` metadata. Raised from 2 because both memory and knowledge are now isolated natively, which is on par with adk-go.

Not provided; namespace your vector-store collections per tenant. `MemoryProvider` does not receive `app_meta`, so the namespace must be fixed when the provider is constructed. No framework primitive.
Filesystem-shaped: per-tenant CLAUDE.md lives under `tenants/<tid>/CLAUDE.md` and the SDK loads it via `cwd`. Works but only as deep as the filesystem-only memory layer.

Memory dirs are global-per-machine (`~/.claude/agent-memory/`, auto memory under `~/.claude/projects/`) or project-scoped (under `cwd`), so isolation is not natural. The hosting doc now documents the recipe: per-tenant `cwd`, per-tenant `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `settingSources: []` and auto memory disabled. Database-backed per-tenant memory is BYO through an MCP tool.

Hierarchical `root_scope` is the natural fit: `Memory(root_scope='/tenant/acme')` scopes all `remember`/`recall` to that prefix. Different tenants need different `Memory` instances, and `Crew(memory=True)` defaults to `/crew/{crew_name}`, which is shared across tenants. BYO wiring: no `Memory.with_tenant(id)` runtime filter, and Knowledge has no tenant concept.

Not automatic. `Retrieve(ctx, query, opts...)` receives ctx so you pass tenant scope through and the retriever adapter's `Options.SubIndexes` or query filter respects it. Framework does not enforce — the adapter does.

Not provided automatically. Retrievers accept a free-form `RetrieverRequest.Options` field you'd use to encode tenant filters (e.g. `Pinecone.namespace`, `Postgres WHERE tenant_id = $1`). Each plugin's `Retrieve` implements its own filter pass-through. No Mastra-style automatic namespacing.

Convention via `BaseStore` namespace tuples (`runtime.store.search((runtime.context.tenant_id, 'memories'), query=...)`); in-process enforcement is BYO. Prefix matching in the Postgres/SQLite stores is segment-aware since 3.1.1, so `('acme',)` no longer matches `('acmecorp',)`. At the HTTP layer `@auth.on.store` injects the tenant prefix server-side so external API callers cannot escape it. First-class enforcement when running under the LangGraph server.

`Memory.session_id` is the only first-class scoping key. For per-tenant separation encode `tenant:user:session` in `session_id`, use a per-tenant `SQLAlchemyChatStore` (different DB, table or schema via `db_schema=`), or pass a tenant-aware `AsyncDBChatStore` via `chat_store=`. No dedicated tenant axis.

Memory is naturally scoped per `resourceId` (in the `memory: { thread, resource }` tuple). The reserved `MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY` makes it server-controlled so a client cannot read another tenant's memory. For cross-tenant separation at the vector level, prefix index names with tenant id.

Scope-by-identifier: Mem0 `user_id`/`agent_id`/`application_id` (storage scope split from search scope since 1.14.0), Cosmos memory user profiles, and vector filters on a tenant field. .NET's isolation key is documented as reusable for memory, but registering a provider 'does not automatically partition application-owned memory' (`AgentIsolationKeyProvider.cs:15-24`). Tenancy = encode the tenant into a scope identifier yourself.

Sandbox memory isolation is by `MemoryLayoutConfig` (`memories_dir`, `sessions_dir`), 'not on agent name', so each tenant can get its own layout or sandbox snapshot (`docs/sandbox/memory.md:136-160`). `FileSearchTool(filters=...)` can scope hosted vector-store search; other vector indexes you namespace by `tenant_id` yourself. No tenant axis or enforcement. Raised from 1 as a correction: the layout helper existed in May but was missing from the report.

Not enforced by the SDK, but there are real hooks: sandbox `memory()` supports configurable memory directory layouts (`memory.mdx`) so each tenant can have its own workspace/memory directory, `RunContextAwareSession` (0.15.0) passes the `RunContext` so a custom session can route by tenant, and `fileSearchTool({ vectorStoreIds })` takes per-tenant vector store IDs. No tenant axis or enforcement. Scored the same as openai-agents-python, which has the equivalent layout helper.

Harness `Memory` takes `namespace: str | Callable[[RunContext], str]`, resolved once per run and 'never exposed as a tool argument' (`memory/_capability.py:74-75`), so one agent instance can serve many tenants without the model choosing the scope. The docs caution that namespace isolation 'is not an authorization system' for shared or custom stores. Vector/RAG scoping remains BYO and the Harness is 0.x. Raised from 1; held at 3 because enforcement is host-side and not server-injected like langgraph/mastra.
Not first-class. You scope vector-store collections per tenant yourself (e.g. namespace by `tenant_id` in your Postgres/Qdrant schema).

note: Per-store scope, one store per tenant
details: Not automatic, but with real primitives. `BedrockKnowledgeBaseStore` takes a `scope` applied as a search filter and stamped on writes (default metadata key `namespace`), `FileMemoryStore` namespaces storage under `memory/<store name>`, and any `Storage` can be namespaced. The docs recommend many store instances differing only by `scope`; you still build one store/manager per tenant and pick it per request. Raised from 1.

note: Per-store scope, one store per tenant
details: The `MemoryStore` interface has no tenant or user fields; a store scopes through its own configuration. `BedrockKnowledgeBaseStoreConfig.scope` is applied as a metadata filter (key default `namespace`) alongside `filter` and `accessControlList`, and the docs recommend one store per tenant; `FileMemoryStore` scopes by `name`. You build the `MemoryManager` per tenant or request; the SDK will not derive scope from `invocationState`. Scored the same as strands-agents-python.
BYO — namespace yourself in your vector DB (prefix keys with `tenantId:`, or use a separate index per tenant).

First-class SKILL.md loader (tool/skilltoolset/) following the agentskills.io v1.2 spec. YAML frontmatter (name, description, license, compatibility, metadata, allowed-tools) with strict validators and a standard skill-name/SKILL.md plus references/, assets/, scripts/ layout enforced at load time.

Top-level Agent.skills parameter backed by libs/agno/agno/skills/. SKILL.md uses YAML frontmatter (name, description, license, metadata, compatibility, allowed-tools) and validate_skill_directory enforces required fields plus optional scripts/ and references/ subfolders.

AutoAgents has no SKILL.md analogue, no Skill trait, no skills directory convention. The framework's only abstractions are Rust agent structs and tools; a markdown workflow skill would have to be hand-rolled outside the framework.

Skills are a native concept in the underlying Claude Code CLI; the Python SDK exposes only the skills option to enable/filter them (types.py:2309-2329; names validated at connect since 0.2.129). The SDK itself does not define or validate the SKILL.md schema, but markdown skills with YAML frontmatter (name, description) are the canonical Claude Code format; the repo carries its own example at .claude/skills/verify/SKILL.md.

Same as the Python SDK — SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter is the canonical Claude Code format, but it is CLI-validated, not SDK-validated. The TS SDK only surfaces an Options.skills filter and an SDKSystemMessage.skills field.

lib/crewai/src/crewai/skills/ is a full subsystem (parser, loader, validator, models, load_skill tool, AMP registry client with local cache). SkillFrontmatter is a frozen Pydantic model enforcing name regex, length limits and directory-name match, plus optional allowed-tools (parsed, still not enforced), metadata, license, compatibility. Also accepts inline SKILL.md strings and 'org/name@version' registry refs. Standard scripts/, references/, assets/ layout.

First-class via adk/middlewares/skill/. SKILL.md uses YAML frontmatter typed as FrontMatter struct (name, description, context mode, optional agent/model). Markdown body is the skill instructions or sub-agent prompt; closest match in any Go framework to Claude Code's SKILL.md model.

Skills middleware (plugins/middleware/skills.go) reads SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter, but the schema is minimal: only name and description are typed (skillFrontmatter struct, skills.go:78-82). No license, compatibility, allowed-tools fields; body has no validated schema.

Grep for SKILL.md, loadSkills, class Skill across libs/ returns zero matches. Skills (a la Claude Code's SKILL.md) are not a first-class concept; engineers BYO via BaseStore + pre_model_hook or by routing through the separate langgraph-deepagents template repo.
LlamaIndex has no SKILL.md analogue. The closest community offering is LlamaPacks, but those are pip-installable codebases, not lightweight markdown workflow skills.

Mastra implements the Anthropic Agent Skills spec end-to-end (workspace/skills/types.ts). SkillMetadata is fully typed (name, description, license, compatibility, user-invocable, metadata), validateSkillMetadata plus validateSkillContent() (1.69.0) enforce the schema, and skills support local, external and managed content sources. Skills can now be attached at agent level without a Workspace: paths, inline createSkill() objects, or a per-request resolver.

First-class and now stable (experimental marker removed in Python 1.11.0, .NET 1.13.0); only MCP-sourced skills (MCPSkillsSource) remain experimental. Aligned with agentskills.io (ADR 0037, renumbered from 0021). SkillFrontmatter validates name, description, license, compatibility, allowed_tools and metadata, with validators for name/description/compatibility; standard SKILL.md plus references/, assets/, scripts/ layout.

Skill BaseModel (sandbox/capabilities/skills.py:526) implements the canonical SKILL.md frontmatter, but skills are scoped to SandboxAgent / shell execution rather than general workflow templates. Typed scripts, references and assets dicts. A second hosted path references OpenAI-hosted skills by skill_id+version via ShellToolSkillReference (hosted container shell only).

Skills are a SandboxAgent capability only (sandbox/capabilities/skills.ts). SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter is parsed via parseSkillFrontmatter; SkillDescriptor types name, description, content, scripts, references, assets, compatibility, deferred. Outside SandboxAgent the concept does not exist.

First-party but pre-1.0: pydantic-ai-harness 0.x (now in the monorepo, version-locked to core) ships a Skills capability that loads SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter (name defaults to directory name and must match; description required, >1,024 chars warns) following agentskills.io (skills/_loader.py:51-76). license/compatibility/metadata are accepted; behavioural fields (allowed-tools, model, hooks, context) are accepted but not implemented, with one aggregated warning. Core pydantic-ai has no SKILL.md loader. Capped at 4 for the 0.x harness; same level as Genkit Go's minimal-schema loader. Previously 1 (skills were treated as third-party only).

Rig has no SKILL.md primitive, filesystem scanner, or WorkspaceSkills equivalent. The word skill does not appear in the documented API; the closest analogs are ToolDefinition.description and Agent.preamble, both hand-rolled.

AgentSkills vended plugin (vended_plugins/skills/) implements the agentskills.io spec. SKILL.md with YAML frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, metadata, license, compatibility) is validated by _validate_skill_name and directory-name match (lenient or strict mode).

AgentSkills vended plugin (@strands-agents/sdk/vended-plugins/skills) compatible with Claude Code's SKILL.md; not part of the core agent. YAML frontmatter validated by Skill.fromContent: name regex, length limits, directory-name match, plus allowed-tools (experimental, parsed but not enforced), license, compatibility, metadata. Path sources now load through the agent sandbox at initAgent.

Skills now exist only on the experimental HarnessAgent (@ai-sdk/harness): skills is an array of {name, description, content, files} objects (harness-v1-skill.ts:5) that the SDK renders to a SKILL.md with name/description frontmatter (write-skills.ts:522-531). No other frontmatter field is modelled, nothing is parsed from user-authored SKILL.md files, and ToolLoopAgent/generateText still have no skill loader (uploadSkill is only a provider upload relay). Scored on capability and capped for experimental maturity. Previously 0 (provider-opaque only).

Toolset exposes three first-class tools (list_skills, load_skill, load_skill_resource) plus a system-prompt XML listing of skill name+description appended on every request (toolset.go:107-117). Agent discovers via the injected list and invokes via load_skill.

Hybrid invocation: metadata (name, description, scripts list, references list) injected as <skills_system> XML in the system prompt; bodies fetched via auto-generated get_skill_instructions, get_skill_reference, get_skill_script tools. The Anthropic Agent Skills pattern, fully realized.

CLI exposes a built-in Skill tool to the model; calling Skill(name=X) loads the SKILL.md body into the conversation. Observable from Python as ToolUseBlock(name=Skill). Discovery is CLI-driven and gated by options.skills filter; SDK does not expose programmatic registration.

Same Claude Code mechanism as the Python SDK: skill list (name+description) injected in the system prompt; LLM invokes by emitting tool_use with name Skill. Filtered by Options.skills; SDKSystemMessage.skills surfaces the filtered set.

Since 1.15.9 path and registry skills stay at METADATA level: name+description go into the prompt as <skill> tags and the agent gets a load_skill tool (skills/tool.py:22-69, wired in agent/core.py:631-652) that returns the body, emits SkillUsedEvent and is renamed on tool-name collision. Inline SKILL.md strings and activate_skill()-ed skills are still injected into the system prompt in full. No tool to read bundled resources, so below ADK/Agno/Mastra. Previously 3 (system-prompt injection only), upstream change.

Pluggable Backend interface exposes a single skill tool (renameable) to the LLM. Three invocation modes via frontmatter context field: inline (returns markdown body), fork (spawns sub-agent with skill as system message), fork_with_context (sub-agent inherits parent history).

Middleware injects a <skills> system prompt block listing names+descriptions and exposes a use_skill(skillName) tool. Calling it reads the SKILL.md from disk and returns the body as the tool result. Filesystem rescanned on each Generate call.

No skill discovery or invocation primitive in the framework. BYO via BaseStore + pre_model_hook to inject skill bodies as SystemMessage, or a custom skill_read tool — every piece must be built by the host.
No skill invocation mechanism in the framework. The closest first-party mechanism is tool_retriever on a FunctionAgent for dynamic tool retrieval, but those are tools, not skills.

Three first-class tools (skill, skill_search, skill_read) plus a SkillsProcessor that injects <available_skills> XML metadata into the system prompt with an explicit instruction. Adds BM25/vector/hybrid search across skill content — beyond the basic load mechanism shipped by other stacks.

Three tools per ADR 0037: load_skill, read_skill_resource and run_skill_script (the last only registered when a skill has scripts); skill names+descriptions are also injected into the system prompt. Since 1.10.0 all three require approval by default (opt out via disable_*_approval flags or ToolApprovalMiddleware auto-approval rules). Stable since Python 1.11.0.

Skill metadata injected as a ### Skills section in the system prompt; for lazy mode a synthetic load_skill tool is added. Invocation is system-prompt instructions plus shell/file-read access in the sandbox — not a dedicated skill tool per Mastra's model.

Capability.instructions injects an available-skills section into agent instructions; when lazy, a load_skill tool materializes a skill on demand into .agents/<skill>/. Eager mode materializes everything up front.

Each skill becomes a deferred capability: a name+description catalog is appended to instructions and the model calls the core load_capability tool, whose result is '# Skill: <name>' plus the body (docs/harness/skills.md:70-82). Works, but through the generic on-demand-capability tool rather than a skill-specific tool, and the body lands in client-visible message history. Harness is 0.x, so capped at 4; comparable to Genkit's use_skill. Previously 2 (BYO or third-party).
No skill invocation primitive in Rig. The LLM only sees what is in the preamble or dynamic_context; there is no skill-as-tool or skill-as-hook mechanism.

Hybrid: <available_skills> XML block injected into the system prompt with name+description+location, plus a skills(skill_name) activation tool that returns full instructions and a listing of bundled resource files. Activated skills are tracked in agent.state and persist across turns.

Same pattern as the Python plugin: BeforeInvocationEvent hook injects <available_skills> XML into the system prompt; a registered skills tool accepts skill_name and returns the full body. Activation tracked in agent.appState across turns.

On HarnessAgent the skills are written to the runtime's home (e.g. $HOME/.agents/skills) in the sandbox and the external runtime (Claude Code, Codex, ...) discovers and invokes them; for the SDK it is neither a host tool call nor SDK prompt injection. Adapters without native skill files fall back to including the skill content in the prompt. Per-turn swap via prepareCall. Experimental and delegated, so below Claude Agent SDK's native Skill tool; ToolLoopAgent has none. Previously 0.

Only frontmatters (name+description) are appended to the system prompt; bodies are fetched only when the agent calls load_skill, and resources only via load_skill_resource. Matches Claude Code's lazy loading model.

Body never enters the system prompt — only metadata does. agent_skills.py:117-125 explicitly documents the Browse / Load / Reference / Scripts progressive workflow. Bodies and references are fetched only on tool invocation, including a get_skill_script tool with optional subprocess execution.

Frontmatter (name+description) goes in the system prompt; full body loads on Skill(name=X) invocation. Confirmed by ContextUsageResponse.skills exposing the frontmatter breakdown. Driven entirely by the underlying CLI.
Same as Python SDK: metadata in system prompt, body fetched on Skill tool use. Options.skills filters which skills appear in the prompt. Driven by the underlying Claude Code CLI.

Lazy by default since 1.15.9 (was eager in May): three disclosure levels (METADATA, INSTRUCTIONS, RESOURCES, skills/models.py:25-40); body loads only on load_skill, and loaded instructions are scoped to that execution. The RESOURCES catalog is only produced by an explicit host-side load_resources(), so the model does not see resource listings on activation (unlike Strands). Previously 3 (prompt-eager), upstream change.

Tool description sent to the LLM enumerates available skills (name + 1-line description) via renderToolDescription; the full markdown body is only loaded when the LLM invokes the skill tool. Keeps initial context small with hundreds of skills.
System prompt lists available skill names+descriptions only; body fetched only when LLM calls use_skill(skillName). Files are read on every invocation (no in-memory cache between Generate calls).
No skill primitive, hence no progressive disclosure. BYO patterns (vector search + pre_model_hook, or a skill_read tool) can implement it but the framework provides nothing.
No skill loading mode. tool_retriever provides progressive disclosure for tools, but not for markdown skill workflows.

Only <available_skills> metadata is injected via SkillsProcessor; bodies are fetched via the skill tool, resources via skill_read with optional line ranges, and skill_search with BM25/vector/hybrid is offered. Stateless: if context is compacted, the model calls again.

Skill names+descriptions go into the system prompt (~100 tokens per skill per ADR 0037); bodies are fetched on demand via load_skill, resources via read_skill_resource and scripts via run_skill_script. Standard Anthropic progressive-disclosure model, stable since Python 1.11.0.

Both eager (Skill(...) inlined, scripts/references/assets materialized into sandbox) and lazy (LazySkillSource exposes index up front, body fetched via load_skill tool) supported. Progressive-disclosure prompt explicitly tells the LLM to open scripts/ instead of retyping code.

Two modes: eager (materialize everything into .agents/<skill>/ and show full metadata) and lazy (lazyFrom: localDirLazySkillSource shows only the index; LLM calls load_skill to materialize). Skills can also be marked deferred.

Lazy: the catalog is metadata-only and stable across runs, so it stays in the cached prompt prefix; bodies load on demand and loaded capabilities stay loaded for the rest of the run and survive history replay. Bundled resources are not loaded at all (see composition). Harness is 0.x, so capped at 4. Previously 2 (third-party only).
No progressive disclosure for skills. Closest BYO would be dynamic_context with a vector store of skill embeddings to RAG-select snippets at prompt time.

Only descriptions and names appear in the system prompt up-front; bodies loaded on demand via the skills tool. Activated skills tracked in agent.state['agent_skills']['activated_skills'] and survive across turns in a session.
Only metadata (name+description+location) goes into the system prompt; body fetched on-demand via the skills tool. Activation tracked in agent.appState[stateKey].activatedSkills.

The docs position skills as 'available on demand' instead of always in context, and discovery is lazy where the runtime has native skill directories (metadata indexed, body read on demand). Adapters without native skill files include the content eagerly, and the SDK cannot inspect or steer disclosure. Experimental HarnessAgent only. Previously 0.

Standard skill-name/SKILL.md plus references/, assets/, scripts/ layout is first-class and resources are read through load_skill_resource, but scripts are only readable (no execution tool). Composition via MergedSource lets you stitch sources together (errors on duplicates). allowed-tools is parsed and returned but not enforced. No skill-includes-skill mechanism; bodies must call each other through tool descriptions.

Skills bundle scripts/ and references/ as first-class (validated via validate_skill_directory). get_skill_script can read or execute (subprocess) bundled scripts with path-traversal protections. No imports: [other-skill] in frontmatter; cross-skill composition is text-driven only.

Cross-skill references are implicit via skill bodies that mention each other, plus plugins (SdkPluginConfig) which bundle multiple skills, plus AgentDefinition.skills which scopes which skills a sub-agent sees. No SDK-side composition primitive — bundling lives at the CLI/plugin layer.

Can reference other skills by plugin-qualified names (<plugin>:skill-name), call sub-agents from the skill body, and AgentDefinition.skills preloads skills into a sub-agent. Bundled assets are accessed via Read/Bash on relative paths inside the skill directory. New: Query.reloadSkills(), SessionStart reloadSkills and a ProposeSkills tool (proposes, does not install). CLI-layer composition; the SDK adds no primitives.

scripts/, references/, assets/ directories are first-class, but the RESOURCES catalog is only injected after an explicit load_resources(), and the LLM still needs a file-read tool to open them. A skill cannot include another skill or call a sub-agent; it is a prompt fragment. No change in score since May; registry refs and sources de-duplicate by name (org/name for registry skills) but do not compose skills.

Strongest composition story: fork mode lets a skill spawn a sub-agent that itself has tools, sub-agents, and skills (full recursion). Skill body can reference files in its BaseDirectory passed via the sub-agent's instruction template. Skills can call other skills if the sub-agent has the skill middleware installed.

use_skill reads the SKILL.md body and returns it as the tool result; no first-class scripts/, references/, or assets/ subfolders in the loader. Composition is purely text-driven via skill bodies that mention other skills.
No skill composition primitive.
No skill composition primitive.

Skills bundle references/, scripts/ and assets/ as first-class; skill_read accesses any path with optional line ranges and binary detection, and inline createSkill() skills carry in-memory references. skill_search across content (BM25/vector/hybrid) lets skills find each other indirectly. No skill-imports-skill directive.

Skills ship references/ and assets/ alongside SKILL.md plus scripts/ executed via a pluggable SkillScriptRunner, with approval-by-default for script execution (the earlier require_script_approval flag was replaced by disable_run_skill_script_approval). Source-level composition via Aggregating/Filtering/Deduplicating/Caching SkillsSource; sources now receive SkillsSourceContext(agent, session), and MCP-served skills (experimental) are supported. No extends/include mechanism between skills.

Skill model has typed scripts, references, assets dicts. Progressive-disclosure prompt explicitly instructs the LLM to open scripts/ and reuse assets/. Skills do not cross-reference each other directly, but a body can mention other skill names for the LLM to load.

SkillDescriptor carries scripts, references, assets entries. Sources include inline, filesystem dir, and gitRepo. Injected instructions explicitly steer the LLM to load only specific reference files and reuse scripts/assets. Lazy loader can request loading another skill at runtime.

Harness Skills does not enumerate, read or execute bundled references/, assets/ or scripts/ (${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR} placeholders stay literal); agents with FileSystem/Shell capabilities can read them but Skills gives no path. No skill-includes-skill mechanism. Several Skills instances combine into one catalog (duplicate names fail at run start), and a code-defined on-demand Capability can bundle tools, hooks and settings (not expressible in SKILL.md). Score unchanged at 2: composition did not improve while the other three rows moved up.
No skill composition primitive.

Skills bundle scripts/, references/, assets/ which are listed in the activation response (capped at maxResourceFiles, default 20). Skills cannot directly call other skills, but the activated instructions can instruct the LLM to invoke other skills via the skills tool (text-driven chaining).

Skills bundle scripts/, references/, assets/ subdirectories; activation response includes a listing capped at maxResourceFiles (default 20). LLM reads them via separate file-reading tools. Skills cannot directly reference other skills or call sub-agents.

HarnessV1Skill.files lets a skill bundle references, templates and scripts (skill-relative paths; absolute paths and '..' rejected) next to SKILL.md. Skill-to-skill references and sub-agent calls are runtime behaviour, not modelled by the SDK. Experimental HarnessAgent only; ToolLoopAgent not applicable. Previously 0.

Five first-class mechanisms: agents-as-tools (tool/agenttool), LLM-driven transfer_to_agent, v2 collaboration modes (ModeSingleTurn/ModeTask sub-agents auto-installed as tools on the parent, task agents return via finish_task), v2 graph workflows (workflow.New with agent/function/join/parallel-worker nodes) and legacy parallel/sequential/loop workflow agents. All run inside the runner; a YAML path exists but is internal.

First-class Team primitive auto-injects delegation tools (delegate_task_to_member(s), task-list tools). Four orchestration modes (coordinate/route/broadcast/tasks) cover most fan-out patterns; Workflow steps, RemoteAgent/RemoteTeam over HTTP/A2A and StudioRunnerTools extend it. Members can be Agents or nested Teams.

No SubAgent/handoff/delegate primitive. Multi-agent is expressed via actors subscribing to a shared runtime Topic; the parent publishes a Task and matches TaskComplete events by sub_id/actor_name. An agent-as-tool wrapper is BYO (implement ToolRuntime over an Arc<BaseAgent>).

Sub-agents are first-class via the bundled CLI's built-in Agent tool (historically Task) plus AgentDefinition (description, prompt, tools, model, skills, memory, background...). The parent LLM emits a tool_use that the CLI dispatches; the sub-agent runs its own loop with isolated context. Also loadable from .claude/agents/*.md.

First-class via the CLI's built-in Agent tool (renamed from Task in 0.3.142) plus AgentDefinition, from Options.agents or markdown files under .claude/agents/. New since May: a Workflow tool (agent()/parallel()/pipeline() scripts), named agents addressable while running, and isolation 'worktree'/'remote'. The special sub-agent semantics cannot be disabled.

Two awkward paths: Crew with hierarchical process + DelegateWorkTool (LLM picks coworker), or Flow @start/@listen with explicit Python orchestration. No first-class agent-as-tool primitive for in-process fan-out. A2A protocol adds heavyweight cross-org option.

Agents-as-tools (NewAgentTool) and DeepAgent (deep.New, task tool over registered sub-agents) are the recommended paths. Transfer handoff (SetSubAgents) and workflow agents (Sequential/Parallel/Loop) still work but are marked NOT RECOMMENDED in code. Prebuilt supervisor/deep/planexecute patterns sit on top; capability is unchanged, the deprecation signal is ergonomic only.

First-party but experimental: middlewarex.Agents (WithExperimental gate, breaking changes allowed between minors) generates delegate_to_<agent> tools plus a <sub-agents> prompt block, with MaxDelegations, history seeding, artifact merging and async background tasks. Stable Genkit still only offers hand-written agents-as-tools. Scored on capability and capped at 4 for experimental status; no handoff or workflow primitive. Previously 2 (BYO only).

No first-class SubAgent/handoff primitive in this repo. Subgraphs are added as nodes, wrapped as tools (langgraph-supervisor/deepagents are separate packages), or reached via RemoteGraph over the HTTP API. Tool-dispatched sub-agents are now named via lc_agent_name. Static compile-time registration; flexible but requires state-schema design.

First-class AgentWorkflow + can_handoff_to declarative handoff graph (auto-injected handoff tool), plus agents-as-tools by wrapping .run() in a FunctionTool. Configuration is Python-only (no markdown manifest).

First-class agents field on Agent (statically, dynamically per request, or via SubAgent interface). Runtime synthesizes agent-<name> tools via listAgentTools(). Network mode wraps supervisor pattern explicitly.

Three mechanisms: agent.as_tool(), BackgroundAgentsProvider (renamed from SubAgentsProvider and now in both Python and .NET; start/wait/get/continue task tools), and the released orchestrations package (Sequential, Concurrent, Handoff, GroupChat, Magentic builders; Workflow.as_agent). Matches the breadth of openai-agents and strands, so raised from 4.

Two first-class local mechanisms: Agent.as_tool() (now with run_config, max_turns, hooks, session, needs_approval, structured parameters) and typed Handoff with HandoffInputFilter. An experimental OpenAI-hosted multi-agent model (0.18.2+) lets a root GPT model spawn sub-agents on OpenAI's service, but rejects handoffs. Both local paths are fully integrated into the Runner.

Both handoffs (synthesized transfer_to_<agent> tool, loop switches the current agent) and Agent.asTool() (structured parameters, customOutputExtractor) are first-class. A third, experimental OpenAI-only hosted Multi-agent model (OpenAIHostedMultiAgentModel) lets the service spawn a sub-agent tree.

Core is still agent-as-tool delegation, but the first-party pydantic-ai-harness (0.52, version-locked to core, in the monorepo since 2026-09-26) adds a SubAgents capability (delegate_task with per-delegate budgets, timeouts, max_calls, depth cap, markdown agent files) and DynamicWorkflow (model-written orchestration scripts in a sandbox). Capped at 4 because the harness is pre-1.0. Previously 3 (BYO delegation).

Agents-as-tools only: Agent::into_tool() (and From<Agent> for DynamicTool) builds a runtime-named DynamicTool in the rig-agent crate; Agent no longer implements Tool directly. No handoff, workflow or transfer primitive.

Multiple first-class mechanisms: agent.as_tool() (also auto-applied when an Agent is passed in tools=, with delegate=True to hand the turn to the child), Graph for deterministic DAGs, Swarm for model-driven handoff, and A2AServer/A2AAgent plus a vended a2a_client tool for cross-process agents. The Beta harness adds a background subagent tool.

Three first-class SDK patterns: agent.asTool() (auto-applied when an Agent is in tools[], delegate:true via the AgentDelegation plugin), Graph DAG with bounded parallelism, and Swarm with structured HandoffResult. harness-ts adds a separate subagent tool. Analysed from harness-sdk/strands-ts, which supersedes the archived sdk-typescript repo.

No sub-agent primitive in the ai package; the documented pattern is wrapping a child ToolLoopAgent inside tool({ execute }). With HarnessAgent plus the Claude Code adapter, sub-agents are runtime-native (Claude Code's Task tool) and the AI SDK only surfaces their activity. No registry or manifest in the SDK itself.

Agents-as-tools and single-turn/task tools run in parallel when the LLM emits several calls (platform.RunTasks, overridable). Graph workflows spawn one goroutine per ready node (capped by WithMaxConcurrency), ParallelWorker handles per-item fan-out, and the legacy parallelagent uses errgroup. Several complementary parallelism paths.

Sync run executes members sequentially (delegate_task_to_members loops). Async arun fans out with asyncio.gather and multiplexes streaming through an asyncio.Queue, so concurrency requires team.arun and an async model. Unchanged since May.

Each actor receives published messages in its own tokio task; subscribers process concurrently after the sequential publish loop returns. Parallel is the natural mode; no dedicated parallel-agent primitive, pub/sub gives it for free.

Parallel sub-agent fan-out is first-class in the CLI; the SDK ships _SubagentContextMixin for hook attribution when multiple sub-agents interleave on the control channel. background flag and stop_task add explicit control.

The parent LLM can emit several Agent tool_use blocks in one turn (or use parallel() in a Workflow script); the CLI dispatches them concurrently and fires PostToolBatch once. Agents are background-by-default from the model's side. New caps: nested sub-agents off by default (depth 1) and at most 20 concurrent sub-agents.

Corrected: the May report wrongly said only the first tool runs per turn. Both executors run multiple native tool calls in parallel on a ThreadPoolExecutor (max 8), so a manager emitting several delegation calls can fan out, and Task.async_execution=True runs tasks as Futures. Hierarchical delegation is still one coworker per call with no orchestration, and persona fan-out is best hand-rolled as Flow + asyncio.gather. Raised from 2 (correction).

Agents-as-tools run in parallel by default: ToolsNode executes the N agent-tool calls of one assistant message in N goroutines. The explicit ParallelAgent (sync.WaitGroup + goroutines, forked run contexts) is marked NOT RECOMMENDED but still works. Strong coverage.

Within one Generate call, tool dispatch fans out on goroutines, so several delegate_to_<agent> calls run concurrently. The experimental Async option adds background delegation with wait_for_background_tasks (all/first), check and abort tools; MaxDelegations caps calls per generate. No worker pool; capped at 4 as the dedicated tooling is experimental.

Send API dispatches each item to its own task (PregelRunner.tick). create_react_agent v2's tools node uses this to run multiple tool calls in parallel. Strong primitive but you assemble the graph yourself.

AgentWorkflow itself is serial (single active agent). Parallel fan-out happens through agents-as-tools: the parent LLM emits parallel tool calls and the workflow runtime executes them concurrently via @step + ctx.collect_events.

Sub-agent invocations are tool calls dispatched via foreach(toolCallStep, { concurrency: 10 }). Concurrency drops to 1 only when approval/suspend is in play. Parallel by default, opt-out via requireApproval.

Corrected: Python as_tool sub-agents run concurrently when the model emits several tool calls (function loop uses asyncio.gather by default, allow_concurrent_invocation=False to serialise); the May report wrongly said sequential. .NET requires opting in (AllowConcurrentInvocation). BackgroundAgentsProvider runs tasks concurrently in both languages with wait_for_first_completion, and ConcurrentBuilder gives graph fan-out/fan-in. Raised from 3 (correction).

When the LLM emits several as_tool calls in one turn, execute_function_tool_calls dispatches them concurrently, bounded by max_function_tool_concurrency. Programmatic Tool Calling (Responses beta) and hosted multi-agent (experimental, max_concurrent_subagents) add model-driven fan-out. Deterministic fan-out is still BYO asyncio.gather; no fan_out() helper.

Multiple asTool invocations in one turn run in parallel, bounded by toolExecution.maxFunctionToolConcurrency, with sibling cancellation on failure. Handoffs are sequential by definition; experimental hosted Multi-agent defaults to three concurrent sub-agents.

Parallel when the parent emits several delegate_task calls: core runs tool calls as concurrent asyncio tasks and the harness documents them as independent sub-agent runs. DynamicWorkflow scripts use asyncio.gather in a sandbox with max_agent_calls limits. Guaranteed fan-out needs DynamicWorkflow or a hand-written gather. Capped at 4 (pre-1.0 harness). Previously 2 (BYO gather).

Parent tool calls in one turn run with buffer_unordered(runner.concurrency.max(1)). Default concurrency is 1 (sequential); set .tool_concurrency(n) to opt in. Results are committed in call order after the batch settles.

Multiple toolUse blocks in one turn run concurrently in ConcurrentToolExecutor (asyncio tasks); Graph runs ready nodes concurrently via asyncio.gather; Swarm is sequential by design. Calls to the same child instance are serialised by a lock, so fan-out needs distinct child agents. Harness subagent runs in the background.
Parent uses toolExecutor:'concurrent' by default with Promise.race scheduler. Graph schedules ready nodes up to maxConcurrency:Infinity with AND-edge semantics. Strong default fan-out.
No SDK-level fan-out primitive. Parallel sub-agent execution is hand-rolled inside the parent tool body via Promise.all. Multiple tool calls within a single step are parallel at the parent level.
