row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: Vended tools: bash (host, ignores the sandbox), shell and fileEditor (both sandbox-routed; view/create/str_replace/insert, no anchors), httpRequest, webFetch (markdown or sub-agent 'agentic' mode, v1.18), notebook, sleep, handoffToUser (v1.19), a2a client (main only) and an experimental stop tool; plugins add skills, memory and context tools. No web search, glob, grep or monitor in the SDK (harness-ts adds web_search/read/write/edit). Raised from 2 because the SDK now has shell, editing, fetch and HITL tools that work against a Sandbox, but it stays well below the Python companion's breadth.

row: Built-in tools (web search, file ops, exec)
details: The SDK still ships no native Read/Edit/Bash/Glob/Grep/WebFetch for ToolLoopAgent; you author them, import them via MCP or provider-executed tools. New since May: toolSearch() for deferred tool loading, an experimental code-mode tool (model-written JS calling your tools in QuickJS), and HarnessAgent built-ins (read/write/edit/bash/grep/glob/webSearch) that are executed by an external runtime such as Claude Code, so their quality is the runtime's. Raised from 1 for these additions; still a thin first-party catalog.

functiontool.New[TArgs,TResults] takes a typed Go function and auto-infers JSON schema via jsonschema reflection on struct tags. Per-tool RequireConfirmation (or dynamic provider), IsLongRunning, OnToolErrorCallback, InputSchema/OutputSchema overrides. Concise smallest tool (~5 lines + handler) with typed args/results. Strong DX for Go.

@tool decorator inspects signature + type hints + docstring (docstring-parser) and builds a Function Pydantic model with JSON schema. Decorator options include name, description, strict, instructions, show_result, stop_after_tool_call, requires_confirmation, requires_user_input, user_input_fields, external_execution, pre_hook/post_hook/tool_hooks, cache_results/cache_dir/cache_ttl. First-class typed tool authoring.

#[tool(name, description, input)] proc macro on a struct plus an async-trait ToolRuntime::execute impl; ToolInput derive generates the schema. v0.4.0 made the derive production-safe (cached ToolInputSchema, compile-fail tests for a missing derive). The smallest tool is still about 20 lines of Rust ceremony (struct, derives, impl, serde_json::from_value), so it is typed but verbose; execute gets no context argument.

@tool(name, description, schema) decorator with schema being a {name: type} dict, TypedDict (fixed 0.1.51), raw JSON Schema, or Annotated[type, 'description'] (0.1.52). Wrapped via create_sdk_mcp_server and routed through the SDK MCP JSON-RPC bridge. Clean and typed; one small extra step to wrap into an MCP server vs. a direct function-tool API.

tool(name, description, zodSchema, handler) is the canonical API; schema is Zod v3 or v4 used for both LLM-facing JSON schema generation and runtime validation. Wrapped via createSdkMcpServer and namespaced as mcp__server__tool. First-class typed authoring.

Subclass BaseTool with name, description, args_schema: type[BaseModel], _run(...). Auto-derives args_schema from _run signature if omitted. Built-in result_as_answer (ends loop on tool return), cache_function, max_usage_count, _claim_usage. @tool decorator also available. Strongly typed and ergonomic.

utils.InferTool(name, desc, fn) generic helper auto-infers JSON schema from Go struct tags (jsonschema/description). utils.InferOptionableTool for options-aware tools, utils.NewTool for manual schema, or implement tool.InvokableTool directly. Runtime validation via sonic unmarshal; errors propagate to model. Clean typed API.

genkit.DefineTool(g, name, desc, fn) takes a typed Go function and infers the schema from struct tags (jsonschema_description, enum); supports WithInputSchema override, WithStrictSchema and ToolContext. An experimental genkitx API adds multipart output and typed interrupts. Smallest tool is about 3 lines. Caveat from the refresh: a tool error, including invalid input, ends the generate call (ErrToolFailed) instead of being fed back to the model, so self-correction requires returning problems as normal output.

@tool decorator from langchain_core.tools auto-generates JSON schema from signature + docstring. Pydantic/dataclass arg classes supported. async def is supported natively. Subclass BaseTool for richer control with name/description/_run. Mature, ergonomic — Pydantic v2 validation on each call.

Two methods: pass a typed Python callable directly (FunctionAgent wraps via FunctionTool.from_defaults) or build FunctionTool.from_defaults with explicit name/description/callback/partial_params overrides. Schema auto-generated via create_schema_from_function using Pydantic. Runtime validation raises ValidationError caught and wrapped in ToolOutput(is_error=True).

createTool({id, description, inputSchema, outputSchema, execute}) takes Zod schemas for both input and output; JSON schema auto-generated. Supports requestContextSchema for tenant-context validation. Tools receive a typed ctx with writer/agent/abortSignal. First-class typed authoring with output schema validation, a step beyond most peers.

Python: @tool decorator over a function or class, optional input_model: type[BaseModel] for strict schema; Pydantic-validated. .NET: AIFunctionFactory.Create infers schema from C# parameter metadata + DescriptionAttribute. approval_mode declarative. Both runtimes are typed and ergonomic.

@function_tool decorator parses signature and Griffe-style docstring (griffelib) to build a Pydantic params model + strict-mode JSON schema. RunContextWrapper/ToolContext as first arg, needs_approval boolean or callable. Output types: ToolOutputText/Image/FileContent. Strict-mode default produces guaranteed-JSON. Best-in-class typed authoring.

tool({name, description, parameters, execute}) accepts Zod, raw JSON Schema or (since 0.16.0) Standard Schema, builds a FunctionTool with strict-by-default validation, optional outputSchema runtime validation, timeouts, approvals and guardrails. Invalid input produces a redacted model-visible error and the run continues. Generic over context, parameters and result; allowedCallers and toolNamespace add grouping. Strongly typed and concise.

@agent.tool / @agent.tool_plain decorators on typed Python functions. Schema auto-derived from type hints + docstrings via _function_schema.FunctionSchema. RunContext[Deps] for typed dependency injection. ModelRetry mechanism turns Pydantic validation failures into structured retry prompts. Per-tool max_retries. Best-in-class Pydantic-native ergonomics.

Tool trait (description/parameters/call with &mut ToolContext/map_error) plus #[rig::rig_tool], which derives the schema from a function signature (Option<T> optional, ToolContext parameter recognised), and DynamicTool for runtime-defined tools. Output is any Serialize value into a rich ToolOutput, typed errors map to model-visible feedback via with_model_feedback, and a typed per-run ToolContext reaches every tool. Raised from 3 because the macro path is now a few lines and context/error handling are first-class; the manual trait impl is still about 30 lines.

@tool decorator extracts name, description, and JSON schema from signature + docstring + type hints (Pydantic-backed via create_model). tool_context: ToolContext parameter activates context-aware mode. Class-based tools implement AgentTool.stream returning a ToolGenerator. Pydantic-validated; invalid args yield ToolResult(status='error').

tool({name, description, inputSchema, callback}) accepts a Zod schema (runtime-validated) or a raw JSON schema (no validation; callback receives unknown). Subclass Tool for custom streaming. Concise and typed when Zod is used.

tool({description, inputSchema, execute}) with Zod 3 or 4 schema. Full surface includes contextSchema, onInputStart/Delta/Available, toModelOutput, needsApproval, outputSchema. Runtime validation via parseToolCall; experimental_repairToolCall can patch invalid calls before they surface to the LLM. First-class typed authoring.

New functiontool.NewStreaming takes a Go iter.Seq2 of string chunks. In a live (bidi) session each chunk is fed back to the model as it arrives and the model can stop the stream; in ordinary runs chunks are concatenated into one result, so neither the model nor the HTTP client sees mid-execution output. Streaming tools also skip Before/After/OnError tool callbacks. Raised from 1: a real primitive exists, but it is limited to live mode and bypasses policy hooks (report 13.3).

Tools can be Python generator functions; FunctionCall.execute detects isgenerator(result) and stores the generator (tools/function.py:1057-1064). The model adapter must consume it. There is no first-class "tool yields progress events to the LLM mid-execution" pattern — chunks are aggregated for the LLM.

ToolRuntime::execute returns a single Value, not a stream. A tool cannot yield progress events back to the model mid-execution. The execute signature has no Context access, so even out-of-band Event::SendMessage requires capturing a sender at tool construction time.

SDK MCP tool handlers must return a single {"content": [...]} dict — no streaming from third-party SDK MCP tools. The CLI itself streams tool output (e.g. Monitor) but that's only for built-in tools, not user-authored SDK MCP tools.

Partial. Bash/MCP/Agent calls can run in the background and report via task_notification; SDKToolProgressMessage emits elapsed-time heartbeats for UIs; the built-in Monitor tool turns a process's stdout or a WebSocket into events the model sees as they arrive. A user-authored SDK MCP tool still returns a single CallToolResult, so mid-execution partial results from your own tools to the model are not supported (issue #213 open).

A tool's _run returns a single value (string or Any cast to string). No mechanism for a tool to yield partial results to the model mid-execution. Only option for long-running tools is to log progress to the event bus (or stdout) and return a single final string.

StreamableTool returns *schema.StreamReader[string] (components/tool/interface.go:53-57); the tool yields chunks the framework concatenates and forwards. EnhancedStreamableTool extends the same shape to multimodal results. First-class streaming.

Since v1.10 a tool running under streaming generate can call tool.SendPartial or SendChunk (experimental package go/ai/exp/tool) to emit partial tool-response chunks; the loop serialises them across parallel tools and clients see role 'tool' chunks flagged IsPartial. Partials are client progress only; the model still sees the tool's final return value. Raised from 0; capped at 4 because the API lives in an experimental package, and non-streaming calls make it a no-op.

A tool that takes runtime: ToolRuntime can call runtime.stream_writer({"progress": 0.5}) to emit CustomStreamPart frames mid-execution (tool_node.py:1663-1730). Visible to clients on stream_mode='custom'. First-class progress streaming through the LangGraph event bus.

Tools receive the live Context and can call ctx.write_event_to_stream(...) inside the tool body to emit custom events to consumers mid-execution. Tools do not yield partial results back to the LLM mid-call though — the tool still returns a single value to the model.

Tools yield mid-execution progress via ctx.writer: ToolStream (packages/core/src/tools/types.ts:417), producing tool-output chunks in fullStream. Tools can also suspend(payload) via ctx.agent.suspend for HITL pauses with custom payloads. First-class streaming.

Correction: the refreshed report states that tools cannot stream partial results to the model and there is no tool-side progress stream; the .NET progress-events claim from May is no longer supported. The remaining small primitives are enqueue_messages (a tool can queue messages into the running session for the next model call), polled MCP long-running tasks and sub-agent stream callbacks. UIs only see tool start/finish via the agent stream.

Function-tool API returns when the async function returns — no yield-based incremental output to the model. Hosted ShellTool streams stdout deltas and ApplyPatchTool streams patch progress, but those are special-cased hosted-tool flows, not a generic API. Pattern for long-running tools: return a job_id and poll, or use a sub-agent.

execute returns a Promise<Result> — no yield-based incremental output to the model. Tools must buffer and return a single final string. For long-running tools the recommendation is to use HITL approval pause as a poor substitute.

Tools can call ctx.emit(event) to stream CustomEvents to consumers without adding to model context; the Vercel adapter maps it to preliminary tool-output chunks, and Harness BackgroundTools let a tool keep running while the agent continues. The model still receives only the final return value. Raised from 2 to 3, the same level as LlamaIndex's ctx.write_event_to_stream, which is the equivalent mechanism; it stays below the first-class tool-writer APIs of LangGraph, Mastra and Vercel.

A tool's call returns one Output; there is no incremental yield or progress event from a running tool. 0.43 also removed partial tool-argument streaming (tool calls now stream whole). A tool can only publish host metadata via insert_result after completion.

Tools return an AsyncGenerator; yielded values are wrapped as ToolStreamEvents (tools/executors/_executor.py:227-256) and surface to the agent stream. The final yield must be a ToolResult which the executor extracts. First-class streaming tools.

Tool callbacks can be async generators yielding ToolStreamEvent or arbitrary values (strands-ts/src/tools/tool.ts:93). Yielded values become ToolStreamUpdateEvents; the final return becomes the ToolResultBlock. First-class streaming tools.

Tool execute can return AsyncIterable<OUTPUT> (packages/provider-utils/src/types/tool-execute-function.ts:38). Each yielded chunk becomes a tool-output-available chunk with preliminary: true, then a final non-preliminary chunk. Useful for tools that progressively reveal output. First-class streaming.

Hook-style gating exists even without a policy layer: BeforeToolCallback can return a result to block a call, tool.FilterToolset hides tools from the model, and RequireConfirmation / RequireConfirmationProvider (plus WithConfirmation for any toolset) give per-tool HITL approval. There is still no allow/deny policy engine, no canUseTool equivalent and no sandbox providers; tools run in-process and the default is allow. Raised from 1 for calibration against Rig's new hook-plus-allow-list model and Eino/LangGraph, which have the same mix of deny hook, visibility filter and approval pause; this is a calibration fix, not a new upstream feature.

Gates: requires_confirmation/requires_user_input/external_execution on @tool, tool_hooks that deny server-side, admin approvals, JWT scope RBAC on HTTP routes (default-deny once authorization is on). Hardening since May: injected-override stripping, MCP tool_name override blocked, centralised safe_join path containment, CodingTools.run_shell opt-in. Sandbox providers: E2B, Daytona, Docker, Superserve; CodeMode runs an in-process IPython kernel (not a sandbox) and skill scripts run on the host via subprocess. Default-allow for registered tools.

AgentHooks::on_tool_call returning Abort is the per-call allow/deny primitive; there is no allowlist structure or HITL approval and the agent-level default is allow. v0.4.0 hardened the built-in tools: filesystem tools are root-scoped by default (no absolute paths, .., symlink escapes), document fetching blocks private networks, and local MCP processes are denied unless a McpProcessPolicy allows them. WasmRuntime (wasmtime) and CodeActAgent (rquickjs, no imports/network/process) sandbox code; no E2B/Daytona/Modal integration. Held at 3: strong built-in tool boundaries, thin agent-level ACL.

SandboxSettings (types.py:873-916) controls macOS sandbox-exec / Linux seccomp bash sandboxing, with autoAllowBashIfSandboxed, excludedCommands, allowUnsandboxedCommands, SandboxNetworkConfig (allowedDomains/deniedDomains/allowManagedDomainsOnly/allowMachLookup). permission_mode ∈ {default, acceptEdits, plan, bypassPermissions, dontAsk, auto} where auto uses a model classifier and dontAsk denies anything not pre-approved. can_use_tool per-call interception. No E2B/Daytona/Modal adapters.

Full permission stack: canUseTool, PreToolUse/PermissionRequest/PermissionDenied hooks, PermissionMode (default/acceptEdits/bypassPermissions/plan/dontAsk/auto), declarative PermissionUpdate rules persisted per scope, allowedTools/disallowedTools, per-MCP-server McpServerToolPolicy and permission-mode override, permissionPrompts:'none', and an OS sandbox (bubblewrap/seatbelt) with network allowlists and credential masking. No E2B/Daytona/Modal adapters. Caveat from 0.3.286: omitting permissionMode now follows Claude Code (auto classifier or a settings default), so servers must set it explicitly; canUseTool can also be shadowed by allow rules or auto mode. Still the most complete sandbox and permission surface in the survey.

Allow/deny via Agent(tools=[...]) construction-time. max_usage_count cap per tool. before_tool_call hook returning False blocks execution. MCP ToolFilter restricts server-exposed tools. AMP RBAC scopes per-org-role. E2B and Daytona are first-party in crewai-tools with persistent/one-shot/attach lifecycle modes. Default-deny for tools (only what you pass via tools=[...]). Strong sandbox integrations, allow/deny is construction-time-only in OSS.

Allow/deny lists are BYO via BeforeAgent filtering of the tool list, and WrapInvokableToolCall can deny a call or raise an interrupt for human approval. New in the refresh: a ValidateCommand hook on the local shell backend and an ACP client backend that routes file and terminal operations to the editor, which owns the permission prompts; the AgentKit Python sandbox for filesystem operations already existed. Core tools still run with the host process's permissions and the default is allow. Raised from 1 to sit with LangGraph (wrap_tool_call plus interrupt) and Strands at 2.

ToolApproval middleware with AllowedTools list — any tool not on the allowlist triggers an interrupt and requires explicit RestartWith({toolApproved:true}) approval. Filesystem middleware uses os.Root sandbox (no .., absolute paths, or symlinks) with strict size caps (256KB chunks, 10MB files). Default-allow globally; ToolApproval flips to default-deny + allowlist. No E2B/Daytona/Modal sandbox adapters.

wrap_tool_call is the sole per-tool ACL hook; engineers wire the policy in the wrapper. No declarative allow_tools=[...] list. No sandbox provider integrations in this repo — engineers wire E2B/Daytona/Modal as @tool wrappers around their SDKs. Default-allow; wrap_tool_call is opt-in for tightening.

No canUseTool-style hook. Permission is enforced by what tools you put in tools=[...] at agent construction. Inside a tool you can raise to refuse, but no declarative ACL. Sandbox integrations: llama-index-tools-code-interpreter (local, not sandboxed by default), Azure code interpreter, AWS Bedrock AgentCore. No E2B/Daytona/Modal first-party packages. Default-allow.

Correction: sandbox providers were first-party in May but under-credited. workspaces/ ships daytona, e2b, modal, docker, vercel, blaxel, cloudflare-sandbox, railway, agentcore and more, plus LocalSandbox wrapping commands in macOS Seatbelt or Linux Bubblewrap. Permission layers: per-tool requireApproval (boolean or function of input), run-level requireToolApproval, persisted per-category approval policies in AgentController sessions, activeTools filtering, beforeToolCall blocking and RBAC/FGA on HTTP routes. Default-allow for tools (default-deny for HTTP routes when auth is configured), and no declarative rule language, so 4 not 5.

approval_mode on FunctionTool/@tool, ToolApprovalMiddleware (Python) and ToolApprovalAgent (.NET) with standing-approval rules, and FunctionMiddleware raising MiddlewareTermination for canUseTool-style denial. Framework-shipped risky tools are now default-deny/approval: skills tools, file write tools and shell (always_require; never_require needs acknowledge_unsafe) while custom @tool functions default to never_require. Sandboxes: Hyperlight micro-VM, Docker shell (ContainerUser, DockerNetworkMode), Monty, LocalCodeAct; no E2B/Daytona/Modal. MCP server sampling is denied by default.

Strong stack: needs_approval (bool or callable) on function, shell, apply-patch, custom and agent tools, per-server MCP require_approval, input/output tool guardrails (now also pre-approval and MCP-wide), is_enabled and tool_filter visibility, per-tool timeouts, and hosted-shell network allowlists. Sandbox Agents ship Docker, Unix-local and seven hosted providers (Blaxel, Cloudflare, Daytona, E2B, Modal, Runloop, Vercel) with hardening for mount credentials and network, but the report labels Sandbox Agents beta and notes Unix-local adds no OS confinement. Lowered from 5 under the shared maturity cap (beta sandbox is the main differentiator); default posture is allow with no global deny list.

tool({needsApproval: true|predicate}) approval gate bound to the normalised invocation (fails closed on invalid args), isEnabled visibility, per-tool and MCP-wide input/output guardrails, preApprovalInputGuardrails, MCPServer.toolFilter and hosted MCP allowedTools/requireApproval. Sandbox providers: Docker and UnixLocalSandboxClient in core (Unix-local does not confine host shell commands) plus E2B, Modal, Daytona, Vercel, Cloudflare, Runloop and Blaxel extensions; the sandbox beta label was removed on main only (unreleased at analysis time). Default posture is allow; lighter than the Python sibling.

Core offers requires_approval / ApprovalRequired with HandleDeferredToolCalls, before_tool_execute (raise or SkipToolExecution as canUseTool), PrepareTools per-step ACLs and default-deny for unknown tool names. The first-party Harness (0.x) adds ToolGuardrail with allow/block/replace/retry/approve, Shell allow/deny lists, and sandbox capabilities (Modal, E2B, Sprites, Bubblewrap, SSH) that host FileSystem/Shell/Coder. Capped at 4 because the sandbox and guardrail pieces are 0.x Harness packages; docs themselves say LocalWorkspace is not a sandbox, and no Daytona integration. Default-allow for declared tools.

on_dispatch can skip(reason), stop the run, deny or patch tool arguments; on_invalid_tool_call handles unknown or malformed calls; RequestPatch::active_tools sets a per-turn tool allow-list; tools can refuse via ToolExecutionError::refused; and examples build in-process and durable approval gates on these hooks. Still allow-all-registered by default, no per-tool ACL type, no sandbox providers or built-in sandbox. Raised from 1 because the hook can now rewrite arguments and a per-turn allow-list exists.

New policy layer: interventions return Proceed/Deny/Guide/Confirm/Transform per lifecycle point (fail-closed option), vended HumanInTheLoop has an allowlist with optional LLM risk classifier and trust-on-approve, and CedarAuthorization evaluates per-tool Cedar policy with a fail-closed principal resolver. A Sandbox abstraction (host default, BYO-container Docker, SSH) routes the vended shell/file_editor, but there are no hardened providers or E2B/Daytona/Modal integrations and the default posture is allow with host execution. Raised from 2: the best policy layer outside Claude's SDK, held at 4 for the minimal sandbox side.

Same policy ideas as Python: InterventionHandler deny/guide/confirm, HumanInTheLoop (flips to approval-by-default with allowlist and LLM risk classifier), LLMSteeringHandler and Cedar via cedar-wasm with call-count limits. Sandbox is wired into Agent (host default, BYO-container Docker with no hardening flags, SSH), but the persistent bash tool ignores it. Direct agent.tool.X calls bypass hooks, interventions and middleware, a standing hole for policy enforcement. Raised from 2 and held one below the Python sibling because of those two gaps.

toolApproval (global, per-tool map or function receiving runtime context and messages) returns approved/denied/user-approval; the new @ai-sdk/policy-opa builds that function from Open Policy Agent, experimental signed approvals add HMAC replay protection, plus activeTools, per-tool timeouts and tool fingerprinting against MCP drift. Experimental_Sandbox has first-party Vercel microVM and just-bash providers (E2B/Daytona/Modal not first-party). Capped at 4 for the experimental sandbox/signing pieces. Default-allow: no toolApproval means tools run, and HarnessAgent permissionMode defaults to allow-all.

`tool/mcptoolset/` wraps the official `modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk` (now v1.8.0, `go.mod:18`). `mcptoolset.Config` (`set.go:102-145`) takes a `Transport` or, new, an `Endpoint` that builds a streamable HTTP transport, plus `Auth`, `RequireConfirmation`; tools are filtered with `tool.FilterToolset` / `AllowedToolsPredicate`. Session is created lazily; non-text results are rendered instead of dropped; Agent Registry can resolve MCP servers. Drops straight into an `Agent`'s toolsets.

`agno.tools.mcp.MCPTools` (`libs/agno/agno/tools/mcp/mcp.py:242`) is a `Toolkit` built on `fastmcp.Client` that exposes an external server's tools to the agent in one line. It handles structuredContent-only results, `_meta`, audio and paginated `tools/list`, with static `headers` and a dynamic `header_provider`. `MultiMCPTools` was removed in v3, so you use one `MCPTools` per server; `MCPToolbox` covers Google's toolbox.

`McpToolsManager` (`autoagents-toolkit/src/mcp/client.rs:144`) connects to one or many MCP servers from a config file, lists tools (paginated) and wraps each as an `McpToolAdapter` implementing `ToolT`. v0.4.0 adds Streamable HTTP next to stdio, so remote servers no longer need host-built code, plus `server_instructions()`, `prompts()`, `resources()` and partial-connect tolerance. Gaps are no legacy SSE, no OAuth and the `mcp` cargo feature gate; raised from 4 because the stdio-only gap is closed.

`mcp_servers` on the options object (`types.py:2010-2017`: dict, JSON file path or inline JSON) is consumed by the bundled Claude CLI, which is the actual MCP client. Full transport set including in-process SDK servers; in-process servers now run on the `mcp` library with resources and prompts support (0.2.140).

`Options.mcpServers` (`sdk.d.ts:1955`) takes stdio/SSE/HTTP/in-process configs, also loaded from `.mcp.json`, settings and plugins unless `strictMcpConfig` is set. Mid-session `setMcpServers`, toggle and reconnect APIs exist; since 0.3.221 `options.mcpServers` servers connect before the first turn. MCP Apps `_meta` and `readMcpResource()` (alpha) were added. The CLI does the actual MCP client work.

`mcp/config.py:12-123` ships `MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerHTTP`, `MCPServerSSE`; `Agent(mcps=[...])` (`agents/agent_builder/base_agent.py:379`) accepts bare slugs (resolved via AMP integrations), URLs or typed configs, with per-server `ToolFilter` and optional tools-list caching. `@CrewBase` projects also get `mcp_server_params` / `get_mcp_tools()` over `crewai_tools.MCPServerAdapter`. MCP `isError` results now surface as tool failures.

Two eino-ext adapters: `components/tool/mcp/` (mark3labs SDK) and `components/tool/mcp/officialmcp/` (modelcontextprotocol go-sdk), both returning `[]tool.BaseTool` with schema translation. The official adapter gained `ServerName`/`ToolNameMapper` for multi-server collisions, paginated listing, description/result policies and typed errors; `components/prompt/mcp/` exposes MCP prompts. Agentic model adapters also support provider-side remote MCP.

`go/plugins/mcp/` is a full plugin built on `mark3labs/mcp-go`: `NewGenkitMCPClient` for one server (`client.go:98`) and `NewMCPHost` (`host.go:53`, now returns an error) for several. Tools, prompts and resources can all be consumed (`GetActiveTools`, `GetPrompt`, `GetActiveResources`).

MCP client support is provided by the separately-versioned `langchain-mcp-adapters` package which exposes MCP server tools as standard LangChain `BaseTool` instances. Works inside any `ToolNode` / `create_react_agent`, but not bundled in `langgraph` core.

`llama-index-tools-mcp` (v0.6.0) ships `McpToolSpec` (`base.py:19`), which consumes any `mcp.ClientSession` and turns its tools into `FunctionTool`s with `allowed_tools`, partial params and optional resources. It now builds on the `mcp` 2.x SDK (`pyproject.toml:44`), a breaking change for hosts that pin `mcp` 1.x. `BasicMCPClient` picks stdio, SSE or streamable HTTP from the URL or command.

`MCPClient` (`packages/mcp/src/client/configuration.ts:90`) consumes external MCP servers and exposes their tools to agents; stored MCP clients can be managed over HTTP (`packages/server/.../stored-mcp-clients.ts`). Since `@mastra/mcp` 2.0 the client probes servers with `server/discover` and falls back to the legacy handshake. Server instructions can be forwarded into agent system prompts. Note `@mastra/core` is analysed at an alpha HEAD.

Python `MCPTool` base (`_mcp.py:871`) with `MCPStdioTool` (3499), `MCPStreamableHTTPTool` (3709), `MCPWebsocketTool` (4318); extras include progressive disclosure, sampling guardrails, OTel spans, experimental long-running tasks (`MCPTaskOptions`) and security labelling of results. .NET uses the ModelContextProtocol C# SDK, with `Microsoft.Agents.AI.Mcp` adding task-aware functions and MCP skills.

`MCPServer` ABC (`src/agents/mcp/server.py:562`) with `MCPServerStdio` (`:1962`), `MCPServerSse` (`:2112`), `MCPServerStreamableHttp` (`:2290`); attach via `Agent(mcp_servers=[...])` (`agent.py:201`) with per-turn tool discovery. `MCPServerManager` pairs connect/cleanup and, since 0.20, serializes overlapping lifecycle operations. `HostedMCPTool` covers OpenAI-hosted connectors; MCP SDK v2 is supported with protocol probing.

`agent.mcpServers: MCPServer[]` with `MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerStreamableHttp` and legacy `MCPServerSSE` (`packages/agents-core/src/mcp.ts:314, 392, 504`). Tools are merged each turn via `Agent.getMcpTools(runContext)` (`agent.ts:1136`) across all paginated pages, with `toolFilter`, `toolMetaResolver` and server-wide tool guardrails.

V2 unified the old `MCPServerStdio/SSE/StreamableHTTP` classes and `FastMCPToolset` into one `MCPToolset` (`pydantic_ai_slim/pydantic_ai/mcp.py:717`) on the FastMCP `Client`, covering tools, resources, prompts, sampling, elicitation, OAuth and background tasks. `load_mcp_toolsets(config.json)` handles multi-server configs, and the `MCP` capability can use provider-native MCP or run the server locally. It is a regular toolset, so it drops into any agent.

MCP client lives in its own `rig-rmcp` crate since 0.43 (facade feature `rmcp`), wrapping the `rmcp` SDK. `McpTool` becomes a context-aware `DynamicTool` and `McpClientHandler` keeps a tool sink in sync on `tools/list_changed` with timeouts (`crates/rig-rmcp/src/native.rs`, `handler.rs`). `AgentBuilder::rmcp_tool(s)` were removed, so wiring goes through `DynamicTool`/handler, and the crate is native-only (no wasm). Kept at 4: capable but less drop-in than the config-driven peers.

note: MCPClient with filtering and background thread
details: `MCPClient` (`tools/mcp/mcp_client.py:216`, a `ToolProvider`) wraps the official `mcp` SDK with `ToolFilters`, `prefix`, background-thread session management and `on_tools_changed` refresh. New: `url=`/`headers=` construction, `load_servers` reading a standard `mcpServers` JSON, `continue_on_error`, elicitation/progress callbacks and per-call cancellation. Supports `mcp>=1.23,<2.2` with a 2.x compatibility layer.

`McpClient` (`strands-ts/src/mcp/client.ts:148`) goes directly into `AgentConfig.tools`; `agent.initialize()` registers its tools and `toolsChanged` re-registers them. `McpClient.loadServers` reads a JSON `mcpServers` config (released since v1.8.0) with `toolFilters` and `prefix`. On main the client swaps to `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.0, unreleased at analysis time (v1.19.0 still uses `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.x).

`@ai-sdk/mcp` `createMCPClient(config)` (`packages/mcp/src/tool/mcp-client.ts:289`) returns a client whose `.tools()` yields a `ToolSet` that drops into `agent.tools` or `streamText`. Added since May: `maxRetries`, MCP Apps support, server-name propagation, `deferLoading` for tool search. The `experimental_createMCPClient` alias is deprecated.

note: no server side in Go SDK
details: ADK Go does not expose an agent's tools as an MCP server. `examples/mcp/main.go` builds an in-process MCP server with the go-sdk, but only to demo the client; v2.1-v2.5 changed nothing here. Exposure would be a standalone server written against the upstream SDK.

`AgentOS(mcp=True | MCPConfig(...))` serves MCP at a configurable `/mcp` path (`os/mcp.py:2984`) with a default operator surface of 8 tools (`run_agent`, `run_team`, `run_workflow`, `continue_run`, `cancel_run`, sessions...). `MCPConfig.tools` publishes agents, teams, workflows, toolkits and functions as individually named MCP tools with annotations; stateless mode, DNS-rebinding protection and a server card are included. Making the default tools opt-in under `MCPConfig` is on main (unreleased at analysis time); lifecycle is managed by AgentOS.
AutoAgents can consume MCP servers but does not expose its own tools as one. Server-side is fully BYO via `rmcp` directly.

`create_sdk_mcp_server` + `@tool` (`__init__.py:251, 491`), or since 0.2.140 any hand-built `mcp.server.Server`, run in-process and are served to the bundled CLI only (`McpSdkServerConfig`, types.py:648). The SDK has no standalone entrypoint to publish tools to other MCP clients; running the `Server` with `mcp`'s own transports is straightforward but BYO. Same capability as TS (`createSdkMcpServer`), so aligned at 3 rather than 4. Both stay above BYO-only stacks because the SDK ships the server builder and typed tool helpers.

`createSdkMcpServer` (`sdk.d.ts:613`) builds an in-process server visible only to this SDK's CLI subprocess; other processes cannot connect to it. To expose tools to other agents or clients you write a standalone server with `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`.

Correction: the `_mcp_server_adapter` on `@CrewBase` crews is an `MCPServerAdapter` client used to consume servers (`project/crew_base.py:251, 303-328`), and the 'custom MCP server' docs page cited in May did not exist. eino-ext has no `eino.NewMCPServer` helper and no documented pattern; you expose Eino tools through the `mark3labs/mcp-go` or official go-sdk server APIs yourself, which is fully host-built code. Moved from 1 to 0 in the calibration pass: nothing is provided or documented, the same evidence as adk-go, AutoAgents and Vercel AI at 0.

`mcp.NewMCPServer(g, mcp.MCPServerOptions{Name: ...})` (`go/plugins/mcp/server.go:51-110`) exposes Genkit-registered tools and resources to MCP clients via `ServeStdio()` or `Serve(transport)` (`server.go:262-280`). One Go process can be an MCP server and client at the same time.

Every deployed agent on `langgraph_api` automatically gets an `/mcp` route, opt-out via `disable_mcp: true` in `langgraph.json` (`libs/cli/langgraph_cli/schemas.py:471-472`). Schemas are populated for MCP at runtime; same-process server.

`workflow_as_mcp(workflow)` (`utils.py:77-141`) wraps any `Workflow` (including an `AgentWorkflow`) as an MCP server (now the `mcp` SDK's `MCPServer`, previously `FastMCP`), exposing it as a single tool and streaming workflow events as MCP log messages. Whole-workflow granularity rather than per-tool.

`MCPServer` (`packages/mcp/src/server/server.ts:155`) exposes Mastra tools, agents (as `ask_<agent>` tools) and workflows. The 2.0 rebuild is stateless (no `initialize` handshake or session header; suspended tools answer `input_required` with a signed `requestState`), which helps horizontal scaling. Transports are stdio and streamable HTTP; `MastraApiMCPServer` was removed.

`Agent.as_mcp_server(server_name=...)` (`_agents.py:1812`) exposes an agent as a single MCP tool and returns an MCP `Server` you can serve over any transport. `agent-framework-hosting-mcp` (alpha) adds `AgentMCPTool` / `WorkflowMCPTool` helpers for app-owned servers. The Azure Functions MCP trigger cited in May has moved to the durable-extension repo.

No 'expose my agent/tools as an MCP server' wrapper and no documented pattern; you use the `mcp` SDK directly. `HostedMCPTool` consumes OpenAI-hosted servers and does not serve. Moved from 1 to 0 in the calibration pass: BYO with nothing provided, level with adk-go, AutoAgents and Vercel AI.

The SDK does not expose its own agent or tools as an MCP server and documents no pattern for it; `hostedMcpTool` consumes hosted MCP via the Responses API, and exposing your tools means hand-rolling a server with `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`. Moved from 1 to 0 in the calibration pass: nothing provided, level with the other BYO-only stacks.

Correction: no API exposes an `Agent`'s tools as an MCP server (the May report overstated the FastMCP adapter). The documented pattern is your own FastMCP/`mcp` server whose tool calls an agent (`docs/mcp/server.md:9-34`); Pydantic AI can also be the LLM behind MCP sampling (`docs/mcp/server.md:71`). Rated like other BYO-only stacks, with a small documentation edge.

No adapter exposes Rig tools or agents as an MCP server; `rmcp::ServerHandler` appears only in tests (`crates/rig-rmcp/src/tests/dispatch.rs:57`). The report's BYO route is a `ServerHandler` that forwards to `ToolServerHandle::execute`, but no helper or documented pattern exists and Rig's `ToolServer` is an internal registry, not MCP. Moved from 1 to 0 in the calibration pass, level with the other BYO-only stacks without a documented pattern.

Correction: `strands-mcp/` (PyPI `strands-agents-mcp-server`) serves Strands documentation search to coding assistants, not your agent's tools. The SDK has no way to expose an agent's tools as an MCP server and documents no pattern; you build one with the `mcp` package. Moved from 1 to 0 in the calibration pass, level with the TypeScript SDK and the other BYO-only stacks.

`strands-ts` does not expose an agent's tools as an MCP server (`@modelcontextprotocol/server` appears only in tests) and documents no pattern. `strands-mcp/` in the monorepo is a separate Python package that serves Strands documentation to coding assistants, not a way to expose agent tools. Moved from 1 to 0 in the calibration pass: in-process exposure has to be hand-built, level with the Python SDK.

`@ai-sdk/mcp` is client-only; there is no public API to expose your tools as an MCP server, so you use `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`. The Claude Code harness bridge creates an internal MCP server inside the sandbox (`packages/harness-claude-code/src/bridge/index.ts:41`), but it is not a reusable API.

note: stdio HTTP SSE via official SDK
details: Any go-sdk `mcp.Transport` (`CommandTransport` for stdio, `StreamableClientTransport`, SSE, in-memory) or the new `Endpoint` shortcut that builds a streamable HTTP transport. `Auth` requires streamable HTTP and errors with stdio (`set.go:113-118`). In-process use is possible with the in-memory transport but there is no ADK-specific helper.

Client: `MCPTools(transport='stdio' | 'sse' | 'streamable-http')` (`mcp.py:260`) plus `protocol_mode='legacy' | 'auto'` for the newer sessionless MCP spec. Server: Streamable HTTP, optionally `stateless=True`, with `allowed_hosts` DNS-rebinding protection. No in-process client transport.

v0.4.0 adds `StreamableHttpClientTransport` (`client.rs:435-437`, `McpRemoteServerConfig { url, headers }`) beside `TokioChildProcess` stdio (`client.rs:412`). Legacy SSE is not wired and unknown protocols map to `Unsupported`; there is no in-process or custom-transport path. Raised from 2: the two transports that matter now work out of the box.
`McpStdioServerConfig`, `McpSSEServerConfig`, `McpHttpServerConfig` (`types.py:623-647`) plus `McpSdkServerConfig` for in-process tools bridged over the CLI control protocol (`types.py:648-665`).
stdio, SSE, streamable HTTP and in-process SDK servers are in the public `McpServerConfig` union; a `claude.ai` proxy config is internal. WebSocket is not in the public union.

Stdio, streamable HTTP, and SSE are each implemented as a dedicated module under `mcp/transports/` (`stdio.py`, `http.py`, `sse.py`); no in-process / SDK-direct transport — every MCP server runs in a separate process or remote service.

Inherited from two SDKs: `mark3labs/mcp-go` (stdio, SSE, Streamable HTTP) and the official go-sdk (stdio, SSE, Streamable HTTP). `officialmcp/session.TransportConfig` selects by `Type` and accepts a custom `Factory` returning any `mcp.Transport`, which also covers in-memory use.

`StdioConfig`, `SSEConfig`, `StreamableHTTPConfig` are first-class (`mcp/client.go:31-60`); v1.13.x honours a custom `StreamableHTTPConfig.HTTPClient`. No in-process transport: a local Go function is simply a Genkit tool.

note: client stdio plus HTTP server HTTP only
details: Client side covers stdio + HTTP via `langchain-mcp-adapters`; server side (the `/mcp` route on `langgraph_api`) is HTTP only. No SSE on the server, no in-process transport advertised.

note: stdio SSE streamable HTTP plus in-process
details: `BasicMCPClient` (`client.py:21-23`) auto-picks stdio, SSE or streamable HTTP from the URL or command (`client.py:53-65, 229-274`); the streamable-HTTP client now uses `httpx2` under the `mcp` 2.x migration. `workflow_as_mcp` covers the in-process server case.

In 2.0 the standalone HTTP+SSE transport was removed (`startSSE`, `connectSSE`, session ids), leaving stdio and Streamable HTTP on both client and server (`client.ts:553, 621`; `server.ts:1083, 1101`). The May 'in-process transport' claim is downgraded: only `server.executeTool()` runs a tool in-process, with no in-memory client-server transport. Lowered from 5 (upstream removal plus correction).

Python ships stdio, streamable HTTP and WebSocket (`MCPWebsocketTool`); .NET gets stdio and HTTP/SSE via the MCP C# SDK. Correction: there is no in-process MCP transport; `as_mcp_server()` returns an MCP `Server` you can serve over any transport, including the `mcp` SDK's in-memory streams. Kept at 5 given breadth and parity with OpenAI Agents JS.

`MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerSse`, `MCPServerStreamableHttp` cover the three wire transports. No first-party `InProcessMCPServer`; recommended pattern is `@function_tool` directly when you want in-process.
`MCPServerStdio`, `MCPServerStreamableHttp` (recommended), `MCPServerSSE` (legacy), plus `hostedMcpTool({...})` (`tool.ts:918`) for OpenAI-hosted MCP via the Responses API.

note: stdio SSE streamable HTTP plus FastMCP
details: `MCPToolset` infers the transport from its argument: stdio, SSE, Streamable HTTP, or an in-process `FastMCP` server instance with no subprocess (`docs/mcp/client.md:48-163`). Multi-server JSON configs are supported. The V2 rewrite replaced the separate `MCPServerStdio/SSE/StreamableHTTP` classes.

Inherited from the `rmcp` crate (re-exported as `rig_rmcp::rmcp`): stdio child process, SSE and streamable HTTP, depending on how you build the `rmcp` service (`examples/rmcp`). In-process pairs are possible with `rmcp`'s in-memory transports but Rig adds nothing for it.

`MCPServerConfig` auto-detects stdio (`command`) versus URL-based transports; stdio, SSE and streamable HTTP via `mcp>=1.23,<2.2` (`mcp_client.py:158-184`). `MCPClient(transport_callable=...)` accepts any factory, so an in-memory transport is possible, but plain `@tool` functions are the in-process route.

Streamable HTTP (from `McpClientConfig.url`), stdio (`config.node.ts:79-86`), SSE (`:112-115`) or a custom `transport` object. Stdio and SSE builders are Node-only. In-process MCP would need a server-transport pair built with the upstream SDK.
`packages/mcp/src/tool/` ships stdio, SSE and streamable HTTP transports plus a mock transport for tests. No function-to-MCP wrapper, because native `tool({...})` already covers in-process tools.

`Config.Auth auth.CredentialProvider` resolves a credential per outgoing request through a context-aware RoundTripper (static bearer, API key, OAuth2 token source, ADC, service account, per-end-user GCP credentials; `set.go:113-122`, `auth/transport.go:31-39`). Sessions are created lazily and `connectionRefresher` reconnects after failures (`tool/mcptoolset/client.go:36-62`); config is validated at construction. Gaps: no interactive OAuth consent flow wired to MCP and no health API. Raised from 3 (v2.1-v2.5 outbound auth).

Client: static `headers=` and a dynamic `header_provider(...)` for per-request JWTs; connection failures no longer crash agents, and AgentOS manages connect/close in `mcp_lifespan` (`os/app.py:107`). Server: same `AuthMiddleware` as REST with per-tool scope checks, an OAuth authorization-server option, PATs and `allowed_hosts`. No client-side OAuth, reconnect or health API, which keeps it at 4.

Static env vars (local) and per-server HTTP headers (remote); OAuth is explicitly not handled. Adds deny-by-default `McpProcessPolicy`, `connect`/`disconnect` (`client.rs:298, 323`), per-server `status()` (`Connected | Disabled | Failed`) and cleanup of stale tools after a failed reconnect. No automatic reconnection or health polling; per-server `timeout_ms` defaults to 30 s. Raised from 2.

`ClaudeSDKClient.reconnect_mcp_server`, `get_mcp_status()` (`McpServerStatus` per server, `types.py:743-770`) and `toggle_mcp_server` (`client.py:395-441`); credentials via env or `McpHttpServerConfig.headers`. `strict_mcp_config` blocks project/user/global configs, which matters for multi-tenant isolation. The hard-coded old protocol string is gone; the `mcp` library negotiates for in-process servers and the CLI for external ones.

`reconnectMcpServer()` (`sdk.d.ts:3155`), `mcpServerStatus()` (`connected | failed | needs-auth | pending | disabled`, `sdk.d.ts:3023`), automatic reconnect after transport aborts, background connect with `alwaysLoad` and a startup-wait env var, mid-session `setMcpServers`/`toggleMcpServer`, OAuth with `onElicitation`, per-server timeouts. Open issues include stdio zombie processes after session end (#219).

`headers` for HTTP/SSE, `env` for stdio; AMP slugs get OAuth through the CrewAI proxy (`mcp/tool_resolver.py:201`). `MCP_MAX_RETRIES = 3` (`mcp/client.py:55`) with connect/discovery/execution timeouts, a 5-minute `_mcp_schema_cache` (`:59-60`), typed exceptions in `mcp/exceptions.py`, `ToolFilter`, and a fix that stops stdio servers leaking the parent environment.

New `officialmcp/session` package: `session.Connect` returns a `Session` that transparently reconnects on connection-level errors with concurrent-safe reconnect and a `StartupError` type (`session.go:78-190`); `TransportConfig.HTTPClient` lets you install a RoundTripper that resolves auth per request and survives reconnects. Static `CustomHeaders`/`Meta` remain for the mark3labs adapter. Health and version negotiation are still delegated to the SDK. Raised from 3.

Credentials via `Headers` for SSE/StreamableHTTP, env vars for stdio, or a custom `HTTPClient` (e.g. an OAuth transport). Client lifecycle has `Disable`, `Reenable`, `Restart`, `Disconnect` (`client.go:239-270`) and the host has `Connect`/`Disconnect`/`Reconnect` per server (`host.go:82-133`). No health checks; failures surface on tool calls.

`MakeRuntimeContext` initializes per-run MCP connections in `ert.context` lifecycle-bound to each run. External-server auth defers to standard `langchain-mcp-adapters` (env vars, OAuth flows). No explicit framework-level health/reconnect API.

OAuth via `OAuthClientProvider` and a `TokenStorage` interface (`client.py:24-25`); `DefaultInMemoryTokenStorage` is the default, so production multi-tenant use needs a custom store. Custom `headers=` and a caller-supplied `http_client` are accepted. A new session is opened per call; there is no pooled reconnection or health check.

note: OAuth provider plus server auth bridge
details: Client: `requestInit` headers or `MCPOAuthClientProvider` (`InMemoryOAuthStorage` default, callback-server helper); `MASTRA_AUTH_TOKEN_KEY` forwards the caller's token. Server: OAuth middleware, `authInfo` bridged into each tool's `RequestContext`, W3C trace propagation. `getServerProtocolVersions()` reports negotiated versions and failed connections release their handlers; no health/reconnect API. Raised from 3 on the documented OAuth and auth-bridging surface, level with LlamaIndex.

`MCPStreamableHTTPTool(header_provider=...)` derives per-request headers from host runtime kwargs, never from model arguments (`_mcp.py:3854-3862`), applied to initialization too; provider-backed sessions are scoped per invocation and cookie persistence is explicit (1.19.0). Initialization errors surface, failed HTTP connections are cleaned up, and .NET adds refreshable auth headers and Foundry OAuth consent. No reconnect or health API; version negotiation is the MCP SDK's. Raised from 3, level with Agno.

Headers or custom `httpx`/`httpx2` auth, stdio env, explicit `connect()`/`cleanup()` plus `MCPServerManager`, `max_retry_attempts` with a backoff ceiling (`server.py:903`), `session_id` resumption for streamable HTTP, per-call `_meta` via `tool_meta_resolver`, `require_approval` policies, and server-wide tool guardrails (0.22.1; not applied to `HostedMCPTool`). MCP v2 negotiates the newest protocol with v1 fallback.

Stdio gets parent env; streamable HTTP/SSE take per-server `headers` and credentials in URLs are redacted from errors; hosted MCP accepts `authorization`/`headers`. `connectMcpServers` opens connections in parallel, serializes lifecycle operations and cleans servers before reconnect (`mcpServers.ts:194, 639`); run cancellation reaches MCP calls. Local connections use the MCP TS SDK v2 and negotiate `2026-07-28` with v1 fallback. Raised from 3; no OAuth helper or health API keeps it at 4.

`auth=` accepts a bearer token, `httpx.Auth` or `'oauth'`, plus `headers=`, custom TLS/mTLS and client identification (`docs/mcp/client.md:479-575`). One session per toolset instance is shared by concurrent runs, so per-user credentials need per-run toolsets; under durable execution there is one MCP session per run. Elicitation and background tasks are supported, with new V2 defaults for handlers and timeouts. The May reconnection claim is no longer in the report.

`McpMeta` in the run's `ToolContext` is sent as request `_meta` outside model-visible arguments, useful for tenant/user identity (`rig-rmcp/src/lib.rs:7-17`). `McpClientHandler` re-syncs tools on `tools/list_changed` with call and refresh timeouts. Transport credentials (headers, OAuth), reconnection and version negotiation remain `rmcp`'s, with no health API. Raised from 2.

Headers or OAuth client-credentials (`auth=`) or any `httpx.Auth` (`auth_provider=`) for streamable HTTP; elicitation and progress callbacks; per-call cancellation; experimental MCP tasks. The background-thread session has a startup timeout, `_NON_FATAL_ERROR_PATTERNS` (`mcp_client.py:206`) and `continue_on_error`, with cleanup through `Agent.cleanup()` and finalizers, plus tracing. Raised from 4 to match the TypeScript SDK; version negotiation stays with the `mcp` SDK.

`McpClientConfig` (`client.ts:130-145`): OAuth client credentials (`auth`), custom `authProvider`, `headers`, `toolFilters`, `prefix`, `continueOnError` (renamed from `failOpen`; a failed client retries on `connect(true)`), `elicitationCallback`, OTel toggle, and the agent cancel signal forwarded to tool calls. `tasksConfig` is experimental and effectively disabled (throws on `callTool`). `versionNegotiation: { mode: 'auto' }` probes protocol 2026-07-28; the MCP v2 SDK swap is unreleased at analysis time.

OAuth in `packages/mcp/src/tool/oauth.ts` (now with credential invalidation), custom headers on HTTP/SSE, capability/version negotiation at handshake and configurable retries. `fingerprintTools` / `detectToolDrift` address trust-on-first-use of server-controlled tool descriptions, and `@ai-sdk/policy-opa` can gate MCP tools.

No first-party PII redaction, prompt-injection detection, or hallucination detection; report 18.1 says "Not provided — BYO" via BeforeModelCallback / AfterModelCallback or plugin OnUserMessageCallback / OnEventCallback. Refresh caveats: tail-retention compaction summaries bypass OnEventCallback plugins (session/compaction/compaction.go:181-201), so a redaction plugin can miss them; opt-in GenAI span content can export prompts to the tracing backend; the openaimodel adapter rejects SafetySettings / ModelArmorConfig, so Gemini-side safety settings do not carry over.

First-class BaseGuardrail (libs/agno/agno/guardrails/base.py:8) with check/acheck raising InputCheckError / OutputCheckError. Bundled detectors: PromptInjectionGuardrail, PIIDetectionGuardrail (custom_patterns accepts raw regex strings since v2.6.19) and OpenAIModerationGuardrail, wired declaratively through pre_hooks / post_hooks. LLM-judge prompts fence judged output behind a per-call nonce (v2.8.0). Covers PII, injection and moderation out of the box; hallucination detection is BYO.

Dedicated autoagents-guardrails crate ships prompt_injection.rs, regex_pii_redaction.rs and toxicity.rs guards, plugged into the LLM pipeline as an LLMLayer with Block / Sanitize / Audit policies. Block raises LLMError::GuardrailBlocked and propagates through the executor; guardrail errors are explicitly excluded from fallback so a blocked request is not retried on another provider (fallback.rs:87-88). Python bindings ship as autoagents-guardrails-py wheels with v0.4.0 (released; the whole framework is pre-1.0). No hallucination detection.

No first-party PII redaction, prompt-injection classifier or hallucination detection; BYO via UserPromptSubmit / PreToolUse / PostToolUse hooks. Refresh adds verbatim_prompts=True (0.2.158, types.py:2219-2248), a narrow mitigation that stops the CLI expanding @path / @server:resource / slash commands in untrusted prompt text. That is an input-handling switch, not a content filter or detector, so the score stays 0. The SDK's strength is sandbox/permissions (13.4), not content guardrails.

Not first-party for PII redaction, prompt-injection or hallucination detection. BYO via UserPromptSubmit (block/rewrite input), PreToolUse (validate args), PostToolUse.updatedToolOutput (redact results) and MessageDisplay (display-only rewrite). Built-ins that are not guardrails in the benchmark sense: the auto permission classifier (judges tool calls, not content), refusal handling (stop_reason "refusal" with stop_details) and sandbox credential masking. Same posture as the Python SDK.

Agent.guardrail (agent/core.py:362) and Task.guardrail take a callable or a natural-language description checked by an LLM (tasks/llm_guardrail.py), returning (passed, output_or_feedback) with retry up to guardrail_max_retries (default 3). Refresh adds INPUT / PRE_MODEL_CALL / PRE_TOOL_CALL / OUTPUT interception hooks that can rewrite payloads or raise HookAborted, a usable seam for PII or injection screening, but you write the detectors. No first-party PII redaction, prompt-injection or hallucination detection in OSS; the hallucination guardrail, PII trace redaction and Agent Control Plane policies (Beta) are AMP-only (paid).

Report states "Not first-party": PII redaction, prompt-injection and hallucination detection are BYO through a ChatModelAgentMiddleware (BeforeModelRewriteState for input, AfterModelRewriteState / WrapModel for output). Refresh notes ModelRetryConfig.ShouldRetry can now reject an output that fails a check and retry (adk/retry_chatmodel.go:145-218), a usable output-guardrail hook but still no bundled detector.

Report 18.1: not provided as a first-party primitive in go/; no PII redaction, prompt-injection or hallucination detectors. What exists: ai.ErrGenerationBlocked surfaces provider safety blocks as a typed error (v1.13), aix.WithStateTransform / WithStreamTransform redact what leaves the server for agents, genkit.Handler redacts non-public error text, and A2UI validates model-produced UI. Input/output scrubbing is BYO via WrapGenerate / WrapTool.

Report 18.1: "Not provided — BYO"; PII redaction, prompt-injection and hallucination detection live outside the OSS runtime. Common patterns are pre_model_hook for input scrubbing, wrap_tool_call for tool-output scrubbing, LangChain integrations (Lakera, Presidio, OpenAI moderation) as callbacks or nodes, and the separate langchain create_agent PII middleware package. TracePolicy can strip payloads from traces but is explicitly not a redaction mechanism.

Not first-party in core. The llama-index-integrations ecosystem includes llama-index-guardrails (PyPI) and integrations with Guardrails AI and NeMo Guardrails, but there is no first-party PII redaction, prompt-injection or hallucination detection on the agent loop. Score reflects ecosystem availability without in-tree primitives.

Comprehensive built-in processors under packages/core/src/processors/processors/: moderation.ts (LLM-based), pii-detector.ts and prompt-injection-detector.ts (both with onDetection callbacks), regex-filter.ts (redact strategy), language-detector, unicode-normalizer, system-prompt-scrubber, token-cost-control. Refresh adds ClassifierProcessor (typed classifier policies over input, output and streaming content, 1.69.0) and cyber-refusal-handler (retry on OpenAI/Anthropic cyber safeguard refusals, 1.72.0), both in stable releases. Each processor can abort('reason', { retry?, metadata? }); processToolResult lets guardrails scan tool outputs; model-backed guardrails fail open with a warning by default (1.67.0). Hallucination detection goes through scorers, not a processor.

Prompt-injection defence through FIDES information-flow control (IntegrityLabel, ConfidentialityLabel, LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware, PolicyEnforcementFunctionMiddleware, SecureMCPToolProxy; security.py; ADR 0024), labelled experimental. Refresh adds the experimental AGENT-HOOKS enforcement bundle in Python and .NET (external interceptors deny or transform at input, model, tool and output points, fail-closed) and keeps the Microsoft Purview policy-evaluation integration. PII redaction and hallucination detection are BYO via middleware or an agent-hooks interceptor. Capped at 4 because the main pieces are experimental and there are no bundled PII detectors.

Most granular guardrail framework in the benchmark: @input_guardrail, @output_guardrail, @tool_input_guardrail and @tool_output_guardrail with a tripwire mechanism and allow / reject_content / raise_exception behaviours at the tool layers (tool_guardrails.py:40-117). Refresh adds pre-approval tool input guardrails (0.17.6), server-wide guardrails on every local MCP tool (0.22.1), a data-free placeholder for blocked terminal tool output (0.22.0) and redacted errors. No ready-made PII, prompt-injection or hallucination detectors ship; you write them as guardrail functions, so the score reflects framework strength without bundled detectors.

First-class guardrail plumbing, BYO detectors: InputGuardrail, OutputGuardrail, ToolInputGuardrail and ToolOutputGuardrail (guardrail.ts, toolGuardrail.ts), plus handoff isEnabled predicates that gate handoffs. Corrected in refresh: tool guardrails are allow / rejectContent / throwException only and cannot rewrite arguments or output. Refresh also notes server-wide MCP tool guardrails (0.17.1), opt-in pre-approval tool input guardrails (0.11.8), a data-free placeholder for blocked terminal tool output (0.17.0) and sensitive data kept out of SDK logs by default. No first-party PII, prompt-injection or hallucination detector; wrap LLM Guard, Lakera or a classifier agent.

First-party in the pydantic-ai-harness package, now in the monorepo and version-locked to core (0.52, explicitly 0.x: "APIs may still move between minor releases"), so capped at 4. InputGuardrail / OutputGuardrail / ToolGuardrail wrap a guard callable returning allow / block / replace / retry / approve. Ready-made regex/heuristic detectors: redact_secrets, redact_personal_data (emails, Luhn cards, IBANs, US SSNs), blocked_keywords; PromptInjectionDefender (StackOne defender) classifies local tool results for indirect injection; TrajectoryJudge steers a live run. Hallucination detection is BYO; no moderation API wrapper.

Report 18.1: not provided; no PII redaction, prompt-injection detection or hallucination checks. Building blocks only: on_run_start (rewrite/stop input), on_model_turn_finished (retry/stop output), on_outcome (rewrite tool results), and experimental rig-typesafeai typed LLM judgments. Provider refusals are surfaced (Gemini blocks map to refusal: true) and telemetry content is off by default, which reduces leakage but is not a guardrail.

Bedrock Guardrails are first-class for that provider: BedrockModel(guardrail_id, guardrail_version, guardrail_redact_input, ...) with the loop redacting the user message and stopping with guardrail_intervened (agent/agent.py:1739-1744). Refresh adds a generic interventions layer (Guide / Deny on before_model_call / after_model_call), HumanInTheLoop with an LLM risk classifier, and steering promoted from experimental. PII redaction, prompt-injection and hallucination detection remain BYO outside Bedrock, so support is provider-scoped plus a generic seam.

BedrockGuardrailConfig attaches AWS Bedrock Guardrails per call (strands-ts/src/models/bedrock.ts:178) with ModelRedactionEvent rewriting (agent.ts:2184, 2522) and GuardContentBlock for explicitly guarded content. The interventions subsystem (proceed / deny / guide / confirm / transform over invocation, model and tool events) is the generic, framework-agnostic surface, with vended CedarAuthorization, HumanInTheLoop and LLMSteeringHandler. Detectors exist only through Bedrock Guardrails; PII, prompt-injection and hallucination detection are BYO on other providers.

Report 18.1: PII redaction, prompt-injection and hallucination detection are "Not provided — BYO" via LanguageModelMiddleware.transformParams / wrapGenerate, prepareStep or toModelOutput; the policy docs recommend a dedicated moderation step for content filtering. v7 ships safe defaults that are not detectors: system messages in messages are rejected, server error details are redacted from UI streams, SSRF-hardened downloads, tool-approval replay re-validation with optional HMAC signatures, MCP tool drift detection. @ai-sdk/policy-opa gates tool approval, not content.

internal/telemetry wires OTel with GenAI semconv (instrumentation `gcp.vertex.agent`) and emits invoke_agent, invoke_node (per workflow node), generate_content (with finish reasons and gen_ai.usage.*), execute_tool and compaction spans automatically. Setup via telemetry.New(ctx, opts) with OTLP and WithOtelToCloud for GCP Cloud Trace. Prompt/response content on spans is opt-in (OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_MESSAGE_CONTENT). The in-memory DebugTelemetry behind /debug/trace is now only enabled with IncludeDebugAPI. No first-party LangSmith/Langfuse exporter, but any OTLP backend works (report 12.5).

setup_tracing(db=db) or AgentOS(tracing=True) wires a TracerProvider, an AgnoInstrumentor (agent runs, model calls, tools, teams, workflow steps) and a DatabaseSpanExporter persisting to agno_traces/agno_spans. Extra OTLP SpanProcessors plug into Datadog, Honeycomb or Jaeger. Refresh adds ClickHouse as a high-volume trace store, trace latency/error stats by agent/tool/model, and per-user trace ownership. First-class out of the box (report 12.5).

autoagents-telemetry ships a TelemetryProvider trait with bundled OTLP and Langfuse (feature-flagged) implementations, plus a Tracer that subscribes to the event stream (from_direct / from_environment) and converts events to spans. OtlpConfig supports HTTP/gRPC and a RedactionConfig. Solid OTel coverage but needs the extra crate, and you must subscribe before running to avoid missing usage events (report 12.5).

The SDK injects TRACEPARENT/TRACESTATE into the CLI subprocess (subprocess_cli.py:827-852) so CLI-emitted spans parent under the caller's distributed trace; since the refresh it also scrubs stale inherited values and lets explicit options.env win. Install with claude-agent-sdk[otel]. No first-party LangSmith/Langfuse/Datadog adapters, and the spans come from the CLI binary rather than Python code, which limits customisation (report 12.5).

The caller's active OTel context is forwarded to the CLI subprocess so CLI LLM/tool spans parent under the host's trace (CHANGELOG.md:928); the CLI exports traces, metrics and logs via CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY and OTEL_* env vars, with prompt text and tool inputs excluded by default. Hook inputs carry prompt_id matching OTel prompt-level events. No first-party LangSmith/Langfuse exporter, and spans originate in the CLI, not the SDK (report 12.5).

Refresh adds a first-party tracing pipeline (telemetry/tracing/) turning bus events into OTel GenAI-semconv spans, enabled with tracing=True or CREWAI_TRACING_ENABLED and exported to AMP; TraceSession.add_exporter attaches other span exporters. The event bus now has 163 events usable through BaseEventListener. Docs list 16 integrations (Datadog, Langfuse, Langtrace, Arize Phoenix, Braintrust, MLflow, Opik, Portkey, Weave, LangDB and more) and AMP adds a tracing UI. The built-in pipeline defaults to the AMP backend. Still one of the broadest tracing ecosystems (report 12.5).

First-party exporters in eino-ext: Langfuse v1 (batching, masking, sampling), new Langfuse v2 (OTLP/HTTP to Langfuse's OTel endpoint, typed observations for ADK agents/tools/retrievers), LangSmith (dotted_order), APMPlus on OTel, CozeLoop, and new Volcengine TLS (OTLP). Wired via callbacks.AppendGlobalHandlers, after which every component invocation is traced; the failover wrapper span is separate from the inner model span (report 12.5).

OTel-native tracing is on by default: spans for flows, generate turns, model calls, tools, middleware short-circuits and sub-agent runs, plus custom steps via genkit.Run. Refresh adds logs attached to the active span, realtime span streaming to the Dev UI, telemetry labels via context and error classification on spans. The googlecloud plugin ships Cloud Trace/Monitoring/Logging exporters; any OTel exporter works. No first-party LangSmith/Langfuse plugin (report 12.5).

LangSmith is the first-party hosted tracer and auto-traces every Runnable when LANGSMITH_API_KEY is set. There is no native OTel emitter; LangSmith ships an OTel exporter, and Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, W&B and Opik come through the LangChain callback ecosystem. Refresh adds per-node TracePolicy (process_inputs/process_outputs, omit_payload) to trim span payloads, explicitly not a redaction mechanism. Strong if LangSmith is acceptable, otherwise you go through callbacks (report 12.5).

llama-index-instrumentation provides an async/thread-safe dispatcher tree with event and span handlers that preserves trace trees across coroutines. llama-index-observability-otel bridges spans to any OTel backend (parent-context handling fixed in #22485). The callbacks directory now holds 10 first-party integrations (Arize Phoenix, Langfuse, Opik, OpenInference, PromptLayer, UpTrain, W&B, HoneyHive, Literal AI, Argilla); AgentOps and AIM were removed. Narrower integration list than May's '20+' but the core story is unchanged (report 12.5).

@mastra/observability emits spans for AGENT_RUN, MODEL_GENERATION/STEP/INFERENCE, TOOL_CALL, MCP_TOOL_CALL, PROVIDER_/CLIENT_TOOL_CALL, MCP_SERVER_REQUEST, processor phases and workflow steps, plus metrics with cost-aware emission. Exporters cover arize, arthur, braintrust, clickhouse, datadog, deepeval, laminar, langfuse, langsmith, otel (exporter and bridge), posthog, sentry and default storage. Fallback models re-stamp the MODEL_GENERATION span so cost attribution stays correct, loggers inject trace_id/span_id, and metric cardinality protection blocks id-like labels by default (report 12.5).

enable_instrumentation() (observability.py:1556) wires tracer/meter/logger and emits invoke_agent, chat and execute_tool spans following OTel GenAI semconv; instrumentation is now on by default since Python 1.6.0 (disable with ENABLE_INSTRUMENTATION=false). Also covers embeddings, workflow, MCP client and compaction spans, and .NET has OpenTelemetryAgent. Works with Azure Monitor, Aspire (DevUI shows Aspire traces), Jaeger and any OTLP collector (report 12.5).

Built-in TracingProcessor interface with a default BackendSpanExporter shipping to OpenAI's hosted Traces dashboard; add_trace_processor / set_trace_processors swap or extend exporters. docs/tracing.md now lists 30+ partners (W&B, Arize Phoenix, MLflow, Braintrust, Logfire, AgentOps, LangSmith, Langfuse, Datadog, PostHog, Laminar and more). Span types now include Task and Turn spans (toggle via TracingConfig) alongside Agent, Generation, Function, Guardrail, Handoff, MCPListTools, Response, Speech and Transcription. trace_include_sensitive_data controls payload capture (report 12.5).

First-party tracer in packages/agents-core/src/tracing with BatchTraceProcessor (bounded export retries on main). Span types are Agent, Function, Generation, Response, Handoff, Custom, Guardrail, Transcription, Speech and MCPListTools, plus new Task and Turn spans on by default since 0.14.0. The default exporter goes to OpenAI Traces; replace with setTraceProcessors. AgentOps, Respan and PromptLayer are documented external integrations, but there is no first-party OTel/LangSmith/Langfuse exporter, which limits parity with the Python SDK (report 12.5).

The Instrumentation capability (capabilities/instrumentation.py) and InstrumentationSettings (default version 5) emit spans for agent runs, model requests and tool calls using OTel GenAI attribute names, with conversation id via baggage. Logfire is the first-party backend and any OTel collector works. Harness capabilities (Guardrails, SubAgents, compaction, ManagedPrompt) add attributes. Clean and minimal (report 12.5).

note: OTel GenAI semconv via tracing crate
details: Both streaming and non-streaming loops emit info_span! with GenAI semconv fields (gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.usage.* incl. cache and reasoning tokens), plus chat and execute_tool spans with outcome and error type. invoke_agent now adopts an ambient span, every modality (embeddings, images, audio, rerank) opens a gen_ai span since 0.43, and content recording is opt-in (default off). OTel export via tracing-opentelemetry (report 12.5).

Tracer (telemetry/tracer.py:84) creates agent, event-loop-cycle, model-invoke, tool-call, multi-agent and new memory spans using gen_ai.* semconv. New opt-in controls through the OTel semconv env: gen_ai_span_attributes_only and gen_ai_unredacted_attributes, which redacts sensitive attributes such as gen_ai.input.messages unless listed. Exports via OTLP when OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT is set; the harness auto-configures an exporter from OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER (report 12.5).

setupTracer() (strands-ts/src/telemetry/config.ts) configures a global TracerProvider; the agent emits spans for invocation, each loop cycle, each model call and each tool call (now with tool arguments/result), plus new memory spans. Exporters: OTLP HTTP, console or anything on the global OTel SDK. A lightweight in-memory AgentTrace tree is always collected and exposed on AgentResult.traces. Unlike the Python SDK there is no span redaction in strands-ts (report 12.5).

The Telemetry interface (now stable in v7) exposes lifecycle callbacks (onStart, onStepStart/End, onLanguageModelCallStart/End, onToolExecutionStart/End, onObjectStep*, onEmbed*, onRerank*, onEnd, onAbort, onError, plus experimental evaluate/transcription) and executeLanguageModelCall/executeTool wrappers for nested-span propagation. @ai-sdk/otel is the OpenTelemetry implementation, @ai-sdk/devtools is a local trace viewer, and HarnessAgent adds trace-tree and file reporters. No first-party LangSmith/Langfuse exporter; community integrations go through OTel (report 12.5).

Every session.Event carries author, timestamp, content and actions and is append-only (no update paths). New since v2.1: a first-party BigQuery Agent Analytics plugin hooks all 12 plugin callbacks and batches structured events (clustered by event_type, agent, user_id) to BigQuery via the Storage Write API. That is a ready-made who/when/what sink, but it is a separate Go module and GCP-specific, and nothing is tamper-evident (no hash chain or signing). 'Who' is only as good as UserID (matches the caller with authz.NewStrict()). Raised from 3 on the new first-party sink (report 12.6).

Released v3.0.11 already persists runs (user_id, status, timestamps), traces, hashed PATs and an agno_approvals table with resolved_by/resolved_at. Unreleased at analysis time (main, 22 commits past v3.0.11), agno.os.authz.audit adds two append-only trails via DbAuditSink: decision audit (principal, route, required vs held scopes) in agno_authz_decisions and change audit (role/assignment mutations with actor and before/after) in agno_authz_audit, with a pluggable AuditSink. Scored 4 on capability and capped at 4 as unreleased; no hash chain, so not tamper-evident (report 12.6).

Events carry sub_id, actor_id and actor_name; you add timestamps and identity on receive. No tamper-evident or sequence-numbered audit log primitive; engineers subscribe to the event stream and ship to their own sink. v0.4.0 hardening (provider trace logs emit request summaries, hardened secret store) reduces leakage into logs but is not an audit feature (report 12.6).

The SessionStore mirror is your audit log: every transcript line (tool calls, results, prompts, mode changes) flows through SessionStore.append(). include_hook_events=True adds a hook-execution stream (HookEventMessage). MessageOrigin on user/result messages now records who initiated a turn (human, task-notification, scheduled-trigger, peer, channel) and ResultError gives a structured failure record. No tamper-evident chain, but the substrate is built in (report 12.6).

The local JSONL transcript is append-only and records tool calls, results, permission denials and model responses; a SessionStore mirror gives a second copy. result.permission_denials now includes path-scoped deny-rule blocks and system/permission_denied is emitted even without canUseTool, with typed reasons. For a true audit log, push PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PermissionDenied/PermissionRequest hook events to your own sink. The report calls it not first-class and not tamper-evident (report 12.6).

The event bus emits structured events with timestamps, emission_sequence, parent/previous ids and an execution UUID; HookDispatchedEvent records every hook decision with abort reason and source, and the checkpoint event_record allows post-hoc reconstruction. Persistence needs a custom listener, there is no hash chain or signature, and no 'who' (no user identity in the framework) (report 12.6).

No dedicated audit primitive distinct from tracing. Engineers register a callbacks.Handler (or per-run adk.WithCallbacks) and emit structured audit events to their sink. No tamper-evident logging (report 12.6).

Tracing and logs are the only built-in observability primitives. Snapshots record what happened in each agent turn (messages, status, error, timestamps) but not who triggered it, and there is no audit-log interface or tamper-evident sink. Engineers wrap tools with WrapTool to log to a write-once store, or put caller identity in Custom state (report 12.6).

Not provided as an audit stream. Engineers hook on_chain_start/on_chain_end/on_tool_start/on_tool_end and ship to an immutable sink (S3, BigQuery, ClickHouse). The checkpoint history (get_state_history) is a replayable record of state transitions per thread but is mutable storage, not an audit log (report 12.6).

Not first-class. The instrumentation event stream plus your own sink (Postgres/S3) is the recommended approach, and nothing is tamper-evident. Since 0.14.23, LLM start events and callback payloads use BaseLLM.to_payload(), a non-sensitive metadata dict, so auth fields beyond api_key no longer reach trace sinks, which matters when traces go to a shared backend (report 12.6).

Spans and metrics are the primary audit signal, persisted in storage/domains/observability with trace queries on identity, outcome, tag, metadata and feedback predicates. Feedback carries a review-workflow status, RBAC and FGA denials surface at the middleware layer, and tenant-scoped deletion supports retention. No first-party tamper-evident audit log; you would mirror spans to an append-only sink. Kept at 3: more audit-aware than BYO peers but without a dedicated audit sink like Agno's unreleased one (report 12.6).

No dedicated tamper-evident audit log; traces are the audit substrate. FIDES LabelTrackingFunctionMiddleware (security.py:1257) records which labelled content flowed through which tools, useful for prompt-injection forensics but not a general audit log. Agent-hook interceptors see every input/model/tool/output point and are a natural BYO audit sink (report 12.6).

Not first-class and tracing is not tamper-evident. For audit, hook RunHooks.on_tool_start/on_tool_end (with ToolContext.tool_call_id) and approval decisions into your own append-only log (report 12.6).

Tracing spans capture LLM and tool inputs/outputs when traceIncludeSensitiveData is true, which still defaults to true for trace spans (run.ts:651); only SDK logs dropped payloads by default in 0.14.0. Nothing is tamper-evident; build an append-only sink with addTraceProcessor or record from agent_tool_start/end listeners (report 12.6).

No dedicated audit log. Options are OTel spans with metadata/baggage for who, the Harness StepPersistence events and tool-effect ledger (append-only per run, idempotency keys), SpendRecordedEvent listeners for billing records, and FileChangeRequestEvent for file writes. None is tamper-evident; ship to a write-once sink yourself. Kept at 2 because the report states no audit log exists (report 12.6).

Not provided as an audit facility. Usable feeds are tracing spans (content only if opted in) and the effect-bus Recorder (AgentBuilder::record_to), which receives every dispatch, stream event and outcome with ids and parent dispatch; EffectLogRecorder in rig-cassette makes it serialisable. Neither is tamper-evident or records 'who' unless you add it. Credentials are redacted in diagnostics (report 12.6).

Not first-class. BYO sink on MessageAddedEvent / BeforeToolCallEvent / AfterToolCallEvent, or an intervention handler that logs every decision; Cedar decisions are not persisted as an audit log. Not tamper-evident (report 12.6).

The hook event stream is the natural audit source (events have toJSON() for wire transport), but the report finds no audit primitive: the interventions registry is where policy decisions happen yet no signed or append-only ledger ships, and ToolLedgerProvider is a steering call history, not an audit log. Direct agent.tool calls skip hooks and interventions, so an audit hook on BeforeToolCallEvent misses them. Lowered from 3 (correction): the May rationale credited interventions as 'closer to a tamper-evident policy log', which the refreshed report does not support; now level with Strands Python and the other BYO-hook frameworks (report 12.6).

Not provided; use telemetry callbacks plus your own logger, with no tamper-evident log primitives. @ai-sdk/policy-opa has a shadow mode that evaluates and records policy decisions alongside an existing approval function, useful as a decision log but not a general audit log (report 12.6).
