Tokens land on every non-partial session.Event via Gemini's UsageMetadata (prompt/candidates/total/cached/thoughts/tool-use prompt) and persist to the DB row; streaming usage is kept on the final aggregated response and compaction summaries report their own usage. ADK still provides no per-turn/session/tenant rollup helpers: you sum events by InvocationID or session yourself, or aggregate rows from the BigQuery Agent Analytics plugin.

MessageMetrics on each assistant message, RunMetrics on RunOutput (including background memory/learning model usage), SessionMetrics persisted with the session, and ModelMetrics per (provider, model_id); reasoning and cache-read/write tokens are tracked. AgentOS also aggregates metrics per user per day (agno_metrics, since v3.0.0). Per-tenant is BYO.

Usage is emitted only as a per-call StreamChunk::Usage (v0.4.0 added Ollama and Google backends) with prompt/completion/total tokens; serde aliases accept OpenAI and Anthropic field names. No per-turn, per-session or per-tenant aggregation in the framework; the telemetry crate forwards to OTel where you build the rollups.

AssistantMessage.usage per LLM call, ResultMessage.usage and a now typed model_usage (ModelUsage with cache tokens, costUSD, canonicalModel, provider) per turn, TaskUsage for sub-agent tasks, plus get_context_usage(). Running totals are reported within a connection and reset on ConversationResetMessage, so cross-connection and per-tenant rollups are BYO.

SDKAssistantMessage.message.usage per call, SDKResultMessage.usage per main-loop turn, and SDKResultMessage.modelUsage as the cumulative per-model record (incl. sub-agents and side calls, with thinkingTokens, cache tokens, provider, canonicalModel), plus AgentOutput.usage per sub-agent and Query.getContextUsage(). Resumed or forked sessions continue from earlier totals since 0.3.277; per-tenant is BYO.

TokenCalcHandler accumulates LiteLLM callbacks into UsageMetrics with prompt/completion/cached/reasoning/cache-creation fields, exposed on LLMCallCompletedEvent, TaskOutput.token_usage, CrewOutput.token_usage and Crew.usage_metrics — per-tenant rollup is BYO since CrewAI has no tenant primitive.

ResponseMeta.Usage on each assistant message (and AgenticResponseMeta, and callbacks' CallbackOutput.TokenUsage) carries prompt, completion and total tokens plus cached, cache-write (new v0.9.21) and reasoning sub-details. Eino provides no first-party rollup; per-turn and per-session aggregation is done in your own callbacks.Handler.OnEnd or TurnLoop.OnAgentEvents.

ModelResponse.Usage carries a very rich GenerationUsage (tokens plus characters, images, audio, video, cached, thoughts), but it only reflects the last LLM call of the tool loop. Multi-turn aggregation needs a WrapModel middleware or trace spans, and the experimental AgentOutput/SessionSnapshot carry no usage fields; per-session and per-tenant rollups are BYO.

LangChain UsageMetadata on every AIMessage with input/output/total tokens, audio details, cache_creation, cache_read and reasoning sub-fields; per-call and per-turn are first-class, but per-session and per-tenant rollups require summing usage_metadata across thread state or installing a BaseCallbackHandler.

ChatResponse.raw exposes provider-shape usage per call and the TokenCountingHandler callback accumulates prompt_llm_token_count and completion_llm_token_count across the run, but everything beyond per-handler-instance aggregation (per-session, per-tenant) is BYO via instrument_tags spans.

LanguageModelUsage (input, output, reasoning, cachedInput, cacheCreationInput incl. 5m/1h split) flows through MastraModelOutput.totalUsage, onStepFinish and onFinish, and is persisted on conversation messages. @mastra/observability also extracts token metrics from MODEL_GENERATION spans so they can be aggregated per thread, resource, user, organization or session via getMetricAggregate.

AgentResponse.usage_details and ChatResponse.usage_details report input/output/total plus cache-creation, cache-read and reasoning token counts; INNER_ACCUMULATED_USAGE accumulates usage across inner chat-client calls in one agent run, and .NET aggregates across looping agents since 1.18.0. gen_ai.usage.* attributes and a token-usage histogram go to OTel (instrumentation on by default in Python 1.6.0); per-session is only observable in the trace backend.

Usage on result.context_wrapper.usage with request_usage_entries per call, raw provider usage preserved (0.20), per-turn and per-run rollups on turn/task spans, per-checkpoint totals (0.22), and AdvancedSQLiteSession.store_run_usage/get_session_usage for persisted per-session totals (SQLite extension only). Per-tenant is BYO via trace_metadata.

Usage class on RunContext.usage (public as result.state.usage) accumulates inputTokens, outputTokens, totalTokens, requests and requestUsageEntries across a run, with per-call usage (and optional rawUsage, 0.15.0) on ModelResponse and generation spans; failed model calls still record billed usage (0.17.1). Per-session and per-tenant are BYO.

ModelResponse.usage exposes RequestUsage per call and AgentRunResult.usage the summed RunUsage (requests, tool_calls, input/output/cache_read/cache_write tokens, details dict); sub-agent usage aggregates into the parent by default and gen_ai.usage.*/aggregated_usage.* are emitted to OTel. A conversation total is carried by passing the stored RunUsage back via usage=, and the 0.x pydantic-ai-harness adds SpendRecordedEvent after every response. Raised from 4 to match peers at 5, now that conversation and sub-agent levels are covered.

CompletionResponse.usage per LLM call and PromptResponse.usage aggregated across the turns of one prompt() call, with PromptResponse.completion_calls[i].usage per provider call; counters are Option<u64> since 0.43 and normalised across providers, and gen_ai.usage.* spans carry cached, cache-creation and reasoning tokens. Per-conversation requires summing prompt() calls yourself.

Usage lives in message metadata per assistant turn, agent.event_loop_metrics.latest_agent_invocation gives per-invocation usage and cycles, accumulated_usage gives a running total (input, output, total, cacheRead, cacheWrite tokens), and BeforeModelCallEvent exposes projected_input_tokens plus Model.estimate_utilization. This is equivalent in shape to the TypeScript SDK, which scores 5, so Python is raised from 4; neither has a reasoning-token field. Per-tenant is BYO.

Message.metadata.usage per assistant message, AgentResult.metrics.accumulatedUsage across invocations, plus an AgentMetrics object with cycleCount, agentInvocations[] (capped at the latest 50), per-tool callCount/successCount/errorCount/time and latestContextSize/projectedContextSize. Cache-read/write tokens are tracked, but there is no reasoning-token field; per-tenant is BYO.

LanguageModelUsage on every call (onLanguageModelCallEnd), StepResult.usage per step and GenerateTextResult.usage per run (in v7 the total across steps; totalUsage is deprecated), with thorough sub-token detail (noCacheTokens, cacheReadTokens, cacheWriteTokens, textTokens, reasoningTokens) that supports prompt-cache cost analysis. Per-session and per-tenant are BYO.
ADK Go reports tokens via Gemini's UsageMetadata but does not compute USD anywhere; you maintain your own per-model price table and multiply tokens by $/Mtoken yourself.

Correction: Agno ships no pricing table. BaseMetrics.cost exists and is accumulated into RunMetrics and SessionMetrics, but the only producer is the OpenAI-compatible adapter copying response_usage.cost when a gateway such as OpenRouter returns it. For Anthropic, OpenAI direct, Gemini or Bedrock, cost stays None and you compute USD from tokens yourself.
AutoAgents has no price-per-1k-token table and no USD conversion; cost in dollars is computed entirely by your own code from the StreamChunk::Usage events.

ResultMessage.total_cost_usd is computed by the Claude Code CLI on every turn — including across model fallback — giving the Python SDK an authoritative USD figure for free; explicitly called out in the report as the only stack in the comparison with first-party USD cost on the result object.

SDKResultMessage.total_cost_usd is computed by the CLI's bundled pricing tables on every result, and Options.maxBudgetUsd enforces a server-side dollar ceiling that surfaces an error_max_budget_usd subtype on overrun — unique combination of native cost reporting and native cost capping.

LLM.completion_cost is declared on the LLM class but still not populated by any code path, so OSS CrewAI has no first-party USD computation. Cost is shown only by the paid AMP platform (tracing UI, crewai eval --models) or by external vendors computing it from traces.
Eino reports tokens via TokenUsage and that is it — no pricing table, no cost field, no helper; USD is computed by your code from a price table you maintain (lookup by RunInfo.Type).

Genkit has no pricing table or cost field. The OpenAI-compatible core copies a gateway-reported cost (e.g. OpenRouter) into Usage.Custom["cost"], which is a small primitive with no accumulation or tracking across calls. For other providers you multiply tokens by your own price table or rely on a downstream platform.

LangGraph OSS has no built-in price table, no total_cost_usd field and no max_budget_usd cap — the report flags this as materially different from Claude Agent SDK; cost computation is offloaded to the paid LangSmith platform which extends UsageMetadata with cost fields server-side.

A search of llama-index-core for cost_usd, cost_in_dollars or usd returns no results; USD is computed yourself from token counts and an external pricing table, or via callback integrations like Langfuse/Phoenix.

Correction: @mastra/observability estimates cost with estimateCosts(), using a bundled PricingRegistry (pricing-data.jsonl, ~9.1k rows) with tiered pricing and cache-read/cache-write (5m/1h)/reasoning/audio meters, and attaches a CostContext to each token metric. @mastra/core itself has no table, unknown models yield a no_matching_model error instead of a cost, and the table is a bundled snapshot with no documented refresh path, hence not a 5.

UsageDetails only carries input/output/total token counts; there is no first-party USD computation in Agent Framework — you compute cost in a downstream OTel processor or evaluator using your own per-model price table.

Only tokens are reported (Usage dataclass with input_tokens, output_tokens, cached_tokens, reasoning_tokens, request_usage_entries); you compute USD in a RunHooks.on_llm_end or in a TracingProcessor using a model→$/Mtok table you maintain.
The TS SDK only reports tokens via the Usage class — no pricing table, no cost field; USD is computed from your own pricing table against the per-call RequestUsage entries.

Pydantic-AI ships first-party USD computation via the genai-prices package (Pydantic-maintained) which RequestUsage.extract uses, so per-call and per-run USD is computable directly from RunUsage plus model name and provider without a host-side price table.

New in 0.43: CacheCost::from_usage(...).usd(&CacheRates) prices input tokens (uncached, cache reads, cache writes, cache storage) with caller-supplied per-1M-token rates. Rig ships no price table and does not price output tokens, so it is a small primitive and you still build the table and the output-token maths.
Strands Python has no per-model price table and no cost_usd field anywhere; USD is computed in an AfterModelCallEvent hook by multiplying message metadata usage by your own price table.
Strands TS only counts tokens — the example in the report explicitly shows computing costUsd as inputTokens * 0.000003 + outputTokens * 0.000015 in the host, since the SDK does not provide it.

The ai package itself does not compute cost in USD — no pricing tables, no costUSD field, no tokenCost helper; the only USD figures come from the Vercel AI Gateway's GatewaySpendReportRow REST API (totalCost, marketCost) and only for calls that go through the Gateway, so direct provider calls leave you to compute cost yourself.

Still no tenant or cost rollup, but the first-party BigQuery Agent Analytics plugin (v2.1, separate module) now writes rows with session_id, invocation_id, user_id, usage_metadata, latency and static CustomTags that you can aggregate in SQL against your own price table. Tenant is not a column: use CustomTags or encode it in user_id. Correction: the old suggestion to carry tenant in app: state is unsafe, since app: state is shared by all users of an AppName.

AgentOS now aggregates metrics per user per day (agno_metrics, v3.0.0) and RunMetrics/SessionMetrics give per-run and per-session token totals, but per-tenant rollup is BYO: tag runs with metadata tenant_id or encode tenant in user_id and aggregate from agno_runs/agno_sessions. Correction: cost in those metrics is only the gateway-reported value (usually None), so USD attribution also needs your own price table.

No tenant primitive in the framework, and Events do not carry app_meta, so tenant-tagged cost means mapping sub_id to tenant yourself or tagging spans in a custom TelemetryProvider. Usage events are per-call only.

total_cost_usd and ModelUsage.costUSD are authoritative per turn and running totals are kept within a connection, but they reset on ConversationResetMessage and across connections you accumulate yourself, keyed by SessionKey.project_key or your own tenant id. Held at 2 versus the TypeScript SDK because the report documents no resume-continuity of cost totals for Python.

total_cost_usd and modelUsage are cumulative for a session and, since 0.3.277, a resumed or forked session continues from earlier turns instead of starting at zero, so per-conversation USD is first-party. canonicalModel, provider and costBasis per row help billing pick rates. Per-tenant aggregation is BYO keyed by your tenant id, as the SessionStore is not an aggregation point.

BYO via a BaseEventListener on LLMCallCompletedEvent tagging by tenant; run state is now per-run via ContextVars, but the bus is still process-global so you filter by source inside the handler. No USD in OSS; the paid AMP platform rolls up per org/deployment.

No first-party rollup; the pattern is callbacks.Handler.OnEnd reading tenant from ctx. The eino-ext Langfuse v2 handler propagates user, session, tags and metadata to child observations and the TLS handler has SetSession(WithSessionID, WithUserID), so tenant mapped to user/tag can be rolled up in those backends (tokens only, no USD).

Not provided in the SDK; add tenant via tracing.WithTelemetryLabels(ctx, ...) (applied as span attributes) or a WrapModel middleware keyed by core.FromContext(ctx)["tenantId"], then aggregate downstream in Cloud Trace, Datadog or Grafana. No built-in tenant dimension even in the googlecloud plugin metrics.

Not provided in OSS LangGraph; stamp metadata tenant_id on every run and install a BaseCallbackHandler that joins it with model_name and usage_metadata. LangSmith does this server-side (paid), and sdk 0.4.4 can route a run's traces to an additional LangSmith project, which allows per-tenant projects.

Per-tenant cost is BYO; the recommended primitive is the instrument_tags context manager which tags spans with arbitrary key/value pairs (e.g. tenant_id, user_id) that your OTel or callback exporter then groups on.

Sum estimatedCost over resourceId, threadId, userId, organizationId or sessionId filters with getMetricAggregate/getMetricBreakdown in observability storage, the same query TokenCostControl uses for USD budget caps; traces also carry a trusted tenant scope (1.70.0). Not a one-line per-tenant report API, it needs a storage backend implementing getMetricAggregate, and metric flush adds lag, hence 4.

No first-party tenant rollup; the pattern shown in the report is a custom ChatMiddleware (e.g. TenantTagger) that stamps dm.tenant_id on the current OTel span from ctx.kwargs, then a downstream OTel exporter aggregates.

Per-tenant is still BYO, but RunConfig.trace_metadata and group_id propagate through the trace pipeline, and AdvancedSQLiteSession now persists per-session usage (store_run_usage/get_session_usage, tokens only, SQLite extension). No USD is computed, so conversation cost still needs your own price table.

Per-tenant cost is BYO — attach tenantId to runContext.context and use RunConfig.groupId to bind related runs into a trace group; aggregation happens in your downstream tracing backend rather than in the SDK.

The first-party pydantic-ai-harness (0.x, hence capped at 4) adds SpendLimits: Budget(window='conversation'|'day'|'month'|..., scope=lambda ctx: ctx.deps.tenant_id) acts as a USD counter even with no ceiling, with atomic counters shared via RedisSpendStore and status() reads outside a run. Core also lets you carry RunUsage across a conversation, and Pydantic AI Gateway adds account-level caps outside the process.

Not provided: per-conversation requires summing runs that share a ConversationId and per-tenant means tagging metrics with the tenant from ToolContext. Building blocks are PromptResponse/CompletionCall usage, gen_ai.usage.* spans and CacheCost, plus your own price table.

BYO; the recommended pattern is an AfterModelCallEvent hook that reads invocation_state['tenant_id'] and emits a per-tenant cost gauge to Datadog/OTel after multiplying message metadata usage by a host-side price table.

BYO; per-tenant is done by setting agent.traceAttributes = { tenantId } so every span carries it, then aggregating downstream in the OTel collector — the SDK does not roll up cost or even tokens per tenant itself.

Through the Vercel AI Gateway, getSpendReport supports groupBy user, tag, model or provider with totalCost and marketCost in USD; tag calls via providerOptions.gateway.tags: [tenantId]. Direct provider calls bypass it, and without the Gateway rollup is BYO from LanguageModelUsage; telemetry exposes runtimeContext keys such as tenantId only if allowlisted via telemetry.includeRuntimeContext.

`Runner.Run` takes typed `userID`/`sessionID` (AppName fixed on the Runner) and v2 adds `agent.Identity{UserID, AppName, SessionID}` recoverable from any derived ctx. The REST `Authenticator` puts `authn.Caller{UserID, Claims}` on the request ctx, the same designed entry point as Genkit's `ContextProvider`. There is still no `tenant_id` field, and `WithStateDelta` keys are client-controlled on `/run_sse`. The old report's `app:tenant_id` carrier was wrong: `app:` state is shared by every user of the AppName, so it leaks across tenants unless AppName is the tenant.

`Agent.run(...)` takes typed `user_id`/`session_id` plus `dependencies` and `metadata` dicts, all carried on a `RunContext`; there is no `tenant_id` field (open issue #9831). Over HTTP, `JWTMiddleware(dependencies_claims=[...])` copies verified JWT claims into `dependencies` and overrides client-supplied values, and `RequestContext.trusted` carries verified claims to factories. Strong carrier with a tamper-proof path, but still untyped at the schema level.

v0.4.0 adds `Task::app_meta: Option<serde_json::Value>` set with `with_app_meta()`, a dedicated per-run carrier meant for session/chat isolation and app context. It is an untyped JSON value with no tenant, user or locale schema, and `Context` and `AgentConfig` still have no tenant field. It reaches hooks (`on_run_start`, `on_run_complete`) only, not tools or tool selection.

`ClaudeAgentOptions` has about 60 fields but no tenant or user-context channel into tool handlers (`user` goes to the CLI, not to callbacks). Tenant identity is modelled with `cwd`, `env`, `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, closures inside hooks/`can_use_tool`, and `SessionKey.project_key` (which scopes only session storage). Not a typed run-loop input.

`Options` has about 90 fields with no typed `tenantId`, `userId` or `metadata` (issue #319 asks for it). Tenants are modelled via `cwd`, a per-tenant `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` in `env`, `SessionKey.projectKey`, `managedSettings`, and closure capture inside `canUseTool`/hooks. The vendor hosting guide now documents this pattern, but it is still not first-class.

No `tenant_id`/`user_id` field exists on Crew, Agent, Task, Flow or `ConversationState`. The channels are `Crew.config`/`Agent.config` (visible to hooks), free-form `inputs` (LLM-visible), a caller-chosen Flow `session_id`, and a host `ContextVar` that now reliably reaches tools and hooks because contextvars are copied into executor thread pools. All are host-built conventions; CrewAI is still not architected for in-process multi-tenant serving.

Inputs are `context.Context` plus `WithSessionValues(map[string]any)` — both flow through the entire run but neither is typed. No `Spec T` / `Context T` field like LangGraph's `Runtime[ContextT]`; the idiomatic Go-style ctx-value plumbing works but is untyped.

`ContextProvider` is a designed entry point that extracts `tenantId`/`userId` from request headers into `core.ActionContext` on `context.Context`. New since May: `WithSnapshotPathPrefix(func(ctx) string)` partitions experimental file and Firestore session stores per context-derived tenant key, and `tracing.WithTelemetryLabels` can tag spans. `ActionContext` is still `map[string]any`, not a typed struct, and run inputs have no tenant field.

`StateGraph(context_schema=Context)` declares a typed dataclass/TypedDict for tenant deps that is resolved into `Runtime.context` and frozen for the run. `config['metadata']` tags traces, and since 1.2.3 `ensure_config` merges nested metadata so tenant tags survive into subgraphs. Tenant scope on the thread is convention (stamp `metadata['owner']` in `@auth.on.threads.create`), not a first-class field.

`AgentWorkflowStartEvent` has no first-class `tenant_id`/`user_id`/`metadata`. Tenant info enters via `initial_state` (now deep-copied into `ctx.store['state']`, fixing cross-run bleed in 0.14.23), a pre-populated `Context`, arbitrary `**kwargs`, or an encoded `Memory.session_id`. Functional but untyped and convention-bound.

`RequestContext<TRequestContext>` is a typed Map with six reserved keys (resourceId, threadId, versions, authToken, inheritedMemory, messageAuthor) that take precedence over client-supplied values, and agents can validate it with `requestContextSchema`. Caveat: `mergeBodyRequestContext` accepts a body-supplied non-reserved `tenantId` unless the auth middleware sets it first, so set it server-side from the JWT. A trusted `actor` signal also exists for background work.

Python `Agent.run()` still has no tenant field: identity goes in the free-form `function_invocation_kwargs` mapping or `session.state`. New in .NET hosting is `AgentIsolationKeyProvider` / `ClaimsIdentityAgentIsolationKeyProvider`, a typed tenant or user partition key resolved from the authenticated principal that scopes sessions and A2A tasks. The key is storage and hosting scoped (tools read `AdditionalProperties` or ambient context), and Python has no equivalent, so this stays below the typed-context stacks.

`Runner.run(starting_agent, input, context=TContext, ...)` carries a user-typed `TContext` wrapped in `RunContextWrapper` and threaded through the whole run. Since 0.20 a custom `Session` can declare `wrapper=` to receive the context, which gives a storage-layer tenant hook. First-class typed context; `trace_metadata` tags traces.

`run(agent, input, { context: TContext })` produces a typed `RunContext<TContext>` that flows to every tool, hook, guardrail and handoff. New: `RunContextAwareSession` (0.15.0) passes the run context to every session operation so a custom store can route by tenant. Same first-class typed model as the Python SDK.

`Agent.run(..., deps=AgentDepsT, metadata=AgentMetadata)` exposes both a typed `deps` channel (compile-time-checked) and a free-form `metadata` channel for OTel tagging. The deps generic is part of the agent's type and is enforced at the type level.

`AgentRunner::tool_context(ToolContext)` sets typed, serializable `ContextValue` slots (e.g. `app.tenant_id`, `app.user_id`) per run. Inbound values are never sent to the model and are not persisted in the run, and `ctx.require::<TenantId>()` reads them back typed. There is no built-in `tenant_id` field, but the typed slot channel is a designed per-run input equivalent to LangGraph and OpenAI Agents typed context. Previously scored 1 because the report found only `preamble` and `conversation_id` carriers.

`Agent.stream_async(prompt, invocation_state=...)` accepts a free-form `dict[str, Any]` propagated to hooks, interventions and tools. The monorepo agent guide now states that `invocation_state` belongs to the user and SDK code must not use it for internal state, which makes it a stable caller-identity slot. Still untyped, with no tenant field on the session schema.

`stream(args, { invocationState })` accepts a `Record<string, unknown>` per-call bag threaded by reference into every hook, middleware context and `ToolContext`. The SDK docs state that the key space belongs to the caller. Functional but not typed at the framework level, and session scope is encoded in `sessionId` by convention.

`ToolLoopAgent<CALL_OPTIONS, TOOLS, RUNTIME_CONTEXT, OUTPUT>` is generic over the runtime context type, and per-tool `contextSchema` validates `toolsContext[toolName]` at runtime. `callOptionsSchema` is now enforced before `prepareCall`, so typed per-call options are safe to template. Strong typing alongside LangGraph and Pydantic AI; there is no session object, so no tenant scope on a session.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: v2 unified tool and callback contexts into `agent.Context`, so every tool receives `UserID()`, `AppName()`, `SessionID()`, `State()` (with `app:`/`user:` prefixes) and `Value(key)` for anything placed on the ctx passed to `Runner.Run`. `authn.CallerFromContext` is reachable the same way through ctx chaining (reported as not executed). Auto-propagated, but tenant identity is a ctx value or claim by convention, not a first-class field. Do not carry it in `app:` state, which is shared across users of the AppName.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: If the tool signature includes `run_context: RunContext` (or any parameter annotated with it), the framework injects it and the tool reads `run_context.dependencies['tenant_id']` / `run_context.user_id`. The parameter is excluded from the model-facing schema, and since v2.9 `_drop_injected_overrides` discards a model-supplied value for such names. Team members receive the leader's dependencies. Clean propagation, just not typed at the dependencies layer.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
note: hooks can read app_meta, tools cannot
details: `Task::app_meta` reaches `on_run_start`/`on_run_complete` directly and `on_tool_call(&ToolCall, &Context)` indirectly through `ctx.state().task_history` (a best-effort `try_lock` write, not a documented contract). `ToolRuntime::execute(&self, args)` still has no context parameter, so identity cannot reach the tool itself except through a struct field captured at construction. A hook-level read is a small primitive, not propagation to tools.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: SDK MCP tool handlers receive only `dict[str, Any]` LLM args — no `RunContext`/`ToolContext`. Tenant identity must be captured in a Python closure at server construction (`make_tools(tenant_id='acme')`) or forced via the `PreToolUse`/`can_use_tool` callbacks rather than reaching the tool directly.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Same as the Python SDK: handler is `(args, extra) => ...` with no harness-injected context; tenant flows via closure-captured factory functions, AsyncLocalStorage, or `PreToolUse`/`canUseTool` `updatedInput`.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tool `_run(**kwargs)` still receives only LLM-validated arguments and no context object. Since contextvars are now copied into executor thread pools, a request-scoped `ContextVar` read inside the tool, or a per-request `BaseTool` instance, reliably carries identity, which matches the closure-capture level of the Claude Agent SDKs. The path is entirely host-built, and the hook-based alternative relies on the semi-internal `scoped_hooks()` API.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `InvokableRun(ctx context.Context, argumentsInJSON, opts...)` receives the same `context.Context` you set values on plus per-tool typed options via `tool.GetImplSpecificOptions[T]`. Untyped Go-style propagation, but reaches every tool automatically.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `*ai.ToolContext` embeds `context.Context`, and `core.FromContext(ctx)` returns the `ActionContext` populated by your `ContextProvider`. Auto-propagated with a designed extraction API.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools declare a `runtime: ToolRuntime[ContextT, StateT]` parameter and read `runtime.context.tenant_id` directly. The parameter is excluded from the LLM-visible JSON schema, so identity reaches the tool but never appears in the model-facing surface.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools that declare `ctx: Context` get the live workflow context injected automatically; tenant is read as `state = await ctx.store.get('state'); state['tenant_id']`. Context params are excluded from the LLM-facing JSON schema. Works, but key-by-string lookup.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Every tool's `execute(args, ctx)` receives a typed `ToolExecutionContext` whose `requestContext` is the same Map the caller passed, with `requestContextSchema` for validation and a trusted `actor` for background work. The same context reaches processors, dynamic resolvers and derived copies for sub-agents. First-class auto-propagation.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools declare a `ctx: FunctionInvocationContext` parameter that is auto-injected; `ctx.kwargs` carries `function_invocation_kwargs`, and the parameter is hidden from the model schema. `agent.as_tool()` forwards the kwargs to the sub-agent, but `BackgroundAgentsProvider` runs do not, so identity must be re-injected there. .NET reads `FunctionInvokingChatClient.CurrentContext` / `AIAgent.CurrentRunContext`. Auto-injected but untyped.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools whose signature declares `ctx: RunContextWrapper[TContext]` get the same wrapper threaded through the whole run (with cumulative usage and approvals), and `ToolContext` extends it with per-call metadata. Schema-extraction skips the ctx parameter, so the LLM never sees it.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Every `tool({ execute })` callback receives `(parsedInput, runContext, details)` automatically, with `runContext.context` typed as the caller-supplied `TContext`. Documented contract that every agent/tool/hook in a run shares the same `RunContext` type.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `@agent.tool` functions whose first arg is `ctx: RunContext[DepsT]` get the typed deps plus rich call metadata (`tool_call_id`, `usage`, `retries`, `metadata`, etc.). One of the cleanest typed-deps stories in the survey.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `Tool::call(&self, context: &mut ToolContext, args)` receives a fresh clone of the run's `ToolContext` on every dispatch. The same context is inherited by sub-agents built with `Agent::into_tool()` and forwarded to MCP servers as `_meta` (`McpMeta`), outside model-visible arguments. This is first-class automatic propagation. Previously scored 1 because the old `Tool::call(&self, args)` had no context parameter.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Tools receive `invocation_state` via the executor's update of the dict, and decorated tools can request a `ToolContext` parameter that wraps it. Auto-propagated but untyped.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: `ToolContext` always exposes `invocationState`, `toolUse`, `agent` and `cancelSignal`, threaded by reference so hook writes are visible to later tools, and `asTool()` sub-agents inherit it. Gap: `agent.tool.X.invoke()` direct calls build a `ToolContext` with an empty `invocationState`, so identity does not reach tools called that way.

row: Tenant identity propagation into tool calls
details: Each tool's `execute(input, { context })` receives its own `toolsContext[toolName]` entry, validated against the tool's `contextSchema` (`validateToolContext` throws on mismatch). `runtimeContext` is not passed to `execute`, so tenant data must be placed in `toolsContext`, a tool factory closure or `prepareStep`. Type-checked end-to-end.

`BeforeToolCallback(ctx, tool, args)` can update `args` in place and return `(nil, nil)`; a plugin-level callback applies to all agents and short-circuits agent-level ones. The schema still leaks the field unless you leave it out of `TArgs` and read the tenant from ctx, and there is no injected-arg annotation. New caveat: streaming tools (`functiontool.NewStreaming`) bypass Before/After tool callbacks.

Preferred pattern: keep `tenant_id` out of the schema and read it from `run_context`; `_drop_injected_overrides` stops the model overriding framework-owned parameters. `tool_hooks` middleware is the route for tools you do not own, but the override only works when `args` is mutated in place and is silently lost when the model calls a tool with zero arguments (`function.py:2485-2496`, `:2642`). The old report overstated the hook (correction); there is no typed per-tool fixed-args spec.

Hooks receive `&ToolCall` by shared reference and can only `Continue` or `Abort`, so they cannot mutate arguments. New with `app_meta`: an `on_tool_call` hook can detect a mismatch between the LLM argument and the tenant and abort, which is a validation gate, not injection. Otherwise the only workaround is a tool struct that owns the tenant at construction, which means one agent per tenant.

`PreToolUse` hooks return `updatedInput`, and `can_use_tool` returns `PermissionResultAllow(updated_input=...)`; both run out-of-band in your process. `can_use_tool` can be shadowed by allow rules, permission modes or a PreToolUse allow (the SDK now warns), so use `PreToolUse` for forced args. Hook bypass for background sub-agents was fixed in 0.2.127/0.2.160, so pin a recent version.

`PreToolUse` hooks return `updatedInput` and `canUseTool` returns `{ behavior: 'allow', updatedInput }`; the CLI dispatches with the harness-supplied input. `canUseTool` can be shadowed by `allowedTools`, bypass or the new default `auto` mode, so the report recommends `PreToolUse` for forced args. `canUseTool` now receives `mcpServer` provenance so rewrites can target only your in-process server.

A `PRE_TOOL_CALL` hook can mutate `ctx.tool_input` in place, and since 1.15.3 a per-execution `scoped_hooks()` ContextVar registry avoids the old process-global problem. That API is not exported from `crewai.hooks` or documented, hook exceptions other than `HookAborted` are swallowed fail-open, and the LLM still sees the field in the schema. Workable per request but brittle, so it sits above the old global-hook-only level without reaching the documented-hook peers.

`ToolsNodeConfig.ToolArgumentsHandler` and `compose.ToolMiddleware.Invokable` / `WrapInvokableToolCall` middleware can rewrite the raw arguments JSON before dispatch. Report explicitly contrasts this with LangGraph's declarative `InjectedToolArg` as strictly worse — you write middleware and remember to scrub the JSON schema yourself.

`Hooks.WrapTool` middleware can mutate `params.Request.Input` before calling `next(ctx, params)`. The pattern works but doesn't ship as a built-in, the report calls this BYO, and the field stays in the LLM-visible schema unless scrubbed.

Tools annotated with `InjectedToolArg`/`InjectedState` have those keys stripped from the LLM-visible JSON schema and overwritten in `ToolNode._inject_tool_args` — an LLM that supplies `tenant_id` has it silently replaced with the harness value. Report describes this as the cleanest forced-arg mechanism in the benchmark.

`FunctionTool(partial_params={...})` is a default-filler — LLM-provided kwargs win over `partial_params` because of merge order. Real forcing requires either closure-wrapping the tool (ignore the LLM-supplied field) or reading from `ctx.store` inside the tool; both are conventions, not enforced.

Mastra has no `updatedInput` contract. The recommended pattern keeps tenant fields out of `inputSchema` and reads them from `requestContext` (validated by `requestContextSchema`). The new agent-level `beforeToolCall` hook can block with `{ proceed: false, output }` but cannot return replacement input; in-place mutation of `input` happens to work but is not a contract. `prepareStep`/`processInputStep` can also rebuild tools with closures.

`FunctionMiddleware.process(context, call_next)` can overwrite `context.arguments` before dispatch, and since 1.19.0 the innermost handler re-validates changed arguments so a forced value still passes schema validation. The agent-hooks `pre_tool_call` `transform` verdict is an alternative. There is no declarative pin-arg mechanism, so it stays BYO middleware, with not exposing the argument as the cleaner pattern.

No `PreToolUse -> updatedInput` equivalent: tool input guardrails and `on_tool_start` can only reject or raise. The recommended pattern is to keep tenant out of the tool schema and read `ctx.context`, with a custom `on_invoke_tool` for richer cases. MCP `tool_meta_resolver` injects server-side `_meta` per call, which forces metadata, not arguments.

No argument-rewrite hook exists: `ToolGuardrailBehavior` is `allow | rejectContent | throwException` only, and `callModelInputFilter` works on messages, not pending tool args. The supported pattern is to omit `tenantId` from `parameters` and read it from `runContext.context` inside `execute`. Effective but convention-bound; MCP `toolMetaResolver` sets `_meta`, not arguments.

`@hooks.on.before_tool_validate(tools=[...])` can return a new raw-args dict that replaces the LLM's before validation, and `before_tool_execute` does the same on validated args. Correction: `args_validator` can only reject (`ModelRetry`/`ToolFailed`), not rewrite, so the old report overstated it. Keeping the field out of the schema and reading `ctx.deps` is the strongest pattern. Not a declarative `InjectedToolArg`, but close.

`on_dispatch` can return `DispatchAction::Patch` (helper `rewrite_tool_args`), which replaces the tool arguments while keeping the tool name; the stack rejects patches that change the target, and the streamed committed item reports the patched call. Better still, `tenant_id` can stay out of `Args` and be read from `ToolContext`. This is a first-class hook-mutation mechanism equal to the Strands `BeforeToolCallEvent` level, without a declarative injected-arg annotation.

`BeforeToolCallEvent.tool_use` is writable (`_can_write` allows `tool_use`) and the executor re-reads it after hooks run. An `InterventionHandler.before_tool_call` can also return `Transform(apply=...)` to rewrite the input. Equivalent in effect to the Claude SDK's `PreToolUse` `updatedInput`, with no declarative injected arg.

`BeforeToolCallEvent.toolUse.input` is mutable for hooks, with the model-issued `toolUseId` kept authoritative, and interventions can `transform` the input (hooks at order 0 run before Cedar at order 90). `ExecuteToolStage.Input` middleware can also modify it (not exercised in the report). Caveat: direct `agent.tool.X.invoke()` calls skip hooks, interventions and middleware, so forcing applies only to model-driven calls.

`experimental_refineToolInput` is a first-class per-tool function applied in `parseToolCall` before dispatch, so tools, callbacks, telemetry and approvals see the refined input. It is still `experimental_` and must keep the same JSON shape; the cleanest pattern is `toolsContext` plus `contextSchema` so `tenantId` never enters the LLM schema. `HarnessAgent` has no `refineToolInput`.

`Toolset.Tools(ctx ReadonlyContext)` is called per LLM request and `tool.FilterToolset(toolset, predicate)` can branch on state or a ctx value; `mcptoolset` `ToolFilter` is deprecated in favour of it. Static `llmagent.Config.Tools` are not filtered per request, so wrap them in a Toolset. Sub-agents remain a static list.

`agent.tools` accepts a callable factory that receives `agent`, `run_context` and `session_state` by name; results are cached per `callable_tools_cache_key` (default user then session), or disabled with `cache_callables=False`. `AgentFactory`/`TeamFactory` in AgentOS rebuild the agent per request from verified claims, varying tools, model, instructions and knowledge. Per-run rather than per-step.

`AgentDeriveT::tools()` returns a fixed `Vec<Box<dyn ToolT>>` at agent build time and the `#[agent]` derive macro lists tools statically. No `activeTools`/`allowed_tools`/`prepareStep` mechanism. Per-tenant filtering means constructing a different agent per tenant.

Three layered mechanisms (`tools`/`allowed_tools`/`disallowed_tools`) at construction, plus `set_permission_mode` and `toggle_mcp_server` for mid-session changes, and `PreToolUse` denial as a per-turn veto. No first-party `set_tools()` control request, but multiple knobs cover the use case.

Same construction-time mechanisms as the Python SDK plus mid-session `Query.setMcpServers(...)` to replace MCP servers and `applyFlagSettings({ permissions })` for per-turn permission changes. `AgentDefinition.tools`/`disallowedTools` provide per-sub-agent scoping.

`Agent(tools=[...])` is set at construction and there is no `prepareStep`/`activeTools` mid-run equivalent. Only mid-run dynamism is `BaseTool.max_usage_count` (returns an error string when exceeded). MCP `tool_filter` is connection-level, not per-turn.

`ChatModelAgentMiddleware.BeforeAgent` gives a mutable `Tools` slice once per run, and a removed tool is dropped from both the schema and dispatch. `BeforeModelRewriteState` rewriting `state.ToolInfos` is now the recommended per-turn path, but it controls visibility only, so pair it with a `WrapInvokableToolCall` guard. Filtering in `WrapModel` via `model.WithTools` is now explicitly discouraged. Two-tier story that needs custom middleware.

Tools are declared per `Generate` call with `ai.WithTools(...)`; since v1.12 repeated `WithTools` calls accumulate, which helps compose tenant-specific additions. A `WrapGenerate` hook can replace the `ModelRequest` per turn to hide tools, but the loop still dispatches any registered tool the model names, so enforcement needs a `WrapTool` deny. Registry-level scoping is none, and the report shows no ready-made per-turn filter.

Per-turn filtering is first-class: pass a callable for `model` taking `(state, runtime)` that returns a different `bind_tools([...])` per turn, plus `wrap_tool_call` can short-circuit forbidden tools. `bind_tools` and prebuilt registry filter combine cleanly with the typed runtime context.

Filtering at construction is trivial; per-turn dynamism comes from `tool_retriever: ObjectRetriever` which the framework calls each turn with the current `user_msg_str` (`get_tools` merges static `tools` plus retrieved). Not a tenant-aware filter primitive specifically, but the retriever can branch on tenant from state.

Three first-class layers: dynamic `tools` callable receiving `requestContext`, per-call `activeTools` whitelist, and `prepareStep`/`processInputStep` returning `{ activeTools }` per step; `toolCallStep` rejects hidden tools by name. `ToolSearchProcessor` has a request-aware filter, and per-call version selection exists. Strongest per-tenant tool-filtering surface in the survey.

Per-run `tools` overrides, `AgentMiddleware` overriding run-level tools, and `ContextProvider.before_run` adding tools from `session.state` give per-run tenant-aware selection; `FilteringSkillsSource` now receives `SkillsSourceContext(agent, session)` for per-tenant skills. Mid-run `add_tools`/`remove_tools` exists but is experimental. There is no per-turn `activeTools` callable driven by request context.

`Tool.is_enabled` accepts `(RunContextWrapper, AgentBase) -> bool | Awaitable[bool]` and `Agent.get_all_tools` evaluates it per turn (and again before invocation); handoffs have the same predicate. MCP static and dynamic `tool_filter` receive the run context. Caveats: it gates only `FunctionTool` (hosted tools are always included), and mutating shared tool objects per request is not isolated across concurrent runs.

Per-tool `isEnabled` receives `{ runContext, agent }` and is evaluated in `Agent.getAllTools(runContext)` every turn; handoffs support the same predicate. MCP `toolFilter` callables receive the run context, and on main the current filter is re-applied on each cached lookup. Hosted tools are not filtered by `isEnabled`, and there is no registration-time tenant scope.

Several first-class options: `PrepareTools` capability (passed per run via `capabilities=[...]`; `prepare_tools=` is not a `run()` kwarg), per-tool `prepare=`, `.filtered()`/`.prepared()` toolset wrappers, `@agent.toolset`, dynamic capabilities resolved per run from `RunContext`, and per-run `toolsets=[...]`. Comprehensive coverage with scoping at runtime only.

`on_completion_call` can return `RequestPatch::new().active_tools([...])`, a per-turn allow-list that narrows the advertised tools and is intersected across hooks. Patches are non-sticky, so a tenant hook must return the patch every turn, and it hides tools without blocking a guessed call, so pair it with an `on_dispatch` deny. Previously scored 1 because only per-request agent construction existed.

`Agent(tools=[...])` is the primary surface, and there is still no public per-turn `activeTools`/`prepareStep`. Workarounds are mutating `agent.tool_registry.registry`, MCP `ToolFilters` at load time, or vetoing in `BeforeToolCallEvent` (the tool stays visible). The SDK filters `tool_specs` per model call through `InvokeModelStage.Input` middleware internally, but it is reachable only via the private `agent._middleware_registry`, so using it is a workaround on internal API.

The public `InvokeModelStage.Input` middleware (`agent.addMiddleware`, no experimental label) carries `toolSpecs`, so a handler can filter the visible tools by `invocationState.tenantId` on every model call. It hides tools only, so pair it with a `BeforeToolCallEvent` cancel for enforcement; per-tenant `Agent` construction and registry mutation remain alternatives. Previously scored 2 because the May snapshot had no per-turn filter.

Four coexisting layers on `ToolLoopAgent`: agent-level `activeTools`, per-step `prepareStep` returning `activeTools`, per-call `prepareCall` returning `tools`, and new deferred tool search that respects `activeTools`. `HarnessAgent` adds `activeTools`/`inactiveTools` over built-in and host tools, with adapter-dependent support for built-ins.

v2.4/v2.5 add inbound `adkrest.ServerConfig.Authenticator`/`Authorizer` (header, IAP, Google OIDC, custom; `authz.NewStrict` requires caller == `userId`), putting `authn.Caller{UserID, Claims}` on the request ctx for tools. Outbound, `auth.CredentialProvider` resolves per-call credentials, `auth/gcp` resolves per-end-user Google credentials, and `mcptoolset.Config.Auth` applies a provider to every MCP request. Gaps: defaults are open (Noop), `Caller` is not mapped to `session.UserID` automatically, only user-level authz exists, and `ConsentRequiredError` handling is not wired.

AgentOS authentication propagates the verified JWT `sub` to `RunContext.user_id` (forced for scoped callers), selected claims arrive via `dependencies_claims`, and the caller's bearer token is forwarded to remote agents and MCP. There is no per-tool OAuth vault, so tools calling downstream APIs fetch credentials themselves. First-class auth plumbing at the HTTP layer.
No identity reaches the tool — the runtime has no notion of a principal or auth context. Identity must be captured as a struct field at tool construction.
No SDK primitive automatically threads caller JWT to every tool call. Tenant/auth identity is captured via Python closures into hook/tool callbacks. BYO.

Caller identity does not flow into tool calls. SDK MCP tools run in your Node process (use `AsyncLocalStorage`), while built-in tools run as the subprocess OS user. The hosting guide advises keeping tool credentials out of the agent environment, and sandbox settings now offer credential masking and egress injection.

Caller's identity does not propagate. External-API tools (gmail, slack, salesforce) are configured per-tool-instance with their own credentials; no 'use the caller's bearer token' notion. AMP's Connected Apps binds at user-org level, not per-request.

Caller identity reaches the tool only because the host puts it on `context.Context`. Pattern is documented (extract identity in `BeforeAgent`, set on tool's BQ client) but not built-in — no automatic per-tool-call STS or impersonation.

Whatever your `ContextProvider` puts in `ActionContext` reaches every tool call, including parallel and sub-agent tools. There is no IAM/RBAC layer, and the Firebase plugin ships one auth-policy provider. Cautions: background sub-agent task IDs are not access-scoped, and `genkit.Handler` now redacts non-public error messages to avoid cross-tenant leakage.

`runtime.context` carries identity into every tool, and engineers wire tenant-scoped DB connections or JWTs into it. LangGraph Server's `@auth.on.*` handlers filter threads, runs and store at the HTTP layer; `actions=` is now enforced, but unmatched paths are allowed by default, so add a global default-deny handler. The resolved server identity does not reach tools automatically; you pass it into `context`.
Auth identity is whatever you stash in `ctx.store` and read inside the tool. No built-in identity propagation from an outer HTTP handler.

`MASTRA_AUTH_TOKEN_KEY` forwards the caller's token into tools and MCP servers sharing the server's auth. New: a trusted `actor` signal lets background work run with FGA checks, invoker-bound tool-provider connections receive the live `RequestContext` so OAuth integrations run as the authenticated user, and MCP `authInfo` is bridged into the tool's context. First-class plumbing.

Identity is not automatic for local tools: it reaches them only via `function_invocation_kwargs` (Python) or `AdditionalProperties`/ambient context (.NET). New: MCP `header_provider` maps host kwargs to per-request auth headers, and .NET Foundry hosting passes delegated user identity into the session. Tool approval is orthogonal to identity.

Typed `TContext` reaches every tool call, so tokens, RLS predicates and tenant rules flow without thread-locals; MCP `tool_meta_resolver` forwards identity in `_meta`. New caution: serialized run state includes the app context, so persist only secret handles in `context` or use `context_serializer`. One of the cleanest models alongside Mastra.

Whatever you put in `runContext.context` is automatically reachable from every tool, lifecycle hook, guardrail, and handoff — documented contract that they share the same context type. Tools enforce auth in `execute`.

`ctx.deps` flows to every tool by construction, and the host code that builds deps from the request is the auth termination point. For MCP, build the toolset per run from `ctx.deps` (`MCPToolset(url, auth=ctx.deps.mcp_token)`) because a shared one is a single identity; `ResolveModelId` supports per-tenant provider keys. Strong typed plumbing.

Whatever the host puts in the run's typed `ToolContext` (principal, scoped token newtype) reaches every tool call, sub-agent call and MCP call (`McpMeta` sent as `_meta`). There is no principal type, token validation or per-tool ACL, so the framework gives a typed carrier, not auth. That matches the OpenAI Agents and Pydantic AI typed-context level. Previously scored 1 because tools had no context parameter.

Whatever sits in `invocation_state` reaches every hook, intervention and tool call. New first-party `CedarAuthorization(principal_resolver=...)` evaluates principal, tool action, input and session context before each call and denies when no principal is found (fail-closed). There is still no JWT/OAuth identity object and tools run under host credentials, so you supply identity and per-user credentials yourself.

Identity propagates through `invocationState`, and the vended `CedarAuthorization` maps it to a Cedar principal with `principalResolver`, denying when none is found (fail-closed), with `contextEnricher` forwarding role or environment values. There is no SDK-level auth principal type and tools run under host credentials. Gap: direct `agent.tool.X.invoke()` calls get an empty state and skip interventions.

Identity reaches tools only if placed in `toolsContext[toolName]` (validated by `contextSchema`); `runtimeContext` does not reach `execute`. Since 7.0 tool and runtime context are excluded from telemetry by default, so JWTs do not leak into spans. Typed and clean, but no automatic plumbing.

No token or USD cap and no rate limiter, so nothing is tenant-scoped. `LiveRunConfig.MaxLLMCalls` (`agent/live.go:48`) caps LLM calls per live run and `TriggerConfig.MaxConcurrentRuns` limits concurrent trigger runs globally; token counts are on `Event.UsageMetadata` for the host to aggregate. Raised from 0 to 1 in the calibration pass: per-run caps are a small primitive, level with the other turn/call-cap-only stacks.

`tool_call_limit` caps tool calls per run (open bug #8304), and queue-level `max_concurrency`/`max_queue_depth` and `PublicSurface` quotas are global or anonymous-only, not per tenant. `Metrics.cost` is reported after the fact, and cost budgets are only an open request (#9151). A tenant counter in pre/post hooks is BYO.

Only `ExecutorConfig { max_turns }` (default 10); `RetryLayer` honours provider `Retry-After`, which is back-off rather than a per-tenant limiter. No USD budget or per-tenant tracking; `Usage` from stream chunks is available for BYO enforcement, and events lack `app_meta` for tenant rollup.

`max_budget_usd` is wired to `--max-budget-usd` and ends the run with `error_max_budget_usd`; it is a post-call check, so cost can exceed the cap by one API call. It is a real per-run USD cap but there is no per-tenant aggregation (sum `total_cost_usd` yourself). `RateLimitEvent` surfaces Anthropic rate-limit transitions for back-off.

`maxBudgetUsd` is a per-`query()` USD ceiling enforced by the CLI, plus `maxTurns` and an alpha `taskBudget.total`; resumed sessions continue `total_cost_usd` but the cap still applies per run. `managedSettings.modelPricing` lets you price at negotiated rates. No per-tenant cumulative cap or rate limiter, so aggregate `modelUsage[*].costUSD` per tenant yourself. No longer the only first-party USD cap in the benchmark.

`Agent.max_rpm`/`Crew.max_rpm` use a process-local `RPMController`, not per tenant, and rate-limited provider calls are now retried with backoff. `UsageMetrics` is tokens only and `completion_cost` is never populated. AMP's Agent Control Plane documents a cost-limit policy, but it is AMP-only and not inspectable in this repo.

No USD budget enforcement and no per-tenant token ceiling. A per-run `MaxIterations` cap (default 20, `adk/chatmodel.go:305-308`, `ErrExceedMaxIterations` at `adk/react.go:393`) bounds the loop, and v0.9's `AgentCancelFunc` with `CancelAfterChatModel` stops a run at a safe point with a resumable checkpoint, which a host can wire to its own token counters from `ResponseMeta.Usage`. Raised from 0 to 1 in the calibration pass: a per-run cap plus a clean stop mechanism, level with the other turn-cap-only stacks.

Only per-call caps: `MaxTurns` (default 50) and `middlewarex.Agents.MaxDelegations`. Token usage is on `resp.Usage`, and per-tenant enforcement (for example a Redis counter in `WrapModel` keyed by `ActionContext` tenant) is BYO.

No token-budget or USD-cost cap in the OSS library, and LangSmith Deployment exposes per-deployment rate limits, not per-tenant USD ceilings. The one built-in bound is the per-run `recursion_limit` step cap that raises `GraphRecursionError` (`libs/langgraph/langgraph/pregel/main.py:3005`, `3486`); the report does not mention it, so it was checked in source. Raised from 0 to 1 in the calibration pass: a per-run cap only, level with the other turn-cap-only stacks.
`TokenCountingHandler.token_budget` raises `ValueError` when exceeded — but per handler instance, not per tenant, and counts tokens not USD. No USD budget cap.

`TokenCostControl` (core processor, renamed from `CostGuardProcessor` in 1.59.0) enforces a USD `maxCost` per `run | resource | thread | user | organization | session` over 1h to 365d windows, in block or warn mode, using the built-in pricing registry of `@mastra/observability`. Caveats: it needs observability storage with `getMetricAggregate`, async metric flush lags recent spend, and user/org/session scopes fail open if the keys are missing. Request-rate limiting is not provided. The old report's 'no pricing table' claim was wrong.

No per-tenant or USD cap. `FunctionInvocationConfiguration` caps iterations, function calls, consecutive errors and wall-clock duration per request (`_tools.py:1755-1846`) and `FunctionTool(max_invocations=...)` caps per-tool calls, but none is tenant-scoped or token-based. Tokens are observable via OTel and `UsageDetails`. The Claude wrapper only forwards that SDK's `max_budget_usd` for one agent type. Raised from 0 to 1 in the calibration pass: the richest per-request cap set of the 1s, but still no tenant scope.

`Usage` reports tokens and request counts but has no dollar field, no per-tenant cap and no stop-if-over-budget mechanism. `max_turns`, `ModelSettings.timeout` and per-tool timeouts bound work, not spend. Enforcement happens in `on_llm_end` hooks against your billing store.

SDK surfaces token usage on `RunContext.usage`/`RunResult.state._context.usage` but does not enforce caps. Ceilings via custom `Model` wrapper or `agent_tool_start` listener that throws. No USD budget cap.

Harness `SpendLimits` with `Budget(usd, window=run|conversation|day|month|total, scope=lambda ctx: ctx.deps.tenant_id)` refuses the next request once a tenant window is spent, and `RedisSpendStore` shares atomic counters across workers. Core `UsageLimits.cost_limit` adds a per-run USD cap. Capped at 4 because the Harness is a 0.x satellite package whose APIs may still move; it also only guarantees no request starts after exhaustion, and request-rate limiting is not provided.
Only `max_turns` (turn cap) and `max_tokens` (per-completion cap). No USD budget, no per-tenant rate limit.

`stream_async(limits={'turns','output_tokens','total_tokens'})` stops a single invocation with `limit_*` stop reasons, checked at turn boundaries. It is per call (not cumulative across agent reuse), with no USD cap and no per-tenant ledger, so aggregation and enforcement across calls stay BYO. That is the same level as Pydantic AI's earlier `UsageLimits` and LlamaIndex's `token_budget`.

`stream(args, { limits: { turns, outputTokens, totalTokens } })` caps a single invocation, can be derived from a tenant plan, and rejects unknown keys. It is per call only, with no USD computation and no per-tenant ledger. The limits were already present in the archived snapshot but were missed in May, so this is a correction rather than a new feature.

`stopWhen` supports step-count, tool-name and loop-finished conditions; there is no built-in USD or token cap. A custom `StopCondition` over `steps[].usage` or `@ai-sdk/policy-opa` (which gates tool calls using runtime context and history) can approximate one, but you supply the spend data. AI Gateway spend reports are observational.

Eval REST routes (sets, cases, runs, results) exist only so the web UI gets a clear answer: they return HTTP 501 with 'Use adk-python for eval workflows' (`server/adkrest/internal/routers/eval.go:23-35, 39-108`). Test building blocks exist (`agent.StrictContextMock`, public `session/sessiontestsuite`, `platform` time/UUID seams) but none is an eval harness. The record/replay plugins (`recordplugin`/`replayplugin`, `internal/httprr`) sit under `internal/` and cannot be imported, so you would copy them. The Python ADK ships eval; adk-go users run a sister adk-python process or write their own harness.

`agno.eval.suite` (v2.7.0, released) declares `Case(name, input, agent|team, criteria, judge_mode, expected_tool_calls, scorer, tags, timeout_seconds)` and runs them with `run_cases`/`arun_cases` (`eval/suite.py:61-120, 513-635`); `SuiteResult.to_dict()` is a stable CI contract and results persist in `agno_eval_runs`. It also keeps `AccuracyEval`, `PerformanceEval`, `ReliabilityEval`, `AgentAsJudgeEval`, plus `agno.scorer` (Code/Judge/ToolCall) and `agno.environments` (pass@k rollouts with save/load/diff, SFT export). Raised from 4 because the May caveat (multi-case suites composed by hand) is gone. Minor gap versus pydantic-evals/Mastra: cases are Python objects, not a serialised or generated dataset type.

Standard `cargo test --features full --workspace` runs SDK unit tests; the `crates/autoagents-llm/src/evaluator/parallel.rs` is unrelated to agent-output evaluation. No dataset format, no regression harness.
Report explicitly marks golden datasets, LLM-judge, and CI gates as 'not provided'. Users compose evals around `query()` themselves.

No golden-dataset format, no regression harness. The only test-shaped artifact is the `SessionStore` adapter conformance suite (`examples/session-stores/shared/conformance.ts`) — that tests adapters, not agent behaviour.

`crewai test [-n N] [-m MODEL]` (`lib/cli/src/crewai_cli/cli.py:612`) runs the crew N times and `CrewEvaluator` (`utilities/evaluators/crew_evaluator_handler.py:29`) spawns a `Task Execution Evaluator` agent that prints a quality score table. There is no dataset format: you re-run the crew with hard-coded or `kickoff_for_each` inputs, and the CLI never fails the build on low scores. The `crewai.experimental.evaluation` package remains; the new AMP-backed `crewai eval` needs the paid platform, so it is not counted.
No `Dataset`, `Evaluator` or `EvalRun` primitives. The recommended pattern is Go's `testing` package with recorded `model.BaseModel` mocks.

`go/ai/evaluator.go:142-157` defines `Example` (testCaseId, input, output, context, reference, traceIds) and `EvaluatorRequest{Dataset, EvaluationId}`. Datasets and runs are managed by the Genkit CLI / Dev UI (`genkit eval:run`, `eval:flow`) against the Go process. Built-in Go evaluators (`go/plugins/evaluators/evaluators.go`) are deterministic (Deep Equal, RegExp, JSONata). The cross-language agent conformance harness (`tests/specs/agent.yaml`) tests the framework itself, not user agents.
No dataset or evaluator primitives in this OSS repo. Dataset management and evaluators live in the paid LangSmith product; local-only users wire `pytest` around `graph.invoke(...)`.

`llama-index-core/llama_index/core/evaluation/` ships `RetrieverEvaluator`, `RelevancyEvaluator`, `FaithfulnessEvaluator`, `CorrectnessEvaluator`, `AnswerRelevancyEvaluator`, `GuidelineEvaluator`, `SemanticSimilarityEvaluator`, `BatchEvalRunner`, plus `RagDatasetGenerator`/`LabelledRagDataset`. Coverage skews RAG; agent-behaviour regression means composing primitives yourself or piping to Phoenix/Langfuse/Opik. `MockFunctionCallingLLM` can now emit tool calls (`llms/mock.py:294-360`), which makes deterministic agent-loop tests possible but does not change the score.

Datasets and experiments are first-class (`packages/core/src/datasets/`, `datasets/experiment/`): `mastra.datasets.create()`, dataset items, `runExperiment` with `beforeAll`/`afterAll`/`beforeEach`/`afterEach` hooks, item-level static tool mocks plus `unmockedToolPolicy`, item-level scorer selection, a portable snapshot format with integrity digest, and `organizationId`/`projectId` scoping. `runEvals({agent, dataset, scorers, concurrency})` (`packages/core/src/evals/run/index.ts:230-316`) orchestrates agents and workflows, now with multi-turn `inputs[]`. Results persist via `storage/domains/scores/`. Features cited shipped between 1.46 and 1.70, so they are in the latest stable (1.72.0).

`_evaluation.py` (gated by `@experimental(feature_id=ExperimentalFeature.EVALS)`) ships `EvalItem` (:183), `ExpectedToolCall`, `EvalResults`, `LocalEvaluator` (:1488), `evaluate_agent` (:1600) and `evaluate_workflow` (:1804). Foundry evaluation (`FoundryEvals`, `evaluate_traces`, `evaluate_foundry_target`) moved to `agent-framework-foundry` in 1.18.0, and Foundry Adaptive Evals add rubric generation. There is no dataset file format beyond lists of `EvalItem`. Experimental tag and Foundry-centred design mean production use needs caution (capped below 5).

New in 0.21: `agents.testing` provides `ScriptedModel`, `assert_complete()` for workflow drift, `scripted_sandbox_session()` and realtime/voice equivalents (`docs/testing.md:7-206`). These make no model calls and test orchestration (tool loops, handoffs, guardrails), not model quality. There is no dataset format or eval runner; dataset-driven regression is left to Braintrust/Phoenix/Langfuse/LangSmith over SDK traces. Scored 1, same as Vercel's test-server mocks: a small deterministic-test primitive with the harness still host-built.

New in 0.16.0: `@openai/agents/testing` ships `ScriptedModel` (with `assistantMessage()`, `functionCall()`, `modelResponder()`, `modelError()`), `assertComplete()` for workflow drift, `scriptedSandboxSession()` and `ScriptedRealtimeTransport` (`packages/agents-core/src/testing/scriptedModel.ts:176-255`, `docs/.../guides/testing.mdx`). They are unit-test doubles for runner/tool workflows, not behavioural evals. No dataset format or eval harness; partner platforms (Braintrust, Phoenix, Langfuse, LangSmith) consume the traces. Scored 1 to match the Python SDK and Vercel's mocks.

`pydantic_evals` (first-party, same repo) ships `Dataset`/`Case` (YAML/JSON serialisable, `dataset.py`; V2 requires `Dataset(name=...)`), built-in, custom, span-based and agentic evaluators (`evaluators/`), report evaluators, multi-run and retry strategies, dataset generation (`generation.py`), OTel emission (`otel/`) and Logfire integration. `online_capability.py` samples production runs. `TestModel`/`FunctionModel` and recorded cassettes cover deterministic replay. The most complete first-party golden-dataset toolkit in the benchmark.

The `evals` module (`Eval`, `EvalOutcome`) was removed in 0.40 (`CHANGELOG.md`, #2036), replaced by `rig-cassette` (publishable since 0.43): record provider HTTP exchanges or agent effect logs once, replay in CI, and refuse replay when the run spec or handlers changed (`crates/rig-cassette/src/lib.rs:13-27`, `agent/mod.rs:1-45`). The repo runs ~3,000 provider recordings and ~2,000 effect-log goldens itself (`MIGRATING.md:1492`). Moved from 1 to 2: a real regression harness for recorded behaviour now exists, but there is still no dataset format or scoring harness.

Not in the SDK itself, but first-party sister package `strands-agents-evals` (repo `strands-agents/evals`, v1.4.0 released 2026-09-22) provides experiments/cases, dataset generation (`experiment_generator`), user/tool simulators, red teaming and detectors (`site/src/content/docs/user-guide/evals-sdk/index.mdx`). Capped at 4 because the evals repo is not part of the analysed commit: claims come from the in-monorepo docs site and GitHub metadata, not code reading. Previously 0 ('not provided').

Not provided in `strands-ts`. The SDK has unit and integration tests for its own code (`strands-ts/src/**/__tests__/`, `strands-ts/test/integ/`) but no dataset format or agent-regression runner. The docs site documents a separate Python-only package, `strands-agents-evals` (`quickstart.mdx:34`); no TypeScript evals package was found, so TS users do not benefit from it.

No SDK-shipped dataset format or regression harness; Braintrust, LangSmith or your own harness are explicitly external. `@ai-sdk/test-server` and `MockLanguageModelV4` (`ai/test`) mock providers for deterministic unit tests of agent wiring. Same level of test-double support as the OpenAI SDKs' scripted models.
Report flags 'no first-party rubric / scorer / judge classifier'. You wire an LLM-judge from scratch on top of the Go runtime.

`AgentAsJudgeEval` (binary or numeric 1-10 with threshold), `JudgeScorer` (explicit model, normalised scores, v2.8.0) and `AccuracyEval` (LLM grades output against `expected_output`, defaulting to the agent's own model) are built in. `Case(judge_mode=...)` lets suites mix judge and code scorers. Results persist in `agno_eval_runs` for trend analysis.
No LLM-judge ships. The `evaluator/parallel.rs` in `autoagents-llm` is for parallel execution, not output rubric scoring.
Report marks LLM-as-judge explicitly 'not provided'. Users compose a second `query()` call as judge themselves.
Report explicitly marks it 'BYO'. Compose with another `query()` call against a rubric prompt yourself.

`crewai test` spins up an `Agent(role='Task Execution Evaluator')` to grade each task on a 1-10 `quality` scale via `TaskEvaluationPydanticOutput` (`utilities/evaluators/crew_evaluator_handler.py`). The OSS rubric is hardcoded to completion, quality and overall performance, with no knob beyond `task.expected_output`. The new `crewai eval` (`--models` comparison) grades traced runs on AMP and is not counted because it needs the hosted platform; Patronus is the third-party option.
Eino ships no judge framework. Recommended pattern is to write a function that calls an LLM with a rubric prompt over the agent's output.

Go ships only deterministic evaluators (Deep Equal, RegExp, JSONata). LLM-as-judge is a documented pattern: define your own evaluator with the typed `genkit.DefineEvaluatorAction` (`go/genkit/genkit.go:1716-1725`) that calls `genkit.GenerateText` with a judge prompt and returns an `ai.Score` (numeric/string/categorical). `genkit.DefineEvaluator` is deprecated; the May example is no longer valid. First-class LLM judges live on the JS side, not Go.
Hosted LLM-judges are in LangSmith (paid); `langchain` has `load_evaluator(...)` but is separately packaged. Local LangGraph users compose judges themselves.

`RelevancyEvaluator`, `FaithfulnessEvaluator`, `CorrectnessEvaluator`, `AnswerRelevancyEvaluator`, `GuidelineEvaluator`, `SemanticSimilarityEvaluator` all use an LLM-against-rubric pattern out of the box. RAG-focused defaults, but the breadth and ergonomics are top of the benchmark.

`createScorer(...)` (`packages/core/src/evals/base.ts:1981-2000`) supports code and LLM-judge steps, with processors and `maxSteps` for judges; `notScorable()` skips irrelevant runs and `createClassifierScorer()` turns a typed classifier into a 0-1 scorer. Scorers can gate the agent loop itself (`isTaskComplete: { scorers, strategy: 'all' }`), so the agent retries on judge failure. Built-in scorers ship under `packages/core/src/evals/`.

The `Evaluator` protocol (`_evaluation.py:684`) with `RubricScore` (:653) ships deterministic checks (`keyword_check`, `tool_called_check`, `tool_calls_present`, `tool_call_args_match`); LLM judges come from custom evaluators or Foundry (rubric generation via Foundry Adaptive Evals), not a bundled judge class. Still under the `@experimental(EVALS)` flag, which keeps it below pydantic-evals/agno/Mastra.
`examples/agent_patterns/llm_as_a_judge.py` is a usage example, not a built-in scorer; rubric, parsing, and aggregation are user-built.
`examples/agent-patterns/llm-as-a-judge.ts` shows the pattern (one agent grades another) but no judge primitive ships in the SDK.

Built in: `judge_output`, `judge_input_output`, `judge_*_expected`, `judge_g_eval` (`pydantic_evals/evaluators/llm_as_a_judge.py:174-572`) and the `LLMJudge` evaluator (`docs/evals/evaluators/llm-judge.md`). They plug into the Dataset/Case pipeline and OTel reporting, and `OnlineEvaluation` (`online_capability.py:52`) samples production runs. Strongest combination of built-in judging plus surrounding regression harness.

The `evals` module (`Eval`, `EvalOutcome`, judge metrics) was removed in 0.40, and the report now says 'Not provided as a framework feature'. Remaining options: `prompt_typed::<Verdict>()` / `Extractor` (`crates/rig-agent/src/extractor.rs:34`), the experimental `rig-typesafeai` typed judgments (thin evidence; thresholds stay in app code), and `examples/agent_evaluator_optimizer`. Lowered from 2 because the capability was removed upstream (an `upstream` regression, not a correction).

`strands-agents-evals` (first-party, separate repo, v1.4.0) ships output, trajectory, helpfulness, faithfulness, correctness, tool selection/parameter, skill selection accuracy, skill instruction following and multimodal judges plus custom evaluators (`site/src/content/docs/user-guide/evals-sdk/evaluators/`). Capped at 4 because evidence is docs-only (the evals repo is not in the analysed commit) and the package is not part of the core SDK. Previously 0.

No eval harness in TS. New `GoalLoop` plugin (`strands-ts/src/vended-plugins/goal/plugin.ts:233`) builds a judge `Agent` after each invocation, grades the answer against a natural-language `goal` and feeds failures back until `maxAttempts`/`timeout`; `lastResult(agent)` returns the verdict. It grades live runs, not datasets, so it is a small LLM-judge primitive rather than rubric scoring. The Python `strands-agents-evals` package is not usable from TS.

New: `experimental_evaluate({ model, state, questions })` (`packages/ai/src/evaluate/evaluate.ts:36`) asks named Choice, Score and Boolean questions about one shared state and returns typed answers; evaluation models come from `typeSafeAi.evaluationModel('jev-latest')` or adapters over OpenAI/Anthropic/Google structured output, with telemetry callbacks. It is a rubric-grading call, not an eval runner (no datasets, aggregation or experiment tracking), Boolean P(true) is uncalibrated, and the API is `experimental_`-prefixed, so it is capped below 4. Previously 1 (compose with `generateObject`).

Not provided - BYO. The closest primitive is the record/replay plugins (`recordplugin`/`replayplugin`, `internal/httprr`), which suit snapshot regression tests but live under `internal/`, so you would copy them. Eval REST routes return 501.

`agno.eval.suite.cli(CASES, db=...)` (`eval/suite.py:807-1000`) is an argparse CLI with `--name`, `--tag` and `--json-output` that returns a process exit code (0 pass, non-zero on failures or output errors, 2 when no cases match), so `sys.exit(cli(CASES))` drops into any CI job. No hosted gate and no JUnit output; persistence to `agno_eval_runs` gives trend data. Raised from 2 (v2.7.0 feature, released).

Not provided for agent behaviour. Only `cargo test --features "full" --workspace` ships (`README.md:180`). The repo's own release-readiness gates (version consistency, compile-pass/compile-fail derive tests, #279) protect the framework, not your agent.
Report flags 'not provided'. Users wire pytest around `query()` themselves.

Not provided; build a gate with your own eval harness over `query()`. The repo's `workflow-hardening` check (`.github/workflows/workflow-hardening.yml`) is a reference for running agents safely in CI, not an eval gate.

`crewai test` prints a quality table but has no `--min-score` threshold or JUnit output and exits 0 unless an exception is raised. The report found no pass/fail threshold on the new AMP-backed `crewai eval` either (not checked in code), and no documented PR-gate integration. A CI gate means parsing scores yourself.
No first-party gate. Recommended pattern is to run agent against fixtures in CI, assert outputs match expected or judge-score above a threshold, and block PR.

Not shipped: run `genkit eval:run` / `eval:flow` (JS CLI) in CI against a dataset and assert on scores yourself. No first-party gate or JUnit output; the `/docs/go/testing/` page covers testing patterns.
OSS repo ships nothing. Typical pattern is a pytest job running a sample of `graph.invoke(...)` against golden datasets and blocking merge on regression.
No first-party gate. Report says wire `BatchEvalRunner` into your CI and assert on scores; primitives are rich but the gate plumbing is yours.

First-party since 1.47.0: `runEvals({ gates, scorers })` returns a `verdict` (`packages/core/src/evals/run/index.ts:55, 159`), gate-only runs since 1.51.0, and it runs inside Vitest; caller-driven experiments (1.61.0) let an external orchestrator own the loop. Results persist for trend dashboards. Minor gaps: no bundled CI workflow template, no JUnit output, and the process exit code is host-written. Raised from 3 (`upstream`: gates and verdict were added after the May commit).

Not packaged as a turnkey gate. `EvalNotPassedError` (`_evaluation.py:70`) makes it straightforward to fail a pytest/CI job after `evaluate_agent`, but the wiring is yours; `FoundryEvals` is the managed alternative. Evals remain experimental.

No eval-score gates; BYO via partner platforms. The new `ScriptedModel` + `assert_complete()` (`docs/testing.md:196-206`) gives deterministic offline pytest tests that catch accidental workflow drift, but they are hand-written unit tests, not evals, so the score stays 0 (the report labels this 'partial').

Not provided: no eval gate or scoring threshold. The scripted test utilities (`ScriptedModel`, `assertComplete()`) make deterministic workflow tests practical in vitest/jest CI, but they are unit tests, so the score stays 0.

Run datasets under `pytest` and assert on report scores; `TestModel`/`FunctionModel` give deterministic tests and recorded cassettes provide provider replay (`AGENTS.md:113-116`), which the framework's own suite uses. No packaged CI gate/threshold runner, but the surrounding toolchain is the most CI-friendly of the Python peers without a dedicated CLI.

Not provided as a gate: write `cargo test`/`nextest` tests over cassettes or your own judge. `rig-cassette` replay refuses to run when the agent's run spec or handlers changed, so recorded goldens already act as a regression check in CI. No threshold reporter or JUnit output. Score unchanged at 1; the `eval_batch` basis was removed with the `evals` module.

Via the evals CLI: `strands-evals run --fail-on any|none|threshold:0.8` sets the exit code, `--exit-zero` records only and `--diagnose on_failure` emits root-cause output (`site/src/content/docs/user-guide/evals-sdk/cli/run.mdx:97-128`). You wire it into CI yourself, and the evidence is docs-only (evals repo not in the analysed commit). Same level as Agno's suite CLI and Mastra's `runEvals` gates. Previously 0.
Report explicit: 'Not provided'.

Not provided - BYO: eval is your CI's responsibility. `experimental_evaluate` and `MockLanguageModelV4` can be called from your own test runner, and `@ai-sdk/policy-opa` policies are testable with `opa test`, but there is no gate or threshold mechanism.

The `adkgo`/launcher stack covers `web` (REST, A2A, Web UI), `console` (terminal chat, now with human-in-the-loop prompts), `agentengine` and `prod`/`universal` compositions, plus a YAML CLI that scans for `root_agent.yaml` and `runner.NewInMemory` for tests. v2.5 defaults bind the web server to 127.0.0.1 and refuse cross-origin browsers unless `-webui_address` matches. Trace and graph panels need the opt-in `-include_debug_api`. First-class (report 20.1).

`python run.py` starts AgentOS on port 7777 and pairs with the AgentOS UI. The `agnoctl` CLI scaffolds from templates and runs `agno up/down/restart/status`, and `agno connect` exposes MCP to coding agents. `Agent.print_response()` and `cli_app()` give terminal REPLs.
